title: Game of Thrones: The Mad King review – an action-packed saga of dry ice and fire | Theatre | The Guardian
description: This prequel to the TV series has one joust after another, spectacular stagecraft and plenty of modern resonance
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: This prequel to the TV series has one joust after another, spectacular stagecraft and plenty of modern resonance
Content: Reminiscent of Olivier? … Michael Shaeffer as King Aerys II Targaryen in Game of Thrones: The Mad King.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenReminiscent of Olivier? … Michael Shaeffer as King Aerys II Targaryen in Game of Thrones: The Mad King.Photograph: Johan PerssonTheatreReviewGame of Thrones: The Mad King review – an action-packed saga of dry ice and fireRoyal Shakespeare theatre, Stratford-upon-AvonThis prequel to the TV series has one joust after another, spectacular stagecraft and plenty of modern resonanceMark LawsonSun 9 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDuring the RSC’s 65 years, numerous Lears have lost their minds and frequent Caesars been slaughtered by their courts. Now, though, a tyrant new to its stages faces both fates. He is King Aerys II Targaryen, ancestor of one warring bloodline inGame of Thrones, the dramatisation of George RR Martin’s A Song of Ice and Fire series of fantasy novels that helped TV streamers’ rise to global domination during eight HBO seasons from 2011 to 2019.Some may balk at an institution named for England’s greatest dramatist staging an American drama franchise. There is, though, a compelling economic imperative:rising costs due to current wars(a frequent problem for Martin’s ancient oligarchs too) and Covid-era debts now exacerbated by paying back government loans means that the RSC could use another big commercial transfer – asits musical Matildamay not be immortal.View image in fullscreenChloe Lamford’s striking sacred tree … Noah Ritter as Prince Rhaegar Targaryen in Game of Thrones: The Mad King.Photograph: Johan PerssonThere is also an artistic rationale. Martin has always credited Shakespeare’s English history plays as a model. DramatistDuncan Macmillan– starting from an unexplored reference in the books to a consequential tournament in this universe in 281AC (after conquest) – and director Dominic Cooke bow even deeper to the presiding genius: Michael Shaeffer’s King Aerys, with long white beard and flower-braided hair, strongly resembles Laurence Olivier’s television Lear.You don’t need to read the entrails of a raven to guess the target of the title The Mad King: the various Brutuses plotting his fall conclude that the “paranoid and delusional” monarch will destroy their civilisation. The focus, though, is not just Trumpian. Macmillan references two wider international crises – the instability of heads of state and the weather – and a UK national concern: the endurance of a royal bloodline. The RSC’s patron, King Charles III, might skip this one.There are already two HBO prequels –House of the DragonandA Knight of the Seven Kingdoms– but while those are set up to 200 years before the TV series, Macmillan’s is a much closer prologue. That is a harder task, as he must match up with the season one box set. Fans will be attracted by back stories of telly-legendary characters: one young man is addressed as Eddard Stark, but pleads to be known as Ned. Two leads in the main TV show are babies at the end of the RSC’s three hours and 45 minutes.Macmillan’s dialogue is quasi-Shakespearean with a rough iambic beat. A heavily pregnant princess is “overloaded with the hopes of the realm”. One of many violently bereaved characters tells another: “If a beloved has been wrenched from you, then we are fellow countrymen.” The problem comes when this plausible pastiche of Elizabethan politicking collides with Martin’s supernaturalism.View image in fullscreenVisceral … Elizabeth Ayodele as Princess Elia Martell and Tanisha Spring as Ashara Dayne in Game of Thrones: The Mad King.Photograph: Johan PerssonThe steeds of puppetry and movement directors Nick Barnes and Finn Caldwell – vast skeletal frames manipulated by squads of actors – carry characters in rather too many jousts and battles. Dogs and dragons are similarly simulated. But whatever the efforts and budgets expended, theatre can’t match the stunning dollars-to-burn televisual atmospherics. Chloe Lamford’s set, though, includes a striking sacred tree, intermittently formed by a huge trunk rising to dock with flowered foliage descending. Real flames and mock fog frequently swirl on a cruciform walkway that quarters the stalls of the Royal Shakespeare theatre: a scene of dry ice and fire.‘Can’t stop smiling!’ The wait is over for epic Game of Thrones prequel The Mad KingRead moreActors in adaptations of screen material – such as the currentThe Silence of the Lambs– can choose whether to be avatars of the TV or film stars. Here, the performers must be plausible previews of their future television inheritors. Maxim Ays as Jaime Lannister, Michael Abubakar’s Ned Stark, the Cersei Lannister of Daisy Franks and Hughie O’Donnell’s Lord Varys might all be earlier portraits of the famous, but youth and new lines leave leeway for their own intonations. Even so, the greatest impact is made by characters featured in the main TV show only in dialogue or flashback: Princess Elia Martell and Prince Rhaegar Targaryen, viscerally played by Elizabeth Ayodele and Noah Ritter.The play’s end intriguingly leaves a 14-year gap until the TV series, perhaps allowing for more instalments. Purists will object that, rather than staging Shakespeare-adjacent populist spin-offs, the RSC should be offering its house dramatist’s royal dramas plain. The counter argument is that hitching on to a cultural juggernaut may bring in new sources of income and audiences.The review star system can struggle with shows that some might sell their house to see but others would be reluctant to leave home for. This feels like a five-star production for most devoted throners but a three-star for those who haven’t seen the TV series. Thereby, to channel this show’s infectious tones, the Judging One has trod a path between those stellar prophecies.AtRoyal Shakespeare theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, until 5 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreRoyal Shakespeare CompanyGame of ThronesGeorge RR MartinDuncan MacmillanDominic CookereviewsShareReuse this content

title: This is how we do it: ‘Since I started HRT, we’ve switched roles – he jokes that I want to do it every day’ | Sex | The Guardian
description: After being on the brink of divorce, Antonia and Rob have experienced a radical revival of their sex life
Author: Elena Angelides
Headline: After being on the brink of divorce, Antonia and Rob have experienced a radical revival of their sex life
Content: Illustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianThis is how we do itSexThis is how we do it: ‘Since I started HRT, we’ve switched roles – he jokes that I want to do it every day’After being on the brink of divorce, Antonia and Rob have experienced a radical revival of their sex lifeHow do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymouslyAs told toElena AngelidesSun 9 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAntonia, 56double quotation markThe perfect storm of work stress, menopause and raising kids meant our sex life slowly slipped out of viewRob and I have been together for 33 years but, weirdly, the past 18 months have been the peak of our sex life for me. It took me threatening to file for divorce to bring us back from the brink.If someone told me that the gangly 6ft 6in spotty young man I met on the first day of university was going to be my husband and the father of my children, I wouldn’t have believed it, but that’s what happened. I was drawn towards the dangerous types in leather jackets, but Rob is more like a ginormous teddy bear. By the time we hooked up in second year, we were such good friends that our relationship felt like putting on a pair of comfy slippers. It was so easy, we were two puzzle pieces that slotted together. Our sex life was pretty regular for years – normal, loving, safe.It’s hard to pinpoint when something breaks. But the perfect storm of work stress, menopause and raising kids meant our sex life slowly slipped out of view. I’d be racked with guilt, but couldn’t find it in myself to initiate.double quotation markThree months after starting testosterone, I said to Rob: ‘I want you in bed now’Ironically, it was when I started taking testosterone as part of hormone replacement therapy that I started feeling like a woman again. We have a super king-size bed, and for years we slept on opposite sides, not even touching. But three months after starting the testosterone, I said to Rob: “I want you in bed now.”Now, I initiate more than Rob. We’ve completely switched roles. He often jokes that I want to do it every day – which is not true – but what I love is that we now get to enjoy little moments of intimacy every day. When we have sex, he knows a slower rhythm will bring me to completion. He will wait until I’ve orgasmed and then I will finish him off.The closeness of our intimate life and personal relationship are linked. I try to give less weight to the things that annoy me and celebrate the positive parts of our marriage, and the revival of our sex life has brought our relationship back to its roots. Rob tells me I’m wrong about this, but I think now we have sex more, we bicker less.Share your experienceShare your experiencesIf you’re keen to talk to us about your sex lives you can get in touch by filling in the form below. It is very important that both sexual partners are happy to participate.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. It wasn’t only down to the sexless periods, but also the absence of feeling loved and part of a team.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI like to joke that I noticed Antonia when she was walking away because she has a really beautiful bum. I’ve always called her my “peachy fruit salad”, as she has such peachy breasts. But when we had children, sex became a bit of a chore. Life was busy, and by the time we got to bed, all we wanted to do was sleep. I did grow frustrated when she seemed to stop craving sex at all. She would promise we would do it another day, but it never materialised. Now she’s been prescribed testosterone it’s a helpful indication that the menopausal woman you’re living with – who can fly off the handle at the drop of the hat – still likes you.double quotation markAntonia needs a slower rhythm to help her reach completion, and sometimes I am too tired to do the whole routineThis is how we do it: ‘My ex didn’t find me attractive after I put on weight. With Denzel, I finally feel loved’Read moreBefore, our sex life was quite vanilla – often missionary. But within a week of starting the testosterone, she was wanting it all the time. It was like I had married a new woman. One issue is that we crave it at different times of the day. In the evening, she’s often asking, “Do you fancy a shag?” I am normally knackered and reply, “In the morning, I promise!” She needs a slower rhythm to help her reach completion, and sometimes I am too tired to do the whole routine, whereas I often orgasm from oral sex.It helps that Antonia is more open and imaginative nowadays. On a recent holiday to Italy, we carried out a little experiment: I watched porn to get me going, which meant we both orgasmed during penetrative sex. It helped that I had already reached a certain level of arousal that I could carry on from.Although our intimate life has experienced this recent revival, I wouldn’t say we bicker any less, there is just more of the good stuff too.Names have been changedExplore more on these topicsSexThis is how we do itRelationshipsMarriageFamilyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s rare to hear: I’m black and middle class’ – Symeon Brown on black Britain’s enduring ‘taboo’ | Society | The Guardian
description: Black people are more prominent than ever in the UK’s politics and culture. But are they overwhelmingly from the middle class, as Brown argues in his new book? And if so, why isn’t anyone talking about it?
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Black people are more prominent than ever in the UK’s politics and culture. But are they overwhelmingly from the middle class, as Brown argues in his new book? And if so, why isn’t anyone talking about it?
Content: ‘I’ll never really be read as middle class’ … Symeon Brown.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I’ll never really be read as middle class’ … Symeon Brown.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianSocietyInterview‘It’s rare to hear: I’m black and middle class’ – Symeon Brown on black Britain’s enduring ‘taboo’Emma LoffhagenBlack people are more prominent than ever in the UK’s politics and culture. But are they overwhelmingly from the middle class, as Brown argues in his new book? And if so, why isn’t anyone talking about it?Sun 9 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSymeon Brown and David Lammy went to the same primary school in Tottenham, north London. One went on to a selective secondary school, and became the second black person to hold one of Britain’s great offices of state. The other became a journalist who would go on to survey the country’s black professional class more thoroughly than anyone ever had – and who remembers being told by Lammy that he could “never become prime minister, because you sound like where you come from”.It was 2010, and Brown, interested in politics, was interning for the then Labour backbencher. “And he was right, certainly at the time,” Brown says now.It’s a small exchange, but it sits at the centre of everything Brown’s new book, The Good, the Black and the Boujee, is trying to work out. What separated the two boys from the same Tottenham streets was class. And class, Brown argues, is the elephant in the room in almost every British conversation about race.“In the book, I was trying to reconcile two of what seem to be contrary events,” he says, as we chat over Zoom. “On the one hand, Britain’s black population has never had more cultural stature and economic capital – in politics, music, film, publishing – but those same years produced the Black Lives Matter protests and the toppling ofEdward Colston’s statue into Bristol harbour, and black people saying that it is harder than ever to succeed.”View image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch visiting Windracers, a drone manufacturer, in Fareham, Hampshire last month.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAKemi Badenoch,Stormzy,Daniel Kaluuya,Olivia Dean: are these a reflection of a more equal Britain, or are we simply more comfortable looking at elite black faces while nothing structural changes underneath them? Their success is real, but a handful of people crossing class boundaries is not the same as collective progress.“Black people in Britain are hyper-visible, but also, in many cases, disenfranchised,” Brown says. “And that creates a tension – class has been missing from conversations about race.”To get underneath that tension, Brown interviewed about 1,500 members of Britain’s black middle class about their education, employment, families, aspirations, spending, social values and, of course, class. He touches on some questions that feel taboo within this community, such as why middle-class black Britons tend to date white people. What his findings reveal is something Brown thinks Britain has never quite reckoned with: the fact that, as he says, “to be black in Britain is so often to be assumed to be working class”, and that assumption has masked how the black Britons who come closest to power are actually, disproportionately, middle class.View image in fullscreenSymeon Brown at his home in London.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianNot everyone was pleased that he went looking. “Bona fide black elites don’t like the idea of this book,” Brown tells me matter-of-factly. Some people, once they heard what he was working on, stopped returning his calls. “People felt it was going to be an exposé.”The objection, as he understood it, came from the idea that to be black and middle class doesn’t mean you are anywhere near as privileged as if you were white and middle class. “That may be true,” Brown says, “but it doesn’t mean that we shouldn’t interrogate it.”Britain is a nation obsessed with talking about class and allergic to admitting it has any issue with it. Everyone wants their success to look like the product of hard work and nothing else; nobody wants to concede they had a head start. Black Britons, it turns out, are no exception. “It is very rare to hear someone say, ‘I’m black and middle class,’ in Britain,” Brown says. “The most common response I got from interview requests was: ‘Thanks, but I’m not middle class.’”Part of the reason is that class itself refuses to sit still long enough to be defined. It is nebulous and mercurial, with economic and cultural dimensions that don’t always point the same way. “The middle class itself has always been quite fragmented,” Brown says. “There’s always been variety in terms of social, economic and political capital.”View image in fullscreenMiatta Fahnbulleh, secretary for energy and net zero, on her way to Andy Burnham’s first cabinet meeting last month.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesPerhaps the most visible example of the changing face of Britain is in politics. Britain has had its first black leader of a major political party; it has had a black chancellor and foreign secretary. And yet, for all that representation has grown, Brown thinks it has brought remarkably little benefit. “Ultimately, these people are representing their class interests,” he says. He runs through the roll call: “David Lammy, educated at a school founded by Henry VIII; Kwasi Kwarteng, Eton and Oxbridge; Miatta Fahnbulleh, the current cabinet’s only black minister, privately educated, Oxbridge … Black politicians actually have to have more elite credentials than white candidates,” he says.Brown’s point is less that every politician on his list was born privileged than that advancement often depends on acquiring the educational and cultural credentials prized by the establishment. Lammy, for example, was raised by a single mother in Tottenham after his father left the family; he attended the sought-after state-funded King’s School in Peterborough, which paved his way to university in London, then Harvard Law School.School turns out to be one of the clearest mirrors of class that black Britain has. Among black professionals Brown surveyed, almost one in four had attended a fee-paying school at some point – and, contrary to the popular image of the scholarship kid, 72% of them had their fees paid outright by their parents.“Representation has been the end goal, and I think people have found it unsatisfying,” Brown continues. For him, the muted response among some black and leftwing voters to Lammy’s departure from government illustrated the limits of symbolic progress.View image in fullscreenDavid Lammy, then deputy prime minister, at Downing Street in May.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesBrown sees this as part of a wider pattern of a black British elite that increasingly lacks political imagination, or a model of success without assimilation and establishment acceptance. “I was a child of the 90s; it was a very radical period,” he says. “People were critical of corporate behaviour; my parents and their friends had been galvanised by the anti-apartheid movement. There was a kind of radicalism to black sensibility. But black Britain has now been co-opted by corporate and individualist ideals.”Outside politics, Brown argues that often conversations that are putatively about race are actually about class. He remembers, for example, the debates that used to dominate the heyday of “Black Twitter”, about issues such as “proximity to whiteness” – the notion that lighter skin brought you closer to acceptance. “Completely missing from this is the notion of class,” Brown says. “Because then who has greater proximity to whiteness, Eton-educated Kwasi Kwarteng, or mixed-raceMark Duggan from Tottenham?”The arguments over black dating patterns – who is dating outside their race and why – tend to present themselves in the same way. “People primarily date class before race,” he says. “It’s the most visceral discourse that is happening online, and I thought it was useful to add a data intervention.” Brown found that black women, for example, are more likely to be middle-class professionals than their black male counterparts. “What many women were saying was: ‘I’ve got this level of professional success, I’ve hit these particular class markers, but I can’t find a man who also equals this on the terms that I want,’” he says.View image in fullscreenBroadwater Farm in Tottenham, north London, after the 1985 riots that ravaged the area.Photograph: PABrown grew up in the 90s, in a terraced house on the edge of Tottenham’s once notorious Broadwater Farm estate, an area he describes as “a hub of grime, street life and black radicalism”. His parents were both second-generation British-Jamaicans – his father a “career criminal” and his mother a childcare worker. He describes early years in social housing, when his mother delivered the Yellow Pages for extra cash. He started his professional life as an assistant archivist at theBlack Cultural Archivesbefore joining the Guardian as a researcher on a Scott Trust bursary, and later moved to Channel 4 News, where he is now home affairs correspondent. All of which is to say that he now operates in a decidedly middle-class milieu.When I ask him how he would describe his class status, he laughs. “Everyone always wants to ask me that!” He describes himself, in the end, not as middle class but as “multi-class”, adding: “I’ll never really be read as middle class, because of my accent and other things.”Whatever the terms, Brown is part of an emerging, often young, black professional class that hasn’t assimilated into the frameworks of white cultural sensibilities. He can be found at book launches populated by the “black literati”, and festivals such as Detty December in Nigeria, or Paris’s Fête de la Musique – as Brown puts it, a “middle-class cultural life driven by black cultural products”.View image in fullscreenNigerians celebrate Detty December in a Lagos nightclub.Photograph: Olympia de Maismont/AFP/Getty ImagesThe Cambridge sociologist Ali Meghji, whose research on Britain’s black middle class predates Brown’s, argues that black middle-class identity in Britain tends to take one of three forms: those who don’t see racism as a significant issue and feel a stronger affinity with people of the same class; those who strategically code-switch to match white middle-class taste; and those who deliberately steer their cultural life towards black diasporic culture.Brown himself, and many of his subjects, fit firmly into the third category. Like the traditional white middle class, it’s a sort of “if you know, you know” crowd. And like any middle class, it is also full of gossip, drama and internecine fighting. (“There’s so much beef within the black literati, you wouldn’t believe,” Brown laughs.) “When I go to a book launch, I don’t want to drink warm wine and eat cheese,” he continues. “I want to turn up, hear some bashment, dancehall and soca.”Yet the flourishing of this confident black professional culture is only one half of the story Brown tells. “We’ve never had a greater cohort of black people with this level of cultural or economic capital, but we still have a huge working class that is also, in some cases, disenfranchised from citizenship,” he says. He points to unresolved Windrush cases as an example. Black Britain, Brown argues, has become more stratified – even as the country continues to talk about it as though it were a single, undifferentiated group.That flattening also shapes the way Britain talks about the working class. Political debate routinely treats the “white working class” as a uniquely left-behind constituency, even though black and other minority-ethnic working-class people face the same pressures, often compounded by racial discrimination. The label can turn shared material problems into a racial contest, inviting struggling groups to see one another as rivals rather than people with common interests.And for all the pleasures, rivalries and contradictions of black professional life, the economic foundations of middle-classness are shifting beneath everyone’s feet. Three decades of wage stagnation and rising costs have made the category less secure – and membership of it worth considerably less than it once was. “If we think about what it means to be middle class, whatever your race, at this moment in time,” Brown says, “it means to be poorer, less influential, and doing work of lesser stature than 30 years ago.”The irony, then, is that just as black Britain has developed a sizable middle class – and a culture distinctly its own – the middle-class bargain itself is beginning to fall apart.The Good, the Black and the Boujee: How Black Britain Became Middle Class by Symeon Brown is published by Dialogue (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: As AI guzzles water and energy, we are already facing a choice: datacentres or homes? | John Harris | The Guardian
description: Whitehall wants to triple their number in the UK. Yet in Slough, I saw the impact they’re having on communities, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: Whitehall wants to triple their number in the UK. Yet in Slough, I saw the impact they’re having on communities, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: Illustration: R Fresson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: R Fresson/The GuardianOpinionDatacentresAs AI guzzles water and energy, we are already facing a choice: datacentres or homes?John HarrisWhitehall wants to triple their number in the UK. Yet in Slough, I saw the impact they’re having on communitiesSun 9 Aug 2026 07.03 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareAmid headlines aboutthe UK’s drought, Europe’s wildfires and impossible global temperatures, it was 28C when I arrived in Slough last Monday. I was there to look around Slough Trading Estate, a place that might once have conjured up images of the TV comedyThe Office, many of whose laughs came at the expense of this overgrown patch of suburbia, 20-odd miles west of London.But these days, this area of town – an incongruous mixture of old-school businesses such as Mr Clutch and Angling Direct, and vast, metal-clad leviathans that look like something pulled from JG Ballard – hasbecome a bywordfor the constant expansion of datacentres, those hulking symbols of the vast computing power that big tech now requires, not least because of the ever-more complex workings of artificial intelligence.In many people’s minds, datacentres are also a byword for the two totemic issues of yet another searing summer:heat and water. Across the world, the huge amounts of electricity they demand, mostly generated using fossil fuels, indelibly connects them to the climate emergency. The constant machinations of their crammed-in servers require cooling processes that also use vast amounts of water. So it is that the 21st century’s dominant means of communication intensifies our era’s most terrifying threats.The first building I loitered around was a datacentre owned by the California-based company Equinix. There were 100 or so cars in its “visitor” and “staff” spaces, no corporate branding to be seen – and, up close, the constant sound of a low industrial whirr. On the other side of the street, poetically enough, was a set of offices occupied by ThamesWater, a few of whose employees were taking a break outside. I pointed across the road: did they know what the building contained?“There’s loads of AI bits in there,” said a twentysomething woman called Louise. “I saw something about it on Instagram: all the water they use.” She rolled her eyes. “It’s ridiculous. Loads and loads of water because of all the AI.” On her phone, she foundone of the postsshe had seen. “Slough is quietly running Britain’s AI boom but there’s a problem,” it said. “When a heatwave hits, the machines get thirsty too. Cooling systems work overtime in hot weather, spiking demand for power and water.”Someone suggested I make the five-minute journey to nearby Britwell, a housing estate built for bombed-out Londoners after the second world war. The first person I encountered was a mum from the area called Sheryl. “You notice the noise at night: like a whirring, buzzing sound,” she said. “And since we’ve had all these [new] ones up here, there seems to be more heat round here.”Early research, including arecent preprintof a paper authored by researchers at Cambridge University earlier this year, does suggest that datacentres can have a “heat island” effect, pushing up temperatures in their immediate vicinity by an average of 2C, and as much as 9C. Last month, the trading estate’scorporate owners saidthey had “not seen conclusive evidence demonstrating that datacentre operations on Slough Trading Estate are causing increases in local temperatures”.View image in fullscreenSlough Trading Estate, which houses some of the 40 datacentres in the area.Photograph: Education Images/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesSlough has thedensest cluster of datacentresin western Europe: as many as 40, with more to come. What has happened here is bound up with the trading estate’s recent history as a partly deregulated “simplified planning zone”, the town’s proximity to London (the faster that digital financial transactions can happen, the better), and the apparently flukish fact that Slough sits atop the cables that connect Britain to the US and Ireland. The datacentres the town hosts are owned and maintained by companies that are far from being household names – Equinix, Digital Realty, Iron Mountain – but serve famous customers including Amazon, Google, Oracle and Microsoft.Fierce arguments about datacentres are a big part of the discourse surrounding the upcoming US midterm elections, with Donald Trump taking apredictable position: “You have to convince your community how great these things [are] … You can’t fight it.” But actually, you can. Resistance is now pouring into the US political mainstream: midway through last month, New York became the first state to impose aone-year pauseon new “hyperscale” datacentres, and, as litigation is fought out across the country, there is mounting pressure for other parts of the US to follow suit. The leftist insurgent Abdul El-Sayed, who last week won a Democratic Senate primary in Michigan, has crisply captured the mood: “People really effing hate datacentres,” he says. Even the Republican governor of Texas hascalled for a banon their development in rural areas, and last week ordered that new centres won’t join the state’s power grid until regulators have reviewed their use of water and energy.Increasing numbers of US facilities have their own dedicatedgas turbines; in the UK, high-ups at the energy regulator Ofgem say that100 planned centreshere aim to do the same. US sites are putting added pressure on existing power grids that also use coal and oil, and backup generators powered by diesel are a standard industry feature. Green datacentres areattracting growing interest, but many insiders insist that renewables simply don’t cut it: “Our datacentres have to run 100% of the time so we can’t even consider using [renewables] as a primary source,” one industry kingpintold the Financial Timeslast year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDemocracy is at stake when foolish humans bet on machines being intelligent | Rafael BehrRead moreWith good reason, not many people are minded to listen to private water companies. But only a fortnight ago, Water UK, the organisation that represents firms in the four nations, said that the government’s existing water forecasts were “fatally flawed” and “explicitly exclude” datacentres, which can use up to5m gallons a day, equivalent to the consumption of up to 50,000 people. What that omission says about our readiness for more datacentres – and what will happen during inevitable future droughts – is an interesting question. Would the public be expected to stoically limit their use of water while datacentres carried on guzzling it?All sorts of tensions could soon explode. For all Andy Burnham’s talk of local decision-making, Whitehall’s official aim is still to triple the UK’s number of datacentres by 2030, which could be aided by the fact that they are nowclassed ascritical national infrastructure. In December, a report by the London assemblyrevealedthat datacentres’ electricity requirements had led to stalled housebuilding in the capital; last week brought news of the returned housing secretary, Angela Rayner,approving a redevelopmentof the old Truman Brewery site in east London that had been called in by her predecessor, Steve Reed. It will include a datacentre handling transactions in the City, offices and 44 homes, in contrast to plans supported by the local council centred on 350 new dwellings. Whatever that represents, it doesn’t sound like what the new PM calls “good growth in every postcode”. There may, in fact, be a stark choice lurking in such stories that politicians will soon have to face: homes or servers?On my way out of Britwell, I had a chat with a woman called Jodie, on her way home from Lidl. “My brother said he saw something on TikTok that said if there was a war, Slough would be a target because of the datacentres,” she said. I grimly laughed: “Come friendly bombs and fall on Slough”, and all that? “Let’s hope not,” she said. In the middle distance, the increasingly gigantic datacentres whirred on, and I thought of a few lines from another of John Betjeman’s poems: “And over all the land, instead of trees / Clean poles and wire will whisper in the breeze / We’ll keep one ancient village just to show / What England once was when the times were slow.”John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDatacentresOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingWatercommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Panda of the insect world’: the moscardón bumblebee creates buzz for invertebrate of the year | Environment | The Guardian
description: Bombus dahlbomii, a giant ginger bumblebee fondly known as the flying mouse, is in decline in its native Patagonia due to commercial farming
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: Bombus dahlbomii, a giant ginger bumblebee fondly known as the flying mouse, is in decline in its native Patagonia due to commercial farming
Content: The moscardón bumblebee is a gorgeous ginger giant that can measure up to 4cm in length.Illustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe moscardón bumblebee is a gorgeous ginger giant that can measure up to 4cm in length.Illustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianInvertebrate of the year 2026Environment‘Panda of the insect world’: the moscardón bumblebee creates buzz for invertebrate of the yearBombus dahlbomii, a giant ginger bumblebee fondly known as the flying mouse, is in decline in its native Patagonia due to commercial farmingRevealed: the top 10 invertebrates of the yearPatrick BarkhamSun 9 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe all love bumblebees. Not only are they beautiful, busy and social, they perform pollination services that are crucial for plants, crops and human civilisation.Any bumblebee would be a worthy winner of invertebrate of the year but a gorgeous giant ginger bumblebee fondly known as the flying mouse? Come on!There are about 250 species of bumblebee andBombus dahlbomiiis the largest. The gloriously furry females can measure 4cm in length. These unusually heavy-bodied bumbles, weighing up to 1.5g, are found flying in the temperate forest-clad mountains of Patagonia, in Argentina and Chile.View image in fullscreenBombus dahlbomii is being outcompeted by the European buff-tailed bumblebee, which was introduced for fruit tree pollination.Photograph: Michael Grant Wildlife/AlamyAs a Patagonian endemic, the bumblebee is an important pollinator of native plants such as the Peruvian lily (Alstroemeria aurea) and the Chilean bellflower (Lapageria rosea). The latter is red, which most bees cannot see, so they typically avoid red flowers. But the moscardón visits them because it uses a special receptor system to detect and distinguish the colour red. Its furry appearance is due to long bristles that cover the thorax and abdomen.Unfortunately, the magnificent moscardón is threatened by human actions that go beyond the usual habitat loss and destruction. Populations haverapidly declined since the introduction of two non-native invasive European bumblebees, the ruderal bumblebee (Bombus ruderatus) and the buff-tailed bumblebee (Bombus terrestris), which have been imported to Chile since the 1980s to assist commercial agricultural pollination. These species may be much loved in their natural environments, but in Chile and Argentina they have rapidly spread, not only outcompetingBombus dahlbomiibut bringing in novel pathogens and diseases that are decimating populations of the native bumble.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRevealed: the top 10 invertebrates of the yearRead moreIt’s terrible news for the web of life that intersects withBombus dahlbomii, from native flowers to other endemic species such as mites that live on the giant bumble. But the invasive bumblebees are also helping invasive non-native plant species from Europe, such as broom, spread more rapidly. Today, the invasive bees are too widespread to be eradicated. When will we learn?Bombus dahlbomiireceived a fabulous nomination from the researcher Anton Gradišek in Ljubljana, Slovenia, a partner inan academic project developing bioacoustics– the analysis of sound recordings – to better study the endangered bumblebee. “When we were out in the field, we saw only a handful of them,” he says. “Bumblebees are the pandas of the insect world, and a mascot for biodiversity conservation.”It’sinvertebrate of theyear again! From 3-12 August, every daywe will profile one of the thousands of amazing invertebrates that our readers have nominated. And then, when you’veheard about all of them, we’ll open the voting soyou can choose your favourites. Don’t hesitate to get in touch with thoughts and ideas: email us atenvironment.desk@theguardian.comwith Invertebrate in the subject line.Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentInvertebrate of the year 2026BeesInsectsWildlifeAnimalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Like being in prison’: the ship crews stuck in Gulf since February | Strait of Hormuz | The Guardian
description: US-Iran war has stranded up to 20,000 seafarers, mostly Indian and Filipino crews, with none knowing when the nightmare will end
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: US-Iran war has stranded up to 20,000 seafarers, mostly Indian and Filipino crews, with none knowing when the nightmare will end
Content: ‘The vessels are not prepared to defend themselves against missiles and drones’: ships in the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The vessels are not prepared to defend themselves against missiles and drones’: ships in the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman.Photograph: ReutersStrait of Hormuz‘Like being in prison’: the ship crews stuck in Gulf since FebruaryUS-Iran war has stranded up to 20,000 seafarers, mostly Indian and Filipino crews, with none knowing when the nightmare will endJoanna PartridgeSun 9 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe panicked crew of a cargo ship broadcast a distress signal late on Monday night from their location in thestrait of Hormuz. About 20 nautical miles north of the coast of Oman, the Minoan Pioneer bulk carrier was hit by an unknown projectile, causing a blackout in the engine room and a fire in the accommodation area.The crew scrambled to put out the blaze and called for help from nearby vessels. When they managed to disembark from the Greek-owned, Liberian-flagged ship on Tuesday morning, they realised the third engineer was missing. Days later, he is yet to be found.The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations centre is investigating but has not yet officially confirmed the origin of the projectile, although analysts at the maritime intelligence company Windward noted: “Prior kinetic attacks at this exact location have been Iranian in origin, thoughIrandenies involvement.”In the preceding 24 hours two other vessels in the region, a large- and a medium-sized oil tanker, had reported near-misses.The flurry of incidents casts a spotlight on the danger facing the thousands of seafarers who remain trapped in the Gulf as the US-led war on Iran extends into its sixth month. What should have been a normal journey when they passed through the strait and entered the Gulf back in February has turned into a long and stressful waiting game.Iran has in effect blockaded the waterway, trapping 20,000 seafarers for weeks on end and inflicting a huge psychological toll. One seafarer stuck in the Gulf told the Guardian in the early weeks of the conflict ofthe “impossible” situationthey and their crew were in, which had contributed to another sailor having a breakdown.As the war has dragged on, sailors have become casualties: 17 seafarers have died since hostilities began, the majority following Iranian strikes.The crews stuck in the strait have had their hopes of departure raised several times, before being dashed. April’s ceasefire and the peace deal signed in June by Washington and Tehran bothbroke downshortly after being announced.View image in fullscreenIndian sailors stranded on their cargo vessel when congestion at Port Sultan Qaboos prevented them from docking, leaving the ship anchored off Oman.Photograph: Elke Scholiers/GettySeveral dozen oil and gas tankers seized the brief window offered by thememorandum of understanding(MOU), the ceasefire deal signed by both sides, to exit through the channel, but not all made it through in time. There are still 6,000 seafarers on 500 vessels, encompassing all types of ships, trapped in the Gulf, according to the UN’s International Maritime Organization.“We need to remember that these are innocent people who are trained to do the work, that they are not trained for combat, and the vessels are not prepared to defend themselves against missiles and drones,” said the IMO’s secretary-general, Arsenio Dominguez.For the crews stuck waiting to exit it is like being in “prison”, the head of one of India’s maritime trade unions said. “For the guys who are on board, the question that arises is, when is this going to end? The uncertainty of the ongoing geopolitical tension is causing them stress,” said Savio Ramos, general secretary of the Maritime Union of India, which represents merchant navy officers.“It is like putting somebody in prison and not giving them freedom to move,” added Ramos, a tanker captain with more than two decades of experience moving large oil carriers around the globe. “You don’t know where you’re going, you don’t what you’re doing. It gets to you after some time.”Hormuz mapMost vessels – at least those with responsible owners – are receiving regular supplies of fresh water, food and other goods ferried by small boats from shore, yet most crews have no way of getting out of a perilous situation.Ramos said some of the union’s members who wanted to return home had been able to do so, provided other senior officers were willing to enter the region and replace them.Talks have been taking place, mediated by Oman, which along with Iran borders the waterway. However, the two countries’ proposed deal suggestedTehran would have controlover the flow of traffic entering the Gulf. This would not be popular with shipowners or the wider industry and would be a significant deviation from the freedom of navigation for vessels before the conflict.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTraffic is still passing through the strait, albeit at extremely low levels, since hostilities and attacks on ships resumed following the collapse of the MOU peace deal.Only 52 non-Iranian linked vessels transited the strait in the week from 27 July to 2 August, according to analysts at the shipping publication Lloyd’s List, of which 60% exited the channel and 40% entered.A further 32 Iranian-linked ships passed through the strait during the week. In total, these 84 vessels represent just over 10% of the average 700 ship movements each week before the conflict broke out.This means 70 large oil and gas tankers, owned by mainstream companies that are not subject to sanctions, have been stranded in the Gulf since February, according to Lloyd’s List analysis. A further 65 tankers entered the region following the announcement of the MOU, only to find themselves unable to leave.View image in fullscreenA Thai‑flagged cargo ship on fire after being hit by Iranian missiles in the strait of Hormuz in March 2026.Photograph: Royal Thai Navy/EPAIt is not clear how the stranded seafarers break down by nationality, but the biggest cohorts are likely to be Indians and Filipinos. India is the second largest global supplier of seafarers, with 312,000 working in the industry, after the 460,000 from the Philippines, according to the latest global seafarer report from the shipping associations the Baltic and International Maritime Council and the International Chamber of Shipping.Since the war on Iran began, hostilities have spread to other regionsincluding the Red SeaandIraq. In addition, Russia and Ukraine have beenattacking each other’s vesselsin the Black Sea in an escalation of a maritime conflict in which24 seafarers have been killedsince the start of July.This prompted analysts from Lloyd’s to call July “one of the deadliest months ever for commercial seafarers”.Many in shipping are concerned that the longer the Iran conflict drags on and crews are stuck on vessels in a dangerous region, the fewer seafarers will be willing to travel to dangerous regions – or go to sea at all.The IMO chief, Dominguez, pointed out that without seafarers the “90% of goods that are transported by ships will not be able to reach their final destinations and all of us are going to be impacted”.Explore more on these topicsStrait of HormuzShipping industryIranMiddle East and north AfricaUS-Israel war on IranWater transportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Labour seeking ‘deeper relationship’ with EU under Burnham, new minister says | Brexit | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Hamish Falconer wants ‘sense of renewed pace’ in post-Brexit talks while staying within Labour’s red lines
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Exclusive: Hamish Falconer wants ‘sense of renewed pace’ in post-Brexit talks while staying within Labour’s red lines
Content: Hamish Falconer: ‘We have made some real initial progress on resetting but now we’ve got to deliver.’Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHamish Falconer: ‘We have made some real initial progress on resetting but now we’ve got to deliver.’Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianBrexitLabour seeking ‘deeper relationship’ with EU under Burnham, new minister saysExclusive: Hamish Falconer wants ‘sense of renewed pace’ in post-Brexit talks while staying within Labour’s red lines‘I was on my honeymoon!’: Hamish Falconer’s surprise call-up to Burnham’s cabinetJessica ElgotandLisa O’CarrollSun 9 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK will move faster and be more ambitious on achieving closer ties with Europe under Andy Burnham’s government, his new chief post-Brexit negotiator has said.Hamish Falconer, the new cabinet minister in charge of the EU reset talks, said there was “room to be ambitious” within Labour’s red lines onEurope, which exclude reopening discussions on the single market and customs union, and he would look at the “art of the possible”.He said greater cooperation on services – which might include visa-free travel for British people working in the EU, or mutual recognition of qualifications–was the next big area where the UK hoped to make progress. “I would want a deeper relationship, a more ambitious relationship with the EU,” Falconer told the Guardian.What the EU wants from Andy BurnhamRead more“There’s also a whole range of areas in relation to services where I’d really like it to be progressed. Services is obviously an area where the EU itself is less closely integrated and there’s a lot of discussion within the EU about where to take the productivity challenge for them – that’s a challenge we can recognise here in the UK as well. So, particularly on services, I’m really interested in where we can go further.”Falconer, the son ofthe Labour grandee Charlie Falconer, is a former Middle East minister and diplomat who has experience as a Foreign Office negotiator. He said he wanted “a sense of renewed pace” in the talks – though there is still no new summit date in sight. The long-awaited reset summit, whichhad been proposed for July, was postponed after Keir Starmer resigned as prime minister in June.“We’re committed to our manifesto red lines, but all of my experiences as a negotiator and the art of the possible is in part shaped by the nature of the relationship between two people negotiating,” Falconer said.“I used to be a negotiator with the Taliban. With the EU, this is a negotiation with our friends, with whom we share our values and with whom we feel solidarity.”Earlier this summer, EU diplomats expressed concern that the talks under Starmer had lost momentum, with the second annual summit of EU and UK leaders repeatedly delayed astalks stalled over a youth mobility scheme.Falconer,who returned from his honeymoon when he was offered the post of Europe ministerby Burnham, has spoken already to the EU trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, and senior bloc figures hope he will bring a new energy to talks.View image in fullscreenHamish Falconer arriving at 10 Downing Street in July.Photograph: Thomas Krych/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOne said of his predecessor Nick Thomas-Symonds: “I really liked him but the problem was the UK didn’t open up a window, create the political space for a deal.”They complained that instead of seizing opportunities to get a deal over the line and bank a political win to move on to the next phase, the UK negotiators “kept trying to add things” such as an agreement on services.A source close to Thomas-Symonds disputed this and said good progress had been made on all areas under discussion in advance of the planned July summit.It is believed that the next summit may not be held until October to give Falconer time to get across the detail, and for Burnham to flesh out his foreign policy.Resolving the terms of a youth mobility deal is a key priority, to allow tens of thousands of European and British young people to live and work in each other’s territories.Talks remained deadlocked due to the UK’s reluctance to allow EU students to pay the lower fees charged to UK students, something opposed by cash-strapped universities.Falconer said the deal should “work for both sides” and was mindful of financial pressures on the university sector. “In my constituency in Lincoln, there’s two universities. I’ve got those issues very much at the forefront of my mind,” he said. “It is vital that as we go through this, we have real respect on both sides for what some of the constraints are for each of us.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFalconer said he wanted to apply Burnham’s“Makerfield test”to the EU negotiations, ensuring they would deliver tangible change to ordinary people struggling with the cost of living, including in his own very heavily leave-voting constituency.But he said he would continuously emphasise principles of “European solidarity”, which he said went beyond trade and were backed by shared values, including on defence and security and on how countries could tackle growing dangers such as wildfires caused by the climate crisis.Starmer and Thomas-Symonds had been due to host the second UK-EU summit on 22 July, withprogress already announcedon a deal easing barriers for food and drink exports expected to come into force before summer 2027.The EU that the UK left no longer exists | Mujtaba RahmanRead moreThough there was a warm relationship between Starmer and the EU’s Ursula von der Leyen, the UK had also faced difficulty in fulfilling some of the promised changes agreed atthe last UK-EU summit, including an inability to reach agreement on the UK’s entry into the €150bn Safe fund for defence investment.Talks over UK participation in Safe collapsed last Novemberwith France blamed for setting too high a price for British involvement. Seasoned observers in Brussels say it was also embarrassing for the EU and was “a failure of statecraft” on both sides.Falconer said: “I think that we have made some real initial progress on resetting but now we’ve got to deliver.”Having Downing Street support to give Falconer the political space that EU diplomats want created will be key. And he says he has the experience to deliver.“I used to be a negotiator in the Foreign Office, often doing really hard negotiations. Ultimately, the character of the wider relationship is really important,” he said. “Yes, there are some really important technical questions that we have got to get right.”“But we also need to put this in the big picture … there is also a massive wider European agenda, which is really important to us, and Britain is really important to that agenda too. Security, defence, tech. We are a big part of those discussions and those dilemmas.”Falconer said he would use his role – now at cabinet level – to boost the UK’s participation in solving Europe-wide challenges outside the EU. “We are part of Europe and we feel the threats to Europe, whether it’s in eastern Europe from Russia invading Ukraine, or even wildfires and that shared sense of challenge in dealing with that.”Explore more on these topicsBrexitForeign policyLabourAndy BurnhamEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Netanyahu rejects US-led 15-point Gaza peace plan in rare public break with Trump | Israel-Gaza war | The Guardian
description: Israeli PM says IDF will not withdraw until Hamas is disarmed and rebukes US pressure to end wars without his country’s buy-in
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Israeli PM says IDF will not withdraw until Hamas is disarmed and rebukes US pressure to end wars without his country’s buy-in
Content: Trump will have to decide whether to increase pressure on Netanyahu if he wants his Gaza peace plan to succeed.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTrump will have to decide whether to increase pressure on Netanyahu if he wants his Gaza peace plan to succeed.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesIsrael-Gaza warNetanyahu rejects US-led 15-point Gaza peace plan in rare public break with TrumpIsraeli PM says IDF will not withdraw until Hamas is disarmed and rebukes US pressure to end wars without his country’s buy-inAndrew Rothin WashingtonSun 9 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTFirst published on Sun 9 Aug 2026 14.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael’s prime minister,Benjamin Netanyahu, has rejected a US-backed 15-point peace plan for Gaza in a rare public break with Donald Trump.In a statement on Sunday, Netanyahu said that he was confronting a “wave of rumours about Israeli weakness and Israeli withdrawals on all fronts” and rebuked US pressure to end wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran without Israel’s buy-in.On Gaza, he said: “Israel does not accept the 15-point document. The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal untilHamasis disarmed. And when I say the disarming of Hamas, it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry. And we are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament. Right now, we are talking with the Americans about this issue.”Trump’s Board of Peace in July proposed the 15-point plan, which mandated that Hamas disarmin exchange for providing a full Israeli military withdrawalfrom the Gaza Strip and an eventual transition of power to an independent Palestinian National Committee. Trump had said that the agreement would be implemented in stages, but Netanyahu on Sunday said that he wanted a full disarmament first in order to implement the deal.View image in fullscreenIsraeli attacks have continued on Gaza despite a ceasefire brokered last October.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesThe Israeli leader’s main target in his remarks was the US. Israel has emerged as a key stumbling block in the Trump White House’s plans to broker peace in the region, in Israel’s conflicts inGazaand Lebanon as well as in the war begun by joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran. And Netanyahu, who is facing tough elections in October and pressure from hardliners in his own government, appears ready to test his relationship with Trump in public in order to shore up his reputation as a defender of Israel at home.Israel had already signalled that it would reject the US-led plan. Soon after Trump announced it last month,Israel stepped up its bombing campaign in the Palestinian territory– strikes killed 18 people last Sunday. Netanyahu’s office had previously indicated it would not back the plan, saying: “The version that has been made public does not reflect Israel’s positions.”But Sunday’s rejection was far more forceful and direct, and appeared targeted at the Trump White House, as Trump and Netanyahu both face difficult elections. “Unlike all those who lecture us, we do what needs to be done for Israel’s security, and we can and know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary,” Netanyahu said.The head of Trump’s Board of Peace hit back on Sunday, saying the plan remained the “only way forward”. Nickolay Mladenov, the board’s high representative for Gaza, told Israeli television: “The option we are offering today is the only way forward that ensures this tragedy does not happen again.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIran plots to deal Trump a blow in midterms by keeping him entangled in warRead moreNetanyahu’s rejection is a blow to Trump’s desire to be seen as a broker of peace in foreign conflicts. With US midterm elections due in November, the White House is desperate to negotiate a peace in Iran in order to reopen the strait of Hormuz and help bring down oil and petrol prices.But the conflicts in the Middle East are interconnected and parallel US efforts have continued to bring peace to Lebanon, where Israel has occupied land in what it says is a buffer zone against Hezbollah, and Gaza, where Gulf allies of the US have decried what they say is an ethnic cleansing campaign being carried out by Israel.Like US presidents before him, Trump has found that Netanyahu can be a difficult ally. Bill Clinton, after meeting Netanyahu for the first time in 1996, is reported to have said: “Who’s the fucking superpower here?”More recently, the Biden administration found that its concerns about the human toll in Gaza were ignored, but continued to publicly back Netanyahu and did not significantly suspend military aid to the country for fear of the political blowback that Netanyahu and his allies in the US could cause.In Trump, however, Netanyahu has found a far more unorthodox and unpredictable counterpart in the White House. Netanyahu is a natural ally for Trump, and he has attacked Democrats before the midterm elections for being weak on supporting Israel.Yet more broadly,support for Israel and its war in Gaza is eroding in the Democratic party, and the Republicans have a presidential frontrunner for 2028 in the vice-president, JD Vance, who ispublicly sceptical of Israeland the war in Gaza.Trump will have to decide whether to increase pressure on Netanyahu, potentially alienating some pro-Israel allies, or to allow his efforts for a Gaza peace plan to stall, perhaps indefinitely.The answer will depend heavily on the US president’s own political instincts – are US voters hoping to see Trump emerge as a statesman capable of ending one of the world’s bloodiest recent wars in Gaza, or would a public clash with Netanyahu provoke a revolt among his base? With both countries entering tumultuous election cycles anda generational shift in support for Israel among US voters, the result could redraw the alliance between Israel and the US.Explore more on these topicsIsrael-Gaza warIsraelGazaBenjamin NetanyahuDonald TrumpMiddle East and north AfricaHamasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Parents of baby girl killed at nursery fear unsafe sleeping ‘rife’ in sector across England | Early years education | The Guardian
description: Katie and John Meehan say responses to campaign they launched after death of daughter Genevieve must be ‘wake-up call’
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Katie and John Meehan say responses to campaign they launched after death of daughter Genevieve must be ‘wake-up call’
Content: John and Katie Meehan have worked with the Lullaby Trust to strengthen safety and regulation of nurseries in England.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJohn and Katie Meehan have worked with the Lullaby Trust to strengthen safety and regulation of nurseries in England.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianEarly years educationParents of baby girl killed at nursery fear unsafe sleeping ‘rife’ in sector across EnglandKatie and John Meehan say responses to campaign they launched after death of daughter Genevieve must be ‘wake-up call’Josh HallidayNorth of England editorSun 9 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 09.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe parents of a nine-month-old girl who died after being placed in an unsafe sleeping position at nursery said they feared poor practice may be “rife” across England.Genevieve Meehan suffocated when she wasstrapped face downto a beanbag for an hour and 37 minutes at a nursery in Cheadle Hulme, Stockport, in May 2022.Kate Roughley, the nursery’s deputy manager, wasjailed for 14 yearsin 2024 after being found guilty of manslaughter. One of Roughley’s colleagues was later jailed for the “deplorable” treatment of other babies in her care.Genevieve’s parents, Katie and John Meehan, have led a campaign with the charity the Lullaby Trust to strengthen safety and regulation of nurseries after a series of high-profile abuses.The sector has come under intense scrutiny in recent months after the cases ofVincent ChanandNathan Bennett, nursery workers who sexually assaulted children in their care.View image in fullscreenGenevieve Meehan, who died in May 2022 at nine months old.Photograph: Greater Manchester Police/PAChan was jailed in February for 18 years for molesting young children in a campaign of sexual abuse that was described as “every parent’s worst nightmare”, while Bennett was jailed in March for 24 years for raping and abusing young children in his care.Another nursery worker, Kimberley Cookson, wasjailed in Aprilover the death of 14-month-old Noah Sibanda, who had been physically restrained face-down with a blanket over his head while being put to sleep.As a result ofGenevieve’s parents’ campaign, childcare settings in England will be banned from September from putting babies under 12 months to sleep in anything other than a cot.Ofsted, the regulator, will triple the number of unannounced inspections – adding an extra 3,000 visits a year, boosted by an additional £8m from the government – and inspect nurseries every four years instead of six. Each visit will scrutinise sleeping policies.Katie Meehan, 42, said she was “really shocked” by the extent of unsafe sleeping practice that had been revealed when nurseries wrote privately to the government about the planned changes this year.Some reported leaving babies to sleep in pushchairs “due to space limitations”, according to details shared with the Department for Education (DfE). Others put infants to sleep outside, adopting “forest school models or Scandinavian practices”.By law, nurseries are required to follow NHS safer sleep guidance – which includes laying the baby on their backin a cot or Moses basket– however, in the rules from September, the government will state: “Babies aged one year and under must only be placed to sleep in a cot.”Katie Meehan, who is working closely with the government and Ofsted, said the responses suggested unsafe sleeping may be “rife” across England and that they were a “wake-up call” for the regulator and officials.Some nursery owners said they would be forced to reduce the number of infants they take as a result of the new rules. Several raised concerns that this will ban smaller beds, such as dream coracles, which take up less space than a cot and have been widely adopted in recent years.John Meehan, 40, said he was concerned some nursery owners – many of whom arebacked by private equityfirms – were potentially putting profit before safety.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“There are lots and lots of people out there who just want to do their absolute best and they go into that industry because they want to look after children,” he said. “But my impression from some of the responses is that they are taking too many children and there is a money incentive for them to do so, and that is a real concern.”Ministers are now considering whether to introducemandatory CCTV to all nurseries in England, one of the key aims of the campaign. Olivia Bailey, the former early years minister who spearheaded the latest reforms, is understood to have been very persuaded by the arguments for mandatory CCTV.Katie Meehan said she was disappointed that Bailey lost her role in the reshuffle when Andy Burnham became prime minister. However, she is hopeful Burnham will take up the reforms, having met Genevieve’s family this year when he was mayor of Greater Manchester.She said Burnham was particularly supportive of their call for mandatory CCTV – which was crucial in securing Genevieve’s killer’s conviction – and that he had told them: “Genevieve was a child of Manchester and she was failed. We’ve got to make sure it doesn’t happen again.”The DfE said: “What happened to Genevieve was a tragedy, and her parents’ campaigning has already changed practice across the country. We will keep going until no family goes through what theirs has.Nurseries, vets and shops: the sectors where private equity plays a big roleRead more“The vast majority of settings do a brilliant job, and the response to our updated guidance showed a sector that wants to get this right. But settings have long been legally required to follow NHS safer sleep guidance, and that is why we are working with the Lullaby Trust to make those expectations unambiguous, so there can be no excuses for unsafe practice.”Sir Martyn Oliver, the chief inspector at Ofsted, said: “No parent should have to endure what Katie and John have been through. They have shown remarkable bravery in pursuing change following their daughter’s tragic death.“We welcome the DfE’s additional funding for more frequent inspections, including thousands more without notice visits. We’re also strengthening our inspection practice so that safe sleeping in nurseries and with childminders is now a mandatory part of every inspection and will be reported on for parents to read.”Explore more on these topicsEarly years educationCrimeOfstedChildcareChildrenParents and parentingChild protectionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alleged crime boss Daniel Kinahan’s return to Ireland ends global game of cat-and-mouse | Ireland | The Guardian
description: Kinahan built boxing empire while in exile in Dubai but now faces trial in Dublin charged with directing organised crime
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Kinahan built boxing empire while in exile in Dubai but now faces trial in Dublin charged with directing organised crime
Content: Daniel Kinahan left Ireland in 2016, first for Spain and later Dubai, where he ran a successful boxing business.Photograph: NNA/SOLARPIX.COMView image in fullscreenDaniel Kinahan left Ireland in 2016, first for Spain and later Dubai, where he ran a successful boxing business.Photograph: NNA/SOLARPIX.COMIrelandAlleged crime boss Daniel Kinahan’s return to Ireland ends global game of cat-and-mouseKinahan built boxing empire while in exile in Dubai but now faces trial in Dublin charged with directing organised crimeRory CarrollandLisa O’CarrollSun 9 Aug 2026 14.18 EDTFirst published on Sun 9 Aug 2026 07.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA decade after escaping assassination and fleeing into exile, Daniel Kinahan is back inIreland– but it is not the homecoming he wanted.The alleged leader of the Kinahan organised crime group was extradited from Dubai in an Irish government jet on Sunday and met by a huge security operation in Dublin, marking the end of a global game of cat and mouse with European, US and Gulf authorities.The 49-year-old landed at Casement aerodrome in Dublin on Sunday evening and was taken to the criminal courts of justice in central Dublin to be charged with directing organised crime.A judge told Kinahan that, because of the charge, an application for bail would have to be made to the high court. Kinahan said: “I understand. I think we know I won’t be getting bail, but thank you.”He was then taken 50 miles outside the city to his new home in Portlaoise prison.View image in fullscreenA vehicle arriving at the special criminal court in Dublin, where Kinahan was taken to be charged on Sunday.Photograph: Natalia Campos/ReutersTabloid headlines anticipated his return with glee. “Du-Bye!” said one. “Dan and Dusted,” said another. “Kin Air: He’s Coming Home,” said another.It is a moment long sought by law enforcement agencies that named Kinahan as a leader of a cartel said to control about a third of Europe’s cocaine supply, along with running criminal sidelines in firearms and racketeering.As the founder of the boxing management company MTK Global, the Dubliner was alsoan influential figure in sportsand boasted of friendships with Tyson Fury and other champions.View image in fullscreenKinahan (right) with the boxer Tyson Fury in 2020.Photograph: UnknownKinahan has not been tried but is braced for conviction and a long sentence, according to clips of an interview that he gave by phone fromDubaito the podcaster James English. “I think I’ve already got life in prison. And we have to go through the dance now.”The married father of five said he had “not been an angel” but that accusations against him were overblown. “I believe in a way I’m a scapegoat.” He had not laundered money through boxing promotion, he said, rebutting one of the allegations against him.Kinahan said he looked forward to familiar Irish treats such as a crisp sandwich. “Get back home and have a little bit of batch bread and a packet of King crisps or Tayto.”View image in fullscreenDaniel Kinahan (back right) leaving Dublin’s criminal courts of justice on Sunday.Photograph: Mark Marlow/PAThe bravado, or fatalism, could not disguise a dramatic fall. Fromgilded opulencein the United Arab Emirates (UAE), allegedly at the helm of a criminal empire worth hundreds of millions of euros, Kinahan will reportedly become an inmate at the maximum-security A5 unit within A block at Portlaoise.His father, Christopher Kinahan, launched a family enterprise in the 1980s by importing heroin into Dublin. A polished figure with university degrees and a facility for languages, Kinahan senior, better known as Christy, was convicted of drug offences and money laundering whilecreating a networkthat spanned Latin America, north Africa, the UK and continental Europe.In 2009, a US diplomatic cable named his son Daniel as “an Irish businessman involved in narco-trafficking throughout Europe”. Soon after, Spanish authorities arrested Christy and Daniel and seized assets, but the Kinahans emerged largely unscathed.That changed when a murderous feud with the rival Hutch gang piled up corpses and led to an audacious but unsuccessful attempt on Daniel’s life at aboxing weigh-in at Dublin’s Regency hotelin February 2016. The death of one man, David Byrne, fuelled further killings.View image in fullscreenWanted posters displayed at a press conference at Dublin City Hall after the US government announced it was offering $5m for information on the Kinahans.Photograph: Niall Carson/PAKinahan was never again seen in public in Ireland and operated from southern Spain before settling in Dubai in the UAE, which had no extradition agreement with Ireland. With his father and brother Christopher junior, Daniel remained alert to surveillance attempts but lived openly and turned MTK Global into a boxing powerhouse.That apparent untouchability evaporated in 2022 when the US offered a reward of up to $15m for information that led to the arrest or conviction of the trio. Washington had been reluctant to get involved until lobbied by the then assistant garda commissioner John O’Driscoll, Greg Gatjanis, who ran the US national security council’s strategy for transnational organised crime, told the MacGill summer school last month.“To this day I hold Ireland, the gardaí, as the model [for international manhunts] of how they handled the Kinahan organisation,” said Gatjanis. “Their drug empire probably did not touch the US, but then he started talking about the effects of the Kinahan organisation and the terror they were inflicting. I went from telling him I couldn’t accommodate sanctions because I could not make a case for it to agreeing to starting up an investigation, and that began the entire sanction investigation.”View image in fullscreenFlowers, photos and messages at the site of the former Regency hotel in Dublin, where David Byrne was shot dead during a boxing weigh-in.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PAIn May 2025 Ireland agreed an extradition treaty with the UAE and the net began to close. Sean McGovern, a cartel lieutenant wanted for murder and directing organised crime, wasextraditedthat month and jailed for 24 years.Daniel Kinahan wasarrested in Aprilthis year. UAE authorities rejected his appeal last month, clearing the way for extradition. Irish military personnel are expected to reinforce police during Kinahan’s transfers to court and prison. Kinahan told the podcast he would be subject to a “circus” and “character assassination”.Gatjanis said no organised crime group lasted for ever. “It’s born, it crawls, walks, runs, starts to decline, ultimately dies.”Explore more on these topicsIrelandEuropeDubaifeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Pilot pulls off Count Binface stunt for Clacton byelection | Clacton byelection August 2026 | The Guardian
description: Plane spends 30 minutes off the Essex coast marking out shape of a bin in apparent tribute to Nigel Farage’s rival
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Plane spends 30 minutes off the Essex coast marking out shape of a bin in apparent tribute to Nigel Farage’s rival
Content: The pilot’s flight path off Clacton appears to be a tribute to Count Binface.Photograph: Flightradar24View image in fullscreenThe pilot’s flight path off Clacton appears to be a tribute to Count Binface.Photograph: Flightradar24Clacton byelection August 2026Pilot pulls off Count Binface stunt for Clacton byelectionPlane spends 30 minutes off the Essex coast marking out shape of a bin in apparent tribute to Nigel Farage’s rivalNadeem BadshahSun 9 Aug 2026 13.03 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA pilot has traced the shape of a bin with their flight path near Clacton beforeCount Binfacechallenges Nigel Farage in a byelection on Thursday.The light aircraft spent around half an hour between 2,100ft and 4,150ft above the sea near theEssexcoastal town zigzagging to mark out the shape of a bin, according to data from Flightradar24.The plane took off from Earls Colne airfield near Colchester at 2.48pm on Saturday and landed at 4.13pm. The aircraft is in private ownership, according to Flightradar24, and the pilot’s identity is unknown.Voters will go to the polls in Clacton in a byelection triggered by the resignation of Farage, theReform UKleader.View image in fullscreenCount Binface supporters canvassing in Clacton, where Nigel Farage is expected to win a byelection on Thursday.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPACount Binface, a self-proclaimed space warrior who wears a bin-shaped helmet, is Farage’s main rival. There are also three candidates from the Official Monster Raving Loony party and numerous independents.All the main Westminster parties are boycotting the byelection, which they have dismissed as a stunt.A survey by Survation on behalf of Mandate Research suggests Farage will win 73% of the vote while Count Binface could get 20%.Farage resigned after it emerged that he was being investigated by the parliamentary standards commissioner over a £5m gift from the cryptocurrency tycoon Christopher Harborne, which he received before taking his seat in the Commons.The investigation, which is looking at whether he should have declared the money when he arrived in parliament, was suspended on his resignation but is expected to resume should he win the byelection.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf he is found to have broken the rules, and a suspension of more than 10 days is imposed, it could trigger a recall petition and the prospect of the Reform UK leader losing his seat, forcing a further contest.Farage has repeatedly insisted the gift –revealed by the Guardian in April– was not linked to his political career.
