He has said he had no intention of returning to politics until June 2024, just before the election.Explore more on these topicsClacton byelection August 2026ByelectionsCount BinfaceNigel FarageClacton on SeaEssexReform UKnewsShareReuse this content

title: Zuckerberg faces questions over why superyacht reportedly declined to help stranded boat | Alaska | The Guardian
description: Small cruise ship rescued skiff in south-east Alaska even though Meta billionaire’s $300m megayacht was closer
Author: Eric Berger
Headline: Small cruise ship rescued skiff in south-east Alaska even though Meta billionaire’s $300m megayacht was closer
Content: A spokesperson for Zuckerberg said the ‘assist was already under way’ by the time the yacht crew reviewed the radio request.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersView image in fullscreenA spokesperson for Zuckerberg said the ‘assist was already under way’ by the time the yacht crew reviewed the radio request.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersAlaskaZuckerberg faces questions over why superyacht reportedly declined to help stranded boatSmall cruise ship rescued skiff in south-east Alaska even though Meta billionaire’s $300m megayacht was closerEric BergerSun 9 Aug 2026 15.06 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 20.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMark Zuckerberg has faced questions over why a small cruise ship in south-east Alaska rescued a stranded skiff and its crew when his 387ft superyacht had been closer.The Silicon Valley billionaire’s yacht, worth a reported $300m, is said to have “repeatedly” declined to assist when a nearby boat called for help last week.Zuckerberg, CEO of Facebook and Instagram owner Meta Platforms, was not on board at the time, a spokespersontold Forbes.When a nearby 21ft skiff ran out of fuel between Petersburg and Juneau, theAlaska Beaconreported operators of a cruise ship that was further away than Zuckerberg’s yacht came to the rescue.“I’m on a small-ship Alaska cruise with my son,” a passenger on the UnCruise Adventures ship Wilderness Legacy postedon Bluesky.“Our boat rescued a stranded vessel last night and apparently we did that after the Coast Guard radioed Mark Zuckerberg’s yacht – which was closer – and they repeatedly refused to respond. (There was near unanimous booing when the captain announced this).”But Brian Baker, a spokesperson for Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, told Forbes that the couple were not on board his yacht, named Launchpad. The yacht crew had been operating on a different radio channel, Baker told Forbes. “The assist was already under way” by the time they reviewed the broadcast, he said.Even if he was not on his ship, the report is unlikely to boost public opinion of Zuckerberg, who has faced criticism over the societal impact of his social media platforms; his newwarm relationshipwith Donald Trump; andhis lavish,insular lifestyle.“I live in Juneau and I’ve been having to look at that excessive eyesore parked up in [Auke Bay] for too long now,” aReddit userwrote of the yacht in response to the rescue story. “Fuck Zuckerberg.”Explore more on these topicsAlaskaMark ZuckerbergMetanewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham vows crackdown on ‘rip-off’ business practices to ease cost of living | UK cost of living crisis | The Guardian
description: First of PM’s ‘everyday fixes’ to be banning fake discounts and making it easier to cancel unwanted subscriptions
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: First of PM’s ‘everyday fixes’ to be banning fake discounts and making it easier to cancel unwanted subscriptions
Content: Andy Burnham is seeking to put the cost of living at the heart of his premiership.Photograph: Fred Duval/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham is seeking to put the cost of living at the heart of his premiership.Photograph: Fred Duval/SOPA Images/ShutterstockUK cost of living crisisBurnham vows crackdown on ‘rip-off’ business practices to ease cost of livingFirst of PM’s ‘everyday fixes’ to be banning fake discounts and making it easier to cancel unwanted subscriptionsAndy Burnham: I’ll end the rip-offs that people hateAletha AduPolitical correspondentSun 9 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 20.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has promised a series of measures to tackle the cost of living, including a ban on fake discounts and making it easier for people to escape unwanted subscriptions.The crackdown on “rip-off” business practices is expected to benefit consumers to the tune of £400m a year and will be the first in a range of “everyday fixes” to be implemented in the coming months.Writing for the Guardian, the prime minister said his government would step in wherever it could as he sought to put the cost of living at the heart of his premiership.“We won’t be able to solve every frustration overnight,” he wrote. “But where the government can save people money, remove an unnecessary obstacle or simply make something work better, we should and we will.”The government will ban misleading pricing practices that retailers use to make discounts appear better than they really are, including fake “was” prices, invented reductions and misleading recommended retail prices.View image in fullscreenThe government wants to ensure RRP prices cannot be used misleadingly.Photograph: Rosemary Roberts/AlamyMinisters will consult in the autumn on the precise practices covered and how the ban will work, before introducing the changes through secondary legislation.Downing Street hopes the measures can be implemented as soon as possible and does not expect a lengthy parliamentary process.The changes are intended to stop retailers inflating the price of an item before cutting it to give shoppers the false impression they are receiving a bigger discount.Burnham wrote: “If something is advertised as half price, it should actually be half price. We’ll make sure that when families snatch a deal, they can be confident they’re actually saving. That’s the least they deserve when budgets are so tight.”The government is also speeding up new protections against subscription traps, bringing forward their introduction from next spring to January. The rules will force businesses to provide clearer information when people sign up, regularly remind customers about their subscriptions and make it easier for them to cancel. Customers will also be given a 14-day cooling-off period after a trial ends or a long-term contract renews.The average person has about three subscriptions and spends about £500 a year on them, according to government figures. There are about 155m active subscriptions across the UK, and about £1.6bn a year is spent on unwanted ones.View image in fullscreenNew rules will make subscriptions clearer and easier to cancel.Photograph: Srdjan Randjelovic/AlamyMinisters estimate consumers will save an average of £14 a month for each unwanted subscription they are able to leave early.“Too many companies want you to sign up in seconds but then make it feel impossible to leave. It’s exhausting,” Burnham wrote.The challenge for the prime minister will be whether smaller consumer-oriented interventions can provide savings households notice when many are still under pressure.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe two measures will be followed by more over the coming months as he attempts to show voters his government can make a noticeable difference to household finances.Burnham also promised “bigger plans to make life easier and fairer for people over the longer term”, but Downing Street has yet to set out what those will include.Burnham wrote: “As far as I’m concerned, whatever the size, big or small, if it’s a problem for you, it’s a problem for us. That’s why I’ve made it clear from day one that creating room to breathe is my number one priority, and the whole of government is united on that.“Every single unexpected payment, rip-off or hidden catch chips away at hope. That might sound dramatic – but it’s true. Every single one is another message that thiscountry is built to catch people out rather than help them get on.”Citizens Advice welcomed the changes but said they “can’t be the end of the story”.The announcement comes as Burnham prepares to spend the rest of his summertravelling around Britainin an attempt to reconnect the government with voters, particularly in areas where Labour has lost support.“I’ll be asking people what action they want to see on the cost of living,” Burnham wrote. “Because if we want to find the problems that make everyday life harder, we need to listen to the people dealing with them.”Downing Street has not said whether what Burnham hears on the tour will shape the next round of “everyday fixes”.Explore more on these topicsUK cost of living crisisLabourAndy BurnhamRetail industryEconomic policyConsumer affairsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was on my honeymoon!’: Hamish Falconer’s surprise call-up to Burnham’s cabinet | European Union | The Guardian
description: New EU negotiator, who previously helped free Taliban hostages, thought it was safe to book holiday during recess
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: New EU negotiator, who previously helped free Taliban hostages, thought it was safe to book holiday during recess
Content: Hamish Falconer in Lincoln city centre. He was in Greece when he found out about his appointment as minister of state for intergovernmental and European relations.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHamish Falconer in Lincoln city centre. He was in Greece when he found out about his appointment as minister of state for intergovernmental and European relations.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianEuropean UnionProfile‘I was on my honeymoon!’: Hamish Falconer’s surprise call-up to Burnham’s cabinetNew EU negotiator, who previously helped free Taliban hostages, thought it was safe to book holiday during recessLabour seeking ‘deeper relationship’ with EU under Burnham, new minister saysJessica ElgotDeputy political editorSun 9 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Hamish Falconer left his career as a Foreign Office diplomat for the hostile environment of a Labour party selection process, one of his last acts was a negotiation to free six hostages from the Taliban.When he won the key marginal seat of Lincoln in the 2024 general election, he did not expect to be back in those offices on King Charles Street quite so quickly – he was appointed Middle East minister just two weeks later.Two years on, he is one among the first three of his generation of MPs to reach the cabinet, and he is back around the negotiating table, this time with the EU.One of his oldest friends, Anneliese Midgley, is another of the three MPs from the 2024 intake toreach the cabinet, as Andy Burnham’s chief whip. Falconer had trusted Midgley – a close confidant of Burnham – to keep him in the loop about cabinet moves.But the tight secrecy of Burnham’s first appointment meant that he was caught off guard by his promotion, while on his honeymoon in Greece. “We got married in June but delayed the honeymoon until recess, and thought: what could possibly go wrong?” he said.“I thought it would be fine; Midge hasn’t told me not to go. Within 24 hours, I got a call saying: ‘Sorry, you have to look at flights.’ I was like: ‘I’m on my honeymoon!’ And the vibe was: you sort of have to be here for your first cabinet meeting.“So a combination of flights managed to get me back and forth, but on the 5am Jet2 flight, I might have been the only person wearing a suit.”He will attend cabinet as minister for European relations, taking the reins of negotiations with the EU for the next joint summit.While he is careful to praise his predecessor, Nick Thomas-Symonds, Falconer said he wanted to up the speed and ambition of deepening ties with the EU. “This is right at the centre of everything this government is trying to do: cost of living, energy,” he said.“Yes, there are some technical questions we need to get right. But the bigger picture is there is a massive wider European agenda. We want to be part of those discussions on security, defence, tech, about where Europe is going.”Falconer is the second generation of his family to attend cabinet – his father, Charlie Falconer, was Tony Blair’s justice secretary. He was long tipped as one of the most ambitious of the new intake of Labour MPs and has spent much of the past two years flying to summits and negotiations on Gaza and Iran.EU relations, climate crisis and Gaza: why Ed Miliband is fired up by Foreign Office challengesRead moreHe has answered a record-breaking number of urgent questions in the House of Commons from MPs, on Israel and Gaza, Iran and Sudan and the Chagos Islands.“I found it so strange coming back into the Foreign Office, where apparently I still had stuff I had left there,” he said. “People I knew incredibly well, people I’d had dysentery with in South Sudan, they wouldn’t call me Hamish any more, they would only call me minister. So it was a real head-spin.”When Falconer took on the brief – nine months after the 7 October Hamas massacre and the subsequent Israeli onslaught on Gaza – there was deep suspicion of Labour because of Starmer’s early comments about the right of Israel to cut off energy and water to Gaza. Burnham has since apologised for how disillusioned many voters became with Labour over those comments.“I came in with this knowledge that there had been a lot of upset and concern about what Keir had said … the LBC interview, and so I was determined that we would make a real contribution,” Falconer said.“I feel so proud to be the first Middle East minister who recognised the Palestinian state. I will literally never forget the kids we helped rescue from Gaza, all the students who started their lives here.”But it never felt like enough, Falconer admits. Many in his party wished the government could have gone much further with evacuations, aid and sanctions.“It was a terribly difficult job to do for two years because I would feel that the country was desperate not to see the horrors of Gaza continue … they couldn’t bear – rightly – that there was malnutrition among children, that there was still terrible loss of life,” he said.“There are so many incidents that were burned into my mind. I think over the last two years we did really important and historic things. But nobody could look at the last two years in the Middle East and not feel just such a depth of sadness. And my God, I carried that with me, and will still carry that with me.”View image in fullscreenDisplaced Palestinians walk amid the rubble in Jabalya, north of Gaza City. Hamish Falconer says, ‘Nobody could look at the last two years in the Middle East and not feel just such a depth of sadness’.Photograph: Mohammed Saber/EPAFalconer is speaking from his constituency office in Lincoln, yards from the cathedral in a city which is the sole patch of red in a county once solidly Conservative but where Reform have been growing dominant. It is home to the constituency of the Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice, and the mayor is the former Conservative MP turned Reform UK defector Andrea Jenkyns.There is a palpable sense of relief from Falconer that Labour has some chance, under Burnham, to get another public hearing. “I can see what the alternative is. I see it every day. I work with a Reform mayor – actually that’s probably overstating how practical a conversation I can have,” he said. “I really know what is at stake because it is right outside my city, and this is such an important battle to get right.What the EU wants from Andy BurnhamRead more“The truth is, the right are not offering any answers for the country. I could have snorted with laughter at some of the proposals that were being made by Reform in recent weeks, which were so obviously unserious.”Burnham’s key weak spot has often been said to be foreign policy – and he has made it known he intends to spend far less time on the world stage than his predecessor, which has worried some officials and international leaders who admired Starmer’s commitment to Ukraine and to diplomacy in the Middle East.Falconer said it was “not fair” to describe the prime minister as uninterested. “I’ve known Andy a long time. He is incredibly engaged,” he said. “He’s someone who is good at forming relationships, and that’s so important in international relations.”But the “Makerfield test” should still be applied to foreign policy, how actions will affect the kinds of voters who delivered Burnham his landslide in his Wigan byelection.“It’s not a hard or complicated test,” Falconer said. “I am really focused on delivering something that my constituents will feel in their day-to-day lives. In my constituency office, I’m sat across from a small gas turbine producer. I want to make it easier for them to trade in Europe, to continue to grow.“I know through my job, I can make that better. That is true of businesses right across the city. That is what I think the Makerfield test, the Lincoln test, is all about.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionEuropeprofilesShareReuse this content

title: ‘You live for those breakthroughs’: an investigation into military tribunals on US airbases meant protecting those who spoke out | Media | The Guardian
description: Guardian journalists have been uncovering how cases involving US military personnel that bypassed British courts. It involved telling the stories of women who have been denied important rights and protections, and safeguarding them as sources
Author: Gautam Malkani
Headline: Guardian journalists have been uncovering how cases involving US military personnel that bypassed British courts. It involved telling the stories of women who have been denied important rights and protections, and safeguarding them as sources
Content: Complainants are often not given the same protections in the US military court martial process as they would have got in a British court.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComplainants are often not given the same protections in the US military court martial process as they would have got in a British court.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesInside the GuardianMedia‘You live for those breakthroughs’: an investigation into military tribunals on US airbases meant protecting those who spoke outGuardian journalists have been uncovering cases involving US military personnel that bypassed British courts. It involved telling the stories of women who have been denied important rights and protections, and safeguarding them as sourcesSupport investigative journalism todayGautam MalkaniSun 9 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen reporters talk about protecting their sources, it isn’t always about protecting a source’s identity. Some sources are prepared to go public. Others may have already shed their anonymity before a journalist gets in touch with them. But they all still need to be supported and safeguarded as their stories are brought to light.“I try to ensure there are no surprises for them,” says Harry Davies, a Guardian investigations correspondent. “You have to prepare them for the exposure and talk them through what it will mean.”Over the past six months, Harry and a team of Guardian journalists haveuncovered the stories of womenin the UK who have accused US servicemen stationed or operating in Britain of serious crimes, including rape and sexual assault. The women had been denied rights and protections they could have expected within the British justice system because the American servicemen were instead tried in opaque US military tribunals held in US airbases – often forlesser offencesthan they would have faced had the cases been heard in British courts. And the juries in these tribunals consist of fellow US military personnel, often from the same base.One of the women our reporters spoke to was willing to waive her anonymity. Others chose to retain it. All of them were given the usual support and protections as sources for the Guardian’s subsequent reporting.“We talked them through the process and ensured that it was their decision and we weren’t pressuring them into it,” says Harry. “They can’t be fully involved in our journalistic process because it needs to be completely independent and separate from the people we’re writing about, but we can keep them informed about how certain things are going to be described. We can talk through what it means to have your photograph taken and also about how a story may be received, even if those reactions are often hard to predict.”The reporters on the Guardian’sBase justice investigationwere all too aware that some of the women might have already been retraumatised by the relative lack of protections and safeguards in the witness stand during the US military tribunals – which are known as courts martial. Harry and fellow investigative reporter Rob Evans had applied to attend one such tribunal last April at RAF Lakenheath, the largest US base in Britain.That’s where they heardthe case of Sarah Steele, an academic from Cambridge who had been strangled and assaulted by the US fighter pilot Capt Jacob Wulfson. Prosecutors also accused him of drugging her, as well as sexual assault and “aggravated sexual contact” – a crime that doesn’t exist in the UK, where the offences would likely be categorised in British courts as rape. An all-male panel of eight US air force officers found Wulfson guilty of strangulation but acquitted him of the sexual assault and aggravated sexual contact charges.View image in fullscreenCapt Jacob Wulfson’s case was tried at a court martial on a US airbase according to US military law, despite his alleged crime taking place while he was off duty and in an English city.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Benjamin SmithHarry and Rob observed first-hand how victims of alleged sexual offences can be subjected tomuch more invasive questioningand potential intimidation in a US court martial than they would in a British court hearing. Steele later described her experience in the witness stand: “The ordeal I went through was incredibly distressing and degrading. It felt intrusive and archaic.”How the US bypasses British courts to try its military over crimes in the UKRead moreTheir reporting from Lakenheath also conveys how uncanny US airbases can feel. The stores are stocked with American candy, the base has its own shopping mall, and the currency used in its shops and cafes is dollars. To reach the emergency services, you dial 911. “You’d see an American ambulance or police cars and other indicators that you’re in a sort of quasi-sovereign territory behind fences,” says Harry. “It’s not quite a parallel reality but it is a bit like walking into a part of the US.”Above all, they were struck by how hidden the whole thing was. “What Sarah had been through, and what we experienced in the court martial – these things would never have been known about if Rob and I hadn’t been there. The only real public record of it was a series of very limited entries on an obscureUS militarywebsite.”Harry and Rob had a hunch that there must be other similar cases out there, and that Sarah Steele’s ordeal formed part of a much bigger picture. Emine Sinmaz, a senior Guardian reporter, helped them with this painstaking work of finding other cases and also by knocking on doors, trying to find people willing to speak out and be sources, and by helping the team support and protect those sources.“For an investigation like this, you end up drawing on the skills and expertise across the whole team,” says Harry. “Emine is such a brilliant reporter, she’s really dogged and is great at old-fashioned shoe-leather journalism. And Rob somehow manages to prise out bits of information from bureaucracies by finding the right questions to ask – whether it’s the British police, American military police, the US Air Force or the Pentagon.”Harry recalls how they felt when they realised that Steele’s experience was very far from an isolated case: “You live for those breakthroughs. And it also laid down a challenge because we suddenly saw that there was a lot of reporting we could now go and do, and tangible leads and concrete information we could use.”Steele waived her anonymity for the Guardian’s subsequent reporting to help raise awareness about the scale and impact of this parallel legal system for US military personnel accused of committing crimes in the UK.While the team has protected the identities of other victims of alleged offences, the US military personnel convicted of some of the charges brought against them are neither nameless nor faceless thanks to the Guardian’s picture researchers and designers who have ensured each of the powerful stories in our Base justice investigation is accompanied by equally powerful imagery.“To be able to show the faces of these men was incredibly important to the story,” says art director Alex Mellon. “They have managed to avoid facing the British courts and public, so to be able to place them front and centre is really powerful.”Alex also explains the prominence of the stars and stripes: “The inclusion of the US flag in the illustrations highlights the power it symbolises. The flag is usually used as a patriotic symbol. But in hiding behind it, these servicemen have brought it into disrepute. I wanted the concept as a whole to feel like inverted patriotic images.”View image in fullscreenThe British government is conducting a review of British crimes prosecuted by US military after Guardian investigaiton.Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyThose stories are also brought to life by photos of the fighter jets that the servicemen either flew or worked on. Jim Hedge, a picture editor, is effectively the Guardian’s go-to person when it comes to photos of military equipment, having previously written about modern combat aircraft and studied it as part of his degree. “You have to get those details right,” Jim explains. “It’s very easy to undermine all our colleagues’ hard reporting work if we unwittingly use a picture of the wrong plane – and fighter jets and tanks have started to look very similar in recent years as military budgets have been squeezed.”Jim also commissioned the photographs of Steele. “A big part of that commissioning job is a duty of care to vulnerable people,” he explains. “Even if a source is happy to let us show their face, we need to be careful not to show anything that might identify where they live.”When handled correctly, the public exposure that a source might face when they waive their anonymity can also be empowering for them. “This investigation had, at its heart, a woman experiencing an extraordinary situation – and a situation which I think many people didn’t even know was possible,” says Harry. “And that seems to have caught people’s attention.”Indeed, the first stories in the Base justice series, published in June, sparked immediateconcerns from government ministersabout the way US military personnel were avoiding the British justice system, despite being accused of committing serious crimes on UK soil. Likewise, we have published amoving response from an MPabout the way the courts martial system denies accusers important rights and protections.Last week, it emerged that the UK government and police chiefs have launched a review into why UK police forces have been ceding jurisdiction to US military investigators. Meanwhile, ministers have met with Steele to discuss her case and the broader issues it raises. A government spokesperson said Steele had “shown incredible bravery in coming forward”, and that ministers had“committed to identifying and learning any lessons from this case to ensure that victims are supported and treated with the seriousness, dignity and compassion they deserve”.The Guardian is able to undertake impactful investigations such as this thanks to readers who support our work financially. title: ‘I’ve definitely lost followers’: influencers face backlash over Meta ‘pervert glasses’ content | Meta | The Guardian
description: Using ‘spy glasses’ made by Facebook owner leads to floods of negative comments, say content creators
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Using ‘spy glasses’ made by Facebook owner leads to floods of negative comments, say content creators
Content: Meta’s tech has prompted concerns about privacy and surveillance.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreenMeta’s tech has prompted concerns about privacy and surveillance.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersMeta‘I’ve definitely lost followers’: influencers face backlash over Meta ‘pervert glasses’ contentUsing ‘spy glasses’ made by Facebook owner leads to floods of negative comments, say content creatorsSammy GecsoylerSun 9 Aug 2026 09.37 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was hardly an offensive video. Amid the buzz of the Tour de France finale, Oliver Hooson filmed himself whipping up a delicious-looking flat white for a fellow cycling enthusiast. But after posting the footage on social media, the comments that soon rolled in were a real shock. “PERV,” read one. “Out here pushing creep glasses,” said another. His mistake? Documenting the moment with Meta’s “spy glasses”.Despite being marketed as the latest must-have gadget, Meta’s smartglasses, which can record video footage while being worn, have faced a vicious backlash, particularly relating to concerns about surveillance. There are widespread fears about the glasses being used to film people, especially women, without their consent, and the resultant footage being posted on social media. This has earned them the label of “pervert glasses”, and content creators, no matter how they are used, have faced a flood of negative comments for deploying them.View image in fullscreenOliver HoosonThings reached a peak this summer when Kylie Jenner collaborated with Meta to launch a pair, leading to a flurry of influencers showing off their trendy, Kardashian-approved goggles. Some content creators have been forced to apologise for plugging the specs. Rida Tharana, a content creator with 1.6 million followers on Instagram,“took accountability”for taking part in a Meta campaign to promote the glasses, criticising men who misuse them to “record and harass women”. Self-described pickup artists have used the glasses to film themselves trying to chat up women in public without their knowledge, sometimes making disparaging, misogynistic comments afterwards.Hooson says that, while some of the comments lefton his videowere “savage”, he is fully in support of their message. “It definitely caught me off guard. It was a real ignorant move,” he says, adding that he hates that the glasses are being used against “women mainly being filmed against their knowledge”. The backlash was even coming from those close to home. “Funnily enough, my wife predicted it. She was going to post a banterous comment in a similar tone to the others but she didn’t press send.”After posting the video, Hooson, whoshareshis passion for home design and cycling to his 224,000 Instagram followers, says he lost a “good 50 to 100” followers. He called the term “pervert glasses” a “defence mechanism” to dissuade people from using them. “If everybody gets round that they are pervert glasses, which evidently they have, then it’s a really easy way of limiting sales and the usage of them,” he says. “People do not need any more of their privacy stripped away. I’m fully in support of that.”Could Meta’s ‘pervert glasses’ be banned across the UK? – The LatestRead moreHis interest in the glasses, which he received at a PR event, was far more innocent. “I saw [chefs at] high-end restaurants filming themselves with the glasses on, showing off their process. It was stupid, poetic and beautiful to watch. I wanted to have a play about and show people the things that I enjoy doing,” he says, adding that it is very hard to capture a point of view (POV) angle otherwise. “It was intended as a simple way of capturing a human POV of my morning coffee routine or my fast cycling descents. I think that’s vastly different from somebody going into the centre of Soho and asking somebody a divisive question and clipping them up for views without their knowledge,” he says.But, for now, it’s not worth using the glasses. “Would I rather just not have that little fun point-of-view shot for the greater good? Yes, I would definitely get rid of them,” he says.While the glasses have proved unpopular with some online, they sold 7m pairs in 2025 alone. Meta says the tiny, flashing LED light that activates on the glasses will let people know when they are being filmed, but there have beenmultiple instancesof people complaining they have been videoed without prior knowledge.In one instance, a woman told the BBC a man had recorded her, and thendemanded moneyto remove the videos from social media. Another womandescribed being recordedduring sexual encounters without her consent. Last month, police in Scotland said they wereinvestigating a far-right TikTokerwho allegedly filmed himself making sexualised comments to young women and telling a Sikh shopkeeper about a plan to “breed out the white race” without their knowledge.Restaurants, theatres and pubs in the UK, including Wetherspoons, have even joined in on the backlash,banning the Meta glassesover privacy fears.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTell us: do you believe you have been filmed by Meta’s smartglasses without your consent?Read moreDeena Lang, a parenting influencer, first got her hands on a pair of the glasses from Meta. “I didn’t really know what they were capable of,” she says, but she thought they could be a cool gadget for her son. This was especially true as the family were heading to Europe for a trip and the glasses could, very usefully, translate foreign text live.But things took a turn when Lang wore them to a cooking class. After looking at the footage she had captured, she says she was “horrified because I just kept catching people giving me dirty looks or side-eye. For me, that was a real awakening.” Sheposted the footageto her 110,000 followers on Instagram with faces blurred out to act as a “cautionary tale”. She was soon flooded with comments criticising the glasses.She says she felt “a lot of embarrassment” for using them in a public place in the first instance but understood where the criticism had come from, especially after looking at how they are used in nefarious ways. “I still think they can be used for good. People who are blind said the glasses had helped them navigate life better but the negatives just far outweigh the positives,” she says. “I heard from some people who were dancers that men were invading their privacy and wearing them into the clubs. Others said they caught their waxers wearing them during appointments.“I don’t believe that we are in an age where technology like this can exist without people with bad intentions making use of it.”As for now, the glasses remain out of sight. “They’re in a drawer,” she says.A Meta spokesperson said: “We designed our AI glasses with privacy and safety features built in from the start – informed by engagement with safety experts, including women’s safety organisations. Our glasses have always had an LED light that activates whenever someone captures a photo or video for their gallery.“They also feature tamper detection technology, and we are updating the glasses to disable the camera if they detect the LED was physically tampered with or destroyed. No other kind of camera has done this and we’re proud to lead the industry forward.”Explore more on these topicsMetaPrivacySurveillanceSocial mediaDigital mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Magic tricks, Palestinian circus, and a ‘kinky Hamlet’: the must-see shows at 2026’s Edinburgh fringe | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: From big-name standups to dance performances and experimental plays, here are our picks for an excellent festival ‘It’s like managing depression – you need to remember basic self-care’: fringe veterans share their wisdom with eager festival newbies Explore the rest of our coverage of the Edinburgh festival 2026
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: From big-name standups to dance performances and experimental plays, here are our picks for an excellent festival ‘It’s like managing depression – you need to remember basic self-care’: fringe veterans share their wisdom with eager festival newbies Explore the rest of our coverage of the Edinburgh festival 2026
Content: Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026Magic tricks, Palestinian circus, and a ‘kinky Hamlet’: the must-see shows at 2026’s Edinburgh fringeFrom big-name standups to dance performances and experimental plays,here are our picks for an excellent festival‘If you’d done that in the 90s, you’d be torn to shreds!’: comedy icons share their survival tips with Edinburgh first-timersExplore the rest of our coverage of the Edinburgh festival 2026Kate WyverSun 9 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKirsty Mann: CorpseTo 30 August,Red lecture theatre atSummerhallKirsty Mann bought a house – and it came with a ghost. Winner of the best theatre award at Adelaide fringe, this real-life one-woman comedy horror is dark, funny and deliciously disturbing.Ayo Adenekan: Homeland InsecurityTo 30 August,Cab Vol 2 atMonkey Barrel ComedyFollowing his sellout debut, Black Mediocrity, the Scottish comic and SNL writer is back with a “romantic hour” of finely observed comedy. Think summer romances, chased dreams and messy endings.View image in fullscreenA maze-ing … Ben Hart.Photograph: Sarah ClinchBen Hart: The LabyrinthTo 30 August,Palais du Variété atAssembly George Square GardensThe ever surprising magic shows of Ben Hart are always a fringe highlight. With skilful sleight of hand, mind reading and card trickery, he’s good enough to win over any fool who thinks they don’t like magic.Campitalism: Three Gays Try to Fix the EconomyTo 31 August,Attic atPleasance CourtyardThree financially illiterate LGBTQ+ people demystify finance in this drag-satire debut from BOY Theatre. There may be no money in the arts, but they’re making art about money. Could be a camp equivalent of The Big Short.Dee Allum: RaumdeuterTo 30 August,Pleasance CourtyardDee Allum tackles the World Cup and the trans experience in this follow-up to her debut show, Deadname. What does it mean to cheer for England when it doesn’t feel like you’re getting anything back?View image in fullscreenFame academy … Demi Adejuyigbe.Photograph: Jonny RuffDemi Adejuyigbe Sells OutTo 30 August,Queen Dome atPleasance DomeLast time he promised audiences one backflip. Now the skilled skit-comedian and writer on The Good Place is ready with his next challenge to complete: becoming famous.Kwami Odoom and Jack Henry: Support GroupTo 31 August,The Penny atGilded Balloon Patter HouseKwami Odoom (fresh from Soho theatre’s Tender) doesn’t know how to be a dad. Jack Henry (multi-award winner and nominee) doesn’t know how to be “gay, sane and sexy at the same time”. Will their hour of standup offer more clarity?View image in fullscreenAussie rules … Lizzy Hoo.Photograph: Giulia McGauranLizzy Hoo: Says Hoo?To 30 August,Studio Four atAssembly George Square StudiosOversharing Australian Lizzy Hoo is at the fringe for the first time, thanks to winning a big Melbourne comedy prize. With her two-drinks-in storytelling, you’ll feel like you’re best buds by the end of the show.Max Olesker: Making the CutTo 30 August,Pleasance DomeThis theatre comedy is adapted from Olesker’s memoir, which is about his realisation that he’s not Jewish enough for the Orthodox woman he’s fallen for – and the rollercoaster that follows. From one half of Max & Ivan, the brains behind Clash of the Comics.SanctuaryTo 31 August,Ace Dome atPleasance DomeTracing the hard-fought effort to open an Aids hospice in 90s Suffolk, this time-twisting debut from the National Theatre’s casting director Jacob Sparrow won the exciting new Leodis prize for playwrighting.View image in fullscreenSão solid crew … Border Bodies.Photograph: Adriano Escanhuela PhotographyBorder BodiesTo 30 August,DB3 atAssembly @ Dance BasePart of the fringe’s São Paulo Showcase, Border Bodies features the Brazilian company TF Cia de Dança, whose show explores ideas of community and togetherness.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe PlotTo 31 August,Main Hall atSummerhallAfter a run of finely tuned fringe hits, writer-director Emma Howlett is back with a tale of radicalised young men and the stories we tell ourselves, as we dive into the foiled gunpowder plot of 1605.View image in fullscreenBard to the bone … HAM.Photograph: Holly RevellHAMTo 30 August,Old Lab atSummerhallFringe favourites Hotter Project lied about their last show being their farewell. We’ll forgive them as they return with this “kinky eco-hijacking” of Hamlet. Expect nudity, messy hijinks and some weird feelings about your next ham sandwich.Edinburgh festival 2026: 10 terrific shows we’ve already reviewedRead moreShedinburghTo 30 August, ShedinburghMaybe it’s cheating to pick an entire lineup – but each show here is one night only. Head to the shed for bold new work from the likes of Sam Nicoresti, Inua Ellams and the Femmes of Colo(u)r Comedy Club.View image in fullscreenThe Palestinian Circus: Step and a Half.Photograph: UnderbellyThe Palestinian Circus: Step and a HalfTo 29 August,The Lafayette atUnderbelly’s Circus Hub on the MeadowsBlending Palestinian folk dance with contemporary circus, this swirling show is a celebration of freedom, heritage and resilience. Presented in partnership with Medical Aid for Palestine.BadgersTo 30 August,Traverse 2 atTraverse theatreMade by the team behind the Bristol Old Vic’s Outlier, Badgers questions our obsession with true crime. Writer-performer Malaika Kegode leads this shape-shifting show about folk tales, podcasts and the art of letting go.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)TheatreComedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalCircusStreet dancefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: OnlyFans for Therapy review – a brave and unsettling emotional exposure | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Veering from confident to crumbling, Verona Verbakel delivers a vivid show mixing humour with trauma
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Veering from confident to crumbling, Verona Verbakel delivers a vivid show mixing humour with trauma
Content: Big in Belgium … Verona Verbakel in OnlyFans for Therapy at Zoo Playground, Edinburgh.Photograph: Kaat Pype/Soraya AzbiriView image in fullscreenBig in Belgium … Verona Verbakel in OnlyFans for Therapy at Zoo Playground, Edinburgh.Photograph: Kaat Pype/Soraya AzbiriEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewOnlyFans for Therapy review – a brave and unsettling emotional exposureZoo Playground, EdinburghVeering from confident to crumbling, Verona Verbakel delivers a vivid show mixing humour with traumaMark FisherSun 9 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe are all familiar with the cliche of the influencer narrating their daily routines – or should I say, their journey? – and trying to convince us, and perhaps themselves, they are living their best life. We know, too, about the websites offering intimate access in exchange for cash.But what if the online medium were put to more honest purposes? What if, instead of endless positivity, it presented a painful recovery from trauma?View image in fullscreenHaunted … Verona Verbakel in OnlyFans for Therapy.Photograph: Soraya AzbiriIt would, suggests writer and performerVerona Verbakel, be cheaper than paying for therapy. After a back-of-the-envelope calculation, she estimates she would need 2,599 sessions with a psychiatrist at £70 a time to get her through a lifetime of recovery. The cost, either in cash or in continued trauma, has to be paid by someone.The exposure in her solo show, OnlyFans for Therapy, is of the emotional not the naked body kind. It concerns a woman haunted by the abuse she suffered as a five-year-old and the additional anguish of an investigation when she was 18. Confident and assured one minute, she crumbles the next – the damage for ever just beneath the surface, raw and inescapable.Part of the Big in Belgium programme, Karolien De Bleser’s production has a characteristically Belgian disregard for theatrical convention. Verbakel’s role is to sit, stony-faced at a laptop, occasionally catching our eye, and seemingly indifferent to the content of the first-person videos she shows in sequence.At turns upbeat and tearful, Verbakel appears in videos that vary from lying in bed wearing a sleep mask and reciting a drily comic list of emotional triggers to the actor making painful expeditions to the scene of the original abuse and breaking down as she does so. The direct-to-camera honesty of the online world makes the pain all the more vivid in a brave, unsettling show.AtZoo Playground, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsIn the UK, theNSPCCoffers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In the US, call or text theChildhelpabuse hotline on 800-422-4453. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact theKids Helplineon 1800 55 1800; adult survivors can seek help atBlue Knot Foundationon 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found atChild Helpline InternationalExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsTheatreInternetreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The secret lives of theatre workers: ‘People were having full sex in the stalls’ | Social etiquette | The Guardian
description: Domestic dramas, bodily fluids, drink, drugs, rudeness and worse … ushers and box office staff have seen it all. So much for the myth of the ‘genteel’ theatregoer
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Domestic dramas, bodily fluids, drink, drugs, rudeness and worse … ushers and box office staff have seen it all. So much for the myth of the ‘genteel’ theatregoer
Content: The show must go on … today, ushers are often called upon to do much more than show customers to their seats.Photograph: Hulton Archive/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe show must go on … today, ushers are often called upon to do much more than show customers to their seats.Photograph: Hulton Archive/Getty ImagesSocial etiquetteThe secret lives of theatre workers: ‘People were having full sex in the stalls’Domestic dramas, bodily fluids, drink, drugs, rudeness and worse … ushers and box office staff have seen it all. So much for the myth of the ‘genteel’ theatregoerGeorgie WyattSun 9 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Theatre still has a sheen of respectability, so people feel they can behave badly because where they are cancels out how dreadful they are being,” says John, who has been a box office manager for 15 years. From my early 20s to my mid-30s, I too worked in the box office, at some of London’s top theatres. During my decade in the job, I witnessed audience behaviour ranging from the odd and the outrageous to the outright belligerent. If you are under any illusion that theatre audiences are classy, allow my former colleagues to disabuse you of that notion.The misuse of phones is one of the most common offences. In April,Cynthia Erivostopped her one-woman West End production ofDracula mid-performance to urge an audience member to stop filming. Former Love Island winnerAmber Davies,starring in a tour of Legally Blonde, last month asked staff to kick out an audience member who was filming the performance from the front row of a Dublin theatre. And in May, Rosamund Pike spotted an audience member texting during the climax of her performance in Inter Alia. After the curtain call,Pike returned to the stage and shamed the behaviour, without singling out the culprit. Part of me hoped that, like a teacher, she would make the individual in question read their texts out to the rest of the theatre.View image in fullscreenBox office staff on duty at His Majesty’s Theatre, Haymarket, London, 1924.Photograph: Topical Press Agency/Getty ImagesFront of house (FoH) theatre staff are all too familiar with such disturbances. It’s “distracting and rude” and “hugely disrespectful to the people who have worked tirelessly to create the show,” says Jackie, 35, from Hertfordshire, who has been an usher since 2021. Naomi, an usher since 2016, says that when she has asked audience members “to stop filming the performance”, she has been called a Nazi or told: “This is worse than the Soviet Union!”Ushers had to be particularly vigilant during one show at the London Coliseum that included acrobatics and aerial stunts. “Audiences don’t realise how distracting phone use is,” says Naomi. Not only did she have to tell them to stop filming, she also had to plead with them not to use the flash, as it can distract performers during their acrobatic tricks. “At the interval, an audience member told me I was acting like a member of the Gestapo.No one is putting them in front of a firing squad. I was just asking them to sit and enjoy the show.”Working as a box office assistant, I soon realised that I needed to know the running time. When a customer speaks to you, it is nearly always to ask about this – they get all dressed up, pay a fortune for tickets, but cannot wait for the show to end. I also learned that the box office is the first port of call for official complaints; it’s unbelievable how often people ask for a refund because they “didn’t like the show”. My technique was to respond with excessive empathy: “Oh no, I’msosorry you didn’t enjoy the show – that’ssucha shame. Poor you!” Without fail, this outpouring of sympathy would throw them, and their complaint lost all momentum. A former colleague, Emma, recalls having to keep a straight face when a customer complained: “There were too many wars in War Horse.”In the box office, there is usually a glass panel between staff and the public. Ushers have no such luck. Laura, 35, who moved to London from the West Midlands and has worked as an usher for more than 15 years, recalls one particularly horrifying experience. During the performance of a high-profile rock musical, an older male audience member handed her “a plastic pint cup filled with warm urine”, smiled, then disappeared back into the crowd without a word.double quotation markIf people have spent their money, whether it's £10 or nearly £200 a ticket, they feel they can do what they wantBodily fluids are an alarmingly common problem. Laura witnessed a disturbing incident during an electronic music concert. “At the back of the stalls, I saw a woman squatting and taking a dump on the floor. By the time the cleaners turned up, it had been spread across the floor and on to unwitting people’s shoes.” Another West End usher, Adi, went to the aid of a customer who, during an expensive West End musical, was vomiting over the balcony on to the people below. He proceeded to vomit all over Adi. Not wanting to disturb the show any further by leaving, Adi stood at the back, picking regurgitated sun-dried tomatoes off himself throughout the second act.Hannah, a veteran box office assistant in London, says ushers regularly had to knock on the doors of the boxes to stop audience members from “the giving and receiving of oral sex during The Wizard of Oz”. Apparently, the actors playing the evil winged monkeys flew in from the rafters and got “an eyeful”.View image in fullscreenTheatregoers show their true colours when an A-lister is off sick.Photograph: Picture Post/Getty ImagesInterrupting sex is a familiar part of the job. Lizzie, who worked as an usher in the West End for more than 10 years, says: “A couple were having full sex in the stalls during a magic show.” The woman was drunkenly straddling the man in his seat. “We didn’t know what to do, so the duty manager, who had just clocked out, had to come back and politely tell them to stop.” At one north London theatre, says Lizzie: “A couple were having sex in the disabled toilet. The usher gave them a five-minute courtesy knock so they wouldn’t miss the show.” They got to their seats just in time for the curtain.John says some theatregoers have a sense of entitlement. “If people have spent their money, whatever the price, £10 to nearly £200 a ticket, they feel they can do whatever they want.” John recalls one woman arriving to collect tickets from the box office and insisting that he give her his half-drunk cup of water because she was thirsty. He persuaded her to try the bar.double quotation markA man lifted his wife’s feet on to his lap, took off her shoes and massaged her bare feet in the middle of the stallsLawrence, who has spent 20 years as a theatre usher, says some audience members act as if they are at home. “People cannot sit for more than 20 minutes without getting up for a loo break or another alcoholic drink.” Bare feet are also a bugbear. “The number of times I’ve seen audience members take off their shoes and socks and put their feet on the chair in front of them is unreal,” says Lawrence. Nadia has seen something similar. “A man lifted his wife’s feet on to his lap, took off her shoes and massaged her bare feet in the middle of the stalls,” she says. Another usher recounted finding toenail clippings in the stalls: “They were too big and yellow to be from fingers!”To ensure everyone enjoys an uninterrupted show, the role of the usher often goes way beyond their job description. One former colleague had to intervene when a couple who had split up after buying tickets to a hit West End show each turned up with a new partner, thinking they were entitled to both tickets. “They arrived just before the curtain went up. It appears it wasn’t an amicable breakup, as it quickly erupted into a full-blown screaming match over who would see the show. It happened four rows from the front of the stage and everyone could see and hear. When they showed no signs of sorting it out themselves, the ushers intervened. They awarded the tickets to the girlfriend because they were in her name.” The rest of the audience were treated to two shows – a five-star West End musical and a full-blown domestic drama.To avoid disruption, FoH are adept at removing disruptive customers discreetly. Jimmy, an usher, spotted a young teenager looking unwell. The lad had used a family trip to a classical music concert to experiment with ketamine. “I could tell he was in a K-hole,” says Jimmy. The ushers came to his aid and swiftly removed him from the auditorium. He begged them not to tell his parents that he had taken ketamine (and they never did).Jimmy came to the rescue again at the same high-end London venue when a Cirque du Soleil production was showing. He had to call an ambulance for a group of teenagers who had got carried away. “Their parents had bought them tickets for VIP areas with free booze. Before the show started, they had to be taken out in wheelchairs to waiting ambulances and have their stomachs pumped.”Then there are those who nap. Hannah recalls one incident. “The show began, and a woman in the front row put her feet on the stage and fell asleep,” she says. “They had to wake the woman up without disturbing Adrian Lester, who was in the middle of a 20-minute opening monologue.”View image in fullscreenNo telling what she might find … an usher deploys her torch, 1954.Photograph: Bert Hardy/Getty ImagesTheatregoers are particularly likely to show their true colours when, God forbid, the A-lister they are expecting goes off sick. An overwhelmed young usher had to deal with angry customers who had arrived to see Hollywood heartthrob Josh Hartnett in a West End production of Rain Man, only to find that he was off sick with gastric flu. “I thought they’d tear the place apart,” she says. “They didn’t just demand refunds; they expected them.” Most theatres now have written into the terms and conditions something along the lines of: “The absence of a specific actor (even a star performer) does not entitle you to a refund or exchange.”But from my experience, you need to be ready to duck for cover the moment you say: “Sir, if you read the T&C’s …”Rudeness to staff ranges from a simple lack of politeness – “The art of ‘hello’ is gone. People come up to me and just yell ‘Toilet?’,” says Lizzie – to the extremely insulting. “I was called a ‘cold-hearted bitch’ for not letting in a latecomer to the Proms,” says Laura.FoH staff are often out-of-work performers and creatives. “FOH are arguably some of the most talented individuals you’ll ever meet, who are grafting hard to make their dreams a reality,” says Lizzie. If that doesn’t make you watch your manners the next time you go to the theatre, you might end up on our “list”. Or, as one theatre calls it, “the wall of wankers”. That’s show business, baby.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
