title: Dining across the divide: ‘She’s got a real downer on Nigel Farage – I think he’s a charismatic guy’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description:
A Labour-voting ex-headteacher and a police officer keen on Reform hit it off, but would they find common ground on immigration or Andy Burnham?

• Want to meet someone from across the divide? Click here to find out how
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: A Labour-voting ex-headteacher and a police officer keen on Reform hit it off, but would they find common ground on immigration or Andy Burnham?• Want to meet someone from across the divide? Click here to find out how
Content: Steph and Stephen. All photographs: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSteph and Stephen. All photographs: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianDining across the divideLife and styleDining across the divide: ‘She’s got a real downer on Nigel Farage – I think he’s a charismatic guy’A Labour-voting ex-headteacher and a police officer keen on Reform hit it off, but would they find common ground on immigration or Andy Burnham?Zoe WilliamsSun 9 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenSteph, 66, ChesterOccupationRetired primary school headteacher. Now does consultancyVoting recordAlways Labour, and is the local women’s officer for her partyAmuse boucheSteph has a bald dog named Archie, and unfortunately he doesn’t like having his head touched. He nearly snapped the Duke of Westminster’s hand offView image in fullscreenSteve, 51, Connah’s QuayOccupationPolice officerVoting recordNormally Conservative; Reform UK last time; would consider Restore Britain in the futureAmuse boucheProbably his best day with the police was when a young woman said, “You’re Jason Statham – you look like Jason Statham.” He logged it, and a colleague added to the log: “The lady was very intoxicated.” He and his mate Sean are starting a Jason Statham podcast, one film at a timeFor startersStephHe’s absolutely lovely. We really hit it off. There’s a lot of depth to his anecdotes, he’s a good storyteller and he listens. The fact that he then comes out with, “I think Rupert Lowe’s wonderful; I would stand as a Restore councillor,” I think is because he’s had his head warped by his time in the police force.SteveMy 15-year-old son said, “I bet you’re gonna get a 7ft guy with a beard, in a dress.” I thought, what if I get a student who’s really loud? Then Steph walked in, and we hit it off straight away.StephWe shared the sea bass.SteveI had garlic pitta, a steak.View image in fullscreenThe big beefStephNigel Farage is a nasty, angry, divisive man. He stands there and says, “I’m not racist, I’m not homophobic, my best friend’s black,” then he throws a grenade and all the neanderthals react. They’re anti-immigrant. Steve couldn’t see that – he was just going for the reasonableness of some of the policies and ignoring the ripple effect that the language has. Why is it bringing out all the racists? Why aren’t we having reasonable conversations about their other policies? Because of Nigel Farage. The leadership needs to change, then I might look at their policies.SteveShe’s got a real downer on Nigel Farage. I think he’s a charismatic guy. I had higher hopes for him two years ago than I’ve got now. Rupert Lowe gives his monthly salary to charity, so I think he’s in it for the right reasons. He says what he thinks – he doesn’t say it to appeal to the widest possible audience. When they had that big falling out, I thought, you’ve got such a small party, the time to fall out is when you’ve got three or four hundred MPs.StephAs for Restore policies, some of them are bonkers; some of them are so weak, you think, fine, do that.SteveSteph’s got high hopes for Andy Burnham. I just think, the man’s lost a leadership election before to Ed Miliband. You lost to that charisma vacuum and now you’re the saviour of the country?View image in fullscreenSharing plateStephI think immigration is fine as it stands. I don’t think we should go to 10 years before you can get indefinite leave to remain. At the moment it’s five years, and I know what a hard slog that is: I’ve seen it up close. We’re encouraging our children to go off and see the world, so the likelihood is that they’ll fall in love with someone from a different country. I think illegal asylum seekers are such a small percentage, it’s been blown out of proportion.SteveEven as somebody who considers themselves rightwing, I think if somebody’s come here and made a positive contribution, let them stay. Obviously, I have no problem with legal immigration – the only thing I did say is that a lot of the time, politicians say we need more immigrants to fill these jobs. But there are one and a half million Brits unemployed. We should have a block on all new asylum claims until we’ve cleared the backlog.View image in fullscreenFor aftersStephHe said he thought we were in agreement over Kemi Badenoch’s impressive leadership. I absolutely don’t want to put my name to that.SteveAfter a shaky start, Kemi Badenoch is coming into her own a little bit now. I can see myself voting Conservative again.View image in fullscreenTakeawaysStephHonestly, he was really nice. We didn’t stop – we chatted the whole time.SteveI think we’ll probably keep in touch, because she was messaging me this morning, going, “What do you think of a wealth tax? What do you think of the royal family?”View image in fullscreenAdditional reporting: Kitty DrakeSteph and Steve ate atMarayin ChesterWant to meet someone from across the divide?Find out how to take partExplore more on these topicsLife and styleDining across the divideSocial trendsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Readers reply: What do you wish you could buy in vending machines? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical concepts
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical concepts
Content: Japan: a vending enthusiast’s dream.Photograph: Jacob Wackerhausen/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJapan: a vending enthusiast’s dream.Photograph: Jacob Wackerhausen/Getty ImagesNotes and queriesLife and styleReaders reply: What do you wish you could buy in vending machines?The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical conceptsRead this week’s new question:How is it physically possible to continue breaking sporting records?Sun 9 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve heard that in Germany you can buy sausages in vending machines. What should be sold in machines that isn’t offered at the moment?Sybil Freestone, OregonSend new questions tonq@theguardian.com.Readers replyReasonably priced train tickets.EddieChorepostCome on – be sensible. I’ll take angel wings, magic beans and pots of gold but reasonably priced train tickets? Madness.RobRoy1975Anyone who has travelled in Japan has encountered the ubiquitousjidōhanbaikivending machines selling cans of hot and cold drinks. The hot coffee is terrible, but I’ve bought some in desperation on train platforms or in stations when the lines at coffee kiosks were too long. And, of course, having a can of Boss Coffee with the kitschy image of the pipe-smoking man (Tom Selleck lookalike?) in your hand is too tempting to pass up.Nancy Cadet, New York, by emailI was quite impressed to see vending machines with bottles of whisky in them in Japan. I suspect they wouldn’t have lasted very long in this part of the world.BruthaHave you seen the anime about the guys reincarnated in a vending machine that sells anything? No, it’s not a joke. I wish.BalckeView image in fullscreenCoffee culture … vending machines in Tokyo.Photograph: Bruce Yuanyue Bi/Getty ImagesMortgages for affordable houses?GirlyouknowitstrueBooks, preferably good secondhand ones. There’s no need for any more instant food gratification – unless the machines are in the middle of nowhere, like the ones supplying baguettes, and occasionally half bottles of champagne, which you sometimes encounter in rural France.Jane Reed, by emailThere’s a wine bar in my town that has a wine vending machine. It’s lovely.Uphillstruggleuk[You] see them all over Spain.JohnH1973The first wine vending machine was made by Hero of Alexandria, in first-century Roman Egypt.TarlachmoorhouseA new boyfriend! A divorce.SpinnyAn EU passport.WindydayWhen I was a child, the ladies’ loos in our poshest local department store, Schofields in Leeds, had a vending machine that dispensed a squirt of perfume if you put in sixpence (I think) and pressed a button. There was a choice of four or five. I can’t remember them all but my mother liked Yardley’s flower fragrances such as Freesia, while my grandmother favoured Lenthéric’s Tweed. I’ve never seen this anywhere else.MistyPI think there should be cat vending machines. There is a glut of unwanted cats. Maybe another vending machine with plumbers …David Neville, by emailI would like small packets with a single nappy, two wet wipes, one soapy hand wipe and a nappy disposal bag – biodegradable if possible. To be deployed in baby changes in museums, rail stations, airports and all good coffee shops everywhere. Parenting is hard.2opinionatedCigarette vending machines were everywhere when I was a lad. Most notably on the platforms of the London Underground.BristolBoyThat brings back memories. Also, those machines on the platform that sold odd-sized chocolate bars – they were more square than the rectangular shop-bought ones.reggiepurrinSeen plenty selling cheese and wine in France and Germany – even seafood. On a recent trip, we found one on Germany’s Baltic coast selling eggs and vodka – ideal for breakfast!David Bridle, Brightlingsea, Essex, by emailMore than 40 years ago, in Strasbourg I think, we bought merguez in lengths of baguette from a machine. It was about the only thing available on a Sunday afternoon. More recently, we bought baguettes in a small village on the boulanger’s day off. I have also bought chips in Amsterdam – not bad.Janet Carne, by emailView image in fullscreenFresh juice and fruit in an automatic vending machine in the Netherlands.Photograph: barmalini/Getty Images/iStockphotoVat-grown babies. To save the effort of conceiving, bearing and delivering them. Failing that, kittens.haztomRaising them too – option B3 for a 10-year-old, D7 for a 20-year-old.RobRoy1975Fruit salad, freshly made on demand. And if they can do that, a poached egg on toast while they are at it.daleawayA long time ago I had a holiday job in the kitchen of a factory, and we did prepare poached eggs for the vending machine the men used after we’d gone home. No toast, however.EastWestCatsAreBestOne of the places where I used to work had a snack vending machine that was topped up every month. If there were any out-of-date or close-to-date items they were given away to us for nothing – and there were usually loads of chocolate bars and crisps to be had that day, so people would stock up. Then it wouldn’t be used for a while and the cycle would repeat itself until the company decided it wasn’t viable and took it away. It was my favourite vending machine.Starling7[The supply of] Narcan, drug testing strips and safe usage supplies in vending machines was covered in the Guardianhere.Kalluna34Psychology and self-help books. They are in high demand at our library, but are also notoriously not checked out properly or not brought back.NerdvanianHelp-yourself books, then?jno50Vending machines in toilets could sell incontinence pads.ArthurDalesWorld peace. And cash. You could have a machine that works as an automated teller.SavoryCharacterAren’t cash machines a kind of vending machine?Starling7Some are. They sell you the right to access your own money for a hefty fee. Looking at you, Paddington station.EastWestCatsAreBestI think a pizza could be selected, dropped through a slot into an oven and cooked before being posted out to the consumer.misruleI’ve just come back from France where there are lots of these machines. You can choose hot or cold (to heat at home). Not the best pizza but a welcome meal when there are no other eating options nearby.C0lumb1daeA DIY “rejuvenation tank kit” that cancels out all ravages of time, illness and climate crisis stress. And not at a cost that only billionaires can afford!GalliantUp a mountain in Valais in Switzerland a few years ago, there was a little deli full of fresh wonders – plus a vending machine outside that served up all the ingredients for raclette: bag of spuds, raclette cheese, wine, etc. It was so delightful that I just stared and smiled. My Swiss friend thought I was cracked.maryyBut how were you supposed to cook it, unless you’d lugged your portable raclette grill up the mountain on the off-chance?haztomView image in fullscreenMaking the big choices … a vending machine in Madrid.Photograph: Jose Gonzalez Buenaposada/Getty ImagesMy local pool has a vending machine for swimsuits. And you can get extremely good cheese from a vending machine at Besançon station [in eastern France].EastWestCatsAreBestCancoillotte?TomboNo, just comté and morbier, but very good quality.EastWestCatsAreBestI’ve seen cheese and sausage vending machines throughout Switzerland, in or near hiking trails. Local goods, emphasis on the word “good”.EgoOnePacers, Marathons, and those green ET: the Extra-Terrestrial custard creams I used to get from Bromley’s Walnuts Centre vending machine after swimming.joshthedogThe perfect vending machine would be a “Santa Claus machine”, potentially a form of “molecular assembler”. Essentially, it’s a sci-fi type idea where a machine, given raw materials at molecular level and instructions, can produce any physical object you could imagine. The closest to something like this existing is probably a ribosome: the small components of every biological cell that use mRNA strands as the instructions. They assemble any proteins the cell needs from amino acids. If that’s not mind-blowing enough, the molecular-assembler-type vending machines would, in turn, be able to assemble molecular-assembler-type vending machines.leadballoonMore gluten-free snack options.StellaASPlasters. We have vending with condoms, lube, etc (mostly in bus stations – don’t ask me why), so there is space to spare to include plasters for little cuts, blisters, etc.BalckeWe’ve now got little shops here in south-west France that are like vending machines, but you go inside them. It’s like a tiny corner shop. You sign up, then scan your phone at the door, which lets you in. You do your shopping, swipe the items and pay by card, then scan again to open the door and exit.GoldgreenSame in rural Austria and Germany.HoofitoffAnything sold in a refill shop could be adapted for sale by vending machine, as long as you bring your own container. Last year, in Bath, I saw a vending machine for milk. Excellent initiative.IreneLavingtonA talent for music or art – or preferably both. If that’s not possible, then peace of mind. If none of the above are possible, then Smith’s Bovril crisps.AD2023Instructions on how to put your disappointing purchase back into the machine.IcommentthereforeIamAs someone on chemotherapy who is prone to accidents, new underwear would be nice.IlikeicecreamThat would also be useful to all those who menstruate. Dark knickers, cotton, plain, in sizes XS to 2XL, please.redstar1000A genuinely great suggestion. With a little baggy for the other pair.LadyzakisHardback academic textbooks that hit the bottom of the cabinet with an alarming thunk. Why? Well, in a world in which it’s possible to buy sausages (Germany), fresh eggs (Japan) and sex toys (Spain) from a vending machine, I see no reason to not cater to every possible niche. Oh, and prime ministers. Or are we pretty much there already?DorkaliciousAwww! Give Andy a break.AdnilsetabMini pieces of art and secondhand books. Posh snacks.Pawscrosssed53Second hand books are free at “book-stops”, and bus or train stations, and “phone box libraries” all over the place.confused23View image in fullscreenA light in the darkness.Photograph: MarioGuti/Getty ImagesI’m not saying that sausage vending machines don’t exist, but I’ve never seen one.PhineasPPhagbrakeThere’s one in Bangor.VanillaRadioAnd in Lincolnshire.GirlyouknowitstrueI like the idea of a vending machine that allows you to donate to a charity. There would be a broad selection; everything from mental health to foreign aid. You could pay a tenner and, in return, the charity gets a sizeable proportion of the cash and you get a booklet explaining what they do and how the charity uses the donated funds.You could read the booklet on your commute and recycle it when you arrive. No strings, quick and meaningful, and with the choices in front of you everyone gets a fair shout, although the charities at eye level may do better. It’s a spontaneous purchase that could make you feel you were making a real difference.deepbluepete66Kindness, hugs and love to our planet. Ooooh, and seeds for bees.Pawscrosssed53Parking tickets. There are far too many car parks now in which you can’t park if you don’t own a smartphone.SpoilheapSurferGenius idea! You could get a ticket as you enter, and before you leave, return it to the machine to let you pay the charge. It would then give it back and you return it again to get through the exit! So simple.confused23A family member has set up an egg vending machine. There’s no pun coming up, I promise. It operates brilliantly.VanillaRadioEggxcellent idea.DorkaliciousI’ve often thought, while waiting for ages to be served in a crowded and understaffed pub, that machines selling the usual alcoholic drinks might be useful.PeteTheBeatI used to frequent a bar in Austria that had a draught beer-dispensing machine – you tapped your credit card and it dispensed a half litre of beer. The ultimate beer on tap.HoofitoffI grew up in northern Europe, where every bakery had a vending machine outside, into which went a selection of the unsold bread and pastries at the end of each day.HoofitoffThey would be useful, as everything seems to be closed in rural Germany and Austria on a Sunday – especially in the mornings, when it’s hard to even find a cafe open.PeteTheBeatAt an airport I was recently at, they had a vending machine full of different versions of Top Trumps.LhurgoyfI’ve always fancied running a vending machine business, so … vending machines?saltybaconThat’s quite fractal!greendreamerExplore more on these topicsLife and styleNotes and queriesRetail industryFood & drink industryRobotsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Subscriptions you can’t easily cancel, sales that aren’t sales – I’ll end the rip-offs that British people hate | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: These everyday hassles are small, but they add up – especially in a cost of living crisis. That’s why my government will tackle them head-on, says UK prime minister Andy Burnham
Author: Andy Burnham
Headline: These everyday hassles are small, but they add up – especially in a cost of living crisis. That’s why my government will tackle them head-on, says UK prime minister Andy Burnham
Content: ‘Each everyday fix will be designed to put a bit more money back into people’s pockets.’Photograph: mihailomilovanovic/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Each everyday fix will be designed to put a bit more money back into people’s pockets.’Photograph: mihailomilovanovic/Getty ImagesOpinionLabourSubscriptions you can’t easily cancel, sales that aren’t sales – I’ll end the rip-offs that British people hateAndy BurnhamThese everyday hassles are small, but they add up – especially in a cost of living crisis. That’s why my government will tackle them head-onAndy Burnham is the UK prime ministerBurnham vows crackdown on ‘rip-off’ business practicesSun 9 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareIt’s remarkable how much of modern life can seem designed to wear us down. Every “sale” seems to come with an asterisk. Consumer contracts often find a way of costing more than you expected. And too many companies want you to sign up in seconds, but then make it feel impossible to leave. It’s exhausting.They might not be the issues that keep you up at night. But they’re often the reason you go to bed ticked off. Westminster has got used to telling people that these everyday hassles are just part of life. The response has too often been a shrug of the shoulders or just calling it bad luck.I don’t think that’s right. Because these everyday hassles affect millions of people. And they add up. Every single one is an unnecessary cost. And when the cost of living continues to weigh heavily on so many people’s lives, we need to be pulling every single lever we can to help ease that.But they add up in another way too. Every single unexpected payment, rip off or hidden catch chips away at hope. That might sound dramatic – but it’s true. Every single one is another message that this country is built to catch people out rather than help them get on.I want people to start believing in Britain again. But we’ll only get there by building a country that feels fair. And that means getting a grip on those issues that get people’s backs up day in, day out. So we are going to do things differently. We are going to get on with the everyday fixes that make life easier and more affordable. As far as I’m concerned, whatever the size, big or small, if it’s a problem for you, it’s a problem for us.That’s why I’ve made it clear from day one that creating room to breathe is my number one priority, and the whole of this government is united on that. We won’t be able to solve every frustration overnight. But where the government can save people money, remove an unnecessary obstacle or simply make something work better, we should – and we will.We are kicking off with a couple of first steps on those everyday hassles that people tell me about time and time again.First, we are putting an end to phoney bargains. We are taking on poor practices that make people’s lives harder. If something is advertised as half price, it should actually be half price. We will make sure that when families snatch a deal, they can be confident they’re actually saving. That’s the least they deserve when budgets are so tight.Second, we are making it as easy to leave a subscription as it is to join, and businesses won’t be able to renew a subscription without notifying you. New rules will come into force in January 2027, in time for when people often start new subscriptions, or cancel the ones they have, for the year ahead.There are about 155m active subscriptions in the UK, with consumers spending an estimated £1.6bn a year on ones they don’t actually want – a direct hit to family budgets. The changes we are introducing will save an average of £14 a month for every unwanted subscription.These are just a couple of our everyday fixes. There will be more to come over the next few months and bigger plans to make life easier and fairer for people over the longer term.Each everyday fix will be designed to put a bit more money back into people’s pockets, to make daily life a little fairer and to give people a bit more hope that politics really can work for them again.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI will also be asking people what action they want to see on the cost of living. Because if we want to find the problems that make everyday life harder, we need to listen to the people dealing with them.So over the summer, I will begetting out to regions across countryto hear directly from people about the challenges they face and the changes they want to see.Westminster has spent too long asking people to wait for life to get better. This government is determined to make it better and to bring back hope. My message to people is simple: this will be a cost-of-living government and we will be on your side to prevent you being overcharged, trapped or misled.Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United KingdomExplore more on these topicsLabourOpinionConsumer rightsUK cost of living crisisFamily financescommentShareReuse this content

title: Britain is paying the price for failing to invest in its young people | Richard Partington | The Guardian
description: Alan Milburn has outlined a generation cut adrift by austerity. We must grasp the nettle and rebuild a preventive state
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: Alan Milburn has outlined a generation cut adrift by austerity. We must grasp the nettle and rebuild a preventive state
Content: ‘Rather than investing in public services early to stop problems from developing, the state is in firefighting mode.’Photograph: lovethephoto/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Rather than investing in public services early to stop problems from developing, the state is in firefighting mode.’Photograph: lovethephoto/AlamyEconomics viewpointYouth unemploymentBritain is paying the price for failing to invest in its young peopleRichard PartingtonAlan Milburn has outlined a generation cut adrift by austerity. We must grasp the nettle and rebuild a preventive stateSun 9 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareMost people think Britain is not working as it should. For young people, the situation is at its most acute: onlyone in four believe that everyone in society has a fair crack. Most think the game is rigged.It is clear why the generation who grew up during the post-2008 crash austerity years and in the shadow of the Covid pandemic are downbeat: the level of public service provision their parents enjoyed is gone, living costs are rising, the AI revolution is changing everything, and the planet is on fire.That is why Alan Milburn’s review intoyouth unemploymentis vital. Britain missing out on the talents of 1 million young peoplenot in education, employment or training(Neet) is a problem that extends well beyond the jobs market. It is about how the building blocks of a just and prosperous economy have been whittled away, and is a call to action to put things right.As with so many of the country’s problems right now, some of the big drivers of youth inactivity stem from the austerity years. That is not to say that other contributing factors – not least Labour’s management of the economy, AI upending youth jobs, and the cost of living crisis – are not playing a role. But there is mounting evidence that the consequences of the Tory spending cuts are maturing with disastrous consequences.Milburn says the risk of a child becoming Neet can be traced to their earliest years in preschool. To look back, therefore, at the past 16 years of change in education policy, youth services and the public sector more broadly – the lifespan of the generation just entering the workforce – is instructive.Primary schools to be told to identify children at risk of future unemploymentRead moreAcross the board, funding has been cut. Within youth services in England,spending is down by 76%, a loss of £1.3bn. Thousands of youth clubs have been closed and social workers lost. Meanwhile the per-pupil level of spending for schools in England wasfrozen for 14 years. Investment in school buildings, many of which have been affected by theRaac – or crumbling concrete – crisis, also collapsed by a quarter.The tragedy is that, rather than spending on the prevention of bad societal outcomes, Britain has instead ended up allocating vast sums to the consequences of the failure.The situation is stark in the Neet crisis. For every £1 the state spends on employment support for young people, it shells out £25 on benefits. With the rise in inactivity for a generation cut adrift, the cost is only set to climb without intervention.Sure Startis another cautionary tale. The Conservatives effectively scrapping the network of family hubs opened by Labour was supposed to save money. But research shows that as the funding dried up, spending on looked-after children and safeguarding rose by more than half. The cost of helping disadvantaged families did not vanish; the support simply shifted from prevention to crisis management.It is a pattern repeated across government. Rather than investing in public services early to stop problems from developing, the state is in firefighting mode. For Andy Burnham, the task will be to end this shortsighted approach by rebuilding what the thinktank Demos calls apreventive state– a model involving investment to support the foundations of society.The size of the economic, fiscal and social prize would be substantial.The NHS provides a clear example. As much as 40% of the NHS budget goes towards treating preventable conditions. Preventable illness accounts for half of GP appointments and 70% of inpatient hospital bed days. After years of underinvestment the service is also highly inefficient.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat can Dublin teach us? Milburn goes on a quest to solve youth jobs crisisRead moreRecent research by theHealth Foundation, however, shows that restoring the deteriorating health of the UK’s population to the level of 2014 would boost GDP by 2% and generate a £72bn dividend for the public finances.In similar analysis, theOffice for Budget Responsibilityhas said the spiralling health budget could be kept in check by investing in prevention. In a “better health” scenario, the Treasury watchdog estimates the national debt would be about 45% of GDP lower by the 2070s as a result.The challenge for ministers is that the costs to the economy and to government finances of the Neet crisis is £125bn a year and rising. Getting more young people into work would, though, revitalise the life chances of millions and drive up labour participation – boosting the economy and public finances.Ahead of the autumn budget, there is a compelling argument for Burnham’s government to take action. However, building a preventive state will come with challenges for a prime minister hemmed in by the UK’s current tight fiscal predicament, and who is in a hurry to show progress.Moving money upstream is difficult because the savings from preventive spending take time to materialise, and spending on acute need and welfare cannot be simply turned off. Nowhere is this clearer than in early-years services, where reforms can take a lifetime to show up in the numbers.That timing problem is why the Treasury has often been sceptical. The costs appear immediately, while the savings arrive years later – often benefiting a different government. The incentives favour firefighting over fixing.However, refusing to make the transition is a bad choice. Britain is already paying the price of a crumbling NHS, rising welfare bill, jobs market inactivity, and consequent weak economic growth.Milburn’s review is therefore a critical test of whether Britain will grasp the nettle to rebuild a preventive state from the ashes of the austerity years. The alternative is to settle for a country hamstrung by the costs of failure, where young people feel lost.Explore more on these topicsYouth unemploymentEconomics viewpointEconomic policyUnemploymentYoung peopleInequalityUK cost of living crisisAusteritycommentShareReuse this content

title: The hill I will die on: Remove those earphones – you’re blocking out the music of humanity | Stefan Stern | The Guardian
description: Beyond the white noise lies a vibrant world of possibility, so take your headphones off and listen to your surroundings. It may even save your life, says author Stefan Stern
Author: Stefan Stern
Headline: Beyond the white noise lies a vibrant world of possibility, so take your headphones off and listen to your surroundings. It may even save your life, says author Stefan Stern
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onTechnologyThe hill I will die on: Remove those earphones – you’re blocking out the music of humanityStefan SternBeyond the white noise lies a vibrant world of possibility, so take your headphones off and listen to your surroundings. It may even save your lifeSun 9 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 13.31 EDTShareEr, excuse me. Hello? I’m sorry, but would you mind taking your … I SAID, WOULD YOU MIND TAKING THOSE EARPHONES OUT FOR A SECOND, PLEASE?I try, in the main, to be a live-and-let-live kind of person. Patient. Considerate. But this patience is being tested to breaking point by the proliferation, the epidemic, of almost-ubiquitous earphones.The world must be shut out, apparently. The wearer has nothing to learn or gain by listening to anybody else in their vicinity. They would rather be elsewhere, plunged into music or a novel or maybe a noisy pavement phone call, which will remain, sadly for the accidental eavesdropper, a slightly odd one-way exchange only.The hill I will die on is that there is a fascinating and beautiful world out there, filled with conversation and laughter and the possibility of making new friends and acquaintances. But instead of taking part in all that, people prefer to plug in their earphones, tune in and drop out.*This phenomenon seems to be 21st-century proof of Pascal’s belief that the “inability to sit quietly in a room alone” is the source of all our problems. There must be constant, piped-in noise. Silence is the enemy.The hill I will die on: I really don’t like ‘like’ – or other imprecise and redundant speech | Louis de BernièresRead morePerhaps this is another consequence of Covid lockdowns. We got used to being on our own, working at home, earphones in, to save flatmates or family members from the distraction of other conversations. Back in the workplace, the earphones have stayed in. Maybe this can help with concentration, a protest against the enforced intimacy of the open-plan office. But it makes life harder for colleagues who may want to ask a quick question, or for a benign boss – other types of boss are available – to show some interest in you, when they are “managing by walking around”.Imagine if, two centuries earlier, Wordsworth had wandered lonely with his AirPods in. Would he have ever heard the “still, sad music of humanity, / Not harsh nor grating, though of ample power / To chasten and subdue”?OK, maybe it is polite on the bus or the train to stick the earphones in and avoid creating noise pollution. People who are neurodivergent may want to block some things out. But personally, I usually enjoy listening to the conversations you can hear, in a range of languages, on public transport. I knowthat Nigel Farage objects to that sort of thing, but the rest of us don’t have to.I say: take the earphones out, lend me (and everyone else) your ears and enjoy the world around you. Choose real life. At the very least, staying alert could save you from getting run over, or mugged.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd, you know, if there weren’t so many of these earphones permanently on display, then maybe people would stop launching so manypodcasts.* I make an exception forthe new audio version of my latest book, you’re allowed to listen to that.Stefan Stern is co-author of Myths of Management and the former director of the High Pay Centre. His latest book is Fair or Foul: The Lady Macbeth Guide to AmbitionExplore more on these topicsTechnologyThe hill I will die onWork & careerscommentShareReuse this content

title: Is your ill fate bad luck or a curse? You could ask Ted Lasso, but why not consider the psychology  | Helen Pilcher | The Guardian
description: From Mayo to Birmingham City, sports lore is rife with powerful hexes. There’s nothing mystical about the dread and self-doubt they can induce, says science writer Helen Pilcher
Author: Helen Pilcher
Headline: From Mayo to Birmingham City, sports lore is rife with powerful hexes. There’s nothing mystical about the dread and self-doubt they can induce, says science writer Helen Pilcher
Content: Mayo celebrate winning the 2026 All-Ireland Gaelic football title after 75 years – and 11 finals losses.Photograph: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMayo celebrate winning the 2026 All-Ireland Gaelic football title after 75 years – and 11 finals losses.Photograph: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesOpinionPsychologyIs your ill fate bad luck or a curse? You could ask Ted Lasso, but why not consider the psychologyHelen PilcherThe hit TV show confirms that sports lore is rife with powerful hexes. But there’s really nothing mystical about the dread and self-doubt they can induceSun 9 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 05.06 EDTShareAs the new season of Ted Lasso started, I was reminded of one of the show’s stranger storylines. When Dani “Football is life!” Rojas gets injured, his teammates blame the incident on a curse said to haunt the treatment room.Absurd? Perhaps. But sports curses aren’t just fictional plot devices. Football is fertile ground for stories of mysterious forces, blamed for everything frommissed penalties to decades of failure.Take Mayo’s Gaelic football team. After they won the All-Ireland title in 1951, the story goes that a local priest cursed them, declaring they would not win another final until every member of that team had died. Over the next 75 years, Mayo reached 11 more finals – and lost them all. Paddy Prendergast, the last surviving member of the 1951 squad, died in 2021. Then Mayo made it to the final again last month and won. This prompted the Canadian prime minister Mark Carney, who has family ties to Mayo, to announce on X: “The curse is broken.”Birmingham City – a team close to my heart – has its own curse story. The club is said to have endured decades of disappointment after a100-year hexwas placed on its home ground in 1906. And this year, Harry Kane missed a close-range chance in England’s Fifa World Cup match against Ghana, shortly after a “witch-doctor” claimed to havecast a spell on him. Coincidence?There are, of course, many possible explanations. Maybe supernatural forces really were at work. Maybe the teams had bad luck, made tactical errors or were simply beaten by better opponents. Or maybe, once the curse became part of the team’s folklore, it acquired a life of its own. In this scenario, it doesn’t matter whether the “spells” were ever cast, or whether players personally believed in them. What matters is that the idea gained a cultural foothold. Retold by fans, journalists and commentators, the stories shaped expectations about what might happen next. And expectations can have very real effects.Psychology has a name for the power of negative expectations: the nocebo effect. The phenomenon is best known in medicine. A person takes aplacebopill but is warned it may cause side-effects. Often, they experience them anyway.The symptoms are real, even though the tablet isn’t causing them. The same principle can play out in sport. Philip Hurst and colleagues at Canterbury Christ Church University have shown that when runners are given an inert supplement but told it will negatively affect their sprint performance,they run slower. Give them the same supplement but tell them it will improve their performance, it has little effect. This hints that in sport, negative expectations may have more of an impact than positive ones.View image in fullscreenTed Lasso tries to lift his team’s curse with a late-night cleansing ritual.Photograph: YouTubeNow, imagine a football player walking on to the pitch. The trigger hardly matters. A “curse”, a run of defeats or a teammate’s throwaway comment can all plant a seed of doubt. After that, every misplaced pass, heavy touch or missed chance can seem like proof that something is off. Confidence falters. A game that once felt instinctive becomes something to overthink, until doubt itself starts to undermine performance.What begins in one player’s mind can also become a team-wide narrative. Players absorb cues from team members, supporters, critics and the media, quietly internalising the atmosphere that surrounds a team. Psychologists call this social contagion: the spread of emotions, behaviours and beliefs through groups. Over time, these shared beliefs can become part of a team’s identity, shaping how it responds under pressure. The result is a feedback loop: the story shapes expectations, expectations shape behaviour, and behaviour can appear to confirm the original story. The question is: how do you break the cycle?Perhaps we can learn a thing or two from Ted Lasso and the real-life managers who faced similar scenarios. Lasso’s solution was a late-night cleansing ritual, with players throwing treasured possessions into a container which he set alight. Meanwhile Birmingham City’s Barry Fry tried a more “fluid” approach, by urinating on the pitch’s four corners.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhether these rituals had any mystical power is beside the point. Their value was psychological. They created a reset – a chance for the team to draw a line under the past and start expecting a brighter future. For Mayo, that reset has finally arrived. The next generation of players and supporters will inherit a different memory – not of the final they could never win, but of the one they finally did. As former Mayo player Colm Boyle put it after their victory: “The shackles are off.” The curse may only have been a story, but now Mayo can tell a different one.Helen Pilcher is a science writer and author of Life Changing: How Humans Are Altering Life on Earth and This Book May Cause Side EffectsExplore more on these topicsPsychologyOpinionTV comedyIrelandcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Democratic party needs to do more than represent wealthy progressives | Dustin Guastella | The Guardian
description: New research shows that a class gap on the left threatens any winning coalition – but there are ways to address it
Author: Dustin Guastella
Headline: New research shows that a class gap on the left threatens any winning coalition – but there are ways to address it
Content: ‘Maybe professional-class progressives could learn a thing or two from their working-class counterparts.’Photograph: Justin Lane/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Maybe professional-class progressives could learn a thing or two from their working-class counterparts.’Photograph: Justin Lane/EPAOpinionDemocratsThe Democratic party needs to do more than represent wealthy progressivesDustin GuastellaNew research shows that a class gap on the left threatens any winning coalition – but there are ways to address itSun 9 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 14.59 EDTShareDebates on the left are typically framed as a division between moderates and progressives, with the two sides wrestling over how best to form a governing coalition. Yet, in many ways, this divide obscures a much bigger fault line: the class divide. The fact is, many of the Democratic party’s ideological factions consist almost exclusively of college-educated professionals. As a result, the priorities of this class tend to dominate the party’s appeals. The priorities of working-class voters, meanwhile, are an afterthought.A new report from Jared Abbott, the director of the Center for Working Class Politics, and Joan Williams, author of Outclassed: How the Left Lost the Working Class and How to Win Them Back, looks at ways to bridge the yawning class divide that threatens the possibility of forming a winning coalition.They developed an original survey to explore the various attitude “gaps” between the broad working class (defined as non-college educated, middle income workers) and the liberal upper middle class (Democratic-leaning college graduates with a household income in the top 25%).Democrats need to rethink their image of a ‘man of the people’ | Judith LevineRead moreThe resulting report, titledThe Left’s Coalition Crisis: Understanding the Massive Divide Between Working Class and College Educated Voters, and How to Bridge it, is, according to the authors, “the most comprehensive review available to date” of class-based political attitudes across a number of issue areas.The first thing to note about the gaps between the educated upper middle class and the working class is that the latter overwhelmingly prioritize economic issues, while the former lean toward cultural ones.Of the top 12 political priorities listed by working-class respondents, 11 are economic concerns. The only non-economic issue prized by the working class was a desire to lower the crime rate. Meanwhile, educated upper-income respondents rated cultural and symbolic issues over economic concerns. Of their top 12 priorities, only six were economic. They also rate abstract ideals over concrete, material ones. Educated voters prioritized “resisting authoritarianism” above “protecting social security” and “ending racism” above “protecting Medicaid”.On an issue by issue basis, the largest gaps that Abbott and Williams found were along culture, climate, crime and immigration issues. That is, the very issues many college-educated liberals have built their political identities around. Maybe that wouldn’t be such a problem if these issues were largely downplayed by Democratic party leaders, in favor of shared economic grievances. But that’s hardly the case.Not only do the cultural priorities of the privileged fail to speak to working-class voters’ economic frustrations, but, because Democratic party primaries are dominated by educated upper-income voters, these appeals have come to define liberalism itself.No doubt, the surest way to get a huge cheer at a liberal political rally is to simply mention racism or authoritarianism. Bonus points if you bravely proclaim your unwillingness to “throw X group under the bus”. Such rhetorical gestures have the added benefit of committing candidates to nothing in particular, and thus never threaten potential rich donors.You might say, so what? Who cares if candidates say some throwaway lines about the “marginalized” at a campaign rally; what’s the harm?As Abbott and Williams demonstrate, signaling allegiance to such political priorities is far from costless. Embracing the values and slogans of the privileged tells working-class voters that you are either aloof to, or ignorant of, their priorities.And worse, that you don’t respect working people as political actors. As the authors note, college graduates in Europe and the United States “are more biased against the less-educated than any other stigmatized group”, including racial, religious, and sexual minorities. Blue-collar workers can sense liberal condescension in smarmy injunctions to “be kind”, and they resent what they perceive as upper-class attempts to morally re-educate them.It gets worse. Even if upper-income progressives steer clear of cultural condescension, their economic priorities are also class-bound. While working-class voters prioritize jobs, wages and economic growth, the educated knowledge workers are mainly concerned with high costs. This, too, is a function of the latter’s relatively privileged class position.Democrats are counting on Trump’s unpopularity to save them. It won’t | Osita NwanevuRead moreDespite recent wage erosion, the college-educated set still make much more than their non-college educated counterparts – between 60% and 80%moreon average. This wage premium, combined with our K-shaped economy, means that the well-educated and well-heeled, those in the top 20% of the income hierarchy, nowdrivenearly 60% of all consumer spending.For many educated, upper-income voters – especially those in corporate careers – the defining feature of their economic lives is consuming, not producing. As such, they are extremely sensitive to price increases.Working-class voters are too, but for very different reasons. It’s the devaluing of work that drives their frustrations. As the authors point out, for the working class, and especially for blue-collar workers, it’s work, not consumption, that defines their lives.But long-term wage stagnation, and the disappearance of good stable jobs, has meant that essential goods have become even more difficult to afford. Here, globalization plays a major role. And, on that issue, the data show yet another chasm between the popular classes.While some liberal appeals to “affordability” emphasize the need to scrap tariffs and embrace more liberal immigration rules in order to broaden consumer demand (and lower the agricultural wage-bill), working-class voters are rightly skeptical of these solutions.Restrictions on trade and immigration represent efforts to address the long neglected problems of wage stagnation. Free-trade has devastated the working class, shuttering thousands of factories and sinking many into drug-addiction and despair. At the same time, mass migration has eroded the wage packet for manual workers. For them, addressing affordability must mean policies that speak to the essentially place-bound character of blue-collar life.While professional-class status is portable – effectively equivalent in London, New York, Paris or Washington DC – working-class status is not so liquid. Seniority in a job or trade is not typically a transferrable credential. For these reasons place-loyalty matters a great deal to working-class people.On the other hand, globalization and the growth of “knowledge work” has supercharged select high-income metro areas, where many professionals live and where progressives thrive. Democrats nowrepresentnine of the top 10 highest-income congressional districts in the country.The truth is, educated upper-income voters, be they progressive or moderate, largely benefit from low-wage immigrant labor and cheap foreign goods. Contrary to the place-based loyalty of blue collar workers, they prize their status as global-citizens and cosmopolitan consumers.Navigating these tensions isn’t easy, but Abbott and Williams did find a number of issues that could serve as a foundation for a progressive program of popular-class unity.Getting it right means addressing both the wage and the price side of the affordability equation, downgrading the cultural priorities of the privileged (including on abortion and transgender issues), and grappling with the tension between globalist affinities and local loyalty.By focusing only on those issues that win more than two-thirds of support from both working-class and educated upper-middle-class respondents, they propose a political program with the following planks: allow Medicare to negotiate lower prescription drug prices, protect and improve social security, spend $150bn on infrastructure, expand Medicaid, ratchet up education spending, and raise the minimum wage.The Democrats have one last chance to halt the erosion of US democracy – and it’s less than 100 days away | Timothy Garton AshRead moreThat’s a great start. But it could be improved by an even greater emphasis on working-class priorities. We need new trade rules, revitalized national industry and real pro-labor immigration reform that can help right the wrongs of globalism.We ought to advocate expansive and generous policies that emphasize the importance of family life. Why not make giving birthentirely free, implement national paid-parental leave, and provide affordable childcare?And finally, we need to make expanding and improving badly underfunded local police and fire departments a national priority in order to make every neighborhood and community safe. Such priorities speak directly to felt needs and they signal a genuine political attempt at reorganizing politics around working-class demands, rather than the preferences of the professionals.Putting working-class priorities first will no doubt result in political tensions. Flashpoints around gender, immigration and even class itself, will break out. Getting through those fights will be necessary if progressives ever hope to expand their coalition by reaching into the working class.Plus, who knows, maybe professional-class progressives could learn a thing or two from their working-class counterparts.Dustin Guastella is a research associate at the Center for Working Class Politics and the director of operations for Teamsters Local 623. He is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsDemocratsOpinionUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Super Furry Animals’ foray into football is not part of Big Music’s money grab | Soccer | The Guardian
description: The sponsorship deal between Cwmbran Celtic and the Welsh indie-rockers is a nostalgia trip rather than a cynical attempt to monetise ‘adjacent audiences’
Author: Emma John
Headline: The sponsorship deal between Cwmbran Celtic and the Welsh indie-rockers is a nostalgia trip rather than a cynical attempt to monetise ‘adjacent audiences’
Content: ‘In the last couple of years, the relationship between bands and football teams has turned serious.’Illustration: David Lyttleton/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘In the last couple of years, the relationship between bands and football teams has turned serious.’Illustration: David Lyttleton/The GuardianSoccerSuper Furry Animals’ foray into football is not part of Big Music’s money grabEmma JohnThe sponsorship deal between Cwmbran Celtic and the Welsh indie-rockers is a nostalgia trip rather than a cynical attempt to monetise ‘adjacent audiences’Sun 9 Aug 2026 06.53 EDTFirst published on Sat 8 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTShareAs someone born on the cusp of the gen X-millennial divide, I am the perfect target for today’s 90s nostalgia. I played my modest, teenage part in the Battle of Britpop (verbal skirmisher, Blur division); I fervently sang – and, God help me, believed – thatThings Can Only Get Better. Super Furry Animals were a band I knew only distantly, via the transgressive thrill ofthat song they had with all the swearing in. And yet the news they’ll be shirt sponsor for a Welsh football club this season has managed to whisk me straight back to a time when things seemed simpler, kinder and more hopeful.Nearly three decades have passed sinceSuper Furry Animalslast had their logo on a football kit. Back in 1999, their frontman Gruff Rhys and bassist Guto Pryce, both Cardiff City fans, persuaded their Bangor-born bandmates to lay down their north Wales allegiances for the duration of the Bluebirds’ Welsh Cup run – which was, incidentally, all they could afford. The cup shirts cost them £2,000 and were, according to Rhys, knock-offs made for ice hockey. This year’s beneficiaries are a more modest outfit: Cwmbran Celtic, just relegated from Wales’s second tier. Cwmbran is the town where the band send their stage props for repair, and given the props in question are giant inflatable bears, you wonder whether they could get one installed in goal.Sing when you’re winning: the 20 greatest songs about football – ranked!Read moreSuper Furry Animals aren’t the only 90s band involved: Scottish post-rockersMogwaihave sponsored the men’s away strip, with 10% of the profits from all shirt sales going to a grassroots music charity.There has traditionally been an element of patronage when famous musicians do football, from Elton John’s time as chair of Watford, to Robbie Williams’s 2024 elevation to Port Vale club president. The pattern is a repeating one: local lads (they’re usually lads) make good, and want to give back to the team they’ve followed since they were little. Wet Wet Wet were the first to go down the shirt-sponsorship route with Clydebank in 1993. The team’s shirts turned out to be a more timeless design than the loud, oversized suits that Marti Pellow’s crew wore the day they unveiled them.Slapping your logo on your home side’s shirt was a charitable endeavour, rather than an investment. Nothing underscored this point better than Fatboy Slim’s relationship with Brighton & Hove Albion. The DJ’s record label first sponsored their shirts in the late 90s, back when the team’s financial straits had left them flirting with extinction, and Tony Bloom’s billions were still waiting to be won. It was particularly appropriate back then that Micky Adams’s men should run out on to the field with their chests declaring them SKINT.View image in fullscreenBobby Zamora in Brighton’s home kit sponsored by Fatboy Slim.Photograph: Mike Hewitt/Getty ImagesMusical match-ups have tended, therefore, towards the endearing, not the cool. Jake Bugg sponsored Notts County not to market his own music, but to evangelise the Midlands team on his global tours. And it’s even cuter when bands have sponsored kids’ teams. The late Lemmy of Motörhead was tickled by the thought of a Lincolnshire under-10s team sporting his Snaggletooth skull mascot on their fronts; unfortunately the resultant all-black kit too closely resembled referees’ uniforms and the children were banned from wearing it in league matches. Still, the idea had an enduring appeal: the Prodigy, Biffy Clyro, Sleaford Mods and Franz Ferdinand have all paid for youth kits.In the last couple of years, though, the relationship between bands and football teams has turned serious. The move to monetise the “adjacent audiences” of pop and sporting fandom means shirt sponsorship is no longer a way of artists showing their support, but a marketing and merchandising opportunity in its own right.Spotify’s deal with Barcelona got the ball rolling, with Coldplay, Karol G, Rosalía and Travis Scott each briefly appearing on the shirtfront, and limited-edition replicas costing more than £340 a pop. The footie-kit-as-streetwear trend means bands aren’t “sponsors” any more, they’re “collaborators”. Hence Manchester United’s pre-match shirts don’t bear the name of the Stone Roses, just their album artwork. And while that may have baffled a few younger fans – the club’s website ran a post explaining who the Madchester group were for the gen Z-ers – it still reflects a genuine connection. Ian Brown is a lifelong Red, and the team has walked out to This Is the One since Gary Neville first requested it two decades ago.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenColdplay show off their Barcelona shirts.Photograph: Fc Barcelona Handout/EPAWhereas a year ago, if you’d been asked at a pub quiz what Paris Saint-Germain had in common with a K-pop band, or what Pink Floyd had to do with a Serie A team, you’d have been within your rights to say “nothing”. The answer, now, is clothing ranges – PSG teamed up with the girl group Blackpink to optimise fan engagement in Asia, while Inter marked the 50th anniversary of the album release of Wish You Were Here.All this can be confusing for the simple-minded sports lover like me. What is a culture-forward lifestyle capsule, anyway? It sounds like something Musk and Bezos want to blast to Mars in. Creating a sporting look now involves an advanced understanding of fashion arithmetic: at last year’s Euros it was Admiral x Spice Girls, now it’s the Rolling Stones x England Cricket x Castore. These are powerful equations, as when a 2025 Bohemian FC x Fontaines DC shirt (raised tothe power of Greta Thunbergwhen she wore it on her flotilla to Gaza) = £££££ for charity. Maybe Ed Sheeran’s Mathematics tour top for Ipswich was an omen. Or perhaps this is a fad, and the music industry will soon move on to something new. GQ, which has declared “blokecore” over, says we’ll be wearing classic rugby tops by autumn/winter. Sounds delightfully 90s to me.Explore more on these topicsFootballSuper Furry AnimalsMogwaicommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the two cultures: bridge the divide, starting with A-levels | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Seventy years after CP Snow warned of estrangement between the sciences and arts, breadth in education should be encouraged
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Seventy years after CP Snow warned of estrangement between the sciences and arts, breadth in education should be encouraged
Content: ‘While recent decades have seen successful efforts to boost Stem, at the expense of the humanities and arts, the division between the two has been unaddressed.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘While recent decades have seen successful efforts to boost Stem, at the expense of the humanities and arts, the division between the two has been unaddressed.’Photograph: AlamyOpinionEducationThe Guardian view on the two cultures: bridge the divide, starting with A-levelsEditorialSeventy years after CP Snow warned of estrangement between the sciences and arts, breadth in education should be encouragedSun 9 Aug 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareAfter the playwrightTom Stoppard diedlast year, one of the most striking tributes to his work came from a clinical scientist. Michael Baum explained in the British Medical Journal how, in the interval of a 1993 performance of Arcadia, heexperienced an epiphany. Thomasina Coverly’s attempt to plot the equation for a rose prompted him to realise that chaos theory was the best way to explain breast cancer’s pattern of recurrence. It was, he wrote, “the bond that links the arts and the sciences as one enterprise rather than the contents of two silos”.Mr Baum was not the first person to celebrate the bridging of this gap. CP Snow famouslycriticised the incuriosityof “literary intellectuals” about technology in hisessay The Two Cultures(later turned into a lecture and a book). Whether or not this was justified at the time, many literary intellectuals besides Stoppard have since taken a close interest in science; Richard Holmes’s latest book, about the influence of evolutionary theory onTennyson, is just one example. But the split between the humanities and sciences remains pronounced, and will be evident when this year’s A-level results are released on Thursday.Stoppard’s Thomasina was talking to her maths tutor when she sparked Mr Baum’s chain of associations. For anyone interested in linking disciplines, education is clearly crucial. But while recent decades have seen successful efforts to boost Stem (science, technology, engineering and mathematics),at the expense of the humanities and arts, the division between these two broad fields of knowledge has been unaddressed. So has the issue of early specialisation, with many pupils in England and Wales choosing either one path or the other at age 16.This narrowing is highly unusual internationally. In France, Germany, the US and Scotland, pupils typically study a broader curriculum until they leave school. And while theoretically, English and Welsh teenagers at least have a wide choice of subjects, and there is nothing to stop them from studying chemistry alongside dance or German, timetables can make this difficult, while the competitive nature of university admissions incentivises them to stick to what they are best at, whether that is a suite of essay-writing subjects or physics, maths and further maths.Thistendency to specialisehas intensified recently. Under New Labour, pupils were encouraged to take four subjects in year 12 before choosing three A-levels. But following Michael Gove’s decision to scrap AS assessments, theoptions narrowedboth in terms of the number of subjects studied and the range. Between 2003 and 2021, the proportion of students taking A-levels from a single subject-grouprose from 18% to 35%. Only 5% of the latter cohort studied a combination of Stem, social science and humanities subjects. Last year the governmentcut funding for state schoolsteaching the wide‑ranging international baccalaureate.There is no shortage of challenges facing the new education secretary, Lucy Powell – not least the repeatedlybotched reformof vocational alternatives, and the rise in pupils with special educational needs. That’s one reason why A-levels barely featured in the recentcurriculum review. But the 70th anniversary of Snow’s “two cultures” thesis is a good time to reflect on whether a rethink of 16-to-18 education is due. Young people should be enabled to keep more options open for longer. More people straddling the science and humanities disciplines would be a good thing.Explore more on these topicsEducationOpinionA-levelsExamsSchoolsSixth formScienceMathematicseditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on India’s green growth gamble: it will need more than private finance | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The world’s most populous country needs state-generated demand to industrialise, decarbonise and avoid China’s overcapacity trap
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The world’s most populous country needs state-generated demand to industrialise, decarbonise and avoid China’s overcapacity trap
Content: Workers install solar panels at a renewable energy park in Khavda, Gujarat, India.Photograph: Bloomberg/GettyView image in fullscreenWorkers install solar panels at a renewable energy park in Khavda, Gujarat, India.Photograph: Bloomberg/GettyOpinionClimate crisisThe Guardian view on India’s green growth gamble: it will need more than private financeEditorialThe world’s most populous country needs state-generated demand to industrialise, decarbonise and avoid China’s overcapacity trapSun 9 Aug 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareIndia is attempting to do something the world has never seen before. SoclaimedNiti Aayog, the government of India’s policy thinktank, earlier this year. It said that no major economy has tried to expand GDP nearly eightfold within a generation while simultaneously redirecting its energy and industrial systems to reach net zero within two generations. Hence itsdetailed report’s claim that there is “no historical precedent”.There is something to this. China industrialised at vast scale, but not on a sustainable net zero path. Korea, Japan and Europe became wealthy byindustrialisingbefore decarbonising. Today, rich nations have already satisfied the basic demands of their people and created the infrastructure and high per-capita energy use that India is still trying to build. The world’s most populous country has to do this while also reducing emissions.The climate emergency is all too real for New Delhi. In April, on a single day, all of the planet’stop 50 hottest citieswere in India. Yet the country still relies heavily on coal, especially at moments of peak power needs. This sets up adangerous feedback loop: heat drives cooling demand; cooling demand drives coal-burning; coal‑burning drives temperatures higher. India is trying to change course. Non-fossil fuel sources now account for more than half of installed electricity capacity.The report assumes India reaches $30tn GDP by 2047, with risingurbanisation,industrialisationandliving standards. India’s net zero path will bejudgedpolitically by who bears the costs and who captures the gains. But the thinktank reasons that as India grows fast, so energy and infrastructure demand and investment rise too, and,voilà, India continues to grow fast. This may be a virtuous cycle. But left unexplained is what source of demand gets the process going and sustains it.That requires a political economy of investment. It means explaining who spends first, who guarantees demand, how businesses are induced to keep building whenexisting factories are not fully used, and how private profitability is maintained when consumption’s share of national income falls.India’s solar success partly answers these questions. In a 2025 paper, the political economistMathias Larsenargues that India’s advances in sunlight-powered electricity came because the state created a market, used public sector financial firepower and protected domestic producers. That is not a story of private finance spontaneously allocating capital. It is a story of state-made demand.But solar is one sector. A whole-economy transition may not work the same way. What happens when domestic demand can’t soak up the state-created capacity? China answered that question through exports, but only because of a historically exceptional bargain. Washington opened the American market to China on favourabletrading termsin 1979. Nothing reversed that access. China’s government was allowed to heavily intervene in the macro- and micro-economy to drive rapid industrialisation and growth inside the US-led trading global system.India faces a far more hostile environment. It is industrialising in a world of fragile supply chains,climate trade barriersandChinese export overcapacity. That makes the question of India’s domestic demand more important, not less. The mainstream view still assumes private investors will allocate capital efficiently once cash is mobilised. But that does not explain why firms would invest at the necessary scale unless the state spends first, guarantees markets and coordinates sectors. This, sadly, may be the truth that cannot speak its name.Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionIndiaTrade and developmentGreenhouse gas emissionsSouth and central AsiaeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The culture surrounding ‘ideal’ childbirth has to evolve | Childbirth | The Guardian
description: Letters: Molly O’Brien responds to an article by Natalie Morris about her five-day labour, while an NHS doctor shares her personal experience of feeling ‘othered’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Molly O’Brien responds to an article by Natalie Morris about her five-day labour, while an NHS doctor shares her personal experience of feeling ‘othered’
Content: ‘What is described is not a debate about “ideal birth”, but an account of undiagnosed labour dystocia.’Photograph: Getty/Posed by modelView image in fullscreen‘What is described is not a debate about “ideal birth”, but an account of undiagnosed labour dystocia.’Photograph: Getty/Posed by modelChildbirthLettersThe culture surrounding ‘ideal’ childbirth has to evolveMolly O’Brienresponds to an article by Natalie Morris about her five-day labour, while an NHS doctor shares her personal experience of feeling ‘othered’Sun 9 Aug 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareIt is not clear whether Natalie Morris’s labour began spontaneously or was induced (By day five of my labour, I didn’t want an ‘ideal birth’. I only wanted to survive, 6 August). Nevertheless, what is described is not a debate about “ideal birth”, but an account of undiagnosed labour dystocia.By day four she had contractions but no cervical dilatation, was exhausted, unable to sit down, and knew instinctively she needed help. These are features of pathophysiology that should have prompted reassessment. That failure was not ideology. It was a lack of education and training among both midwives and doctors in recognising difficult labour, also known as labour dystocia. This same issue, with tragic consequences, was highlighted in the Nottingham maternity review. That system’s failure receives far less attention than the “culture wars” surrounding birth.It is also important to be precise about what “ideal birth” means. When Valerie Amos used the term inher report, she warned that “care should not be shaped by fixed assumptions about the ‘ideal’ type of birth; this includes assumptions that favour either physiological birth or the use of non-evidence-based or unnecessary obstetric interventions”. She instead called for individualised, evidence-based care that listened to women’s voices. That balanced position has too often been recast as “normal birth ideology”. This muddies the waters, diverting attention away from individualised functional assessment that includes women’s voices as clinical data, and instead perpetuates a narrative that today’s mothers are older, heavier and less healthy, justifying intervention rates that are exceptional by international standards.The author also identifies another contributor to harm: she was told she would have been admitted earlier had a bed been available. This is a story of workforce education and resource pressures, not of “ideal birth” ideology.Molly O’BrienMidwife and founder of Biomechanics for BirthYvette Cooper is right (Women must not be put under pressure to have ‘ideal birth’, says Yvette Cooper, 5 August). However, if we are serious about improving maternity care, we must look beyond NHS services and address the wider culture surrounding childbirth.I write as both a NHS doctor and a mother. During my second pregnancy, my husband and I joined a local NationalChildbirthTrust (NCT) antenatal group. Because of pregnancy complications, we knew that our son would need to be delivered early by planned caesarean section on the advice of our obstetric team. We also knew that he would likely spend several weeks in the neonatal intensive care unit.When we shared this with the group, we found that there was virtually no discussion of caesarean birth, complicated pregnancies or neonatal care. Instead, we felt subtly “othered”, as though our experience sat outside the accepted narrative of a “normal” birth.I do not believe that this reflects the intentions of the NCT, whose aim is to support parents. Rather, it reflects a longstanding culture that has placed too much emphasis on achieving a particular type of birth. When medically necessary interventions are seen as departures from the ideal rather than examples of safe, evidence-based care, parents can be left with unnecessary feelings of failure.Changing maternity care means changing culture as well as systems. Antenatal education should prepare families for all birth experiences, including induction, caesarean birth, premature delivery and neonatal care.Name and address suppliedHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Let local communities be the stewards of their own wildlife  | Birds | The Guardian
description: Letter: Sjúrður Hammer responds to NatureScot’s decision to prohibit the annual Guga Hunt, where islanders collect gannet chicks on the Hebridean island of Sula Sgeir
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Sjúrður Hammer responds to NatureScot’s decision to prohibit the annual Guga Hunt, where islanders collect gannet chicks on the Hebridean island of Sula Sgeir
Content: A nesting gannet with its young. ‘The guga hunt is a regulated, small‑scale practice embedded in local ecological knowledge.’Photograph: Danny Lawson/PAView image in fullscreenA nesting gannet with its young. ‘The guga hunt is a regulated, small‑scale practice embedded in local ecological knowledge.’Photograph: Danny Lawson/PABirdsLettersLet local communities be the stewards of their own wildlifeSjúrður Hammerresponds to NatureScot’s decision to prohibit the annual guga hunt, where islanders collect gannet chicks on the Hebridean island of Sula SgeirSun 9 Aug 2026 12.24 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareWhat many celebrate as a win for nature conservation is, in my view, a significant step in the wrong direction for our relationship with the natural world (Scottish gannet chick hunt blocked for first time in 400 years, 3 August). The decision to prohibit the community on Lewis from collecting gannets runs counter to the spirit of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which recognises that safeguarding biodiversity will not be achieved by scientists and city dwellers alone. Instead, it affirms that indigenous and local communities hold a legitimate and essential role as stewards and caretakers of their own environments.Too often, people in our part of the world assume that “indigenous and local communities” refers only to distant, exotic cultures or to the shameful legacies of colonialism. But the Kunming-Montreal accord makes clear that this category also includes small, place‑rooted communities in countries such asScotland, the Faroe Islands and Iceland – communities with ancient traditions, distinct languages and ways of relating to nature that have endured for centuries.These cultures are not museum pieces; they are living, fragile social ecologies that are continuously pressured by the modern lifestyles and ethics of capitals and cities.As a seabird biologist who is also committed to the sustainable use of seabirds for food, I do not dispute the population modelling behind this decision, nor do I believe NatureScot has acted carelessly. But as a Faroe Islander, I have been on the receiving end of many conservation campaigns imposed from the outside, and I have seen how easily well‑intentioned policy can become a tyranny of the majority when local voices are sidelined.I would ask the Scottish government to ask themselves if they genuinely feel that the local community has been sufficiently and fairly heard in this matter, and if this decision has been taken in the spirit of the Kunming-Montreal accord.The guga hunt is a regulated, small‑scale practice embedded in local ecological knowledge. Ending it risks alienating the very communities that global biodiversity policy says must be empowered.Conservationthat excludes local actors is not progress.Sjúrður HammerTórshavn, Faroe IslandsHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
