title: Letter: Sir Garry Sobers obituary | Cricket | The Guardian
description: David Graham writes: His whole personality and cricket skills lit up not only the club but also the whole league
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: David Graham writes: His whole personality and cricket skills lit up not only the club but also the whole league
Content: Garry Sobers in 1969.Photograph: PAView image in fullscreenGarry Sobers in 1969.Photograph: PACricketLettersLetter: Sir Garry Sobers obituaryDavid GrahamSun 9 Aug 2026 12.24 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 12.26 EDTShareIn 1963 and 1966Garry Soberstoured England with the West Indies. But in those days it was not so easy for cricketers from other countries to play for the English counties, so for the summers of 1964, 1965 and 1967 he appeared for Norton Cricket Club in the North Staffordshire and South Cheshire league.What a player! His whole personality and cricket skills lit up not only the club but also the whole league. Gerry, Garry’s brother, kept wicket at Norton, and other top visitors included the fast bowler Wes Hall at Great Chell.At the time I was playing in the juniors and second team: from Garry’s many fine innings I can recall a six ending up in the car park – as a result some people would not park there. He was as approachable as he was gifted.Explore more on these topicsCricketobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Why we should support welfare spending | Labour | The Guardian
description: Letter: Labour peer Ruth Lister disagrees with the high number of party members looking to reduce spending on social security
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Labour peer Ruth Lister disagrees with the high number of party members looking to reduce spending on social security
Content: A protest in London last year against cuts to public services and limitations on social welfare.Photograph: GettyView image in fullscreenA protest in London last year against cuts to public services and limitations on social welfare.Photograph: GettyLabourLettersWhy we should support welfare spendingLabour peerRuth Listerdisagrees with thehigh number of party members looking to reduce spending on social securitySun 9 Aug 2026 12.24 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareThe finding that 47% of Labour party members surveyed believe the government is spending too much on social security is depressing (Labour members ‘have tougher view on welfare than you might think’, poll suggests, 4 August). But perhaps it’s not surprising given the relentless false “out of control” political and media narrative, when in fact spending on non-pensioner social security has remained at about 5% of GDP for the past decade.Social security was one of the main victims of austerity, leaving benefits too low to meet basic needs – hence the increased reliance on food banks. If members had been presented with the evidence from academics, thinktanks and charities showing that improving social security represents the most effective way of tackling child poverty, I suspect they may have been more supportive of spending in this area.The Institute for Government has suggested that it should be seen as preventive spending, reducing the demand on acute services. I trust that the “senior strategists in Downing Street” with whom the survey findings were shared won’t take the wrong lessons from them.Ruth ListerLabour, House of LordsHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Tour de France Femmes: Vollering wins second title but tactics row rumbles on | Tour de France Femmes | The Guardian
description: Demi Vollering won the final stage to seal her second Tour de France Femmes title but runner-up Kasia Niewiadoma reiterated her unhappiness with her rival team’s tactics on the penultimate stage
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Demi Vollering won the final stage to seal her second Tour de France Femmes title but runner-up Kasia Niewiadoma reiterated her unhappiness with her rival team’s tactics on the penultimate stage
Content: Demi Vollering lifts up her bike in delight after winning the Tour de France Femmes.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDemi Vollering lifts up her bike in delight after winning the Tour de France Femmes.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesTour de France FemmesTour de France Femmes: Vollering wins second title but tactics row rumbles onDutch cyclist finishes 1:18 clear of Kasia Niewiadoma‘I know what’s right and what’s not,’ runner-up saysJeremy Whittlein NiceSun 9 Aug 2026 14.32 EDTFirst published on Sun 9 Aug 2026 13.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the end, there was no debate. Demi Vollering went clear on the Col d’Èze, overlooking Nice, to win her secondTour de France Femmesfrom rival Kasia Niewiadoma, champion in 2024, by one minute and 18 seconds.The decisive attacks came on the narrow snaking climb of the Chemin du Vinaigrier, past swimming pools and art deco villas, where breakaway rider Isabella Holmgren was finally overhauled and ­Vollering and Niewiadoma again went head-to-head.Tour de France Femmes 2026: Vollering wins stage eight after dramatic late break – as it happenedRead moreThe Polish rider’s last-ditch attack saw her replicate the effortsshe had made on Mont Ventouxon Friday, but it was not enough to dislodge Vollering, who remained glued to her back wheel on the 15% gradients, before finally breaking clear just 600 metres from the top of the final ascent of the Èze.However, Vollering’s stage victory and overall success was set against the backdrop of the row between her and Niewiadoma over what were described as “dirty” tactics employedat the foot of the crucial climbof Saturday’s stage, from Sisteron to Nice.The pair have history and their spat goes back to the 2024 race, when Vollering crashed while wearing the yellow jersey on stage five, and Niewiadoma rode on to the finish, eventually winning the race overall by just four seconds.“I have a lot of respect for Kasia,” Vollering said before the stage, but added that she had been “disappointed when I saw her interview yesterday [Saturday], directly after the finish line, because she really attacked my teammates, and I think it’s not so fair to do that.“I didn’t forget what she did when I was on the ground two years ago. So, if she’s speaking about fair play, then I think she’s not the one that can really say something about that. I find it sad that we attack each other like this after the finish line.”Niewiadoma had angrily confronted Vollering’s French FDJ United-Suez teammate, Célia Gery, at Saturday’s finish on the Promenade des Anglais, accusing her of blocking her path as she tried to follow the Dutch rider on the final climb of the stage.The row continued into Sunday afternoon and was inflamed further when Vollering’s manager, Stephen Delcourt, demanded an apology from Niewiadoma.View image in fullscreenWinner Demi Vollering (centre) alongside runner-up Kasia Niewiadoma (left) and third-placed Elisa Longo Borghini.Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images“For the credibility of her sport, I prefer she apologises,” Delcourt said before the start of the final stage. “Célia is 20 years old, she made the corner fast. I’m sure it was never in Célia’s mind to do something wrong.”Lars Boom, Vollering’s sports director, said that Gery was being “torn apart on social media and is receiving death threats”.“I’ve seen the footage and, from what I can see, there isn’t much in it. Gery still leaves space,” Boom said.Even in the race itself the debate continued. On the first ascent of four, of the Col d’Èze, Vollering and ­Niewiadoma rode alongside each other, deep in discussion before the Dutch rider wagged her finger at Niewiadoma, who then rode off.“I’ve been racing for years,” Niewiadoma said on Sunday morning. “I know what’s right and what’s not. It’s not like I’m making things up. I expressed how I felt, and nothing has changed since then.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenKasia Niewiadoma (right) tries to dig in as Demi Vollering increases the pressure on the final stage.Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images“Demi was extremely strong. It’s an honour to fight against her. I don’t want to take anything away from her performance. I just want to race fairly against her.”Niewiadoma’s husband, former world champion Taylor Phinney, went even further. “Is it illegal? I don’t think so,” he posted on social media, of Gery’s move. “Is it dirty riding? To me, yes.”Dogs, descents and dehydration: Tour de France Femmes 2026 – in picturesRead moreHe compared Gery’s move to “something you would see in a junior race, not a move you’d expect from one of the world’s best teams in the biggest race of the year.”“People can ride how they want, race with respect for others or not,” Phinney wrote. “I met many riders who rode without respect in my day. The peloton remembers who races with class and who does not.”It was also a bitter final day for Marlen Reusser,winner of the stage four time trialin Dijon, who fell on a right-hand bend, while descending the Col d’Èze, and tearfully got to her feet, to finish the stage. The Swiss rider, who had started the day third overall, tumbled down the standings to finish 14th in the general classification.Afterher Ventoux exploits, Niewiadoma yet again had to be content with a podium finish, her fifth in five years. “A day like today only motivates me to come back even stronger,” she said.But this race was Vollering’s vindication, two years after her bitter tears at Alpe d’Huez. “I wanted to make it clear that we didn’t win because of an incident on Saturday,” she said. “I wanted to make it clear that we, as a team, deserved to win a beautiful Tour de France Femmes with humility and pride.”Explore more on these topicsTour de France FemmesCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 1: Arsenal | Premier League previews 2026-27 | The Guardian
description: With most of their rivals changing managers, can Arsenal go back-to-back for the first time in more than 90 years?
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: With most of their rivals changing managers, can Arsenal go back-to-back for the first time in more than 90 years?
Content: Arsenal’s Premier League title parade drew an estimated million-plus people on to the streets of North London. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianWith most of their rivals changing managers, can the champions go back-to-back for the first time in more than 90 years?ByEd AaronsSun 9 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:1st (NB: this is not necessarily Ed Aarons’ prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:1stProspectsEven losing on penalties inthe Champions League finalcould not take any of the gloss off last season as Arsenalended their 22-year waitto be crowned Premier League champions. The celebrations have continued all summer aftersome wild scenes on the streets of north Londonon their return from Budapest, although concerns over the fitness of some key players after their exploits at the World Cup are mounting.Arsenal have acted quickly to reinforce their midfieldby signing Bruno Guimarãesfrom Newcastle given Declan Rice’s workload must be managed very carefully afterplaying through neural painin his hamstring and lower back since December. Thearrival of Greece forward Christos Tzolisto replace Leandro Trossard also looks like a smart piece of business on the left-hand side of the attack. But withVinícius Junior staying at Real Madrid, despite Arsenal’s best efforts, supporters will be hoping there is still a chance that the sporting director, Andrea Berta, could conjure up a heavyweight attacking signing before the window closes given Bukayo Saka’s fitness problems in recent seasons.The back injury thatwill sideline William Salibafor an unknown period could prove even more central to Arsenal’s hopes of retaining their title. A defence that conceded 27 goals last year in the Premier League may struggle without the immense talents of the France defender, even if they can bring in Ezri Konsa from Aston Villa as hoped. Whether Arsenal can maintaintheir dominance from set piecesover the past two campaigns will also be crucial, with more scrutiny expected from video assistant referees after the fallout from their controversialvictory at West Ham in May.Not since 1935, whenArsenalbecame the second team to win three successive league titles, have they retained their crown. Having strengthened the deepest squad in the division still further, they will take some stopping again.Past five seasonsOff-field pictureMoney definitely isn’t an issue for Stan Kroenke. Arsenal’s co-owner becameAmerica’s largest private landownerthis year and has spent more than £1.5bn on new players since becoming the majority shareholder in 2011 through his holding company, Kroenke Sports & Entertainment (KSE). Next on the agenda isan upgrade to the EmiratesStadiumthat could increase the capacity of their home to more than 70,000. Talks have begun with the stadium’s original architects, Populous, over a project that could cost up to £500m. The much-criticised shirtsleeve deal with Visit Rwanda ended last season and has been replaced by the HR company Deel, itself controversial in some sections of the Arsenal fanbase, while Emirates have renewed their longstanding partnership until 2033.Owner-fan relationshipKroenke and his son Josh – who are co-chairs – clearly revelled in carrying out the Premier League trophy at Selhurst Park before it was presented to the captain, Martin Ødegaard,after Arsenal’s final game of the seasonin May. Having once been criticised for running the club “like an investment vehicle”, now they are praised for the enormous effect they have made.Kroenke Jr’s promisethere would be “no standing still once this season ends” was an ominous sign to their rivals given KSE have a reputation as serial winners in a number of sports in America.The managerMikel Arteta’s expected bumper new contract extension – that will make him one of the best-paid managers in the world – has yet to be confirmed, but there is no doubting his commitment to the cause. The Spaniard could not bear to watch as Manchester City’s challenge collapsed against Bournemouth last season and wasin his back garden “building a fire”when Arsenal were confirmed as champions. With Pep Guardiola gone,Arteta has the opportunityto build a new winning dynasty of his own.Star signingView image in fullscreenThe Gunners fans will be hoping to see Bruno Guimarães’ goal celebration on numerous occasions this season.Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesThe arrival of Guimarães was another big statement of intent from Arsenal. The former Newcastle captain wants to win more trophies after capturing hearts and minds on Tyneside and he will provide several options in the already well-stacked engine room. As well as relieving the load on Rice, the versatile 28-year-old Brazil midfielder is capable of fulfilling a number of roles, from deep-lying playmaker to box-to box destroyer. While it remains to be seen how Arteta chooses to use Guimarães when he also has Martín Zubimendi, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Ødegaard and Mikel Merino at his disposal, his talents will only add to the quality in Arsenal’s squad.Stat attackReferees have been told to pay much more attention to grappling during set-pieces this season so it will be interesting to see if this has any effect on Arsenal. Only three teams in thePremier Leaguehad a better non-penalty expected goal difference than the Gunners had from set plays alone.A graphic showing the six teams who had a positive xG difference for set pieces in the Premier League in 2025-26: Arsenal on 14.11, Brentford on 9.02, Newcastle on 7.83, Man City on 3.12, Brighton on 0.45 and Aston Villa on 0.31.Set for a breakthroughMax Dowman wasa record-breaking revelationas he dipped his toes into senior football for the first time last season and the signs are that the 16-year-old could be handed more opportunities after impressing again during pre-season. A brilliant goal and an assist against Girona capped a man-of-the-match display from the right flank. With Saka and Noni Madueke to be eased back in after returning from World Cup duty, Dowman is ready to add to his solitary Premier League start, against Crystal Palace on the final day of last season, and should appear more regularly in cup competitions.World Cup impactRice and Saka arrived in the United Statesfeeling the effects of a marathon seasonand it was to their immense credit that they played through the pain barrier and made it to England’s eighth match of the tournament. Only Thomas Tuchel knows why he left Saka on the bench in the semi-final against Argentina andhis hat-trick in the third-place playoffa few days later showed how potent he can be even with an achilles problem. Both require an extended break before returning to the rigours of club football and Arsenal will give them as long as possible. But such is their importance that it will be sooner rather than later.Explore more on these topicsPremier League previews 2026-27ArsenalPremier LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Hodgkinson believes gold at home European Championships ‘would mean almost as much as Olympics’ | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: Keely Hodgkinson is the headline act as Birmingham hosts and she believes her 800m clash with Audrey Werro is set to be ‘race of the championships’
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Keely Hodgkinson is the headline act as Birmingham hosts and she believes her 800m clash with Audrey Werro is set to be ‘race of the championships’
Content: Keely Hodgkinson believes standards in the women’s 800m are high in Europe, which adds additional cachet to the European title.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersView image in fullscreenKeely Hodgkinson believes standards in the women’s 800m are high in Europe, which adds additional cachet to the European title.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsHodgkinson believes gold at home European Championships ‘would mean almost as much as Olympics’British 800m star is headline act as Birmingham hostsAudrey Werro clash to be ‘race of the championships’Sean IngleSun 9 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKeely Hodgkinson says winning a European gold medal in front of her home fans in Birmingham this week will be nearly as special as her Olympic title in Paris.Hodgkinson is the headline act as the EuropeanAthleticsChampion­ships come to Britain for the first time in its 92-year history, but she insists the intense spotlight on her only increases her determination to win 800m gold.Georgia Hunter Bell: ‘Getting the tube to work I was like … oh my God, I’ve kind of messed up my life’Read more“I don’t really see it as pressure,” the 24-year-old said. “I just see it as more of a motivation. There’s going to be a lot of my family there to support me, and hopefully I’ll be able to stand on top of the podium and have a national anthem in the UK. That would be incredibly special. It would mean as much to me, almost, as winning in Paris.”Part of Hodgkinson’s ­excitement comes from knowing that the world’s four ­fastest women in 2026 will all be competing ­including the Swiss star Audrey Werro, who shocked her in June by running 1min 53.98sec, ­making her the third fastest woman in the race’s history.Hodgkinson, though, believes she is still the best in the world over two laps, and intends to prove it against a field that includes the ­former 400m hurdle world ­champion Femke ­Broeders‑Bol, who has run 1:55 this year.Quick GuideEuropean Athletics Championship: day-by-day guideShowMonday 10 AugustAmy Hunt is a warm favourite for the women’s 100m (9.50pm), but no British athlete has won more European golds than DIna Asher-Smith, the defending champion. Elsewhere, Norwegian superstar Jakob Ingebrigtsen returns from an Achilles injury in the men’s 5,000m (8.40pm) and there’s also an intriguing 4x400m mixed relay final (9.40pm).Tuesday 11 AugustKeely Hodgkinson begins the defence of her women’s 800m title (12.05pm). The big event of the night is the men’s 100m, where Italian Marcel Jacobs is the favourite to defend his crown (9.45pm), with Britain’s Romell Glave his closest challenger. The women’s 110m hurdles (9.30pm) should also be a cracker.Wednesday 12 AugustLocal lad Matt Hudson-Smith is expected to win the men’s 400m gold for a third time (8.50pm), while Emily Newnham should medal in the women’s 400m hurdles (9.08pm), although Slovakia’s Emma Zapletalova is the wide-margin favourite.Thursday, 13 AugustHodgkinson goes  in the women’s 800m semi-finals (12:10pm). A stacked evening card includes a men’s 800m final (9.28pm) where Max Burgin and Ben Pattison should feature and the women’s 200m where Hunt (9.50pm) will be favourite. In the women’s steeplechase (8.30pm), Britain’s Elise Thorner should cap a breakout season with gold.Friday 14 AugustAll eyes will be on the women’s 800m final (9.45pm), which could be the race of the year. In June Swiss star Audrey Werro ran the third fastest time in history to beat Hodgkinson in Stockholm. Can the Brit get her revenge? Former 400m hurdles world champion Femke Broeders-Bol is a live threat too. Elsewhere Karsten Warholm should win another men’s 400m hurdles (8.40pm).Saturday, 15 AugustNafi Thiam’s withdrawal with injury means there will be a new heptathlon champion for the first time since 2016 and Katarina Johnson-Thompson will hope to take advantage (7.45pm). Britain also have medal chances in the men’s and women's 4x100m relay (9.33 and 9.48pm), a strong men’s 1500m featuring Jake Wightman (9.07pm) and the women’s 400m (8.10pm) where Amber Anning should medal.Sunday, 16 AugustBritain will expect a bumper day with Georgia Hunter Bell favourite in the women’s 1500m (9.13pm), along with strong medal chances in the women's and men’s 4x400m relay (9.33pm and 9.48pm) and the mixed 4x100m relay (8.35pm). Early birds can catch the women’s and men’s marathon (7:30am and 8:10am), while Mondo Duplantis will hope to get his season back on track with gold in the men’s pole vault (7.30pm)Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“This is what I train for,” ­Hodgkinson said.“This is the ­exciting moment. I’ve had lots of people come around and challenge me but I’ve medalled at every single championships.“It’s going to be the race of the championships. It’s really ­interesting to look at how the standard in Europe has come on. But I think it’s really exciting – it just means that a European title is just as important, and just as fun, as a world title at this point.”Hodgkinson confirmed she was back at full fitness after injuring both knees in a fall on to a metal grate in late June. “I feel in a good place. ­Obviously there’s a bit of a tough patch in June/July but I’m happy and I’m excited to compete and I just think it’ll bring out the best in me.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“My knees are healed. I’ve got some fat scars but they’re all fine. It was just a sticky one. I didn’t miss any training or anything. It was more just a lot of pain and inflammation. I’m looking forward to putting that behind me.”Britain will hope to get off to a strong start to the championships on Monday, with Amy Hunt the ­favourite for gold in the women’s 100m, ahead of the defending champion Dina Asher-Smith and the Polish star Ewa Swoboda.Hodgkinson, whose 800m campaign begins on Tuesday, with the semi-finals on Thursday and final on Friday, is backing Britain to challenge for the top of the medal table. “I think we’ll get a few surprise medals as well. The team is really strong and I think it’s going to do great things for the sport by ­inspiring the next generation.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsKeely HodgkinsonAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: La Liga president Javier Tebas says ‘Infantino era is over’ at Fifa | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Javier Tebas, the La Liga president, has accused Gianni Infantino of ‘destroying the essence of football’ and said his time is up at Fifa
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: Javier Tebas, the La Liga president, has accused Gianni Infantino of ‘destroying the essence of football’ and said his time is up at Fifa
Content: Javier Tebas has added to the mounting pressure on Gianni Infantino during an interview with Le Monde.Photograph: Ted Shaffrey/APView image in fullscreenJavier Tebas has added to the mounting pressure on Gianni Infantino during an interview with Le Monde.Photograph: Ted Shaffrey/APFifaLa Liga president Javier Tebas says ‘Infantino era is over’ at FifaTebas says Swiss is ‘destroying essence of football’Any reform at highest levels must be ‘genuine’Paul MacInnesSun 9 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJavier Tebas says Gianni Infantino’s position as Fifa president is untenable, claiming he is “destroying the very essence of football” while calling for reform at the highest levels of the game.TheLa Ligapresident, who is a longstanding and vociferous critic of the current Fifa regime, said “the Infantino era is over” and called for control of the game to be expanded beyond the current “elite”.Fifa defends Gianni Infantino and launches attack after ‘effort to undermine’ presidentRead moreWhile Tebas’s remarks will surprise no one within the game, they maintain the drumbeat of criticism directed against Infantino following his determination to continue in post despite his secret and subsequently quashed plans to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors.In an interview with French newspaper Le Monde, Tebas repeated his call for Infantino to resign, an appeal first made after the World Cup but before the sell-off scandal. “For me, Gianni Infantino’s time has long since passed,” he said.“I’m not saying this because of recent events; I have noticed this style of management for a long time, though everyone else seems to be discovering it only now.“Gianni Infantino is not someone who contributes to the growth of football. On the contrary, his projects are destroying the very essence of the sport: the national leagues.“Football is not limited to the elite. For me, the Infantino era is over. What remains to be seen is when that will take effect and how the succession will unfold. I hope it is not just a matter of swapping out some people for others, but of a genuine overhaul.”View image in fullscreenGianni Infantino has received the backing of Fifa in spite of Uefa’s threat to boycott all its tournaments.Photograph: Sam Corum/PAInfantino is battling to stay in post despite an increasingly coordinated attempt by European football officials and others to unseat the 56-year-old Swiss.Uefahas made it clear they regard Infantino’s continued leadership of world football as untenable, the Norwegian FA has called for the president to stand down and a number of European associations have withdrawn letters endorsing Infantino for another term at the head of Fifa.Uefa confirmed on Saturday that a“departure payment”had been made to a female employee who is alleged to have been in a relationship with Infantino while he was the organisation’s general secretary more than a decade ago.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Daily Telegraphreportedon Friday night that the woman received a six-figure sum after the alleged relationship, allegations Fifa dismissed as “categorically untrue”.On Saturday night,Fifapublished a statement accusing Infantino’s critics of attempting to remove him from office before the presidential election next March. “Those who do not have the support of Fifa’s member associations should not seek to achieve through allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through Fifa’s established democratic processes,” the statement read.Infantino has also garnered support from prominent nations outside Europe, including the World Cup co-host Mexico and the finalists Argentina. Uefa say a proposed boycott of all Fifa tournaments remains in prospect, with the women’s Under-20 World Cup due to start in Poland on 5 September.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoLa LigaUefaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: José Mourinho reveals he signed contract to succeed Alex Ferguson at Manchester United in 2013 | José Mourinho | The Guardian
description: José Mourinho claims in a new Netflix documentary, backed up by Alex Ferguson, that he signed a deal in 2013 but reneged on it to return to Chelsea
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: José Mourinho claims in a new Netflix documentary, backed up by Alex Ferguson, that he signed a deal in 2013 but reneged on it to return to Chelsea
Content: José Mourinho became Manchester United manager in 2016 but says he had signed a deal to take the job three years earlier.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJosé Mourinho became Manchester United manager in 2016 but says he had signed a deal to take the job three years earlier.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianJosé MourinhoJosé Mourinho reveals he signed contract to succeed Alex Ferguson at Manchester United in 2013Mourinho: I reneged on deal and returned to ChelseaFerguson confirms story in new Netflix documentaryPA MediaSun 9 Aug 2026 19.24 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 20.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJosé Mourinho has revealed he signed a contract to succeed Sir Alex Ferguson asManchester Unitedmanager in 2013 only to tearfully renege on the deal and return to Chelsea.The football world was rocked when theScottish great announced he was retiringhaving overseen a 13th Premier League title triumph during a spell of unrivalled dominance at Old Trafford.The five big beasts are gone: who will be the Premier League’s next alpha manager? | Jonathan WilsonRead moreUnited have failed to return to the top of the English game since Ferguson stepped down, withhis successor, David Moyes, sackedafter only 10 months in charge.Mourinho was later brought in, spending two and a half years in charge from 2016, but revealed in a new Netflix documentary about his life that he had agreed to come earlier.“I go to Chelsea in 2013 but in that period there is something nobody knows,” the Portuguese said in the documentary, which is entitled Mourinho. “I think I can say because I don’t hurt anyone with the truth, and I think the objective of this work that we are doing is to tell the truth. When I leftReal Madrid, I signed with Manchester United to go to Manchester United after Sir Alex.”Mourinho continued: “I was, of course, very flattered, because Manchester United has an incredible appeal. When I say Real Madrid is the biggest club in the world, I have to say that Manchester United is very, very close.double quotation markHe phoned me and he was crying. He says: ‘Alex, I can’t take it – I’ve given my word to Chelsea.’Sir Alex Ferguson“But one thing is love for football, and another thing is love for a certain club. I think this is more powerful than love for football and, fundamentally, after Real Madrid, I needed to feel that I’m loved.”Ferguson was one of the footballing figures interviewed for the new documentary and admits he was under the illusion Mourinho was accepting the offer, only for the situation to change in a matter of hours.“Early evening he phoned me and he was crying,” the United great said. “And he says: ‘Alex, I can’t take it – I’ve given my word toChelsea, and I’m not going to break my word.’ The reason he gave to me I could understand, but I was disappointed.”Mourinho had a strong bond with Chelsea after leading them to two Premier League titles, an FA Cup and two League Cups during his first spell.View image in fullscreenAlex Ferguson’s long spell as Manchester United manager ended in May 2013.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianThe Portuguese parked differences with the Chelsea owner, Roman Abramovich, to return to Stamford Bridge after leaving Real Madrid, winning another league crown and League Cup before being sacked in December 2015.“For me to lose the chance to be the coach to succeed Sir Alex Ferguson was dramatic, but I don’t regret because it was a decision that I made with my heart,” Mourinho, now back in charge of Real Madrid, said.“And I think it is nature that says something that when you do something for love, you are never doing anything wrong. I think it’s nature. I did it for love.“I went back with the feeling of, yes, I go home, but with big responsibility because what I did before is history, and you don’t want to destroy your legacy.”Explore more on these topicsJosé MourinhoManchester UnitedReal MadridChelseanewsShareReuse this content

title: Iraola says Liverpool have work to do as familiar frailties in defence prove costly | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: Andoni Iraola was disappointed by Liverpool’s inability to sustain their good first half as they surrendered a two-goal lead to lose 3-2 against Monaco
Author: Dominic Booth
Headline: Andoni Iraola was disappointed by Liverpool’s inability to sustain their good first half as they surrendered a two-goal lead to lose 3-2 against Monaco
Content: Lewis Koumas (right) congratulates Alexander Isak after he opened the scoring at Anfield.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenLewis Koumas (right) congratulates Alexander Isak after he opened the scoring at Anfield.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersLiverpoolIraola says Liverpool have work to do as familiar frailties in defence prove costlyHead coach frustrated by ‘tired’ performanceMonaco come from two down to win 3-2 at AnfieldDominic Boothat AnfieldSun 9 Aug 2026 13.55 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndoni Iraola told his Liverpool team they have work to do after ­squandering a 2-0 lead against Monaco to lose a second successive pre-season friendly.The former Bournemouth coach last managed a game at Anfield almost exactly a year ago in the memorable opener to the 2025-26 Premier League season, a game the Cherries wereunfortunate to lose 4-2. Now on his debut in the home dugout, Iraola saw his team produce a similarly open display and lose again. It became clear Liverpool’s longstanding defensive frailties are still to be eliminated.Leeds stage thrilling comeback to sink Liverpool in Chicago friendlyRead moreAlexander Isak and Florian Wirtz scored in the first half as the hosts exhibited some free-flowing ­football, butMonacodominated a ­second half that became fragmented as Iraola and Monaco’s Filipe Luís made wholesale changes.“As soon as we have made some changes they start to get tired, we cannot sustain that level, so we have work to do,” Iraola told LFCTV on Liverpool’s “frustrating” regression after a bright start. “They were much better in the second half, in the same way we were better in the first half.”After Liverpool beat Wrexham and Sunderland during a pre-season tour to the US, a4-2 defeat against Leedsbrought back memories of the struggles of last season. This result will cause some concerns with transfer activity dragging.Ronald Araújo is at least due to arrive on loan from Barcelona. Although that deal is not yet complete and Alexis Mac Allister is still to return from World Cup duty, Iraola’s team to face Monaco was strong, with Ifeanyi Ndukwe, 18, and Lewis Koumas, 20, the only fringe players to start if you exclude Kostas Tsimikas, back from a loan at Roma. Jérémy Jacquet and Curtis Jones were not considered because of fitness doubts, with Iraola at pains not to “rush” Jaquet, whosigned from Rennes for £50m, into action after a chequered time with injury.Iraola said: “Jérémy, we were in doubt whether to pick him today, he should be fine for the next one. Curtis [there is] something wrong with his hip, [it] didn’t make sense to risk [him].”Wirtz was sharp, testing Lukas Hradecky with an early shot. Isak’s opener on 16 minutes was met with a hearty cheer from the home faithful, perhaps not surprising given it was just the fourth time the Anfield crowd have been able to celebrate an Isak goal, competitive or otherwise.View image in fullscreenAndoni Iraola was disappointed after watching Liverpool slip to a second successive friendly defeat.Photograph: Lewis Storey/Danehouse/Getty ImagesThe strike came after Ryan ­Gravenberch and Dominik ­Szoboszlai’s slick midfield exchange, the former then finding the Swede, who rifled low into the corner. Koumas and Wirtz both squandered presentable chances, but it was soon 2-0 when the German forced home after a ­goalmouth scramble.Iraola cut a relaxed figure on the touchline throughout and was content with his side’s attacking fluidity. The Spaniard’s preference for a high defensive line was evident throughout, though Alisson was tested far less often than Hradecky until he had to face a 44th-minute penalty after Virgil van Dijk’s trip on Aleksandr Golovin. The Russian stroked home the spot-kick himself to make it 2-1 at the break, giving ­Alisson no chance.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWataru Endo for Ndukwe and Giorgi Mamardashvili for Alisson were the only half-time substitutions from Iraola, who made more sweeping changes just before the hour, with Rio Ngumoha, Milos Kerkez and the summer signing Víctor Muñoz among those introduced.By that stage it was 2-2, after Mamardashvili had saved from Mika Biereth only to see the striker tap in the rebound. Monaco’s goals were greeted with eerie silence given there were almost no away fans. There were some groans from home supporters frustrated at seeing their side fritter away a two-goal lead but Ngumoha’s name was sung when he came on.That Ngumoha was selected on the right wing – Mohamed Salah’s old stomping ground – was lost on nobody, nor was the fact that both the youngster and Muñoz were brought on rather than Federico Chiesa. The Italian did appear after 74 minutes along with Harvey Elliott, who was welcomed warmly back to Anfield after his nightmare on loan at Aston Villa.Monaco carved out the better chances in the search for the next goal, with Flávio Nazinho firing wide, and Oumar Konaté failing to seize on a good through ball, before their 88th-minute winner stemmed from a corner swung in from the left, which Paris Brunner met with a sweet header.There was no Anfield roar to push the hosts on to equalise as there would have been in a competitive match, and Liverpool’s side resembled a reserves squad by the end, but it was still a tame finish nonetheless. Only a double-header against Como – the first of which will be played behind closed doors – now remains before Iraola’s competitive debut away at Newcastle on 23 August, with his home league debut coming against Nottingham Forest a week later. The manager will demand an improvement in the next fortnight.Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolAndoni IraolaMonacoFriendliesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Arteta expects Guimarães to ‘ignite’ Arsenal and help take team to new level | Friendlies | The Guardian
description: Mikel Arteta praised Arsenal’s new signing Bruno Guimarães after watching his side lose 3-2 in the Emirates Cup to Borussia Dortmund
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Mikel Arteta praised Arsenal’s new signing Bruno Guimarães after watching his side lose 3-2 in the Emirates Cup to Borussia Dortmund
Content: Bruno Guimarães is presented to the Arsenal fans before the Emirates Cup match against Borussia Dortmund.Photograph: Jacques Feeney/Offside/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBruno Guimarães is presented to the Arsenal fans before the Emirates Cup match against Borussia Dortmund.Photograph: Jacques Feeney/Offside/Getty ImagesFriendliesArteta expects Guimarães to ‘ignite’ Arsenal and help take team to new levelArsenal lose 3-2 to Borussia Dortmund in Emirates CupMan City’s wide players shine in 3-2 win against AtléticoPA MediaSun 9 Aug 2026 14.46 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 20.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Arsenal manager, Mikel Arteta, has backed “warrior” Bruno Guimarães to “ignite something different” in the Premier League champions. The Brazil midfielder was introduced to fans ahead of Sunday’s 3-2 defeat byBorussia Dortmundin the Emirates Cup after completing his £75m move from Newcastle.The 28-year-old,who has signed a four-year deal, bolsters a midfield which already includes Declan Rice, Martin Ødegaard, Mikel Merino, Martín Zubimendi and Eberechi Eze.Iraola says Liverpool have work to do as familiar frailties in defence prove costlyRead more“You can see the immediate reaction,” Arteta told the club website after Guimarães was given a warm reception by supporters. “I think he describes himself as a warrior. I think he’s a warrior with a tremendous quality as well, and intuition and leadership and charisma that is going to help us. That is going to really ignite something different in the team. I think he’s going to push everybody inside the team as well and that’s the type of player that we need.”After finishing runners-up for three successive seasons,Arsenalended their 22-year wait for the Premier League title last term, in addition to reaching the Champions League and Carabao Cup finals. Guimarães watched on against Dortmund as an Ethan Nwaneri strike and a Viktor Gyökeres penalty were not enough to prevent defeat.Samuele Inácio, Konstantinos Karetsas and Joane Gadou scored for the Bundesliga side at the Emirates Stadium, before Arsenal won a pre-arranged penalty shootout 5-4.“Disappointed that we lost the game,” said Arteta, who gave Ødegaard his first minutes of pre-season following the World Cup and will welcome back his full squad on Monday. “I think there were some poor moments where we were not very recognisable, especially in set-pieces and defending actions and timings that we are normally very efficient [in].“Some other very, very positive attacking combinations, big chances that didn’t finish in anything because of the final pass because they were completely open. But, overall, disappointed because you want to win the games in any context and today, we haven’t managed to do that.”View image in fullscreenManchester City’s Phil Foden falls in a collision with Atlético Madrid’s Morten Hjulmand.Photograph: Greg Baker/AFP/Getty ImagesThe Manchester City manager, Enzo Maresca, praised the impact of his wide players after Antoine Semenyo supplied ⁠assists for Omar Marmoush in a 3-1 victory overAtlético Madridto wrap up their preseason tour ⁠of Asia.Marmoush scored ⁠twice in ​the space of three minutes early in the second half before substitute Rayan Aït-Nouri added a third in stoppage ⁠time, helping City overturn a half-time deficit in front of more than 50,000 fans at Seoul World Cup Stadium.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Overall, it was a ⁠very good test against one of the best teams in Europe,” Maresca said. “Credit ​to the players for the effort ‌they have done. From ‌tomorrow pre-season is finished and the real business starts.”Semenyo finished the Asia tour with four assists in ​three matches, while Savinho also impressed on the opposite flank. Aït-Nouri completed the scoring late on, but Maresca said City still needed greater efficiency in front of goal.“We need to be clinical. It’s something we need to improve,” he said. “Slowly we ⁠are getting there and with Erling (Haaland) we can be even more ​dangerous. Today Omar ​scored twice. This is a ​boost.”Maresca said he was encouraged by the progress made during ​his first three ‌matches in charge ​after succeeding Pep ​Guardiola, with City ending their Asia tour with a draw against Inter, before a penalty shootout defeat, and victories over a K League All-Stars side and Atlético.Explore more on these topicsFriendliesArsenalBorussia DortmundManchester CityAtlético MadridnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump appoints staff secretary Will Scharf as new White House counsel | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Scharf, who helped president win approval for $400m ballroom, to replace David Warrington on 1 September
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Scharf, who helped president win approval for $400m ballroom, to replace David Warrington on 1 September
Content: Will Scharf in the Oval Office with the president last week.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APView image in fullscreenWill Scharf in the Oval Office with the president last week.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APDonald TrumpTrump appoints staff secretary Will Scharf as new White House counselScharf, who helped president win approval for $400m ballroom, to replace David Warrington on 1 SeptemberStaff and agenciesSun 9 Aug 2026 18.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump announced on Sunday that ⁠Will ​Scharf, the staff secretary who helped secure approval for the $400m White House ballroom project, will become ⁠White House counsel and assistant to the president.Effective 1 September, Scharf will replace David Warrington, who will be leaving the administration to join the private sector. Warrington ​formerly served ​as a ​personal counsel and a ​lawyer ‌for Trump’s ​2024 campaign.Trump noted that Scharf previously served as a federal prosecutor and represented him in a number of cases, including at the supreme court. Scharf also led the National ‌Capital Planning Commission, which approved the president’s construction ​of the White House ballroom.“Will is Tough, Strong, and Smart! He also loves our Country, and respects the Law,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Will Scharf will do a great job as White House Counsel!”Appeals court halts construction of Trump’s $400m White House ballroomRead moreThe shakeup in the White House counsel’s office comes at a critical juncture – just months ahead of the midterm elections, where Trump’s Republican party will be fighting to hold on to control of Congress.Democrats have vowed to pursue investigations into Trump and his administration if they are successful in November.The White House counsel’s job is to advise on legal and policy questions related to the presidency. The office is the primary White House contact for the justice department, and it handles presidential pardons, works on judicial appointments and reviews legislation. The office also helps investigate and manage congressional investigations into the administration and lawsuits against the president when he is sued in his official capacity.Trump in July 2025 had named Scharf as chair of the National Capital Planning Commission, the executive branch agency with jurisdiction over construction and major renovations to government buildings in the region.Trump’s ballroom won final approval from the NCPC in April, though a divided federal appeals court ruled Friday that construction onthe project must stopbecause Congress had not approved it. Trump has vowed to appeal to the supreme court.The project is already well on its way and has begun to rise above ground on the east side of the White House.The Associated Press and Reuters contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Three Banksy artworks in London have cost taxpayers nearly £150,000 | Banksy | The Guardian
description: Costs of security and removal efforts have reignited debate over whether work is vandalism or valuable public art
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Costs of security and removal efforts have reignited debate over whether work is vandalism or valuable public art
Content: Banksy’s artwork outside the Royal Courts of Justice in London.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBanksy’s artwork outside the Royal Courts of Justice in London.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesBanksyThree Banksy artworks in London have cost taxpayers nearly £150,000Costs of security and removal efforts have reignited debate over whether work is vandalism or valuable public artNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentSun 9 Aug 2026 10.09 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThreeBanksyartworks have cost taxpayers almost £150,000 in removal efforts, security and other costs, with the bill expected to rise.The largest bill relates to a mural painted on the Royal Courts of Justice in London in September 2025, where efforts to remove it and provide security have so far cost more than £85,000,according to the BBC.The mural depicted a judge in a wig beating a protester with his gavel.Banksyconfirmed the work was his by posting an image on his website and Instagram account.The Ministry of Justice told the BBC, after a freedom of information request, that £50,000 had been spent trying to remove the paint from the wall of the Grade II-listed building on Carey Street. A further £35,000 had been spent on overtime and security.Banksy confirms statue of man blinded by flag in London is his workRead more“The Royal Courts of Justice is a listed building and HMCTS are obliged to maintain its original character,” the HM Courts and Tribunals Service said.The costs have reignited a debate over whether Banksy’s work constitutes vandalism or valuable public art, particularly when it appears on historic buildings. The artist,who emerged from Bristol’s graffiti scene in the 1990s,is one of the world’s most famous street artists. His work has sold at auction for upwards of £18m.The shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, said it was “outrageous” that taxpayers’ money was being spent cleaning up after the artist. “Our courts are a national symbol of justice and the rule of law,” he said. “Banksy’s vandalism should be stopped and he should foot the bill for the costs he imposes on others.”But the art critic Estelle Lovatt defended Banksy’s work and highlighted the benefits for tourism. “Some people visit Buckingham Palace and others visit Banksy’s art,” she told the BBC. “His work brings people together in a way that politics can divide us. He’s like the Pied Piper or a town crier.“It can be intimidating if a mural appears on your building, in terms of the crowds, but he makes art accessible because there’s no gallery fee.”Initial attempts to remove the mural were unsuccessful and contractors have since been using laser technology. If Westminster city council considers the result inadequate, another cleaning method will be required. As a final option, the affected stonework could be removed and replaced.A listed building consent application has also been submitted for railings to be installed across the wall where the mural appeared. The cost of the installation is not yet known.Another Banksy work has generated almost £60,000 in costs for Westminster city council.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenBanksy artwork in Waterloo Place.Photograph: Richard A Brooks/AFP/Getty ImagesA statue of a man carrying a flag appeared in Waterloo Place in the capital, near Trafalgar Square, in April. Banksy claimed responsibility by posting a video of the overnight installation on Instagram.The council said it had spent almost £60,000 on safety barriers, administration and a security guard to monitor the statue.“Ownership of the statue now sits with the council as landowner,” it said. “The council has notified the artist’s agent that it is reviewing options for the short, medium and long term.”In August 2024, another Banksy work appeared on a City ofLondonpolice sentry box. The artist painted a shoal of piranha fish over the box, which had been installed in the 1990s as part of security measures against the IRA.The box was subsequently removed at a cost of £2,200 and was never replaced. It is due to go on display at the London Museum when it reopens in November.Explore more on these topicsBanksyArtLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Canadian government steps in as ‘out of control’ wildfires force thousands to flee | Canada | The Guardian
description: British Columbia battling 102 fires day and night across province, as breakneck speed hampers firefighters’ efforts
Author: Olivia Bowden
Headline: British Columbia battling 102 fires day and night across province, as breakneck speed hampers firefighters’ efforts
Content: Firefighters would traditionally get a break during nightfall, as cooler air would slow the burning, but this is no longer the case.Photograph: BC Wildfire Service/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFirefighters would traditionally get a break during nightfall, as cooler air would slow the burning, but this is no longer the case.Photograph: BC Wildfire Service/AFP/Getty ImagesCanadaCanadian government steps in as ‘out of control’ wildfires force thousands to fleeBritish Columbia battling 102 fires day and night across province, as breakneck speed hampers firefighters’ effortsOlivia Bowdenin TorontoSun 9 Aug 2026 14.20 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 22.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCanada’s federal government has announced it will provide urgent assistance to British Columbia after an onslaught of unprecedented fast-moving wildfires forced about 22,000 people to flee their homes in frantic evacuations.A total of 102 wildfires were raging across the province on Sunday, of which nearly half were categorised as “out of control”, according to the BC Wildfire Service. Of those fires, 78 ignited during the past week.The entire community of Summerland, about 30 miles south-west of the city of Kelowna and home to about 12,000 people, was evacuated overnight on Saturday, along with a further 8,000 people around nearby Peachland. About 10,000 others have been told to prepare to evacuate at a moment’s notice.Anette Boulet was among residents who fled Summerland along Okanagan Lake in British Columbia. As she and her family left around 4.30am Saturday, their home was shrouded in smoke.“You couldn’t see barely. It was just dark, and the ridge, the ridge of fire just coming towards you,” said Boulet, who evacuated to a centre in Penticton.“There’s no words to express it, the fear.”In a social media post on Sunday, Eleanor Olszewski, Canada’s minister of emergency management and community resilience, said she had “approved a request for federal assistance from British Columbia to provide shelter and accommodations for people who have been forced to leave their homes”.“I have tasked federal officials, led by the government operations centre at Public Safety ‌Canada, to work with the province to ensure support reaches those who need it most,” she ​said.MapEfforts to battle the Bald Range wildfire have been hampered by the breakneck speed of its spread.The blaze was first detected late on Friday evening, and grew within hours to more than 40 sq miles (100 sq km) – nearly twice the size of the island of Manhattan – as it raced nearly nine miles toward Okanagan Lake.The province’s premier, David Eby, declared a state of emergency late on Saturday, telling reporters that the blaze had been “like a bomb going off.”Cliff Chapman, BC Wildfire Service’s director of provincial operations, said the prolonged hot and dry weather the province has faced this summerhad resulted in “explosive” fire conditionsnever seen before. Lightning caused by thunderstorms forecast this week could make the situation still worse, he said.Residents were shaken awake in the middle of the night to flee their homes. Jennifer Pascoa, who lives in Summerland, told the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that she had begun to pack when she saw flames licking the nearby mountains.“It happened so quickly. We came home from the beach, we saw the plume of smoke, and then within an hour, the sky was covered in dark, black clouds,” she said.The British Columbia Wildfire Service said 10 standard helicopters and one night-vision helicopter were involved in the response, but had been hindered by thick smoke, turbulence ​and large fires.Thousands told to evacuate in British Columbia as wildfire growsThe Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the country’s federal police force, said an 80-year-old woman died while trying to escape the wildfire that forced evacuations in the Okanagan Lake region.Mike Flannigan, a professor of wildland fire at Thompson Rivers University in Kamloops, BC, said the rapidity of the fires’ spread was indicative of increasingly extreme blazes springing up in Canada and the US.Southern BC and the pacific north-west in the US had had little to no rain in the past six weeks, leaving the regions “bone dry”, he said. “You walk through the forest, it crunches; if you look sideways, you start a fire.”These conditions were being driven by human-caused climate change, he said. “We’re seeing higher intensity fires today than the past … the shorter the timeframe, the more challenging it is.”Before this decade, fire agencies’ policy was that if a blaze was 20km (12 miles) away from a community, there was no cause for immediate concern. The ferocity and speed of these fires meant that such calculations no longer held, said Flannigan, warning that all homes in at-risk regions should have an emergency kit ready to go.“If a fire can run 60km in a day, you should be worried about it,” he said.The Bald Range fire was also an example of how fires could metastasise through the night, he said.Traditional firefighting practices would usually give firefighters a break during nightfall, as the cooler air would slow the burning. “That’s not the case any more. The fire roars through the evening, through the night, and we’re seeing this more and more,” he said.Drought and the sheer power and size of the fires during the day allow them to keep momentum even in the dark. Fire management agencies in BC and Alberta now fight fires after dark using night-vision helicopters.Current conditions indicated that the fire season in BC and the US states of Washington and Oregon could extend into the autumn, Flannigan said.“It looks grim … there’s no rain,” he said, adding that, like California, Canada may begin to have “fire years” instead of a summer fire season.“I’m scared for the coming weeks.”In the US, crews in Washington that for over a week have been fighting three wildfires that began burning in the Spokane area continued clean-up near containment lines. None of the fires were growing, officials said. The fires have damaged or destroyed about 920 structures.Earlier in the week a man was arrested and charged with intentionally setting the biggest of the three Spokane-area blazes.Explore more on these topicsCanadaWildfiresAmericasClimate crisisDroughtnewsShareReuse this content

title: Perseid meteor shower set to dazzle northern hemisphere this week | Meteors | The Guardian
description: Astronomers say viewing conditions promising for this year’s shower, and 50 to 100 meteors an hour may be visible
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Astronomers say viewing conditions promising for this year’s shower, and 50 to 100 meteors an hour may be visible
Content: Ancient statues are seen during the Perseid meteor shower atop Mount Nemrut in southeastern Turkey in August 2024.Photograph: Emrah Gürel/APView image in fullscreenAncient statues are seen during the Perseid meteor shower atop Mount Nemrut in southeastern Turkey in August 2024.Photograph: Emrah Gürel/APMeteorsPerseid meteor shower set to dazzle northern hemisphere this weekAstronomers say viewing conditions promising for this year’s shower, and 50 to 100 meteors an hour may be visibleAssociated PressSun 9 Aug 2026 14.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Perseid summer light show is back, and viewing conditions are especially promising across the northern hemisphere.The meteor shower’s is expected to peak on Wednesday night into Thursday morning, and coincides with a total solar eclipse across Spain, Iceland and Greenland and a six-planet parade – though the best time to view the fireballs will come after totality.As many as 50 to 100 meteors per hour may be visible under ideal conditions, according to NASA. The American Meteor Society estimates 30 to 50 meteors per hour could be seen from rural regions in the US.Random meteors are visible in dark skies on any given night. Meteor showers tend to put on dazzling celestial shows and happen at predictable times every year when the Earth plows through trails of debris left behind by comets and, sometimes, asteroids. Those remnants collide with Earth’s atmosphere at extremely high speeds, producing streaks of light known as shooting stars.The Perseids are debris from comet 109P/Swift-Tuttle, an icy ball that orbits the sun every 133 years and is not scheduled for a return visit until 2125. Observations of this meteor shower date back over 2,000 years.The Perseids are a perennial favorite because they tend to produce brilliant fireballs. Summer temperatures also make this shower popular.“We don’t have to suffer through a cold winter night to get a good view of meteors,” said astronomer Zach Vanderbosch with McDonald Observatory in Texas.The moon will be in its new moon phase during the Perseids’ peak, making viewing conditions even better.“The moon is beautiful, but it’s such a diva,” said astronomer Aparna Venkatesan with the University of San Francisco. “New moon means we don’t have moonlight flooding the sky, and you tend to see way more meteors as a result.”To spot the meteors, go outside after dark, away from clouds and city lights. Venkatesan plans to drive to the Sierra Nevada.The best views will be between midnight and dawn when the constellation Perseus is high in the northern sky. The meteors will appear to radiate from that constellation.Look up and give your eyes a half hour to adjust to the darkness. Vanderbosch recommends picking a patch of sky to focus on until a quick, bright streak passes by – even in your peripheral vision – and to avoid looking at your phone.“There’s just something magical about it,” Vanderbosch said.Explore more on these topicsMeteorsAstronomySpacenewsShareReuse this content

title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez announces decision to freeze her eggs | Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez | The Guardian
description: US congresswoman to share journey online as she criticizes Trump administration’s attacks on reproductive care
Author: Victoria Bekiempis
Headline: US congresswoman to share journey online as she criticizes Trump administration’s attacks on reproductive care
Content: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez on the steps of the Capitol in July.Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAlexandria Ocasio-Cortez on the steps of the Capitol in July.Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty ImagesAlexandria Ocasio-CortezAlexandria Ocasio-Cortez announces decision to freeze her eggsUS congresswoman to share journey online as she criticizes Trump administration’s attacks on reproductive careVictoria BekiempisSun 9 Aug 2026 18.06 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 18.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlexandria Ocasio-Cortezhas announced she is going to freeze her eggs and will be sharing the process online.The progressive New York congresswoman, 36, revealed her decision to undergo fertility treatment in a series of Instagram stories this weekend. “This is a choice that I am making to feel more in control of my life,” Ocasio-Cortez said.Ocasio-Cortez said she had been saving for the procedure for a very long time, and said there was not a lot of information for women interested in doing so.“As women in general, we are not taught about our bodies, we are not prepared for our own lives, whether that is in puberty, whether that is in pregnancy, whether that is in perimenopause, menopause, whether that is in so many different aspects of our lives,” shesaidin one of the stories.Ocasio-Cortez recognized the balancing act that comes with undergoing fertility treatment with her work as a congresswoman. Ocasio-Cortez told viewers that she would be taking her shots in the dressing room before a scheduled ABC interview on Sunday.“I want you all to see that,” Ocasio-Cortezsaid. “Because women can do anything. And I think it’s badass that I’m gonna be giving myself shots in the green room, get my glam on, roll out, talk international events, domestic policy, elections, pop out, live my life, do my thing.”Ocasio-Cortez also showed the medicines and tools, such as syringes and alcohol wipes, used in the process, which involves injecting multiple forms of medication over a period of time that typically lasts around 10 days or more. She joked she would not be injecting herself on a live feed, quipping: “Maybe I should start an ASMR egg-freezing channel.”“Don’t be weird about this, even I know though all of you will be,” she said with a slight smile moments before finding an injection site on her abdomen.She exhaled, injected the medication, and then remarked: “That wasn’t so bad!”During her Sunday interview on ABC, Ocasio-Cortezdiscussedher decision further.“In this political environment where this administration is denying reproductive care to women across the country, from abortion rights to the ability to carry out a healthy pregnancy, I think it’s important for us as leaders to have these conversations and share these processes, especially for working women across the country and normalize them,” she said.Ocasio-Cortez’s announcement drew praise.Amanda Litman, co-founder and president of Run for Something, a political action committee that supports young progressive candidates,saidon X: “I’m just so grateful for her honesty & vulnerability.”Xochitl Hinojosa, a Democratic strategist,respondedto Litman’s post by saying: “THIS. We don’t talk about women freezing their eggs or what women have to go through to start a family. Thank you @AOC for your bravery.”Explore more on these topicsAlexandria Ocasio-CortezDemocratsUS politicsHouse of RepresentativesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lake Mead plummets to historic low water level as Colorado River struggles | Colorado river crisis | The Guardian
description: Levels at reservoir along Arizona-Nevada border dipped below previous record set in 2022, amid water crisis in west
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Levels at reservoir along Arizona-Nevada border dipped below previous record set in 2022, amid water crisis in west
Content: A paddle boat in Lake Mead near the Hoover Dam, far below the bathtub ring of light minerals indicating the lack of water, near Boulder City, Nevada, on 7 August.Photograph: Ty ONeil/APView image in fullscreenA paddle boat in Lake Mead near the Hoover Dam, far below the bathtub ring of light minerals indicating the lack of water, near Boulder City, Nevada, on 7 August.Photograph: Ty ONeil/APColorado river crisisLake Mead plummets to historic low water level as Colorado River strugglesLevels at reservoir along Arizona-Nevada border dipped below previous record set in 2022, amid water crisis in westGuardian staff and agenciesSun 9 Aug 2026 14.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLake Mead, the largest reservoir in the United States, has plummeted to its lowest water level since it was filled some 90 years ago, the latest sign of adeepeningwater crisisin the American west.Water levels at the reservoir, which straddles the Arizona-Nevada border outside Las Vegas, hit 1,040.4ft (317.1 meters) above sea level on Friday, according to federal data. That’s just below the record set on 28 July 2022, according to the US Bureau of Reclamation.The reservoir is a critical storage system on Colorado River, a massive waterway that supplies roughly 40 million people across seven US states, tribal nations and Mexico, and irrigates millions of acres of farmland.Water cuts loom as US unveils long-awaited response to Colorado River crisisRead moreBut theColorado River basinis facing enormous pressure due to a combination of overuse, prolonged drought and extreme heat, and a lack of snowmelt to replenish the river. Lake Powell, the second major reservoir on the Colorado River, isalso at historiclow levels.“It’s extremely significant and extremely concerning. You have three-quarters of the population of the Colorado River basin, some 30 million people, who are directly impacted by risks to Lake Mead,” said JB Hamby, the chair of the Colorado River board of California and a board member of the Imperial Irrigation District, the largest user of the river’s water. Hamby said it is vital for states that use Colorado River water to reduce water use.Drought and dry conditions have stretched along the length of the Colorado and are particularly intense at its source in the Rocky Mountains.View image in fullscreenWater lines are visible on the rocky banks of Lake Powell on 1 August 2026 in Page, Arizona.Photograph: Justin Sullivan/Getty ImagesMelting snow provides important water for the river. This past winter, however, saw the worst snowpack on record for the Colorado River basin, adding more stress on farmers, industry, wildlife and hydropower producers, as well as the cities and towns that rely on the waterway.Years of overuse combined with drought and rising temperatures have been depletingLake MeadandLake Powell, the country’s second-largest reservoir. Both are the lowest they have been in nearly seven decades.To protect the strained system’s ability to produce hydropower, federal officials said Thursday that they will not release cool Lake Powell water from Glen Canyon Dam in northern Arizona to protect a threatened native fish, thehumpback chub, whose habitat is between the reservoirs.Federal officialsrecently announceda short-term proposal to stave off a crisis in the beleaguered waterway, after states that rely on it – California, Colorado, Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico, Wyoming and Utah –failedto reach an agreement on how to share the dwindling resource in the long term.The federal proposal called for the Lower Basin states of Arizona, California andNevadato take less water. The Bureau of Reclamation, which released the plan, said it was flexible: deeper cuts could happen in drier times, while states would have more time to collectively agree on how to manage the scarce resources.Lake Powell, a vital reservoir, plunges toward unprecedented low levels as water crisis deepens in US westRead moreThe government is expected to release a so-called “record of decision” in the coming weeks offering more details on the plan, butexperts have warnedit might not be enough to solve the problems facing the imperiled river.Severe drought in 2022 on Lake Mead, which is held back by Hoover Dam,exposed human remainsand forced water officials in Las Vegas to pump water from deeper within the reservoir to continue to supply water to millions of people.Levels at Lake Powell have dropped so much that it has become difficult to descend far enough to reach the water. Boat ramps have had to move, shut down or be built anew.Lake Mead and Lake Powell are not alone. Of the 54 western reservoirs tracked by the federal Bureau of Reclamation, nine recently recorded their lowest levels in the last three decades.Federal officials do not believe the record will stay where it is. According to modeling done in July, Lake Mead is forecast to continue dropping through much of the rest of the year.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsColorado river crisisArizonaNevadaWaternewsShareReuse this content

title: How clean air clubs are protecting Americans from wildfire smoke | Air pollution | The Guardian
description: Mutual aid groups that started giving out PPEs during COVID are now loaning air purifiers and distributing masks to fume-addled communities
Author: Lex McMenamin
Headline: Mutual aid groups that started giving out PPEs during COVID are now loaning air purifiers and distributing masks to fume-addled communities
Content: Mask Bloc LA volunteers distribute and deliver masks during the Los Angeles wildfires on 15 January 2025.Photograph: Abby MahlerView image in fullscreenMask Bloc LA volunteers distribute and deliver masks during the Los Angeles wildfires on 15 January 2025.Photograph: Abby MahlerBuilding powerAir pollutionHow clean air clubs are protecting Americans from wildfire smokeMutual aid groups that started giving out PPEs during Covid are now loaning air purifiers and distributing masks to fume-addled communitiesBuilding power is supported byAbout this contentLex McMenaminSun 9 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMiquette Thompson’s home in rural Mendocino county has been covered in smoke all week. There are the nearby Feliz and Woodside fires in northernCalifornia, which have burned more than 1,000 acres, as well as thewildfiresdevastating Oregon and Washington that are sending smoke their way, too.“It’s become not unusual,” she said of walking outside and seeing a hazy sky.The wildfire smoke meansdangerous air qualityfor her under-resourced, “wee rural little area”, Thompson said. Wildfire smoke is potentiallyunsafe for all populations, but particularly for elderly people and those with respiratory conditions. Hospitalizations for asthma go up 10% on smoke days, according to a recentUniversity of California study.Having locally organized around safety amid airborne illness for years – distributing free personal protective equipment (PPE) to neighbors and Covid tests at farmers markets – Thompson said she watched as the local health department failed to distinguish which types of masks help with smoke issues (N95 masksare better at filtering out tiny particles; cloth or surgical masks are less effective). So with her fellow organizers at Mendo Clean Air Club, she began partnering with local businesses that offered to distribute masks, too.Eastern Washington fires destroy 600 structures and force 60,000 to evacuateRead moreMendo Clean Air Club is one of over 40 clean air clubs around the world. Launched by Emily Dupree, a Chicago resident, the first club lent out air purifiers to touring musicians during Covid. Now, Clean Air Clubs andMask Blocs– a mutual aid practice for sharing masks – are offering free masks and air purifiers from their “lending libraries” to help their local communities stay safe from wildfire smoke and monitor air quality. Mask Bloc Los Angeles, for example, handed out more than 300,000 masks in two weeks during the catastrophic January 2025 LA fires.“Covid and climate change are two major pillars of collective denial in the last decade,” said Dupree. “So though our lending library was created in response to one kind of public failure – namely a failure of public health, which is still ongoing – it can serve as a solution in response to this second failure, of governments to adequately address the growing threat of climate change, of worsening wildfires and worsening air quality.”When wildfire smoke was negatively affecting Chicago air quality in July, Dupree noticed that their lending library of 15 purifiers was not fully booked. “It just didn’t sit right with me,” she said. So they started encouraging people struggling with the smoke to reserve purifiers, which they could retrieve from a storage unit; within hours, the library was fully booked, she said.“We are able to mobilize clean air resources extremely quickly because we are not dealing with bureaucracy or red tape,” Dupree said. “We just get the purifiers placed where they’re needed as quickly as possible.”View image in fullscreenMask Bloc LA  offering free masks on 25 April 2025.Photograph: Abby MahlerThis speed and access are particularly helpful for populations with underlying health conditions. When then-presidentJoe Biden declared the Covid emergency “over” in 2023, Shannon Durkin, a Mask Bloc Delaware organizer – who is especially vulnerable due to her cystic fibrosis – thought her life was functionally over, too. Since the first US lockdown in March 2020, and the ensuing anti-public health backlash, she’s felt excised from participating in public life.She has faced discriminationwhen going out in her respirator, surrounded bycollective denialthat Covid and other viral illnesses are still dangerous.In 2024, Durkin and her husband Jimmy helped launch Mask Bloc Delaware, distributing KN95 masks at protests and partnering with other organizing groups, such as the local Food Not Bombs and DSA chapters. In July, they walked around Wilmington, Delaware, as wildfire smoke from Canada permeated the east coast to distribute PPE. The Durkins said people were surprisingly enthusiastic about receiving it, not even realizing the possible health risks of the air quality. They were also able to drop masks off at various local businesses for distribution.At least one person dead in California wildfire allegedly sparked by chainsawRead moreOrganizers say the work of Clean Air Clubs and Mask Blocs feels more necessary than ever, as the current administration continues to cast doubt on theusefulness of masksandthe severity of the Covid pandemicthat in 2020killed more than 350,000 Americans.Thompson said she navigates any Covid hesitancy by explaining to residents how it can affect their health, their families and their livelihoods. “The big message that’s gotten through in a rural, underfunded region is that we can’t afford to get sick or to get long Covid,” said Thompson. “A lot of us are manual laborers or use our bodies for work in some way. We just don’t have the resources here to manage that.”Awareness of Clean Air Clubs continues to grow; Dupree even created aGoogle docbreaking down how others can start their own. Organizers say being part of these mutual aid groups can offer hope in a time of hopelessness.“A lot of people, when they’re looking at the various horrors of the world, can feel overwhelmed and then stuck regarding what they should do about it,” said Dupree. “But what this shows us is that even if you decide to focus on one problem, it turns out usually what you come up with is going to be able to pivot and solve other problems that you didn’t initially try to address. There’s a kind of freedom in that.”Explore more on these topicsAir pollutionBuilding powerWildfiresCoronavirusfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Falkland Islanders call for referendum on plans for massive salmon farm | Falkland Islands | The Guardian
description: The 3,500 population is divided over the venture, which would bring investment and jobs, but critics claim the environmental cost would be too high
Author: Karen McVeigh
