Headline: The 3,500 population is divided over the venture, which would bring investment and jobs, but critics claim the environmental cost would be too high
Content: Aerial view of part of the Falkland Islands in the south Atlantic. A proposed salmon farm in the archipelago has divided the 3,500 population.Photograph: Don Johnston/Getty Images/500pxView image in fullscreenAerial view of part of the Falkland Islands in the south Atlantic. A proposed salmon farm in the archipelago has divided the 3,500 population.Photograph: Don Johnston/Getty Images/500pxSeascape: the state of our oceansFalkland IslandsFalkland Islanders call for referendum on plans for massive salmon farmThe 3,500 population is divided over the venture, which would bring investment and jobs, but critics claim the environmental cost would be too highSeascape: the state of our oceans is supported byAbout this contentKaren McVeighSun 9 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 11.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is among the world’s last pristine wildernesses, with unique coastal waters rich in krill and squid that attract sea lions, elephant seals, dolphins and whales, and where penguins, of which there are five different species locally, outnumber people.But plans to make theFalkland Islands, one of the most remote and furthest-flung British overseas territories, a new frontier for salmon farming has split the 3,500-strong population. Now, people opposed to salmon farming are calling for a referendum because they have lost confidence in a consultation process they claim is biased towards the industry.Unity Marine, a joint venture between Fortuna, a local fishing company, and Danish firm F-land ApS, want to farm 50,000 tonnes of salmon annually in 16 locations, in what would be the largest industrial inshore development in the archipelago’s history.Farming 30,000 tonnes annually could add £35m a year to the territory’s economy, equivalent to 11% of GDP, and provide 133 jobs,according to an assessmentcommissioned by the Falklands Islands government.Salmon Free Falklands(SFF), set up by local people to oppose the proposal, said that a referendum will allow residents to decide once and for all, without fear of further challenge.View image in fullscreenA salmon farm in Hordaland, Norway. Campaigners in the Falkland Islands are worried about the effects of salmon waste on the environment.Photograph: Marius Dobilas/Alamy“It is then the people who will get to decide what happens in their own country,” said Sally Poncet, of SFF. She says she has lost confidence in the consultation process, which began on 7 August and will run until 30 October.Reports commissioned by the Falklands government as part of the consultation are based on unverifiable data provided by Unity Marine, Poncet claimed. There is “insufficient information” on the impact that the industry would have on the islands, she said. She is also concerned, from researching the impacts of farms elsewhere, that salmon waste would affect the kelp, a spawning ground for squid, a commercially important species and other wildlife, she added.The government has made clear its reports are at present looking at a number of different scenarios for the proposed farms before it commissions full environmental impact assessments.Louise Cherrie, a former member of the environmental protection authority in Tasmania, Australia, who now runs a consultancy and is providing advice to SFF, claimed the reports, one of which determined the estimated value of the proposal, were “bordering on worthless”.“The carrying capacity has not yet been determined by a rigorous scientific process,” said Cherrie. This refers to how many farmed salmon the area can support. “The regulation and impacts have not yet been costed, so it is not a cost-benefit analysis that the Falklands Islanders can make an informed choice on,” she added.Missing from the environmental report, for instance, is how any mass mortalities of fish,common in the salmon industry elsewhere,would be disposed of on the remote islands, she said.Dr Tom Appleby, the head of legal affairs at the NGO Blue Marine Foundation, said: “It is extraordinary that the Falklands Islands government have got themselves in a position where they are providing reports to the public in this consultation that do not use independently verified primary data. The reports are so littered with disclaimers as to the sources of information as to be meaningless.”Initially, in 2022, the government had said no to the salmon farm. Then, Unity Marine asked for – and was granted – a judicial review challenge on the basis that an island-wide consultation should have preceded the original decision. Both parties then agreed to a consent order which quashed the 2022 decision and outlined the consultation process that is now under way.View image in fullscreenA rockhopper penguin on Sea Lion Island, Falklands, where penguins outnumber people and the coastal waters are rich in wildlife.Photograph: Vicki Jauron, Babylon and Beyond Photography/Getty ImagesJames Wallace, the managing director of Fortuna, said: “Unity Marine did not apply for a licence to operate, but rather allowed the Falkland Islands government the time requested to investigate the feasibility of commercial-scale salmon farming in the Falkland Islands, which included determining the social, environmental and economic impacts. The government also requested an indicative business plan from Unity Marine to help provide an idea of what may be possible from the company’s perspective.“We are now in that investigative process, with independent preliminary reports published and public consultations happening.Crabs, kelp and mussels: Argentina’s waters teem with life – could a fish farm ban do the same for Chile?Read more“It is our expectation that an informed decision-making process about whether salmon farming at scale is right for the Falkland Islands must include a robust environmental impact assessment, that can answer the specific questions raised by local residents in public consultations to help determine if the risks can be successfully mitigated and that the benefits are truly realised.”A representative of the Falkland Islands government said that it was “neither advocating for nor opposing salmon farming”.The reports it had commissioned were “to inform public discussion by examining possible outcomes and impacts under different assumptions, rather than to provide final approvals for any specific project”, the spokesperson said.The government rejected suggestions that the environmental impacts of salmon farming had not been clearly presented. The carrying capacity report, it said, had been commissioned “purely for demonstrating how the modelling process would be applied to a potential project”, and was not a determination of the carrying capacity of the Falklands.A third report, on socioeconomic impacts, did not quantify future regulatory costs, it said, because they “cannot be accurately estimated” at this stage.Explore more on these topicsFalkland IslandsSeascape: the state of our oceansFish (Food)Fish (Environment)FoodMarine lifeEndangered habitatsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘These are human fires, not wildfires’: Dunwich reflects on the devastation | Suffolk | The Guardian
description: As residents, nature wardens and experts consider the damage to the heathland and how to restore it, the climate crisis is foremost in their minds
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: As residents, nature wardens and experts consider the damage to the heathland and how to restore it, the climate crisis is foremost in their minds
Content: Firefighters monitor the situation as smoke rises from wildfires near Dunwich Heath on 31 JulyPhotograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenFirefighters monitor the situation as smoke rises from wildfires near Dunwich Heath on 31 JulyPhotograph: Tolga Akmen/EPASuffolk‘These are human fires, not wildfires’: Dunwich reflects on the devastationAs residents, nature wardens and experts consider the damage to the heathland and how to restore it, the climate crisis is foremost in their mindsPatrick BarkhamandPippa NeillSun 9 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 04.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlocal community pulling together, emergency services saving homes and caravan parks from catastrophe, and farmers and nature reserve wardens working to rapidly create fire breaks to halt a marauding fireball 40 metres high – there was plenty to praise the week after aswathe of east Suffolk burned.But local people were also in tears at the blackened, ruined state of more than 112 hectares (277 acres) of Dunwich Heath, mourning the devastation of a much-loved nature reserve alongside neighbouring Minsmere. The rare birds that inhabit the reserve have lost crucial habitat, while the rare invertebrate species there will have been “decimated”, according to the reserve staff.The fire started on Wednesday 29 July; the cause is still unknown, butSuffolkFire Service said the fire took hold at a “ferocious pace” owing to the hot weather, dry conditions and changing winds. More than 100 firefighters have attended the scene since then, and crews from 18 fire services were in attendance.View image in fullscreenA scorched Dunwich Heath this weekPhotograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianA week later, the above-ground fire has been subdued. The fire service has measured temperatures below ground exceeding 600C and surface temperatures of 60C. Hot winds and a lack of rain leave the dry, sandy region in a state of high alert for further outbreaks, with many evacuated residents advised not to return home. Locals and visitors have been kept away from an area of Dunwich Heath because the fire exposed unexploded ordnance from the second world war.The impact on wildlife has been vicious. The reserve is home to some of the rarest bird species in the UK, including nightjars, nightingales and Dartford warblers. “The vegetation that is essential for supporting that birdlife, the structure of the gorse and the trees, all appears to have gone. So, in essence, the habitat they would rely on to nest, to feed, to shelter and to roost at night has gone, so they won’t have anywhere to return to,” said Adam Rowlands, the area manager for theRSPB.As well as rare birds, the site is home to a wide range of rare invertebrates, including the narrow-mouthed whorl snail,antlions, and green tiger beetles.“We know from previous fires that invertebrates aren’t well equipped to escape fire so they will have suffered mortality,” Rowlands said. And even if they did survive, the loss of the landscape meant they now had nowhere to return to, he added.View image in fullscreenThe wildfire has decimated local invertebrates and left rare birds without homes.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianWhile the police investigation into the cause of the latest in a series of devastating global-heating-exacerbated wildfires across Britain is ongoing, the fires had not stopped burning by the timeright-wing media and commentatorsbegan reporting that “rewilding” was to blame. But when the Guardian asked residents about the fire, its cause and future prevention, rewilding was on no one’s lips.Conservationists firmly rebutted the claim that an enthusiasm for rewilding – “leaving underbrush, fallen and overgrown vegetation alone”, according to the Times columnist Libby Purves – had contributed to the fires.“It’s worth stressing this was not a rewilded landscape, this was a traditionally managed, classic 20th century conservation landscape,” said Jonathan Spencer, the former head of the environment for ForestryEnglandand an expert on rewilding and other conservation techniques.The fire occurred on the old areas of Dunwich Heath, an open and naturally dry mosaic of heather and gorse which has been managed in a similar way since the 1800s. It did not spread to areas of restored heathland created on former arable land in recent decades by the RSPB and the National Trust.View image in fullscreenCrews from 18 fire services helped to put out the wildfires on Dunwich Heath.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAAccording to the RSPB and National Trust, on whose heathlands the fires raged, the land is managed like most other lowland heaths, with regular cutting of scrub, including heather and gorse, to encourage young growth and keep areas warm and open for rare species, such as adders and silver-studded blue butterflies. Bracken is removed, and the area is traversed with firebreaks and a wet ditch, which helped prevent the fire’s spread.The rewilding critique was “missing the point”, according to Rowlands. “We don’t have any land at Minsmere that would be defined as rewilding,” he said. “We get criticised by the rewilders for being too interventionist. That’s not a criticism of rewilding, we need a variety of approaches in nature conservation, but it would be incorrect to say this incident was related to rewilding activity.”View image in fullscreenDunwich Heath on Saturday, after the fire was put out.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianPaul Forecast, a regional director for the National Trust, said: “The wild habitats themselves probably saved the fire from being much worse.” He said he was in tears when he was allowed back on to the burned heath for the first time.“We already had firebreaks built in, we removed dead material, and having different age structures means you maintain more moisture in the ground,” he said. “It’s been heath for hundreds of years. It’s not the heath that’s changed, it’s the environment around it. These are not really wildfires, they are often started with human barbecues, cigarette butts or litter, but the key thing is climate change. We’re getting much longer, hotter, dry spells. We’re seeing fires on farmland, we’re seeing fires on some of the most proactively managed land. We have to face that climate change is a primary driver of that.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe sense of loss was palpable among local people at the state of their heathland, while businesses in the village of Dunwich – which was untouched by fire and open for visitors – were despairing over the impact on tourism. A 4-mile stretch of beach during the peak summer holiday season featured a lone angler, one family and two swimmers. Christian Elsley, a co-owner of Flora tea rooms on Dunwich Beach, had eight members of staff serve just 17 customers last Saturday; normally they would serve more than 200.View image in fullscreenCo-owner Sarah Elsley in Flora tearooms, which saw customer numbers drop from more than 200 a day to just 17.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianA textile artist, Rachel Robinson, said: “The whole area is a mix of anxiety and depression. It’s not just about us, ‘Oh, poor Dunwich’, it’s the whole of Europe and a lot of the UK. It’s very alarming. It feels a bit ironic this summer. We thought that the developing world would be the hardest hit by climate change. No, Europe is. That’s a shock.”Sarah Peel, the assistant manager of Dunwich museum, praised the efforts of villagers in Westleton and Dunwich, including nature reserve wardens and farmers who laboured alongside firefighters to supply water or halt the fire’s spread. “Those National Trust and RSPB teams were so brilliant for this,” said Peel. “One of the fantastic things that’s come out of this is just how strong the communities are, and the connections we have.”So how can fire resilience be improved? One local who did not want to give his name said the authorities needed to reinstate the larger firebreaks of old, and criticised the lack of fire paddles and fire buckets with sand that used to be stationed in forests and fire-risk areas so passersby could quickly subdue small fires if they spotted them. “Now they don’t do it because of health and safety,” he said. “It’s mad.”View image in fullscreenRachel Robinson, a textile artist who sells her homemade works for a charity at Dunwich beach, says wildfires are not just a local issue, but one for all Europe.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianConservationists are optimistic that a more fire-resilient wildlife habitat can be created in fire-ravaged Suffolk, the Peak District and the Cairngorms.Spencer, who is advising the National Trust, said this fire-resilient habitat could be achieved through rewilding. Releasing beavers, for example, could create large wetlands which would act as fire breaks, just as the wetlands of RSPB Minsmere protected Sizewell B nuclear power station from the Dunwich Heath fire. Other rewilding techniques, such as winter grazing with large herbivores, could reduce thatch and fuel loads. And a more diverse patchwork of deciduous trees, scrub and open land – rather than a monoculture of pine plantations or grouse moors – further reduced fire risk.Why Britain is breathing the world’s wildfire smokeRead moreHowever, Spencer conceded there were no simple solutions on lowland heaths such as Dunwich, which is a naturally sandy dome and cannot be “rewetted” by beavers. Clay-lined ponds, firebreaks and possibly even light, controlled burns in early spring, as practised in the New Forest, could help reduce fire risk, he said.At the RSPB, Rowlands said they were always willing to learn and seek to adapt the recovering heathland to be more fire resilient.“Our charitable objectives are to benefit nature, benefit wildlife and encourage people to enjoy and learn and be aware of wildlife, and we’ll continue to seek to deliver those in a safe and resilient way. With this change in climate, we all need to learn all the time.”Explore more on these topicsSuffolkWildfiresClimate crisisBirdsWildlifeEnglandConservationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Home Office tells Italian man his right to stay in UK after Brexit was ‘error’ | Brexit | The Guardian
description: Man is told he should not have been granted settled status so he can no longer sponsor Brazilian wife to remain
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Man is told he should not have been granted settled status so he can no longer sponsor Brazilian wife to remain
Content: The Home Office has told at least 100 individuals  ‘errors’ were made in awarding them settled status.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Home Office has told at least 100 individuals  ‘errors’ were made in awarding them settled status.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesBrexitHome Office tells Italian man his right to stay in UK after Brexit was ‘error’Man is told he should not have been granted settled status so he can no longer sponsor Brazilian wife to remainLisa O’CarrollSun 9 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 16.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 33-year-old Italian engineer who has been in London since 2018 has been plunged into a battle with theHome Officeafter officials told him they made a mistake allowing him to stay in the UK after Brexit.Fabio, who initially came to London to finish his doctorate and who has built a successful career working on energy and climate change, says he is shocked by the development as he has not broken any rules sinceBrexit.He was given settled status under the EU settlement scheme, permanent residency given to qualifying EU citizens after five years in the UK.The Home Office has now told him this was “in error” – and his wife, who he has been with since arriving in the UK, now has no right to remain as a qualifying family member of someone with settled status.While officials told him he could remain in the UK as they would not be removing his settled status, despite their claim to have made a mistake, the consequence of their error is that his wife now has no right to be in the country with him.“It was quite devastating for both of us. We have been here for a long time. We have done everything by the book, and we’ve always felt very welcome here and I always thought this is somewhere I could grow my career.“It is so upsetting and frustrating to know that we are now in this vulnerable position just as we were thinking of building a family, buying a place for ourselves. Now all our plans must stop,” he said.Fabio, whose name has been changed, is one of more than at least 100 individuals who have been contacted by the Home Office to say an “error” had been made in awarding them status under the EU settlement scheme.The Home Office wrote to him in April as part of a review that appears to have been triggered by his Brazilian wife’s application for status under the EU settlement scheme.He too was born in Brazil but is an Italian dual national by birth and provided a certificate to demonstrate this from the Italian consulate in his settled status application.Officials have now told him the evidence of his Italian citizenship was “insufficient”, and they needed proof that he was Italian before the Brexit cut-off date of 31 December 2020.“It has therefore been decided that, on the basis of the information and evidence currently available, your settled status under the EU settlement scheme was granted in error,” the Home Office said.It added he was no longer “relevant EEA citizen” and he would therefore not be able to sponsor a family member, his wife, to remain in the UK.Catherine Barnard, professor of EU law at the University of Cambridge, said she was astonished by his case, which suggested the Home Office was creating a two-tier system.“This appears to be contrary to the withdrawal agreement on the basis of which his rights were granted. The Home Office cannot punish him by saying he has only second-class rights and, in particular, that he doesn’t have family rights so long as he retains settled status,” she said.She points to article 13 (4) of chapter two of the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, which states “the host state may not impose any limitations or conditions for obtaining, retaining or losing residence rights”.The Home Office has contacted at least 100 people, but possibly many more, to tell them they made “an error” in awarding status.Monique Hawkins, acting chief executive of the3million, said stripping people of rights in such a way would affect “whole families” as people faced a “cliff-edge loss of their rights” without any of the “proportionality assessment” required under the withdrawal agreement.The Independent Monitoring Authority, the statutory body set up to implement the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, has also said it is worried that the Home Office moves “may be incompatible with the EU withdrawal agreement”.It has written to the Home Office to raise “discretionary decisions” about the original applications for post-Brexit residency being made by caseworkers revisiting historic decisions.It has asked any EU citizen who is experiencing difficulties tocontact them.Mala Savjani, partner at Wilson Solicitors in London, which is acting for Fabio, said it was “not clear why” the government was “targeting EU nationals who have dual nationality”.She added: “In order to come to its conclusions, the Home Office is having to make, sometimes unverified, assertions about complex areas of other EU member states’ nationality laws. It is not evident what the policy objective is.”The Home Office said: “It is longstanding government policy that we do not routinely comment on individual cases.”However, officials said the case was “not a breach of the withdrawal agreement” and “those who have been granted EU settlement scheme (EUSS) status in error are not withdrawal agreement beneficiaries and, unless they can [provide] evidence they meet the requirements for that status, have no basis of qualification under the EUSS”.Explore more on these topicsBrexitImmigration and asylumHome OfficeEuropean UnionnewsShareReuse this content

title: London mayor orders council to drop plan to ban new pubs and bars in Soho and West End | London | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Sadiq Khan urges Westminster council to adopt ‘positive vision of economic growth’ of nightlife
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Exclusive: Sadiq Khan urges Westminster council to adopt ‘positive vision of economic growth’ of nightlife
Content: People ‘vertically drinking’ outside the Dog and Duck pub in Soho.Photograph: fotoVoyager/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople ‘vertically drinking’ outside the Dog and Duck pub in Soho.Photograph: fotoVoyager/Getty ImagesLondonLondon mayor orders council to drop plan to ban new pubs and bars in Soho and West EndExclusive: Sadiq Khan urges Westminster council to adopt ‘positive vision of economic growth’ of nightlifeHelena HortonSun 9 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSadiq Khan has ordered Westminster council to scrap a policy that would ban new pubs and bars from opening in Soho and the West End of London.This comes after the Guardian revealedthe council’s new licensing policyasks pubs to stop customers from standing up while consuming beverages, which it calls “vertical drinking”. The policy is under consultation and also asks pubs to have table service rather than allowing orders at the bar.There was widespread anger at the plans to direct those applying to open new bars and restaurants in Westminster to implement the restrictions.The mayor ofLondonhas new powers, granted by the government this year, to intervene in licensing decisions. He is using these for the first time to ask the council to rewrite the draft policy.The Conservative Westminster councillors decree in the draft policy that newly licensed pubs should have to serve last orders at 10pm, and nightclubs should shut by 11.30pm on weekdays and at midnight on weekends.It also labels the entirety of Soho and theWest Endas a “cumulative impact zone”, which means no more pubs, bars or night clubs should be allowed to open unless under exceptional circumstances. This is despite the West End being one of the most popular nightlife areas in Europe.Khan pointed out that Home Office alcohol licensing data shows that only 41 licence applications were made in the West End cumulative impact area in 2023-24, with only 16 granted.Data also shows only 3.5% of applications that went to a licensing subcommittee in Westminster were approved exactly as applied for between 2023 and 2026, and pub and wine bar applications were down 80% in 2022-24.There are also plans to label Mayfair and the Victoria area as special zones where nightlife is restricted due to noise and other “nuisance behaviours”.Khan is asking the council to scrap all of these zones and allow new bars and pubs to open, in his formal response to the consultation. He is also directing it to get rid of the “core hours” policy and allow venues to be open late into the night.The prime minister, Andy Burnham, waded into the rowthis weekwhen he said standing up to drink in pubs was “British life” and should not be curtailed by local councillors.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Guardian view on pubs: football gave them a boost – now they need another | EditorialRead moreKhan said: “Licensing decisions that could make or break our city’s nightlife have, in my view, been skewed towards the interests of a handful of highly vocal residents and councillors, without giving enough weight to the effects on London’s wider economy and culture.”He added that the draft proposals “undermine City Hall’s efforts to make London’s nightlife the best in the world”.In his formal response he asks the council to “remove this cumulative impact policy altogether, instead setting out a positive vision of the economic growth that is being promoted, rather than the activity that is to be restricted”. This means the ban on opening new bars and pubs in Soho and the West End other than in exceptional circumstances would be lifted.The mayor said that Manchester city council is an example of a local authority that allows economic growth and supports bars, pubs and restaurants.Khan said: “Manchester city council’s policy has adopted a more enabling approach, with no core hours policy, no cumulative impact policy and a clear vision for what they are looking to promote across their different local neighbourhoods.“As envisioned by the Licensing Act 2003, there is a presumption to grant licences for pubs, bars, clubs and other premises where applicants can demonstrate effective management and compliance with the licensing objectives.”Westminster city council has been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsLondonHospitality industrySadiq KhanWest EndPubsRestaurantsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Most X accounts posting about Belfast and Southampton unrest were based outside UK | The far right | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Analysis shows 55% of accounts were overseas – and seven of 12 most-read posts came from US
Author: Carmen Aguilar García
Headline: Exclusive: Analysis shows 55% of accounts were overseas – and seven of 12 most-read posts came from US
Content: The analysis underlines that US rightwing actors are seeking to influence the UK and boost their position on X in moments of disorder.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe analysis underlines that US rightwing actors are seeking to influence the UK and boost their position on X in moments of disorder.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe far rightMost X accounts posting about Belfast and Southampton unrest were based outside UKExclusive: Analysis shows 55% of accounts were located overseas – and seven of 12 most-read posts came from USCarmen Aguilar García,Michael Goodier,Pamela DuncanandDan SabbaghSun 9 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than half the accounts that posted on Elon Musk’s X about the rioting in Belfast and the civil disorder inSouthamptonin June were based outside the UK, an analysis by the Guardian can reveal.Of the 8,672 accounts whose combined posts about the events exceeded 1,000 views, just 45.3% were shown as from the UK, according to the social media platform’s own location function.One in six (16.8%) came from the US, 4.5% from Ireland, and about a quarter from all European countries other than the UK.Seven of the 12 most-read tweets aboutBelfastand Southampton came from the US – including one from Musk himself and two other US “alt-right” commentators – while an eighth was linked to North America.The analysis underlines that US rightwing actors are seeking to influence the UK and boost their position onXin moments of disorder – an exploitation of flashpoint events that has only intermittently attracted political attention in Britain.Q&AMethodologyShowThe Guardian collected 43,000 tweets mentioning Belfast, Southampton, Henry Nowak or Vickrum Digwa posted on X during the period of the unrest in both cities.This covered the period from 2 June to the end of 3 June for Southampton and from the evening of 8 June to the end of 9 June for Belfast.For X accounts whose combined tweets reached more than 1,000 views, we extracted their location and the number of times they have changed their username as shown in the “about this account” tab.Using a large language model (LLM), the team first classified which posts were directly related to the protests in Belfast and Southampton, and then categorised them as containing explicit or implicit racist language or anti-immigration comments. For those about Belfast, we also classified tweets as containing calls inciting to violence.A team of three people manually verified more than 5,500 posts, statistically testing the accuracy of the model to be robust and in line with academic standards.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Nearly a third of all 43,000 posts on X relating to the two incidents contained racist or anti-immigration comments. Almost one in 10 relating to Belfast contained calls for violence or paramilitary or vigilante action.Imran Ahmed, the chief executive of the Centre for Countering Digital Hate, said the data demonstrated that X had become “a weapon of choice” for hostile foreign actors seeking to manipulate shocking and divisive content.Their goal, he added, was “to amplify local tragedies and crises, intensify racist narratives, and incite violence in communities they have never set foot in and to whom they have no real connection.”A post from Musk after the life sentencing of the killer of 18-year-old Henry Nowak, who had been falsely accused of racism by police after being stabbed in Southampton, has been viewed more than 28m times.“Legacy mainstream media, same ones who wrote about George Floyd millions of times, are dead silent about Nowak,” Musk posted shortly before 3pm on 2 June, in effect promoting his own platform at a time of heightened tension and disorder in the Hampshire port.View image in fullscreenElon Musk posted about race and immigration in the UK twice as often as he did about SpaceX in the run-up to the aerospace company’s IPO in June.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersEleven police officers were injuredon the night of 2 June in Southampton as people claiming to protest over Nowak’s murder marched to the site of his death. This followed a rally, addressed by the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, outside the city’s main police station.Musk is based in the US and has not visited the UK since November 2023. A Guardian analysislast monthfound he posted about race and immigration in the UK twice as often as he did about SpaceX in the run-up to the aerospace company’s initial public offering in June.Security experts including Fiona Hill, a former adviser to the US and UK governments, have warned that the UK is asoft target for online manipulationby overseas actors because it does not take the idea of civil, or “psychological”, defence seriously.Dr Julia Ebner, a researcher at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue and the University of Oxford, said flashpoint episodes such as in Southampton and Belfast had become “strategic events” for far-right actors seeking to amplify and exploit them.“They are using the UK as a negative example, smearing the UK to promote their own narratives of western civilisational decay or social collapse,” Ebner said. “But the other purpose is to influence UK politics, and European politics more widely,” using crisis moments to “promote a strong, strengthened far-right wave across the world”.Four of the top 12 most-seen tweets came from UK accounts: two were by the leader of the Restore Britain party, Rupert Lowe, whom Musk has endorsed; another was from GB News, while the most popular, with 37.6m views, was written by the “anti-woke” rightwing political commentatorKonstantin Kisin.Other accounts located in the US were anonymous, though familiar. @EndWokeness posted a blurry still image of a black man attacking a white man in Belfast on 8 June, saying the full video was “too graphic” to post. It attracted 16.3m views.The assault, a stabbing in which the victim, Stephen Ogilvie, lost an eye, promptedthree nights of racially motivated riotingtargeting non-white people in Belfast. An asylum seeker from Sudan was charged with attempted murder and at least 23 people were arrested.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA vehicle set alight during riots in Belfast in June.Photograph: Peter Morrison/APThe @EndWokeness account, which has 3.9m followers, was cited by aparliamentary committeeafter it amplified a false claim that the 2024 attack in Southport, in which three girls were killed, was carried out by a Muslim man.The account has been linked byan open source analystto Jack Posobiec, a rightwing influencer who promoted the Pizzagate conspiracy, a false accusation that leading US Democrats were engaged in satanic child abuse at a child-friendly pizza restaurant in Washington DC.Another leading poster was the US rightwing influencer Benny Johnson, who accused the New York Times of writing nothing about Nowak and thousands of pieces about the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis in 2020 – though Nowak was murdered in the UK.The analysis of the most-viewed accounts did not reveal any posts from Russia or China – bothcountries that have been behind online disinformation campaigns – though it is possible that posters successfully disguised their locations using virtual private networks (VPNs).X shows location data for most profiles, inferred by the platform from user IP addresses, though government accounts are excluded. Last November, after the feature was introduced, X’s then head of product,Nikita Bier, said it was more than 99% accurate. When it was launched, it revealed that some pro-Scottish-independence accounts were based in Iran.But there weresigns of inauthenticityin popular posts. Two of the top most-seen tweets came from the US-based C3 (@C_3C_3) account, accusing “legacy media” of not reporting about the Nowak case. Its profile picture is a baby wearing a Make America Great Again cap; the username has changed 14 times previously.One UK account, which tweeted at least six times about the murder of Nowak, with almost 3,800 combined views, had changed its name more than 400 times. NewsSceneUK – subsequently changed to BritifyFooty – wrote in one tweet about the “huge crowd of patriots outside #Southampton Police Station”.Accounts posting from overseas that changed their usernames more than 20 times included one in Kenya that wrote after the Belfast stabbing: “When the state fails to protect people, the streets find their own language.” Another, from Europe, described the Nowak case as “a globalized, calculated and malicious evil” affecting “every White person and every White nation”.Close to a third – about 13,000 – of the Belfast and Southampton tweets, whether from the UK or abroad, were racist or anti-immigrant, according to the Guardian analysis. When analysed separately, a quarter of the posts that were only about Southampton were racist or anti-immigrant, compared with a third of those that were only about Belfast.One UK-based poster, writing a day after the Belfast stabbing, claimed they hoped the attacker was British-born because “race is the issue, not immigration status”. The post registered 2m views.Valerie Wirtschafter, an expert on online foreign influence operations from the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank, said she believed violent events such as those in Belfast and Southampton were “a point of exploitation” in which “outside agitators” had an opportunity to make a disproportionate impact.Their position was helped by X and other social media companies cutting content moderation, she said, but in particular by “algorithms and how they collide with the basic cognitive processes of humans. We are more attracted to things that are shocking.”Explore more on these topicsThe far rightXElon MuskFar rightFar right (US)InternetBelfastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Christine Borland obituary | Art | The Guardian
description: Turner prize nominee whose installations, sculptures and films returned repeatedly to the histories embedded within bodies
Author: Sorcha Dallas
Headline: Turner prize nominee whose installations, sculptures and films returned repeatedly to the histories embedded within bodies
Content: English Family China, 1998, by Christine Borland, on display at Turner: Always Contemporary, Walker Art Gallery, Liverpool, 2025.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEnglish Family China, 1998, by Christine Borland, on display at Turner: Always Contemporary, Walker Art Gallery, Liverpool, 2025.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianArtObituaryChristine Borland obituaryTurner prize nominee whose installations, sculptures and films returned repeatedly to the histories embedded within bodiesSorcha DallasSun 9 Aug 2026 11.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 11.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1994, Christine Borland, who has died aged 61 of cancer, opened her first solo exhibition at Tramway in Glasgow. Its starting point was a mail-order catalogue through which human skeletons could be legally purchased for medical teaching.The discovery that a person’s remains could be bought anonymously through the post gave rise to one of the defining questions of her career. Working with forensic experts, police and medical professionals, Borland attempted to reconstruct the life behind one such skeleton, producing a bronze facial reconstruction alongside the original bones.View image in fullscreenChristine Borland.Photograph: Jeremy Sutton Hibbert/ShutterstockThe work,From Life, did not solve a mystery so much as expose one, asking how identity is lost, who is remembered and what obligations remain towards the dead. When it was nominated for the Turner prize in 1997, Borland was recognised as one of the most original voices in British contemporary art.She occupied a singular place within the generation that transformed British art during the 1990s. While many of the Young British Artists became associated with provocation, spectacle or autobiography, she pursued another path altogether.Her work emerged through sustained collaborations with technical experts – including museum curators and archivists – treating science not as subject matter but as a partner in artistic inquiry. Long before interdisciplinary practice became commonplace, she demonstrated how artists could work alongside researchers to explore questions that neither discipline could answer alone.Her installations, sculptures and films returned repeatedly to the histories embedded within bodies, specimens and collections. Rather than celebrating scientific certainty, they revealed the ambiguities, ethical responsibilities and acts of interpretation that underpin medical knowledge itself.Among her most affecting works wasPhantom Twins(1997), inspired by 19th-century obstetric teaching models used to train midwives. Borland recreated these instructional objects as leather dolls containing foetal skeletons, transforming instruments of medical education into sculptures that were at once memorials, anatomical studies and reflections on care, loss and the body’s vulnerability.View image in fullscreenBorland’s artwork The Edinburgh Seven Tapestry, celebrating the seven Edinburgh University students who were the first women to study medicine, on display at the Victoria & Albert Museum, London, 2024.Photograph: Guy Bell/Rex/ShutterstockInThe Dead Teach the Living(1997), she questioned the supposed objectivity of forensic reconstruction by exposing the assumptions that shape representations of race and identity.L’Homme Double(1997) invited six sculptors to reconstruct the face of the notorious Nazi medical experimenter Josef Mengele from identical forensic evidence. Each produced a different likeness, demonstrating that interpretation enters even the most rigorous scientific procedures. WithGiant and Fairy Tales(1998), she revisited the lives of two 19th-century people exhibited during their lifetimes as curiosities before their remains entered medical collections, restoring individuality to people history had reduced to specimens.Throughout her work, materials carried meanings of their own. Glass, bronze, porcelain, leather, plaster and bone were chosen not simply for their appearance but for the histories they embodied. Craig Richardson, a scholar of Scottish art, remarked that Borland’s “precise aesthetic serves knowledge”, a perceptive description of an art in which emotional force emerged not through spectacle but through careful attention.View image in fullscreenBorland and Brody Condon’s installation Daughters of Decayed Tradesmen, in the Watchtower, New Calton Burial Ground, Edinburgh, 2013.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianBorn in Darvel, Ayrshire, Christine was the daughter of Chrissie and John Borland,who worked in lace factories.She grew up exploring the countryside, developing an early fascination with plants, ecology and the interconnectedness of living things. After studying environmental art at Glasgow School of Art (1983-87) she took amaster of fine arts degree(1988) at the University of Ulster in Belfast. Living in the city during the Troubles left a lasting impression. Her installationA Lifetime of Love(1993), first shown at Aperto ’93, a show within the Venice Biennale, consisted of worn blankets collected during those years, transforming ordinary objects associated with comfort into quiet witnesses to conflict, memory and care.Returning to Glasgow, Borland served on the artist-run committee of Transmission Gallery (1989-91), helping to foster the city as an international centre for contemporary art.Recognition followed steadily, and she also taught at Duncan of Jordanstone College of Art & Design, Dundee, and Glasgow School of Art in the early 1990s, moving on to academic research in Glasgow (2000-11).In 2012she was appointed professor of fine art atNorthumbria University, Newcastle upon Tyne.As the medical humanities emerged as a field bringing together medicine, history, ethics and the arts, Borland’s work became an important point of reference, showing how art could deepen understanding of care, mortality and human dignity, not by illustrating it, but by asking different questions of it.Those who worked with Borland remembered not only her scholarship but her generosity. Patient, curious and quietly humorous, she listened as carefully as she observed.After being diagnosed with cancer in 2024, Borland continued to work with the same intellectual openness on how we confront mortality, how care is practised and how individual lives retain their dignity even in the face of illness, death or institutional systems that risk reducing people to objects. She changed the way contemporary art could engage with medicine, and in doing so created one of the most distinctive bodies of work in contemporary British art.In 2012 she married the artist Ross Sinclair, who had been her partner since 1994. He survives her, along with their three daughters, Grace, Agnes and Jean.Christine Margaret Borland, artist, born 3 May 1965; died 19 July 2026Explore more on these topicsArtTextile artSculptureCeramicsobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Pakistani grooming gang suspect ‘refuses to give date for return to UK’ | UK news | The Guardian
description: Rukhsar Ahmed was recently elected an MP in Pakistan while on bail over alleged child rape in 1990s Manchester
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Rukhsar Ahmed was recently elected an MP in Pakistan while on bail over alleged child rape in 1990s Manchester
Content: Rukhsar Ahmed is the owner of a former restaurant, the Gujjar Palace, near Manchester’s curry mile.Photograph: SuppliedView image in fullscreenRukhsar Ahmed is the owner of a former restaurant, the Gujjar Palace, near Manchester’s curry mile.Photograph: SuppliedUK newsPakistani grooming gang suspect ‘refuses to give date for return to UK’Rukhsar Ahmed was recently elected an MP in Pakistan while on bail over alleged child rape in 1990s ManchesterShah Meer BalochandRajeev SyalSun 9 Aug 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA grooming gang suspect released on bail in the UK and then re-elected as an MP in Pakistan has reportedly declined to say when he would return to face rape charges.The Guardian disclosed that Rukhsar Ahmed, a former Pakistan state minister, was arrested at Manchester airport in July 2024 on suspicion of raping and trafficking at least two underage girls from care homes in the city’s Rusholme area during the 1990s.He was released on bail and flew to Pakistan nearly two months ago, missing an appointment at a police station after telling officers he was too unwell to fly back to the UK.He was elected an MP for prime minister Shehbaz Sharif’s centre-right Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz party days later.He did not respond to requests for a comment when approached by the Guardian last week.View image in fullscreenRukhsar Ahmed.Photograph: SuppliedIt emerged on Sunday that Ahmed, 61, had been located in his office in Khari Sharif, a village in Mirpur district.According to the Mail on Sunday, he told a reporter he would fly back to Britain to meet his bail conditions, but declined to give a date. “Everything is with my legal team in Manchester and London, they told me I can’t discuss this,” he told the newspaper.“What they done, this media in the United Kingdom and Europe, is out of order. I have not been convicted of anything nor charged for anything, so what is going on? I don’t want to discuss it, because if I discuss it, things may go wrong.”Asked directly whether he had raped two underage girls, he refused to answer, telling the reporter: “You are doing wrong now, I told you not to talk to me like this … please don’t talk to me like this, I told you I have nothing to do with it, OK.”Ahmed published a statement on his Facebook account on Friday. It read: “I categorically deny all the allegations against me and will address these matters through the appropriate forums. On legal advice, I will not comment further while these matters remain ongoing.”Ahmed was a minister in various state governments from 2006 until he lost his seat in 2021.The Guardian understands that Greater Manchester police (GMP) had wanted to restrict Ahmed’s ability to travel abroad as part of his bail conditions, but a judge rejected tougher measures in July 2024.Ahmed was arrested at Manchester airport on 18 July 2024 in relation to past child sexual abuse allegations linked to the Rusholme area, where he lived for many years.According to the report, he received a string of visitors in his office. He is the owner of a former restaurant, the Gujjar Palace, near Manchester’s curry mile.The ongoing investigation relates to allegations from several women about sexual abuse of children at care homes in the early 1990s, when Ahmed was in his late 20s.He is understood to be expected to answer police bail in the next six weeks. If he does not attend, GMP may issue a warrant for his arrest or take steps to extradite him.The Guardian has approached Ahmed for comment again.Richard Scorer, the head of abuse law at Slater and Gordon who has acted in many Manchester grooming gang cases said: “Rusholme has regularly featured in grooming gang investigations over the past 30 years, with many cases involving allegations of children being abused in and around the area.“Not all of those allegations have been adequately investigated. I hope that a comprehensive investigation is taking place here”.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Typhoon Dolphin makes landfall in China as its strongest storm this year | China | The Guardian
description: Tropical cyclone brings torrential rain and high winds to east coast after hitting Japan’s southern Okinawa province
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Tropical cyclone brings torrential rain and high winds to east coast after hitting Japan’s southern Okinawa province
Content: People watch huge waves hit a waterfront in Sanmen county, Zhejiang province, as Typhoon Dolphin approachesPhotograph: cnsphoto/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople watch huge waves hit a waterfront in Sanmen county, Zhejiang province, as Typhoon Dolphin approachesPhotograph: cnsphoto/ReutersChinaTyphoon Dolphin makes landfall in China as its strongest storm this yearTropical cyclone brings torrential rain and high winds to east coast after hitting Japan’s southern Okinawa provinceReuters in BeijingSun 9 Aug 2026 14.13 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 14.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTyphoon Dolphin, the most powerful tropical cyclone to hitChinathis year, has made landfall on the country’s east coast, bringing torrential rain and strong ⁠winds and triggering warnings ​of flooding and landslides.The storm has already swept through Japan’s southern Okinawa prefecture, injuring six people and cutting power to more than 50,000 buildings.Dolphin made landfall near Yuhuan in Zhejiang province at about ⁠5:30pm (0930 GMT) on Sunday, China’s meteorological authorities said. It brought maximum sustained winds of 94mph (151 km/h) near its centre at landfall, equivalent to a category 1 hurricane on the Saffir-Simpson scale.In addition to evacuating at least 30,300 people, Shanghai has cancelled about 1,500 flights, according to the flight-tracking data provider VariFlight.View image in fullscreenA struggles against high winds and driving rain in Dongsha, Zhejiang province, as Typhoon Dolphin makes landfall.Photograph: Huang Zongzhi/Xinhua/APAuthorities moved offshore ⁠workers to safety, ordered vessels back to port and increased checks at reservoirs, mountain streams, landslide-prone areas, construction sites and tourist locations.Torrential ​rain is forecast for Monday across Zhejiang, Shanghai, northern Fujian, ‌north-eastern Jiangxi, central and southern Anhui, and ‌much of Jiangsu. Parts of central and eastern Zhejiang could receive 250-500 mm (10-20 inches) of rain, according to forecasters.Dolphin was forecast to track ‌westward before slowing over central and south-western China and gradually losing strength, the chief forecaster at the National Meteorological Centre, Wang Haiping, told the state broadcaster CCTV.That could prolong heavy rain and increase the risk of flooding and landslides, especially in mountainous areas and along smaller rivers.1:12Typhoon Dolphin batters parts of east and south-east Asia – videoTransport was widely disrupted across the east of the country and more than a million people were evacuated from their homes.A 42-year-old tourist from Guangdong, surnamed Chen, said he had been stranded in Shanghai ‌after his family’s flight, scheduled to depart on Sunday, was cancelled.He said the family had been rebooked on a flight at 10pm on Monday, although they were unsure whether it would be able ​to take off.“To us Guangdong people, this typhoon is as ordinary as having a meal and feeling the wind. It’s just part of everyday life,” he said, adding that the storm did not appear particularly strong by the standards of China’s southern coast.View image in fullscreenA woman wades through floodwater in Shanghai.Photograph: cnsphoto/ReutersIn neighbouring Zhejiang province, the city of Wenzhou relocated more than 900,000 people and opened more than 1,000 emergency shelters. In Fujian province, authorities evacuated 98,900 people from high-risk areas, according to Xinhua.Fujian maritime authorities ​said 55 coastal passenger ferry routes had been suspended, ​all 115 offshore construction projects halted and 290 construction ​vessels moved to sheltered waters.The water resources ministry said the Qiantang, Yong, Jiao and Shuiyang rivers could experience major ​flooding, while smaller rivers in the ‌hardest-hit areas could rise above ​warning levels.Authorities issued an alert for the risk of geological disasters in parts of Zhejiang. Residents in areas covered by a red mountain-torrent warning were told to follow local evacuation orders.Shanghai’s Yangshan port had cleared ships from its berths and moved more than 500 small and medium-sized vessels to shelter as Dolphin approached, the city’s maritime safety administration said.Scientists say global warming has made extreme weather more likely, including more powerful typhoons.Explore more on these topicsChinaAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Italy condemns Spain’s ‘unacceptable’ border controls as Ceuta fallout intensifies | Migration | The Guardian
description: Travellers caught up in migration row as Madrid introduces checks on visitors from Italy in retaliation for Rome’s move
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Travellers caught up in migration row as Madrid introduces checks on visitors from Italy in retaliation for Rome’s move
Content: Spanish police check the documents of travellers from Italy at Madrid-Barajas airport.Photograph: Spanish Police/ReutersView image in fullscreenSpanish police check the documents of travellers from Italy at Madrid-Barajas airport.Photograph: Spanish Police/ReutersMigrationItaly condemns Spain’s ‘unacceptable’ border controls as Ceuta fallout intensifiesTravellers caught up in migration row as Madrid introduces checks on visitors from Italy in retaliation for Rome’s moveAshifa Kassamin MadridSun 9 Aug 2026 10.59 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleItaly’s foreign minister has called Spain’s decision to impose retaliatory checks on travellers fromItaly“incomprehensible and completely unacceptable” as people making their way between the two EU countries were left grappling with the effects of the escalating feud.Spain startedcarrying out spot checkson visitors from Italy at midnight on Saturday. The tit-for-tat move came after Rome infuriated Madridby launching checkson 1 August for travellers from Spain in response to the recent influxof about 72,000 peopleinto Ceuta, a Spanish territory in north Africa.Spanish officials were swift to point out that the Italian checks made little sense, given that by 1 August, the border in Ceuta was back under control and the vast majority of those who had arrived had been returned toMorocco. Ceuta is not part of the Schengen free-movement zone, Madrid has repeatedly stressed, meaning there is little chance of onward travel to continental Europe without EU citizenship or residency.‘We have no tents or blankets’: Ceuta migrants struggle to survive brutal heat and freezing nightsRead moreThe checks by Italy had led to “intolerable” scenes at Italian airports, Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, told reporters. “This measure is, first and foremost, an attack on the dignity of the Spanish people, but, secondly, it is a torpedo fired at the hull of European unity,” he said.In an interviewpublished on Sundayin La Stampa, Italy’s foreign minister defended the move by Rome. “Some order needs to be brought in: we’re not against Spain, but we have a duty to protect our borders,” said Antonio Tajani, voicing concerns about some of the migrants potentially holding jihadist views. “What is incomprehensible and completely unacceptable is Spain’s reaction.”He pushed back against the suggestion that Rome’s actions were symbolic, given the remote possibility of anyone making it to Italy from Ceuta. “Where do they go after arriving inSpain? Italy, as a destination, is the country most at risk. We’re not Germany or Norway.”When asked if Italy’s response was proportionate, Tajani pointed to the reports of fresh calls online for a mid-August mass crossing. “We hope to be able to lift the suspension soon, as soon as the risk is no longer present,” he said.Italy’s interior minister publicly praised Spain last week for its handling of the crisis, but Tajani blasted Spain for not being “as vigilant” as it should have been.View image in fullscreenPassengers caught up in the border controls speak to the media in Madrid.Photograph: Chema Moya/EPAHe linked the influx to Spain’s recent regularisation programme, describingthe move to provide working migrants with papersas a “negative message that puts everyone’s safety at risk,” despite the EU’searlier dismissalof any connection between the Ceuta influx and regularisation.Italy’s government has long criticised Spain’s efforts to regularise undocumented migrants, even as it quietly works on similar plans to give nearly 1.1 million work permits to foreign workers by 2028. Speaking to the Financial Times, oneresearcher describedthe Italian government’s efforts as a “disguised amnesty.”Spain and Italy both have a long history of regularisation programmes. In 2002, Tajani’s party, Forza Italia,carried outone of Italy’s largest such programmes, issuing just over 634,000 permits.Even so, the perception of differences in their approach to migration has pitted Madrid and Rome against each other, with Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, seeking to position herself as a hardliner on migration while Spain’s Pedro Sánchez – who hasdefended the needfor foreign workers to grow Spain’s economy and stave off demographic collapse – said Italy had registered the highest number of irregular crossings in recent years in the EU, with figures that are double those of Spain.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMigrants who crossed into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in north Africa last month.Photograph: Pedro Nunes/ReutersIn recent days, the row has widened to include people making their way between the two countries, a route used by more than 8 million last year.“It’s ridiculous that we’re in this situation,” Elisa Fabbri, 41,told Spanish news siteEldiario.es as she left Madrid-Barajas airport on Saturday. Israel Pérez, a Cuban-born Spanish citizen, described it as an “absurd spiral” that risked pulling everyone down. “If we keep imposing checks on each other, in the end we’ll all end up losing,” he said. “This shouldn’t be happening between two European countries.”In Italy, opposition politicians accused Meloni of unleashing an “unfounded diplomatic crisis” that would ultimately harm Italians. “The cynical propaganda of the Meloni government has produced what was predictable: a boomerang that Italians will pay dearly for,” said Nicola Fratoianni, the leader of the Greens and Left Alliance. “This is a colossal mistake.”The EU commissioner for migration, Magnus Brunner, said on Saturday that he had been in contact with the interior ministers of the two countries. “Both confirmed that the internal border controls are temporary,” he said on social media. “Spanish authorities assured us the events in Ceuta will have no lasting effect on the Schengen area. That is why there are signals from Italy that controls could be lifted soon.”The row between Rome and Madrid after the events in Ceuta hints at sensitivities over migration across the EU, particularly as governments in Italy, France and Poland prepare to face off against far-right challengers in upcoming elections.But the latest Eurobarometer poll, which tracks public opinions every quarter, suggests the focus on migration may be out of step with Europeans’ top priorities. Whenasked about the topicsthat should be a priority for the European parliament, migration ranked sixth, behind issues such as the cost of living, the defence and security of the EU and the economy and job creation.Explore more on these topicsMigrationEuropeSpainItalyEuropean UnionGiorgia MeloniPedro SáncheznewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘You’re hit with a slam of shadow’: Nasa’s air mission to capture rare eclipse data | Solar eclipses | The Guardian
description: Two aviators will take off from Iceland to photograph the sun while flying at high altitude along solar eclipse’s path
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: Two aviators will take off from Iceland to photograph the sun while flying at high altitude along solar eclipse’s path
Content: The sun behind the moon during the Great North American Eclipse in April 2024, seen from in Mazatlan, Mexico.Photograph: Héctor Vivas/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe sun behind the moon during the Great North American Eclipse in April 2024, seen from in Mazatlan, Mexico.Photograph: Héctor Vivas/Getty ImagesSolar eclipses‘You’re hit with a slam of shadow’: Nasa’s air mission to capture rare eclipse dataTwo aviators will take off from Iceland to photograph the sun while flying at high altitude along solar eclipse’s pathIan SampleScience editorSun 9 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter lunch on Wednesday, two Nasa aviators will climb into a research plane and take off from Keflavik airport on a western tip ofIceland. They will climb north towards Greenland and then bank to head south on a gently curving course 40 miles (64km) off the Icelandic coast.Their mission can be described as chasing an eclipse, but in reality the eclipse is chasing them. As the plane cruises at 50,000ft (15,000 metres), the shadow of the moon will race up from behind, crossing the ocean below at more than 2,000mph (3,200km/h). The pilot will aim to reach the point of greatest eclipse, when the largest fraction of the sun is obscured by the moon, at the moment the shadow catches up with them.View image in fullscreenA Nasa aviator onboard a research plane. The mission to capture images of the eclipse on Wednesday is due to fly at altitudes of 50,000ft.Photograph: NASAFor anyone standing directly beneath – or treading water, given the geography – the world will go dark for 2 minutes 18 seconds. But by flying at 460mph along the path of the eclipse, the pilot can extend totality to nearly 3 minutes. Which gives them more time to observe the blotted-out sun.Cary Klemm, a sensor equipment operator at Nasa’s JohnsonSpaceCenter in Houston, who has flown eclipse missions in the past, described the experience at high altitude: “The big difference is that in the cockpit of an aircraft at 50,000 feet, it’s very bright in the sun. There are no clouds above you, and then all of a sudden, you’re hit with this slam of shadow.”View image in fullscreenA WB-57 aircraft at Ellington Field outside Houston, Texas.Photograph: James Blair/Nasa/JSC“You feel the temperature drop off; you’ll notice that you need more light from your instruments, and it’s kind of a weird, eerie shadow that you’re surrounded by. It wraps around the view in the cockpit,” he added.Hidden in the nose cone of the WB-57 aircraft are four cameras. These will take dozens of pictures a second of the occluded sun in different wavelengths of light. The images should capture large, looping ribbons of plasma called prominences and magnetic explosions called nanoflares. Only with the glare of the sun’s disc blocked out are such observations possible.Graphic showing path of eclipse“I’m super-excited,” said Dr Amir Caspi, the principal investigator on the mission at Southwest Research Institute in Boulder, Colorado. “Solar eclipses give us an opportunity to do science we couldn’t do at any other time.”Despite the name, nanoflares pack a punch, each releasing thousands of atomic bombs’ worth of energy as they go off around the sun. The flares at least partly explain one of the sun’s greatest mysteries: why the corona or outer atmosphere is so hot, at more than 1,000,000C, while the surface is a mere 6,000C.View image in fullscreenA Nasa centre at Ellington Field outside Houston, Texas.Photograph: James Blair/Nasa/JSCFor these observations, aircraft are hard to beat. Ground-based cameras have clouds to contend with and atmospheric interference. Space-based cameras are above such concerns, but can send back only so much data. “As you can imagine, this is terabytes of information,” Caspi said.The WB-57 is based on the English Electric Canberra bomber, the RAF’s cold war tactical nuclear strike aircraft, and flies above the clouds in the stratosphere. But other planes have been used for eclipse missions. In 1923, the US navy sent a fleet of biplanes to observe an eclipse, without much success. Fifty years later, scientists persuaded the French to cut holes in the roof of a Concorde prototype; hurtling over the Sahara at Mach 2, they kept up with an eclipse shadow for 74 minutes.View image in fullscreenConcorde passengers view the 1999 eclipse from 55,000 feet over the Atlantic.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyThe more scientists learn about the sun, the better they should be able to grasp space weather, the barrage of energetic particles and radiation that are hazardous to astronauts, satellites and even power grids and communications on Earth. Caspi said: “Understanding space weather is critical for us as a technological species, and it starts with understanding the processes at the sun.”Eclipses are not all about science though. “What percentage of humanity has ever witnessed a total solar eclipse? It’s a fraction of a fraction of a per cent,” Caspi said. “If you’re part of that rare group, you’re connected to the Earth and the sun and the solar system. It’s mind-blowing. It makes you feel very special, but also very small because you are this little mote in the universe.”Explore more on these topicsSolar eclipsesAstronomyNasaSpaceIcelandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Chinese EV sales surge to new high in Europe putting tariffs under scrutiny | Automotive industry | The Guardian
description: Imports this year now account for 14% of the market amid claims vehicles are being dumped in the EU and UK
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Imports this year now account for 14% of the market amid claims vehicles are being dumped in the EU and UK
Content: A Leapmotor production line in Jinhua, China. The company has increased sales in Italy by exploiting a purchase subsidy scheme.Photograph: VCG/GettyView image in fullscreenA Leapmotor production line in Jinhua, China. The company has increased sales in Italy by exploiting a purchase subsidy scheme.Photograph: VCG/GettyAutomotive industryChinese EV sales surge to new high in Europe putting tariffs under scrutinyImports this year now account for 14% of the market amid claims vehicles are being dumped in the EU and UKJasper JollySun 9 Aug 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 11.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChinese electric car sales have risen acrossEuropeto a record high driven by strong demand and low tariffs in the UK and a surge in buyers in Italy.Against a backdrop of claims that Chinese carmakers are “dumping” state-subsidised vehicles in the EU and UK to gain market share, the figures will give impetus to calls for quotas and higher tariffs to protect European manufacturers.The share of electric cars sold by Chinese brands rose to 14.2% across western European markets – or one in every seven battery electric vehicles (BEVs) – in the first five months of this year, according to Schmidt Automotive Research. The 171,800 sales represented an increase in market share of nearly five percentage points versus the same period in 2025.Brands including BYD, Chery, SAIC and Xpeng have targeted Europe for exports, as theChinese industry seeks to dominatethe global electric vehicle market. This has put traditionalEuropean manufacturers under intense pressurewhen tougher emissions rules are forcing them to increase their own BEV sales.Chart showing how China has increased its market share in electric vehicle sales in Europe from 9.4% to 14.2%The increase in European sales comes despiteEU tariffs of up to 35.3%for electric cars made by some Chinese manufacturers, on top of the standard 10% import duty.The UK is the largest European market for Chinese cars because the government hasdeclined to follow the EU’s leadin imposing extra levies. The UK accounted for a quarter of Chinese BEV sales across the 18 biggest Western European markets.AlthoughItalyaccounted for a fifth of the total, Schmidt said this was an “anomaly”. One manufacturer, Leapmotor, sent thousands of its cheap T03 electric cars into the country to take advantage of purchase subsidies from the government. The subsidies meant that the T03 was as cheap as €5,000 at one point – far below even the most keenly priced models sold by rivals.Chinese manufacturers have sold more than 120 different models in Europe this year – compared with about 100 from European brands.However, Matthias Schmidt, the founder of Schmidt research, said China’s share of the BEV market may have peaked, in part because they have shifted some of their focus to plug-in hybrid electric vehicles. PHEVs, which combine a polluting petrol engine with a smaller battery, are not yet subject to EU tariffs.“I think they are hitting a wall when it comes to pure electric models,” said Schmidt. “They will prioritise PHEVs over the next 12 months given hybrids are omitted from extra tariffs placed on BEVs only. With that loophole set to close in the next 12 months, they will aim to maximise that gap in the door for as long as possible.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Given shipping capacity remains limited, more PHEVs means fewer BEVs, which have likely peaked for now. BEVs will take priority again once local EU production comes online.”Oliver Blume, the chief executive of Volkswagen, last month called for that to change. Blume said European PHEVs were uncompetitive against Chinese equivalents. The German newspaper Handelsblatt has reported that the EU is considering extending the levies to PHEVs.The figures also showed a rebound in sales for Tesla across Europe. The US carmaker suffered a steep decline in sales last year amid abacklash against chief executive Elon Musk’s alliancewith Donald Trump and European far-right political parties.Tesla sales rose by 60% year-on-year, helped by an increase in demand for cheaper versions of its Model 3 and Model Y. The Model Y was the bestselling individual model across Europe during the period.Explore more on these topicsAutomotive industryElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsEuropeChinaItalyManufacturing sectorAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Inside a meme factory: meet one of thousands of Indonesians trading political outrage clicks for Facebook cash | Social media | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Adira says she doesn’t know much about her target countries or even know who their leaders are. Instead she’s chasing money from Meta, which pays for engagement
Author: Ariel Bogle
Headline: Exclusive: Adira says she doesn’t know much about her target countries or even know who their leaders are. Instead she’s chasing money from Meta, which pays for engagement
Content: ‘We are seeking dollars,’ one Indonesian content creator says of posting content about Australian and US politics.Composite: Victoria Hart/Guardian design/Getty Images/FacebookView image in fullscreen‘We are seeking dollars,’ one Indonesian content creator says of posting content about Australian and US politics.Composite: Victoria Hart/Guardian design/Getty Images/FacebookSocial mediaInside a meme factory: meet one of thousands of Indonesians trading political outrage clicks for Facebook cashExclusive:Adira says she doesn’t know much about her target countries or even know who their leaders are. Instead she’s chasing money from Meta, which pays for engagementAriel Bogleand Aqwam F HanifanSun 9 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 19.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom her home in West Java, Adira* often starts the day with aFacebookpost about coffee and the busy day ahead. Then she gets to work.In a Facebook group called Team Pauline Hanson, she shares a photo of the Australian senator and One Nation leader and asks its almost 26,000 members for thoughts about Hanson’scomments about Islamand Australia’s way of life.She shares an AI-generated image of a child in a hijab, like the one she wears in her account’s profile picture, in a Facebook group for Charlie Kirk fans. The little girl is holding a sign that asks if it’s OK to serve bacon in school if Muslim students are present.She posts in groups with titles including “I love the USA!”, “JD VANCE 2028” and “Pete Hegseth Fans” but also others focused on creating AI-generated images of attractive pilots.In June,the Guardian revealedthat some of the largest One Nation supporter groups on Facebook appeared to be run by and full of overseas creators who monetise content – many based in Indonesia.Pro-One Nation Facebook groups appear to be run by foreign ‘meme factories’ that monetise contentRead moreTo better understand these meme factories, the Guardian has spoken to Adira, whose account is among the most prolific in one of the largest groups.Adira says she is not getting paid by an agency – instead she is chasing money fromMeta, which can pay for content engagement through its creator program. Nor, she claims, is she getting instructions about which campaigns to post about.“We don’t follow politics overseas, we don’t want to be involved,” she says. “We just, you know, try to earn more dollars. There is no intention to the right or to the left.”According to her explanation of the ecosystem, Adira is in groups on Facebook and WhatsApp with other Indonesians where advice is shared about which groups to post in.Some of these groups have “leaders” who can provide videos and images and give advice about which groups might be worthwhile to post in – although Adira does not answer questions about who these leaders might be and who they might work for.The creators also find groups to post in through platform recommendations. “If I post something, suggested groups will show up,” she says. “I saw the Pauline group and the dollars were good, then you look for other groups with Pauline.”Sometimes she slips up. In TeamPauline Hansonin July she shared a post about a Muslim woman leaving the US because of “Trump’s hate for Muslims” rather than content tailored for an Australian audience.Quick GuideContact us about this storyShowThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know.If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods.Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don't already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDrop, instant messengers, email, telephone and postIf you can safely use the Tor network without being observed or monitored, you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Illustration: Guardian Design / Rich CousinsWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The group, which was founded in April, describes itself as a space for those “who admire the leadership and vision of Pauline Hanson”.The presence of so many Indonesian women in these groups sometimes causes problems, Adira says: “People from overseas get suspicious.”She is part of Indonesia’s infamous “buzzer” economy – accounts that amplify certain messages on social media, usually while hiding their financial incentives.This cyber army is made up of creators who may be trying to make money out of clicks, as well as posters who are linked to advertising companies or certain political parties.
