They can also be state-sponsored, according to Assoc Prof Ross Tapsell, who has researched the industry for the Australian National University.“It comes out of the idea that … they’re making noise online,” he said of the term “buzzer”. “In the way that lots of small insects put together make a really big ambient noise.”While some buzzers are high-profile social media influencers and celebrities, they can also be people who are not earning much at all.“This machine operates by attracting those who are most economically vulnerable,” Angtyasti Jiwasiddi has written in the Indonesian newspaper Kompas. “This job requires zero skills and zero capital, requiring only a cell phone and a few accounts.”The phenomenon is partly the result of Meta’s business model, according to a Queensland University of Technology media researcher Associate Prof Timothy Graham, who pointed to the incentive structure that provides cash for content engagement in an effort to keep eyes on the platform.In 2025, the company says it paid nearly US$3bn to creators for content reels, photos and text posts.Meta did not respond to questions for this report but said seven of the 14 Hanson support groups previously identified by the Guardian in its investigation had now been suspended for “violating our policies”.“If you want to stop the issue, you have to stop Meta farming populations for money,” Graham says. “There’s something harmful about the product.”It appears that Adira runs just one of many Indonesian accounts posting about Hanson and politics in a country she says she knows little about.“We are just seeking dollars,” she says. “We don’t know, like, even who the president is… The Pauline group has great dollars.”*Name has been changed.Do you know more? Email ariel.bogle@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsSocial mediaIndonesiaAustralian politicsOne NationPauline HansonUS politicsFacebookfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: AI push is putting banks at mercy of tech firms, warns Moody’s | Banking | The Guardian
description: Finance sector will gain from the tech but it will need substantial investment and create risks, says rating agency
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Finance sector will gain from the tech but it will need substantial investment and create risks, says rating agency
Content: The reliance of most financial firms on a small set of AI and cloud computing providers risks creating a systemic dependency.Photograph: Ahn Young-joon/APView image in fullscreenThe reliance of most financial firms on a small set of AI and cloud computing providers risks creating a systemic dependency.Photograph: Ahn Young-joon/APBankingAI push is putting banks at mercy of tech firms, warns Moody’sFinance sector will gain from the tech but it will need substantial investment and create risks, says rating agencyKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentSun 9 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe rating agency Moody’s has said the race to adopt AI is putting big banks at the mercy of a small group of Silicon Valley firms, leaving them vulnerable to widespread outages and price gouging by profit-hungry tech bosses.The financial sector’s efforts to integrate AI into day-to-day operations will eventually cut costs and increase revenues across the City and Wall Street, Moody’s said.But that will require “substantial investments”, and with so many rivals racing towards the same goal, many of those benefits will end up being “competed away”.AI will also create bigger risks around data privacy, cybersecurity, fraud and so-called “deposit flight”, as well as an overdependence on a small number of tech firms, the rating agency warned.That will raise concerns for bosses across the financial sector.More than 75%of City companies now use AI, according to a UK Treasury select committee report published in January, with insurers and international banks among the biggest adopters. They are mostly using it to automate administrative tasks or even help with core operations, including processing insurance claims and assessing customers’ creditworthiness.“The reliance of most financial firms on a relatively small set of foundation AI model and cloud computing providers risks creating a systemic dependency,” the Moody’s report said.“This is because a model outage at one major provider could potentially spread quickly across customers and sectors. As AI adoption deepens, regulators may increase their focus on operational resilience and third-party concentration in the AI model stack.”The AI race also risked creating “vendor dependence risk”, Moody’s said, meaning that “a set of dominant AI model and infrastructure providers could, over time, exert control over the price of AI services”. That issue is likely to emerge as the bosses of loss-making generative AI companies, including the ChatGPT creator OpenAI and the Claude owner Anthropic, come under pressure to deliver profits for investors.“While this could pose credit risks to financial firms, they would nevertheless retain control over key assets, including proprietary data,” Moody’s said. Many big banks and insurers also have longstanding experience negotiating down tech contracts, and may be using open-source AI models, and striking key partnerships, to try to offset “dependency risks”.Lloyds Banking Group’s chief executive, Charlie Nunn, recentlydoubled downon AI investment plans with a £13bn strategy that would involve using the technology to lure new business, improve efficiency and increase payouts for shareholders.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat will involve £2bn of cost cuts, which Nunn said would affect staff. “That is going to impact work. It is going to require us to continue to reskill peopleand hire new people, but that’s been my history for 30-odd years in financial services.”Moody’s acknowledged the potential blow to some staff, who could be deemed replaceable as a result of new tech. Its report said there was a 20% chance that, by 2030, AI will be able to do the work of a “solid mid-level employee”.For banks, AI might also make it easier for customers to switch to accounts offering higher interest rates, creating the possibility that large chunks of cash could be moved at short notice. “In this context, depositors’ trust in the institution and the resilience and stability of deposit funding are critical,” Moody’s said.Explore more on these topicsBankingTechnology sectorAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Chris Martin seems nice – but Coldplay make me feel carsick!’: Lucy Beaumont’s honest playlist | Music | The Guardian
description: As a tween, Hull’s finest learned the rap from Waterfalls – now she blubs to prog. But which song from a British singer-songwriter is her guilty pleasure?
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: As a tween, Hull’s finest learned the rap from Waterfalls – now she blubs to prog. But which song from a British singer-songwriter is her guilty pleasure?
Content: ‘I’ve never done karaoke in my life and I never will’ … Lucy Beaumont.Photograph: Debbie EllisView image in fullscreen‘I’ve never done karaoke in my life and I never will’ … Lucy Beaumont.Photograph: Debbie EllisHonest playlistMusic‘Chris Martin seems nice – but Coldplay make me feel carsick!’: Lucy Beaumont’s honest playlistAs a tween, Hull’s finest learned the rap from Waterfalls – now she blubs to prog. But which song from a British singer-songwriter is her guilty pleasure?As told toRich PelleySun 9 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first song I fell in love withCaravan of Love by the Housemartins, when I was four or five. They’re also from Hull, but I think I mainly liked it because my granny and grandad had a caravan in their garden that I used as a wendy house.The first single I boughtI remember buying Thriller by Michael Jackson from HMV in Hull, even though it was before my time. Everyone loved Michael Jackson so I was probably copying somebody at school.The song I inexplicably know every lyric toI know the lyrics to loads of songs, but I actually sat down and learned the rap from Waterfalls by TLC when I was about 12.The best song to play at a partySuperstition by Stevie Wonder.The song I can no longer listen toAnything by Coldplay – particularly Yellow. I have a visceral reaction. It’s not them – Chris Martin seems like a nice guy – but there’s something about the tone that makes me feel carsick.The song I secretly like, but tell everybody I hateSupermarket Flowers by Ed Sheeran. He wrote it about his grandmother dying, but from his mother’s point of view. I think it’s a really lovely song, but I’d never tell anybody.The song that changed my lifeAs a teenager, I was really into hard house. Then, when I heard the first Stone Roses album, it was like nothing I’d heard before. The opening bars of Waterfall are especially rock’n’roll, but also feel so spiritual. It had a massive effect on me.The song that gets me up in the morningMovin’ on Up by Primal Scream – perfect if I’m hungover and have a busy day.The song that makes me cryWish You Were Here by Pink Floyd has been played at a couple of funerals, and it always gets me. I always think how amazing it must be to write something that people play at their most vulnerable moments, and that somehow explains life.The song I do at karaokeI’ve never done karaoke in my life and I never will. But if someone put a gun to my head I’d do These Boots Are Made for Walkin’ by Nancy Sinatra.The song I want played at my funeralAt a funeral, you really listen to music as a group. So I’d have Try a Little Tenderness by Otis Redding.Lucy Beaumonttours the UK23 September to 20 June; tour starts Scunthorpe.Explore more on these topicsMusicHonest playlistComedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming review – brilliant bulletin from Ukrainian frontline dives deep into culture war | Movies | The Guardian
description: A couple attempting to leave Ukraine when the war begins encounter gender identity issues in this bold and challenging film
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: A couple attempting to leave Ukraine when the war begins encounter gender identity issues in this bold and challenging film
Content: The challenge of their lives … I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming.Photograph: X-Filme-Creative-Pool-GmbHView image in fullscreenThe challenge of their lives … I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming.Photograph: X-Filme-Creative-Pool-GmbHMoviesReviewI Rarely Wake Up Dreaming review – brilliant bulletin from Ukrainian frontline dives deep into culture warLocarno film festivalA couple attempting to leave Ukraine when the war begins encounter gender identity issues in this bold and challenging filmPeter BradshawSun 9 Aug 2026 10.34 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 18.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmovie’s themes could hardly be more urgent and contemporary than those on offer in this entirely absorbing film from German director Isabelle Stever and Ukrainian critic turned screenwriter Anna Melikova. It’s a bulletin from the frontline of Russia’s war onUkraine, and from the culture war too. It is about identity and choices made in peacetime when less was at stake. There is a bold and brilliant premise that may at first look artificially satirical but is actually inspired.When Russia begins its attack, the crisis is very specific for a scared young Ukrainian couple, recently engaged: Olya (Tania Myronyshena) and Oleh (Markus Bright). As bombs rain down, they head west in the cramped car of Olya’s elderly mum and dad – with Olya grumpily objecting to her dad’s sexist comments from behind the wheel about female drivers – to stay with Olya’s sister, who is married with a young baby and whose husband, to her fury, has joined up. Oleh’s plan is to get out of Ukraine and live with Olya in the safety of Germany and the EU.But wait. No men between 18 and 60 are allowed out of Ukraine, yet the thing is that Olya and Oleh are a queer couple and Oleh is a trans man, though he hasn’t quite got round to telling his future parents-in-law this. Oleh’s humiliating plan is to swallow his pride and disavow his new identity at the frontier; to betray his own life choices; to demand exit on the grounds that he is really a woman. He even plans to produce his psychiatric certificate, originally intended to underscore the psychological validity of his female-to-male transition, but now to imply the opposite, that there is something crazy in suggesting he is anything other than a woman.Stever and Melikova deliver the film’s sledgehammer punch in a scene showing the female Ukrainian border guards and their towering contempt for Oleh’s desperate cowardice. “You wanted to be a man so much?” they snap. “So stay here and be a man.” They are even more scornful when Oleh starts unzipping his trousers. “We don’t care what’s in your pants.”Oleh’s ordeal of humiliation is linked to the advance of Putin’s forces, but crises of identity are detectable elsewhere. At the local market, a Russian-speaking woman, using the language natural to her and to which nobody objected before now, finds that there is a cold, hostile silence as she speaks. Someone shrilly tells her to speak Ukrainian, and it causes a general brawl in which Oleh sustains a black eye. Language, culture and identity are all combustible elements leading to violence.Olya’s mum is philosophical and fatalistic about everything in ways that exasperate Olya; she has already accepted the problems in her marriage. But Olya’s sister is enraged – and on the verge of a breakdown – at her husband leaving her with their baby to join the army. And so far, this is how this very modern, anti-militarist, anti-war couple Olya and Oleh have always felt: their feelings for each other, their truth, which they have after all gone through a lot to achieve, are the most important thing. Not unreasonably, they thought that would be the great challenge of their lives. And the war exposes painful truths about Olya’s attitude to Oleh’s transition. It’s a terrifically well-shot, well-acted, uniquely challenging movie about a belief system in crisis.I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming screened at the Locarno film festivalExplore more on these topicsFilmWar filmsDrama filmsUkraineFestivalsEuropeGenderreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Chosen in the Wild with Bear Grylls review – in a world of toxic masculinity, this feels radical at points | Television | The Guardian
description: As the survivalist takes the cast of the Christian drama out in the wild to discuss faith, it’s surprisingly moving to find two very confident men so comfortable in their gentleness
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: As the survivalist takes the cast of the Christian drama out in the wild to discuss faith, it’s surprisingly moving to find two very confident men so comfortable in their gentleness
Content: ‘I thought I was going to die!’ Luke Simyan goes skydiving.Photograph: Amazon MGM StudiosView image in fullscreen‘I thought I was going to die!’ Luke Simyan goes skydiving.Photograph: Amazon MGM StudiosTV reviewTelevisionReviewThe Chosen in the Wild with Bear Grylls review – in a world of toxic masculinity, this feels radical at pointsAs the survivalist takes the cast of the Christian drama out in the wild to discuss faith, it’s surprisingly moving to find two very confident men so comfortable in their gentlenessLucy ManganSun 9 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJudas Iscariot is sonice! That’s a surprise. Just goes to show – you betray ONE messiah, the scroll-media gets to work and people forget everything else.I’m joshing, of course. I’m having a little religious joke because The Chosen in the Wild withBear Gryllshas put me in such a good mood. The Judas Iscariot in question is actually Luke Dimyan, the actor who plays him in The Chosen: the multi-season series about the life, death and resurrection of Jesus of Nazareth. The Chosen is a venture by evangelical Christian film-maker Dallas Jenkins that began as a crowdfunded project in 2017 and is now watched by an estimated 280 million people worldwide. Bear Grylls is a fan and a Christian – what could be more natural than him taking members of the cast for survivalist adventures in the Utah desert, to talk to them about faith in between ziplining across chasms, filtering water through socks and rappelling down cliffs?It is precisely because the result does feel so natural that I find myself in such a good mood. The actors are not asked to do too much. Some do a helicopter jump, some don’t. They each do a couple of small challenges, where neither the intrinsic difficulties nor the participants’ hesitations are lingered over, and then they stop for another chat about acting or God while Bear feeds them an MRE (military ready meal) or nugget of survivalist wisdom. No one becomes an emotional or physical wreck.Dimyan is Grylls’ first guest – a wise choice as he is a completely charming, self-confessed nerd (“I worry a lot! I’m constantly worried!”) who names rocks as he makes his way to meet Bear (“I think I’ve passed Jerry a few times,” he notes worriedly) but is willing to skydive on to the canyon trail from 10,000ft. “That’s amazing!” he says cheerfully when he lands. “I thought I was going to die!”At their first pit stop, they talk about Dimyan’s upbringing in a Coptic Egyptian family who didn’t want him to be an actor. “Get paid!” said his dad. “Be safe!” Now, he says, his parents say: “We’re glad we were wrong!” It’s really lovely.So too is the rapport between the men, who discuss their faith in unembarrassed fashion and talk about what Jesus means to them. “Acceptance,” says Dimyan. “He saw people and allowed them to be the best versions of themselves … if you love people unabashedly, they will take that chance.” None of the episodes goes deeply into matters of faith but they have a simple and touching authenticity to them.It is also unexpectedly moving to watch two men – here especially, but in other episodes, too – be so confident and yet so peaceful together. In a world full of toxic masculinity, it feels as radical as any religious profession to hear Bear compliment his companion on his gentleness and to have him poke fun at his own reputation (he tends to let scorpions go these days, he says, unless he’s really desperate to eat).They are also funny together. Dimyan, understandably, can’t quite believe he has to pee on his MRE to activate the heat pack that will make it palatable. Nor, when he has been convinced of the necessity, can he instantly muster the wherewithal. “Normally I can take direction,” he says with his back to us, concentrating. “It just needs a little bit,” Bear shouts over to him. “Look, you get what you get,” says Dimyan.The other episodes stick to this soothing formula, drawing in more of the cast: the Indian American actor Paras Patel, who plays disciple Matthew; Elizabeth Tabish (Lilith/Mary Magdalene); and, in the penultimate outing, Jonathan Roumie (Jesus himself – who gets to roam the Adirondacks instead of the desert, which I think suggests a VIP treatment quite out of keeping with His teachings). I did enjoy the fact that Dallas Jenkins got the final episode. If a director can, he will always place himself just above God.I don’t quite know how to square Grylls’ evident sincerity and good sense on show here with the fact that his most noteworthy recent appearance prior to this was at thebaptism of Russell Brand– after accusations by multiple women of rape and other abuses by the comedian were made public. Brand has since been charged with three counts of rape and other assaults. Grylls was asked during the publicity run for Chosen in the Wild whether his feelings about the baptism had changed. “I think all our faith changes and evolves, and I’d also say I have many doubts as well. I really struggle with so much of it,” he said. But “I think at heart, my faith says … not to judge people and to love people.” I look forward to Brand being judged in a court of law, and I don’t think that’s through a lack of Christian compassion. But on we go.The Chosen in the Wild with Bear Grylls is on Prime VideoExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewBear GryllsReality TVreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Even the good guys were doing bad things’: the wild, twisted story behind the new Tiger King | Documentary | The Guardian
description: Monsters of God is a jaw-dropping new series from the makers of the hit Netflix pandemic smash, exploring the murky world of exotic reptile smuggling
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: Monsters of God is a jaw-dropping new series from the makers of the hit Netflix pandemic smash, exploring the murky world of exotic reptile smuggling
Content: A still from Monsters of God.Photograph: HBO MaxView image in fullscreenA still from Monsters of God.Photograph: HBO MaxDocumentary‘Even the good guys were doing bad things’: the wild, twisted story behind the new Tiger KingMonsters of God is a jaw-dropping new series from the makers of the hit Netflix pandemic smash, exploring the murky world of exotic reptile smugglingAndrew LawrenceSun 9 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1993, a sci-fi blockbuster about an animal theme park that resurrected the dinosaurs sparked more than a flurry of interest in those long-extinct beasts. It left audiences jonesing for the next best thing: a close encounter with a bearded dragon or a ball python. Jeremy McBride, the Emmy-winning film-maker was one of them. “I wanted a pet iguana,” he said. In the wake of the Spielberg classic, reptiles have become fixtures of the modern imagination, adorning zoo exhibits, living room terrariums and every corner of pop culture while underpinning a multibillion-dollar pet trade.Monsters of God review – a messy feud between rival reptile smugglers gets the Tiger King treatmentRead moreBut just as in Jurassic Park, the urgent danger isn’t the prehistoric creatures with the teeth and venom. It’s the people willing to steal, smuggle and kill for them. People like the Pablo Escobar of animal trafficking. “Our next documentary is going to be called Who Backstabbed Who,” jokes Eric Goode, an Emmy-nominated director. “You never know when that knife is going to go in your back because everyone’s trying to make a deal with the feds, with another reptile dealer. Even the good guys were supposedly doing bad things. It’s messy.”Goode’s latest collaboration with McBride,Monsters of God, premiered on HBO this week, and it has all the ingredients to become another monoculture moment in the mold of Tiger King. Where Goode’s pandemic smash was a rabbit hole into the kooky subculture of private zoo owners, this five-part series, executive produced by McBride, explores the sprawling shadow enterprise of traffickers who ransack the globe for the rarest reptiles and sell them for staggering profits. What began as a criminal ecosystem connecting smugglers, individual collectors and major institutions such as the National Zoo soon expanded to include bad actors in other illicit industries who seized on the opportunity to use reptiles as camouflage for their own operations.Based on the 2008 true-crime book The Lizard King, Monsters of God traces the trade’s humble origins to the 1960s, when a cheese salesman named Hank Molt began publishing a reptile price list and mailing it to zoos as they began to recognize the enormous commercial potential in dedicated collections. Molt became an inspiration for reptile enthusiasts who envied his rare finds and the globe-trotting adventures that produced them, while the US Fish and Wildlife Service – dismissed as the “duck cops” – rightly feared his booming business wreaking havoc on native ecosystems and moved swiftly to rein him in.In 1977, Molt was federally indicted on more than 200 smuggling counts and served just 90 days in jail. But that leniency wasn’t enough to contain the reputational damage his case inflicted, particularly among institutions such as the Smithsonian’s National Zoo and its many patrons in Congress. After Molt’s prosecution, the reptile trade’s power structure was revealed: at the center of this tight-knit monopoly, there could be onlyone“lizard guy” inonetown (usually in Florida) – making reptile smugglers comparatively easier to investigate than, say, the mob. After Molt it was his apprentice Tommy Crutchfield, an ostentatious Floridian who poured nearly every dollar he made in trading reptiles back into the hunt for new ones and, fittingly, inspired the title for this series.After Molt dimed out Crutchfield in retaliation for stealinghisbusiness, igniting a decades-long feud between the two reptile obsessives, the crown passed on to Ray Van Nostrand, a Miami hustler who chased bulk profits from common species over rare specimens. Then he crossed paths with Mario Tabraue, a prolific cocaine and wildlife smuggler viewers might remember from Tiger King as the likely inspiration for the cult gangster flick Scarface. Together, they popularized a new method of concealment: packaging rare and venomous reptiles with drugs to disguise shipments and deter inspectors. But the “Pablo Escobar of animal trafficking” title was ultimately reserved for Malaysia’s Anson Wong, the reptile nerd kingpin whosesuspected tiesto Asia’s ruling families and underworld gangs made him law enforcement’s white whale.Monsters of God catches up with these men in their winter years, resulting in wistful reflections on their notorious pasts. Van Nostrand, who died during filming just short of his 80th birthday, was battling dementia and visibly struggles to access his memories in interviews.View image in fullscreenTom Holt in Monsters of God.Photograph: HBO MaxBut Goode and McBride found that they could bring back some of his old spark by pairing him with his son Michael, the Tony Soprano-like successor who expanded the family business while his father was imprisoned, only to wind up imprisoned for turtle trafficking himself. They also shot Van Nostrand at the family’s warehouse facility, ostensibly legitimate again, where he was surrounded by the reptiles that built, lost and rebuilt the family fortune. “We had a whole version of that story with him not in it in a contemporary way,” McBride says. “But we had one editor whose dad was going through dementia at the time who pushed us to show more of that. It’s not every day that you get to interview someone who doesn’t necessarily know what they’re talking about and show that in a way that’s compassionate.”Each hour-long episode raises the stakes, with reptile-loving axeman Slash literally underscoring the twists, turns and spitting-viper cutaways. “He’s such a sweet, normal guy, cares about the issue and wanted to contribute his time,” McBride says. “We’d send him music, and he’d play over it during a lot of particular scenes. We’re gonna put out the vinyl soon.”All the while, you can’t help wondering whether McBride and Goode, doing his Michael Moore thing while calling the shots behind the camera, are sticking their own necks out a bit too far. “What we’re really good at is getting people locked up behind bars,” Goode says, not entirely joking. “There was one guy who was under investigation and went to prison while we were filming him. I’ve decided I’m really good at putting people in prison inadvertently.”Bombs, heists and big cats: TV’s 25 best true-crime shows everRead moreCrucially, no animals were harmed in the production of Monsters of God – something, alas, that can’t be said for a black market that treated dead reptiles as little more than the cost of doing business. The film’s tales of “spoiled inventory” are every bit as shocking and heartbreaking as you’d expect. A longtime conservationist, Goode is relentless about getting viewers to see these creatures as he does, pressing his lens so close to vertical pupils, beaky maws and scaly brows that you can’t help harboring concern for his camera crew.Tabraue, the cocaine cowboy who ultimately served 12 years of a 100-year sentence for his 1989 conviction on narcotics and racketeering charges, had a near-death experience during one shoot after he was bitten by a Gila monster – the only venomous lizard native to the US, McBride hastens to note. “Fun fact: a compound in their venom led to the development of GLP-1 drugs,” he says. “So the very thing that can kill you is now saving people’s lives around the world.”View image in fullscreenEric Goode and Jeremy McBride at the premiere of Monsters of God.Photograph: Rob Latour/ShutterstockIn Monsters of God, the people are the ones framed as beasts – fueled by lust for power, wealth and the narcotic thrill of the chase. The longer you watch, the harder it becomes to distinguish the good guys from the bad. The federal agents who pursued these reptile smugglers are pitched into moral ambiguity the moment they step onto the beat. Some are willing to look the other way for the sake of a conviction; others come to believe their proximity to the trade entitles them to a piece of it.“It’s like the Harvey Keitel movie Bad Lieutenant,” says Goode.“Well,” McBride adds, “it’s even more pathological.”As the crime thriller unravels, the docuseries also shows how smuggling has ravaged reptile populations, pushing some species to the brink of extinction. But one of the documentary’s bigger ideas – how reptile imports have thrown native US ecosystems out of whack – was ultimately left on the cutting-room floor. “We filmed Burmese pythons in the South Florida Everglades,” Goode says. “We filmed iguanas dropping out of trees. The invasive species angle is a big deal, and it really does have an impact all around the world.”But Monsters of God doesn’t do much to help viewers who might have gone into it already feeling ambivalent about zoos. On the one hand, their money-making reptile exhibitions helped create the conditions for the wildlife smuggling business. On the other, where else would people encounter these creatures closely enough to understand why they are worth protecting? “The paradoxical effect of smuggling is that zoos are functionally seed banks for preventing animals from going extinct,” McBride says. “It’s no longer animals coming in. It’s animals going out.”Goode sees that contradiction as part of a larger reckoning. “It’s a bit like saying: how should I feel about America?” he says. “Zoos, like our culture, have a lot of skeletons. They were part of the civic planning of a city and built to be entertaining. But zoos also have a long history of evolving, just like we do in our country.”In the end, Monsters of God is not a spectacle for the sake of it. It’s the Jurassic Park cautionary tale come to life: fascination curdling into obsession.“We’re really interested in making entertaining content,” McBride says. “But we also want to try and tuck in a purposeful message. More than ever nonfiction stories matter a lot. People want to learn something, and we want to help educate them and not just have them watch a freak show all the time.”Monsters of God is available onHBOMaxExplore more on these topicsDocumentaryHBOFactual TVPolitics TVUS televisionTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Grief became my brand’: Freya Bromley on writing about personal tragedy | Books | The Guardian
description: Touring her memoir and talking to others helped the author come to terms with her brother’s death, but the book’s success left her feeling guilty. Had she commodified her family’s pain?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Touring her memoir and talking to others helped the author come to terms with her brother’s death, but the book’s success left her feeling guilty. Had she commodified her family’s pain?
Content: ‘Why is it so difficult to be unhappy around the people you’ve known the longest?’ … Freya Bromley.Photograph: Patch StudiosView image in fullscreen‘Why is it so difficult to be unhappy around the people you’ve known the longest?’ … Freya Bromley.Photograph: Patch StudiosBooks‘Grief became my brand’: Freya Bromley on writing about personal tragedyTouring her memoir and talking to others helped the author come to terms with her brother’s death, but the book’s success left her feeling guilty. Had she commodified her family’s pain?Freya BromleySun 9 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen my memoir about my life after my brother’s death was published, I was very fortunate that people connected with it. It’s not easy to feel good fortune from the worst thing that’s ever happened to you. But I suppose I felt pleased when the experience that had once made me so lonely suddenly became a point of connection.I had not always been an open book. I was 22 when my brother died from a rare bone cancer. The people around me didn’t know what to say about this awful thing, so they pretended it hadn’t happened and I pretended, too. For a few years I was a ghost in my own life. Nothing felt real. I got very good at imitating normality, imagining I was in a video game called Office.There were other simulations such as Dating and Fun Friend Hangout where it was game over when I brought up death. A numbness settled in. Grief, and the subsequent silence around it, had obliterated my sense of who I was. My reality had been shattered, and I was unsure how I fitted within the life I once had. I found that, at this time of my life, even to be looked in the eyes was incredibly uncomfortable. The thought of someone seeing my pain was excruciating. Or perhaps it was the fear of them not searching for it at all.Maybe these years of feeling so unseen made me want to share myself with people through writing. My 2024 book The Tidal Year follows the year I swam in every tidal pool in Britain with a friend. I like to say it’s a memoir about swimming that isn’t really about swimming at all. It’s about loss, and how to find joy in your life as a young person after a tragedy. Readers knew my most intimate moments, and many shared their own. Late at night, I’d receive messages on Instagram with confessions of people’s PTSD. Sometimes people emailed me shocking, explicit details of a death close to them. I was moved that something I’d written had prompted them to contact me. Writing had transformed my life, and I believed that whether it was a book, email or a DM there was power in acknowledging your pain through words.double quotation markI opened up my grief like a suitcase and waited for people to unpack all their sadness into it, then I took it homeAt first, I felt an enormous pressure to reply with something articulate and wise. This was hardest in person. If someone started crying at the signing table, as they often did, there was an awkward distance between us. Should I stand up to hug them? What could I say to make it better? I learned that it wasn’t at all about what I replied. It was about listening. Most people, when they lose someone, don’t get to say the name of their loved one any more. The best thing I could say is: who’s the person you’re missing? What were they like?Having these conversations has been a real privilege. And I must admit I became rather addicted to them. I pitched myself for events, volunteered with bereavement charities, used all my holiday to travel the country visiting bookshops. However, the best thing about the book was also the worst: I’d alchemised my grief into something powerful, positive, productive and I soon became consumed by guilt that I’d commodified our family tragedy. Looking back, I think I felt that if the book did well enough, if it helped enough people, then perhaps I could be redeemed from writing it at all.At events, I opened up my grief like a suitcase and waited for people to unpack all their sadness into it, then I took it home again. On the train, I’d wonder where to put all the stories people had handed me. A brother collapses on a rugby pitch. A mother drowns in the sea. A sister is murdered by her husband … I was thinking about death all the time. Tragic events now seemed quite normal. Perhaps I could have protected myself more, put up a shield between myself and others so I wasn’t so affected by their stories, but what would be the point of having these interactions and not feeling them so deeply? What would be the point of listening and not truly hearing?That summer a men’s book club messaged me to say they’d chosen my book, and I was welcome to join them for a drink. The pub was one I’d mentioned and their attentive reading made me feel special. When I arrived, we had some drinks and spoke about their book club which had seen them through many seasons of their friendship. We drank some more. Someone quoted a passage they found amusing. I felt like the best, shiniest version of myself. Then someone shared that a member of the group had lost his sister recently. A new atmosphere fell over the table, and I realised why I was there. I was drunk now, and my cheeks were red. The man in question gripped his pint and told me he worried he’d never experience happiness again. “You look happy,” he said, “I can’t imagine you ever feel like that.” My stomach twitched with dread that I had performed the wrong version of myself.I often worried whether I looked sad enough, and if people felt I was heartless or fake if I didn’t. Sometimes at readings, people asked me why I wasn’t crying. In publicity meetings for my book, I’d been asked to come up with social media ideas. Are there any significant anniversaries you could post on, they asked. I didn’t want to turn any more sad moments into content, but maybe that’s what I’d signed up for. I suppose I made my brand grief, and I’ve often wondered what happens to the soul of a person with a brand like that.I recently saw the writer and climate justice organiser Mikaela Loach post about being hospitalised for a long-term undiagnosed illness. She said that during a recent meeting with Meta they showed a selection of her posts and revealed that when she cried, they performed best, so maybe she should create more like that. The next day I was served an advert by Instagram aimed at “Creators” that suggested a new Reel template going from “Sad Girl Winter” to “Hot Girl Summer” with space for selfies of crying to camera.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markFiction has given me new ways to untangle the life-changing force that is grief beyond reflecting only on my ownBefore we experience great tragedies, I think we all have this idea that death is something that brings families together. That we will hold each other and cry and bond. In some ways this is true. I have never been hugged tighter than when I saw my big brother, Lawrence, after we got the news that today would be the day. Lawrence had driven across London to pick me up so we could go to the hospital together. I have never been held like that, our bodies colliding on the street as our world fell apart.But what follows can be so devastating. You’re all trying not to knock the bruise. You’re all trying to get by, as best you can. There’s a lot of silence. There’s a lot of crying alone. There are a lot of misunderstandings because you’re all coping in different ways. No one is right, no one is wrong. But sometimes it’s easier to be angry about this, than it is to be angry about the person who’s been taken from you, because at least in one of those situations you have some semblance of control.Although I’d spent two years touring the country talking about grief, I still couldn’t talk about it with those closest to me. Why is it so difficult to be unhappy around the people you’ve known the longest? Even today, I don’t know that I can confidently share my feelings with the people I love. I am just too sad. And I love them too much to show them. I don’t want them to worry, after all we’ve been through. I’m sure that they feel the same.Most of the people who reach out to me aren’t only grieving a person. They’re grieving the version of themselves that existed before. My second book, A Real Piece of Work, is a novel about a family meeting for the fifth anniversary of a death. I wanted this fictional world to be an offering to everyone I’d met – a reckoning with what becomes of a family once the funeral is over. How do our relationships shift when life-changing loss ruptures our existing dynamics? I’m trying to start a family of my own now and I think it’s been important to me to create something real and thorny yet hopeful that captures how most of us are trying our best, even when we misunderstand each other. I do truly believe that.I don’t believe there is such a thing as moving on. We only ever move through and carry it with us. I carry the weight of a lot of stories now, but somehow it feels all the lighter because of the expansive conversations created between people through books.Fictionhas given me new ways to untangle the life-changing force that is grief beyond reflecting only on my own. I’ve just started a new book tour. I still sit at the signing table. And when someone tells me they’re struggling, I ask them about the person they’re missing, so they can say their name again.A Real Piece of Work by Freya Bromley is published by Hutchinson Heinemann.To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com.
