title: Sophie Duker: Hot Beef Injection review – bad encounters with men spun into great comedy | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The standup is on sparkling form as she mines a lifetime of baffling and alarming experiences for a smart, purposeful and very funny hour
Author: Anya Ryan
Headline: The standup is on sparkling form as she mines a lifetime of baffling and alarming experiences for a smart, purposeful and very funny hour
Content: Beef encounter … Sophie Duker is at Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 August.View image in fullscreenBeef encounter … Sophie Duker is at Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 August.Edinburgh festival 2026ReviewSophie Duker: Hot Beef Injection review – bad encounters with men spun into great comedyPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghThe standup is on sparkling form as she mines a lifetime of baffling and alarming experiences for a smart, purposeful and very funny hourAnya RyanSun 9 Aug 2026 10.48 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSophie Duker is done with men. She swears it. And, in her fourth hour, Hot Beef Injection – named after a crude euphemism from80s teen film The Breakfast Club– she is going to tell us exactly why.Duker has had her fair share of relationships, tracking all the way back to her adolescence. “I did hand stuff with a 16-year-old boy,” she announces at the show’s opening. On reflection, though, most of those experiences have left her feeling, well, weird.Hot Beef Injection presents a gallery of men who have intimidated, disappointed or baffled her, from the swaggering alpha male types of Soho to the repairman who deliberately leaves his tools behind in the hope of seeing her again. Later come more sinister stories: getting into a car with a strange man in a time of need and finding herself locked in a room with a man in a position of power at a comedy club. Taken together, they paint a bleak picture – one that will be familiar to many women and that, as Duker quips, Louis Theroux has only recently begun to notice. Throughout it all, Duker has learned to keep smiling.This leads us to the viral question at the show’s centre: would you rather be alone in a forest with a random man or a bear? You don’t need me to tell you which side Duker falls on – I mean, have you seen Paddington? She offsets all the darkness with her trademark breezy wit. And the audience is entirely under her spell. She joyfully targets the “milky whites”, interrogates the single straight white man who has come to her show of his own accord, and does roaring impressions of men in their cars drinking energy drinks.Hostile review – surreal spaghetti western is a wild and wordless rideRead moreThe final payoff feels a little too neat for a show that has, until that moment, been pretty dismissive of all things male. No matter – Duker’s presence is all good-time joy and delight, and this is a show so neatly crafted and intelligent that every routine serves a purpose.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalFestivalsSophie DukerComedy (Stage)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: National Youth Orchestra/Adès review – assured young musicians end their season all guns blazing | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: Thunderous timpani, stereo harps, a supersized horn section and 160 teenagers combined for Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique, Adès’s Dante and a Liszt waltz
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: Thunderous timpani, stereo harps, a supersized horn section and 160 teenagers combined for Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique, Adès’s Dante and a Liszt waltz
Content: Full force … Thomas Adès conducting the National Youth Orchestra at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCView image in fullscreenFull force … Thomas Adès conducting the National Youth Orchestra at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCProms 2026ReviewNational Youth Orchestra/Adès review – assured young musicians end their season all guns blazingRoyal Albert Hall, LondonThunderous timpani, stereo harps, a supersized horn section and 160 teenagers combined for Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique, Adès’s Dante and a Liszt waltzFlora WillsonSun 9 Aug 2026 08.09 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 08.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree big pieces on the programme. 160 teenage musicians almost all on stage throughout. Nochoreography, nobody percussionandnot a kazoo in sight. ByNational Youth Orchestrastandards, this Proms appearance – the all-guns-blazing finale of the cohort’s year together – was positively straight-laced.Yes, there were still whoops when friends and family members greeted individual musicians as they all poured on to the stage. And this remains the only orchestra on the annualPromsroster where 10 horns come as standard and piccolo-playing is a team sport.There weren’t quite 76 trombones, but the supersized eight-strong section here revelled in the brassiest moments ofBerlioz’s Symphonie fantastique, lending familiar music a deliciously outlandish squelchiness. The second movement boasted stereo harps (two on each side of the stage), the third louring, thunderous timpani echoing between stage and gallery. And you really haven’t lived until you’ve heard the Dies Irae motif savagely intoned on four tubas and the catastrophic ending topped by a line of percussionists simultaneously thwacking cymbals.Negotiating quieter passages with an orchestra of this size is the musical equivalent of driving a pantechnicon through a housing estate. But these musicians were instantly responsive to conductorThomas Adès, who crouched, lunged and chopped his way to textures of remarkable lucidity. The ensemble in the opener – Liszt’s Mephisto Waltz No 1 – took a moment to cohere but then boasted conspiratorial woodwind and quiet elegance from the strings. Throughout, Adès was quick to cede control during solos, which were delivered with frankly astonishing assurance.View image in fullscreenYouthful fire … the massed ranks of the NYO.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCThe Purgatorio movement fromAdès’s Danteemerged from gusts of air blown through brass and wind instruments to reach magnificent symphonic tintinnabulations in its final bars. In between was the recorded voice of a Jewish cantor and congregation, woven amid grungy basslines and keening trumpets, a rhapsodic clarinet solo and a millpond-smooth string chorale.It was a shame that individuals and sections were made to stand for their every moment in the spotlight, which had unfortunate school-concert vibes. Playing this polished certainly shows there is no need for gimmickry – even if the results seemed less exuberantly joyful than usual.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026PromsClassical musicThomas AdèsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: BBC Symphony Orchestra/Venditti review – a fervent but lithe-limbed Stabat Mater | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: Nil Venditti’s animated account of Rossini’s choral work embraced its lyricism and theatricality – paired on the bill with the Proms debut of Respighi’s Church Windows
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Nil Venditti’s animated account of Rossini’s choral work embraced its lyricism and theatricality – paired on the bill with the Proms debut of Respighi’s Church Windows
Content: Spirited battle … soprano Federica Lombardi and mezzo-soprano Chiara Amarù are among the soloists in the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Mark Allan/BBCView image in fullscreenSpirited battle … soprano Federica Lombardi and mezzo-soprano Chiara Amarù are among the soloists in the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Mark Allan/BBCProms 2026ReviewBBC Symphony Orchestra/Venditti review – a fervent but lithe-limbed Stabat MaterRoyal Albert Hall, LondonNil Venditti’s animated account of Rossini’s choral work embraced its lyricism and theatricality – paired on the bill with the Proms debut of Respighi’s Church WindowsClive PagetSun 9 Aug 2026 07.06 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 08.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCheered to the rafters at its 1842 premiere, Rossini’s Stabat Mater has held its place in the repertoire ever since. Its nonchalant bel canto tunefulness, however, has attracted its fair share of detractors. True, the famous tenor aria Cujus Animam Gementem, which skips along like a Neapolitan street song, is an unusual setting for lyrics like “Her spirit groaning, saddened and grieving, a sword has pierced”. Yet Rossini writes with sincerity and, especially in the daringly unaccompanied choral sections, considerable power.Nil Venditti was equally fervent. Her briskly animated account with theBBC Symphony Orchestraembraced the work’s lyricism while mining the score for theatrical nuggets in a pacy reading that favoured lithe-limbed drama over heavyweight grandeur. The BBC Symphony Chorus, bolstered by London’s semi-professional Epiphoni Consort, went with her cheek by jowl in a robust and disciplined performance, their crisp consonants landing with pinpoint precision.View image in fullscreenNil Venditti conducting the BBCSO.Photograph: Mark Allan/BBCAn all-Italian lineup of soloists was headed by Federica Lombardi, whose pearly soprano did spirited battle with gleaming brass and driving timpani in the Inflammatus. Mezzo-soprano Chiara Amarù displayed a warm middle register, though she appeared over-reliant on the score. Nicola Ulivieri lent sombre vocal heft to the Pro Peccatis Suae Gentis, while Dave Monaco, a last-minute stand-in for an ailing René Barbera, sang with gleaming tone and absolutely nailed the top D-flat in the Cujus Animam Gementem.If the first half of the programme felt less inspired, it was more the fault of the music than the performers. Respighi’s Church Windows, here making its Proms premiere, is a pale shadow of his Roman Trilogy heardearlier in the season. It has its colourful moments but the melodies, drawn mostly from Gregorian chant, fail to make much of a mark. Venditti gave it her best, the performance effective enough in the opening Flight into Egypt with its Scheherazade-like scales on clarinet and flute. St Michael the Archangel offered plenty of sound and fury though ultimately rang hollow. It was left to the Byzantine glitter of St Gregory the Great to save the day, its papal pomp turbocharged with tolling gongs and thunderous organ.Availableon BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026BBC Symphony OrchestraClassical musicPromsRoyal Albert HallOperareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hostile review – surreal spaghetti western is a wild and wordless ride | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: At the Edinburgh international festival, Olivier Rannou’s lone cowboy encounters desert dangers in a mix of clowning, mime and visual trickery
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: At the Edinburgh international festival, Olivier Rannou’s lone cowboy encounters desert dangers in a mix of clowning, mime and visual trickery
Content: In extremis … Olivier Rannou in Hostile at Church Hill theatre, Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIn extremis … Olivier Rannou in Hostile at Church Hill theatre, Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewHostile review – surreal spaghetti western is a wild and wordless rideChurch Hill theatre, EdinburghAt the Edinburgh international festival, Olivier Rannou’s lone cowboy encounters desert dangers in a mix of clowning, mime and visual trickeryArifa AkbarSun 9 Aug 2026 06.39 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 06.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe lone ranger at the centre of Olivier Rannou’s family-friendly western initially appears as stranded and desolate as one of Samuel Beckett’s anti-heroes. Parched and prone across a table, with a knotted handkerchief on his head, he is marooned in a desert landscape with a water bottle full of sand, a desperate thirst and a scattering of human skeletal remains.He retains an edge of existential angst, struggling to survive in extremis, but also becomes more clown-like by turns. Rannou shows us, through movement, expression and sound, that this cowboy is a wanted man, on the run, wrestling with the dangers of his barren, unpeopled surroundings.There is the hallucinatory sound of dripping water, a fight with a rattlesnake and a saloon bar shootout, enacted solely by Rannou through mime and clowning, along with a delightful invention of props (the snake is conjured from string, the cacti from planks of wood).Émilie Rougier’s electronic compositions accompany his antics, charging the atmosphere with danger and flipping the mood from light to dark. Sometimes, this sound resembles an electric didgeridoo; at other times, tinkly fairground tunes. There is also some lovely lighting design by Alan Floc’h and Alexandre Musset that evokes a relentlessly glaring desert sun or eerie night.View image in fullscreenPlayful … Hostile at the Churchill theatre, Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianIt is comic, cartoonish and brooding. The skeletons are clear memento mori but with comic edges, and there is exuberant silliness alongside this as well as a Beckettian sense of “failing better” that shows him stoically fending off the repeated, Road Runner-like mishaps that befall him.[seagull] review – silence proves golden in innovative if puzzling shot at ChekhovRead moreProduced by French theatre company Bakélite, it is an eccentric and entertaining show. Rannou brings great, easy physicality, although some of it feels rather abstract and you wonder where this one-man spaghetti western is going or what it is ultimately saying.A highlight comes with the visual playfulness of the set, also designed by Rannou. The original table morphs into other objects, ever bigger and more elaborate, including, at one point, a wooden horse which comes to life and slowly clops off the stage. It is all constructed, carpenter-like, by Rannou before our eyes, and it seems as if he is engaged in a delightful act of wood origami.It absolutely amuses, but as a wordless show that does not try to explain itself, it is rather bemusing too.AtChurch Hill theatre, Edinburgh, until 11 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsTheatreComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)ClownsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: William Orbit obituary | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: Musician and record producer who reignited Madonna’s career with his work on her 1998 album Ray of Light
Author: Adam Sweeting
Headline: Musician and record producer who reignited Madonna’s career with his work on her 1998 album Ray of Light
Content: William Orbit in London, 2019. ‘He’s one of the few people I’ve come across in my career who I’d describe as a genius,’ said Miles Copeland.Photograph: Nicky J Sims/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWilliam Orbit in London, 2019. ‘He’s one of the few people I’ve come across in my career who I’d describe as a genius,’ said Miles Copeland.Photograph: Nicky J Sims/Getty ImagesPop and rockObituaryWilliam Orbit obituaryMusician and record producer who reignited Madonna’s career with his work on her 1998 album Ray of LightAdam SweetingSun 9 Aug 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 12.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe career highlights of William Orbit, who has died aged 69, would run to several pages, featuring collaborations withRobbie Williams, All Saints, Prince, Kraftwerk, Britney Spears, Beth Orton and U2, but one of the most celebrated was his partnership with Madonna on her 1998 album Ray of Light.Coming at a point when Madonna had starred in the movie of Evita and had her first child, Lourdes, and her music career seemed to be waning, Ray of Light marked a decisive step into a new world of techno and ambient music. Orbit, who had previously made remixes of Madonna’sJustify My LoveandErotica, proved to be the perfect production partner, and Ray of Light’s blend of styles and textures made it one of Madonna’s most admired achievements, with 16 million copies of the album sold worldwide.“I kind of revere her really, as an individual to work with, as a colleague and as a boss,” Orbit said. “She’s also a collaborator. There’s never a dull moment.” Ray of Light earned Orbit two Grammys, and he won another for his work on the songBeautiful Stranger(1999), performed by Madonna and co-written with Orbit for the Austin Powers filmThe Spy Who Shagged Me. Also in 1999 Orbit produced Blur’s album13, which saw the band making a determined effort to break free from their Britpop origins, and the debut solo album of the Spice Girl Mel C, Northern Star.View image in fullscreenWilliam Orbit and Madonna after winning awards for Ray of Light at the Grammys in 1998.Photograph: YoutubeThe stars had evidently aligned perfectly for Orbit in 1999, since this was also the year when his solo albumPieces in a Modern Stylereached No 2 on the UK chart. This was a selection of classical compositions filtered through Orbit’s electronic treatments.His version of Samuel Barber’s plangent Adagio for Strings gave him a No 4 hit on the UK singles chart ina remix versionby the Dutch DJ Ferry Corsten. Corsten said that Orbit “constantly challenged convention, embraced the unexpected, and created sounds that felt years ahead of their time.”He was born William Wainwright in Shoreditch, east London, the elder son of parents who were both schoolteachers.Classical musicwas the habitual soundtrack in the Wainwright household.William attended Minchenden grammar school in Southgate, but as the biography onhis websiteputs it: “At the age of 15 he chose to leave formal education in favour of being self and world taught.”Years of travelling around Britain and Europe found him “living in squats, fruit-picking camps in Norfolk and Evesham, Worcestershire, and on a grain barge in the Netherlands”.He worked as a builder and a hospital porter, and even a trainee draughtsman at Humphreys and Glasgow, a company that designed offshore oil rigs.View image in fullscreenWilliam Orbit and Nadine Coyle of Girls Aloud in 2010.Photograph: Dave Hogan/Getty ImagesHis musical adventures began with his learning the guitar, which led to him busking inLondonand Paris during his teenage years, and also becoming accomplished enough to play lunchtime gigs at the King’s Head pub in Islington, north London.However, his musical destiny would not be shaped by the guitar but by his aptitude for exploiting the new world of electronic music, synthesisers and galloping advances in recording technology.He took a decisive step in 1980 when he formed the group Torch Song with Grant Gilbert and Laurie Mayer. Based at a disused school in Notting Hill, dubbed the Centro Iberico, between 1984 and 1987 they released three albums of music in an ambient-electronica vein, Wish Thing, Ecstasy and Exhibit A. Their trackPrepare to Energizewas featured in the 1984 Tom Hanks film Bachelor Party. Having disbanded, Torch Song reformed in the mid-1990s and released Toward the Unknown Region (1995).Miles Copeland, who had signed them to his IRS Records label, said of Orbit: “He’s one of the few people I’ve come across in my career who I’d describe as a genius. He had an awareness of playing with space and time that I’ve only ever heard in one act before, and that was Pink Floyd.” Orbit himself said that “sound is like putty, it’s elastic. You can do anything with it.”View image in fullscreenWilliam Orbit in 2007.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/the GuardianIn 1979, Orbit and Mayer had founded Guerilla Studios, which would be the base for Orbit’s label, Guerilla Records. Artists who recorded at Guerilla included the Cocteau Twins, Howard Devoto, Erasure, the Fall, Gary Numan and Sting. In 1988 Orbit also collaborated with the comedians Harry Enfield, Paul Whitehouse and Charlie Higson on the singleLoadsamoney (Doin’ Up the House), which became Orbit’s first hit record when it reached No 4.It was typical of Orbit’s unconventional career that, after decades in the popular music business, it was only after he turned 60 that he suffered traumatic experiences with drugs.He had been living inLos Angeles, but returned to London in 2017, then moved to Chipping Norton in the Cotswolds. A surfeit of cocaine and a selection of mind-altering products prompted a breakdown that led to his being sectioned in St Mary’s hospital, Paddington, for 28 days.Ina 2022 interviewwith Channel 4’s Krishnan Guru-Murthy, coinciding with the release of his album The Painter, he described how he was feeling happy and creative again after “I had four pretty awful years. There was a lot of lifestyle awfulness, some of which I brought on myself, some of which was fate. Stuff that just happens all stacked up to the point where I was unhappy.”The album title reflected the fact that Orbit was also a talented and prolific artist, having begun painting while on a stop-smoking retreat in Nevada where he attended “vino and Van Gogh” adult art classes.“You turn up, get drunk and mess around with cheap acrylics,” he put it, with characteristic self-effacement.William Orbit (William Mark Wainwright), musician and composer, born 15 December 1956; died 23 July 2026Explore more on these topicsPop and rockMadonnaRobbie WilliamsLondonClassical musicElectronic musicComedyobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Tom Chadbon obituary | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Versatile actor whose career spanned The Liver Birds, Doctor Who and an Edward Bond season at the Royal Court theatre
Author: Toby Hadoke
Headline: Versatile actor whose career spanned The Liver Birds, Doctor Who and an Edward Bond season at the Royal Court theatre
Content: Tom Chadbon, right, as Duggan in the Doctor Who adventure City of Death, with Tom Baker as the Doctor and Lalla Ward as Romana, 1979.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreenTom Chadbon, right, as Duggan in the Doctor Who adventure City of Death, with Tom Baker as the Doctor and Lalla Ward as Romana, 1979.Photograph: BBCTheatreObituaryTom Chadbon obituaryVersatile actor whose career spanned The Liver Birds, Doctor Who and an Edward Bond season at the Royal Court theatreToby HadokeSun 9 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 17.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe actor Tom Chadbon, who has died aged 80, was a deft character player, blessed with a versatile voice – his naturally light, delicate, melodious vocal register acquired steel and depth when required – and an almost cherubic physiognomy that could toughen on command. He became well known to television viewers in 1977 as Derek Paynton, the boyfriend, then husband, of Sandra (played by Nerys Hughes) in the long-runningCarla Lanesitcom The Liver Birds (1969-79) and between 2008 and 2011 enjoyed a recurring stint on the BBC series Casualty as the hospital’s director of clinical care, Henry Williams.He will also be remembered as the inept but dogged detective Duggan in the 1979 Doctor Who story City of Death, helping (and sometimes hindering) Tom Baker’s attempts to thwart an alien scheme to steal the Mona Lisa. A comically imaginative caper, filmed partly on location in Paris and co-written byDouglas Adams, City of Death is a high-water mark for Doctor Who and remains the series’ most watched story: the final episode notched up an impressive 16 million viewers. In a perfectly judged performance, Chadbon was both doughty sidekick and comic foil – playing Duggan dead straight (bar the odd well-timed double take when needed) and being hilarious as a consequence.He was born in Luton, Bedfordshire, the elder son of Josie (nee Cook) and her husband, Thomas, a bank manager. The family moved to Jersey when Tom was 12 and he attended Victoria college in St Helier and then Chichester high school for boys. At his father’s behest he became a trainee at a solicitor’s firm, but found the work tedious – and with help and encouragement from the actor Pearl Goodman he got a job as a stage hand at the Chichester Festival theatre. He subsequently enrolled at the Webber Douglas drama school in London, before moving to Rada after one term.View image in fullscreenChadbon, right, with Richard Butler in Cheek by Howard Barker at the Theatre Upstairs, Royal Court, London, 1970.Photograph: Donald Cooper/AlamyOn graduation, he joined the company at the Phoenix theatre, Leicester, before working with the English Stage Company, playing Valentine in Twelfth Night at the Royal Court in London. He remained there for its 1969Edward Bondseason – featuring Saved, Early Morning, and Narrow Road to the Deep North – which became an international and European tour, helping to cement Bond’s reputation abroad.After his television debut in an episode of The Jazz Age (1968), he became a regular fixture on screen, equally at home in drama and comedy. He was one of the leads in the legal drama Crown Prosecutor (1995), drawing on his legal training as the impatient but skilled maverick Lenny Monk, recurred as Dr Kenworthy in the cosy drama Where the Heart Is (2001-06) and played the regular role of the senior officer presiding over cases investigated by the behavioural analyst Tony Hill (Robson Green) in Wire in the Blood (2002-03), based on the books by Val McDermid. He was, though, mostly in demand as a valuable guest star in dozens of series, from Special Branch (1969) to Agatha Raison (2016) via Rumpole of the Bailey (1978), Tales of the Unexpected (1983), Peep Show (2008) and Poirot (2013).View image in fullscreenChadbon in Heartbeat in 2004.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockHis ability to ground the fantastical made him especially useful to the popular genres of science-fiction and fantasy. His lead role in an episode of Out of the Unknown (1971) found him on intense form as the leader of a gang of hypnotically controlled elite soldiers, while inNigel Kneale’s classic The Stone Tape (1972), he was one of a rambunctious team of scientists whose nerves begin to fray as they investigate a haunting. His terrified scream of realisation that the ghost has infested their own computer is a much cited example of abject on-screen terror. His other genre credits included good parts in Blake’s 7 (1979), a second Doctor Who adventure (this time opposite Colin Baker, 1986), and Space Precinct (1995). His last screen role was a cameo in the hit fantasy series Game of Thrones (2017). His popularity was such that he returned to Doctor Who and Blake’s 7 in several audio spin-offs in recent years.On the big screen he made memorable contributions to The Beast Must Die (1974), Tess (1979), Roman Polanski’s film of Tess of the D’Urbervilles, and Dance with a Stranger (1985, with Miranda Richardson as Ruth Ellis) and he appeared briefly in the James Bond filmCasino Royale(2006).Although he eventually retired from theatre to concentrate on screen and voiceover work, Chadbon managed to indulge his passion for Shakespeare before he did so. His favourite role was Leontes in The Winter’s Tale for the Bristol Old Vic (1983) and his last was King Duncan in Macbeth, with Lennie James andHelen McCroryat the Tricycle theatre (1995). He was also filmed performing Hamlet’s To Be or Not To Be speech for the Open University in 1971.View image in fullscreenChadbon in The Beast Must Die, 1974, directed by Paul Annett.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyHe was a highly skilled and experienced voiceover artist, in demand for commercials and corporate work, latterly narrating the documentary Katie Price: In Therapy (2015) for Channel 5. His wicked sense of humour stood him in good stead throughout his career – he had a reputation for being fun to work with and was a self-confessed giggler.His 1966 marriage to Deborah Leathers ended in divorce. In 1977 he married the designer Jane Hennessy, who survives him, as do their daughters, Millie and Felicity, his sons, Dominic and Nicholas, from his first marriage, and four grandchildren, Delphina, Pearl, Sasha and Fynn.Thomas Richard Chadbon, actor, born 27 February 1946; died 18 July 2026Explore more on these topicsTheatreRoyal Court theatreTelevisionDoctor WhoGame of ThronesobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Nas / The Roots review – NY rap legend is in a nostalgic state of mind  | Hip-hop | The Guardian
description: Nas performs his gritty but intricate 90s classics, sharing the bill on the first London edition of the Roots Picnic festival with Questlove and co’s exuberant funk
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Nas performs his gritty but intricate 90s classics, sharing the bill on the first London edition of the Roots Picnic festival with Questlove and co’s exuberant funk
Content: Shoutout to the sousaphone … Nas performs at the Roots Picnic in London.Photograph: Dave Burke/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenShoutout to the sousaphone … Nas performs at the Roots Picnic in London.Photograph: Dave Burke/ShutterstockHip-hopReviewNas / The Roots review – NY rap legend is in a nostalgic state of mindCrystal Palace Bowl, LondonNas performs his gritty but intricate 90s classics, sharing the bill on the first London edition of the Roots Picnic festival with Questlove and co’s exuberant funkAlexis PetridisSun 9 Aug 2026 06.13 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 08.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLooking out over the audience at the Crystal Palace Bowl, Nas feels moved to reminisce about his first visit to London. It was in 1994, around the time he released his landmark debut albumIllmatic; he remembers performing on pirate radio stations and “eating good Jamaican food”. It seems unlikely that he ever thought he’d be back in the capital sharing the stage with a man playing a sousaphone, but such is the power of the Roots Picnic, a US institution for nearly 20 years. Its famously eclectic bill has regularly featured great rappers backed by hip-hop’s premier live band, sousaphone player and all: Lil’ Wayne, the Wu-Tang Clan, Snoop Dogg, Jay-Z.Before Nas appears at the festival’s first London iteration, the Roots play their own set, augmented by a guest appearance from Common. It plays out almost as one long medley which shifts restlessly between their own back catalogue and old funk, soul and disco covers. They do a killer version of James Brown’s The Payback. Awesomely tight, driven by the relentless crack of drummer Questlove’s snare and heavy on jazzy brass solos, it’s a perfect demonstration of the unique musical space they’ve carved out over the years, somewhere between hip-hop and jam band: the Grateful Dead of rap, if you like.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Dave Burke/ShutterstockNas – 10 of the bestRead moreWhen Nas takes the stage, the exuberant mood shifts. It’s no less powerful or funk-driven but it is noticeably darker, befitting the grittiness of his rhymes. His set acts like a career retrospective albeit one noticeably bigger on 90s classics – NY State of Mind, Hate Me Now – than more recent material. It fits with his recent activities. Like Questlove, he seems to have taken on the mantle of a musical custodian, helming a series of albums and comics featuring a roll call of legendary rappers, himself included. Moreover, he offers a reminder of how skilled he is as an MC, his rhymes both intricate and densely packed. Behind him, the screens show old photos from the same era as his first London visit, baby-faced, sitting outside the Queensbridge projects. It’s impossible to tell if he still looks the same today – the peak of his baseball cap renders his face a dark shadow – but what comes out of his mouth sounds as vital as ever.This article was amended on 9 August 2026. It was the rapper Common who made a guest appearance during the Roots’ set, and not Yasiin Bey as an earlier version said.Explore more on these topicsHip-hopThe RootsRaplive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Comedian Mo Gilligan looks back: ‘Drake shared my video, Ian Wright liked a post – then I quit my job in retail’ | Family | The Guardian
description: The standup and presenter on performing at the back of the school bus, his funny aunts and uncles, and swerving a career selling perfume
Author: Harriet Gibsone
Headline: The standup and presenter on performing at the back of the school bus, his funny aunts and uncles, and swerving a career selling perfume
Content: FlashbackFamilyComedian Mo Gilligan looks back: ‘Drake shared my video, Ian Wright liked a post – then I quit my job in retail’The standup and presenter on performing at the back of the school bus, his funny aunts and uncles, and swerving a career selling perfumeHarriet GibsoneSun 9 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMo Gilligan in 1996 and in 2026Mo Gilligan in 1996 and in 2026. Later photograph: Simon Webb/The Guardian. Styling: Andie Redman. Grooming: Sadaf Ahmad. Archive photograph: courtesy of Mo GilliganBorn in Lambeth, south London, in 1988, Mo Gilligan is a comedian and presenter. His online sketches went viral in 2017, which led to his debut tour, Coupla Cans, and the start of his TV career, co-hosting The Big Narstie Show and presenting The Lateish Show. The winner of two Baftas, Gilligan has released three standup specials, most recently In the Moment. His new documentary, Big Chicken: A Fast Food Conspiracy, is available on Netflix now.This was my go-to poseas a kid. The expression is a combination of me being a bit cheeky, my mum telling me I shouldn’t smile with my teeth out, and someone else telling me that I had a nice smile when I did that grin. It was a safe bet, and I would bring it out for every school photo.I grew up on a council estate near East Dulwich, in south-east London. My childhood was spent with my friends and sisters outside – playing football and cricket and climbing trees or garage roofs until someone told us to get down or come inside. It was a multigenerational place to live, and everyone looked out for each other. I was in awe of anyone who was on TV to the extent that if I ever saw a famous person on the street I would ask them for an autograph. Kriss Akabusi opened our Happy Shopper and I got him to sign my jumper. Once I saw a guy who was on The Bill in Sainsbury’s. I wouldn’t stop talking about it in school the next day.double quotation markI learned how to do a Scottish accent when I was quite young because of watching Trevor in EastEndersMy aunts and uncles were funny people who were always taking the mick. If you wore something weird, you would definitely get called out for it. But it wasn’t until I became a teenager that I realised the real value in making people laugh. I was never the kid who could draw well, or know what 105 multiplied by 52 was – instead my currency was being silly.Without realising it, I was developing my style of standup at the back of the bus. I was a big fan of Eddie Murphy and Jim Carrey, and my friends would tell me I was good at doing impressions. Accents, too. I learned how to do a Scottish accent when I was quite young because of watching Trevor in EastEnders. As a young black boy on a council estate, my Australian accent would wow some of the older kids, too. “How’d you do that, bro? You can speak Australian – that’s crazy, man.” Once I realised I could make people on the bus laugh who weren’t even at school – just random passengers, who were smirking when I was doing stupid stuff for my mates – I realised I might be on to something.I am dyslexic, and at school I wasn’t the most academic.Thankfully, I had some very supportive drama teachers who unlocked something in me. I didn’t realise it at the time, but they were teaching me improv techniques, how to think on my feet. Because of them, I ended up studying performing arts and theatre production at Middlesex University, but I didn’t apply myself and I wasn’t sure what to do after I graduated.A lot of people who study drama might get their first foot on the ladder by working front of house in theatres. I had no idea how I would get into that kind of space, so I went to the jobcentre instead. I told them I wanted to work with young people, and they replied: “How about Asda?” After that, I went into retail. It wasn’t my dream career, but I realised I could practise some of my acting skills while also making money, by creating a caricature of myself. My first job was at Jo Malone, selling luxury fragrances and body creams and candles to posh people. Customers would come in and ask what different scents were and I would switch into a new mode: “Ah yes, this is Lime Basil Mandarin. Would you like to try? You don’t want to apply it to the wrist as it crushes the scent.”Whatever job I was doing, I could shape shift into someone new.It was intensive, as I really did try out every retail job: Thomas Pink, Apple, Levi’s. If a chain had already closed I would put it on my CV just to look more experienced. Dixons? Toys R Us? You name it, I worked there. Or pretended to.When I wasn’t getting people to buy stuff, I was building up my standup career. I ran a comedy night at a hotel, and hosted a show every Sunday called The Sunday Show, which was full of up-and-coming creative people – Ed Sheeran would get on stage and play a song, and Cynthia Erivo would do poetry. I was also doing standup at African-Caribbean nights in university towns. I would visit somewhere like Bradford and perform for a crowd of black kids who were a long way from home. I was something familiar to them in an unfamiliar place.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markWhen I got my first Bafta, it was for all the people out there who look like me and sound like me. It can be doneAt the same time, my online videos were growing an audience. I would do impressions and characters and post them on Snapchat, then Instagram. My first proper viral moment was a video about different types of MCs – the MC who misses a drop, the MC who’s from up north, the MC who’s got an American twang, the cockney MC. It was a one-minute compilation that got shared on Link Up TV, GRM Daily and other meme pages. Then Drake shared something of mine, and Ian Wright liked a post. It was getting harder to juggle new opportunities that were coming in, like radio work, as well as selling 501s, so in the end I quit retail. A month later, I got asked to go to LA for the BET awards. I was staying in a hotel for free, on an all-expenses-paid trip, and standing in the same room as Bruno Mars and Mary J Blige. All I had to do was post something on my socials.Standup was still the thing I wanted to pursue the most. I met with a promoter and told them I was ready to do a tour, but they were hesitant as they said working with social media people was sometimes hit and miss. Because of the experience I had on stage, they gave me a chance. When the London tickets were released, it sold out in three minutes.Comedian Joanne McNally looks back: ‘In my 20s, my bulimia was spiralling out of control. My breakdown was the making of me’Read moreWhen I got nominated for my first Baftafor The Lateish Show WithMo Gilligan, I didn’t think I would win. I was up against Frankie Boyle, Lee Mack and Graham Norton, and I had just started my TV career. As it was lockdown, it was happening virtually, so I was in my house and wearing shorts. I decided to put a shirt on, too, just in case the camera panned to me. Then I won. The feeling was strange – all these people falling silent and listening to me. I didn’t want to act like a rock star and give some flippant speech, and I didn’t want to be too sentimental, either. But as those words are immortalised I wanted to say something I cared about.As much as the award was for me, it was really for all of the people out there who looked like me, sounded like me and came from the same kind of places that I grew up. Those big ambitions of being on stage, hosting TV shows, winning awards – none of it feels achievable when you haven’t got the right kind of access or connections. But it can be done. You don’t have to be the kid getting your jumper signed outside the Happy Shopper. You can be the one signing it.Explore more on these topicsFamilyFlashbackMo GilliganPhotographyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My husband won’t make any effort to please me in bed | Sex | The Guardian
description: This may be more to do with ageing than a lack of love. Talk about it – hopefully you can work out a new repertoire together
Author: Annalisa Barbieri
Headline: This may be more to do with ageing than a lack of love. Talk about it – hopefully you can work out a new repertoire together
Content: Illustration: Alex Mellon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Alex Mellon/The GuardianAsk Annalisa BarbieriSexMy husband won’t make any effort to please me in bedThis may be more to do with ageing than a lack of love. Talk about it – hopefully you can work out a new repertoire togetherAnnalisa BarbieriSun 9 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 10.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy husband and I have been together for six years.He is 60, 20 years older than me. We had a baby last year and went through a really difficult time in our relationship. Things are better after some couples therapy, but we are both still unhappy with our sex life.I take a while to orgasm, and he gets very impatient and essentially just gives up (he always orgasms first, and quickly).I also have longstanding health issues that make sex painful. He has always been respectful when I say I can’t have sex because of the pain. But he gets defensive and unkind when I askhim to try new thingsto give me pleasure. He bought sex toysand says these were his way of trying, but Isaw them as a way of him passing off a job he can’t be bothered to do.He recently told me he has been the lover to “lots of” women.I am wondering if he saw himself as the pleasure-giver to those women, rather than their husbands, and that he has now,subconsciously, transferred that into our marriage.He says he had a lot of sex before we met, so has sort of resigned himself to masturbation (I’m not willing to accept that). But he says he wishes I would feel pleasure andthat I deserve it. He has suggested me sleeping with other men – as long as I don’t tell himabout it. WhileI would consider non-monogamy if it was the only option,I wouldn’t want to be sneaking around.I had an active sex life beforewe met, and it was never just about orgasms – it was about the anticipation,and feeling sexy, wanted and emotionally bonded. I’d love that with my husband.I think you’ve hit on something: your husband has been used to being the lover of women without any of the responsibilities attached. Now, he’s a husband, which is a different ballgame. I’d be interested to know how long ago the last of these “relationships” was and why he decided to settle down.I went to sex and relationship psychotherapist Silva Neves. “It sounds as if the sexual problem is to do with connection,” he said. “It’s important for a good sex life to want to get to know our partner’s body, what turns them on, how they like to be touched. But it sounds like there is little interest or curiosity from your husband.”double quotation markIt doesn’t sound like he doesn’t care about you – more that he doesn’t think he can meet your sexual needsNeves felt this could be “to do with ageing, or maybe he has low energy or low testosterone. It doesn’t sound like he doesn’t care about you – more that he doesn’t think he can meet your sexual needs. It may be worth having some proper conversations about that so you can understand what is behind his lack of interest.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMy husband no longer desires me, but engaging an escort has complicated things | Ask Annalisa BarbieriRead moreYou could have an open relationship, but that is on your husband’s terms again, isn’t it? Neves wondered if you could “keep a loving relationship by not putting pressure on yourselves to make sex work, and meet that need elsewhere”? On the other hand, he said, couples can navigate the changes that happen with ageing or after having a baby if both make efforts to adapt. “One way to start is to step outside the usual sexual scripts: I ‘should’ do this, he ‘should’ do that. Instead, how about going back to the drawing board and figuring out a whole new sexual menu together?”If your husband really won’t engage, that in itself is an answer.Sexoften shows cracks in relationships to which we want to turn a blind eye. It doesn’t sound as if you two have ever been sexually compatible. Given the paucity of other details about how you get on, I have to ask: what is worth saving here and do you really want to?Every week, Annalisa Barbieri addresses a personal problem sent in by a reader. If you would like advice from Annalisa, please send your problem toask.annalisa@theguardian.com. Annalisa regrets she cannot enter into personal correspondence. Submissions are subject toour terms and conditions.
