title: We know sleep, exercise and diet are vital for health. But why? | Science and nature books | The Guardian
description: The benefits of all three come down to a crucial piece of cellular kit
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The benefits of all three come down to a crucial piece of cellular kit
Content: Illustration: Elia BarbieriView image in fullscreenIllustration: Elia BarbieriThe big ideaScience and nature booksWe know sleep, exercise and diet are vital for health. But why?The benefits of all three come down to a crucial piece of cellular kitHannah CritchlowSun 9 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 09.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSleep. Exercise. Eat well. It’s the oldest recommendation in medicine, repeated so often it’s become a cliche. We know the advice, even if we don’t always follow it. But have you ever stopped to wonder why these three seemingly different habits have such remarkably similar effects on our brains and bodies?For generations we’ve treated them as separate prescriptions – sleep restores us, exercise strengthens us and food fuels us. Yet neuroscience is beginning to suggest something rather more elegant: they’re all essentially doing the same job.What has changed is not the recommendations themselves, but our understanding of the biology beneath them. The more scientists study the brain, the clearer it becomes that cognition is astonishingly energy intensive. Although the brain makes up about 2% of body weight, it uses roughly a fifth of the body’s energy at rest. Every memory we retrieve, every decision we make and every creative insight carries a metabolic cost. Thought itself is an energy-hungry act.That raises an obvious question: where does all that energy come from? The answer lies deep in evolutionary history. More than 2bn years ago, a primitive cell engulfed a bacterium. Instead of being digested, the bacterium remained, forming a long-term partnership with its host.Over time, this arrangement became one of biology’s most important alliances. The bacterium became remarkably efficient at capturing the chemical energy stored in food and transforming it into ATP, the molecule that powers almost every biological process. The host offered protection, and together they made complex life possible.double quotation markIntelligence depends not simply on the brain’s wiring, but on the uninterrupted flow of energy through that wiringThat partnership is still running inside us today. Mitochondria – the descendants of that ancient bacterium – exist in almost every cell in the body. The exception is the mature red blood cell, which removes them to make space for haemoglobin and improve oxygen transport. Even here, biology reveals its logic: everything is shaped by trade-offs in energy efficiency.For decades, mitochondria were introduced in biology textbooks as the cell’s “powerhouses” – important, dependable but rather dull. The stars of the show were undeniably neurons. Today, that picture is changing.We’re discovering that neurons produce thought, ideas and emotions only because mitochondria continuously transform fuel into the energy they need. Intelligence depends not simply on the brain’s wiring, but on the uninterrupted flow of energy through that wiring. This is a subtle shift in perspective, but an important one.Emerging evidence suggests that healthy mitochondrial functionhelps give rise to intelligence, including drivingarithmetic and processing speed,working memory,healthier brain ageingand greaterresilience to stress. Mitochondria are no longer viewed as passive batteries but as active participants in the delicate balancing act that allows the brain to adapt, learn and flourish throughout life.Suddenly, the oldest health advice begins to make much more sense. Exercise doesn’t simply boost muscle mass, itbulks upthe hippocampus – a key region of the brain involved in learning and memory. It also encourages mitochondria to becomemore numerous and more efficient. We often imagine we’re training our bodies; we’re alsostrengtheningthe ancient energy system that allows our brains to work.Sleep performs a different kind of maintenance. While we’re unconscious, the brain is astonishingly busy. Memories are consolidated and worn-out cellular components – including mitochondria – arerepaired or replaced. So rather than thinking of sleep as simply rest, we can conceive of it, at least partly, as a mitochondrial maintenance shift, aimed at preparing the brain for another day of active learning, adapting and imagining.Then there’s food. Mitochondria rely entirely on what we eat to perform their remarkable chemistry. The quality of that fuel matters. Dietsrich in minimally processed foodsprovide the ingredients for efficient energy transformation, while diets that continually overwhelm the system appear to make that processless efficientover time.Seen through this lens, sleep, exercise and diet stop looking like three separate pieces of lifestyle advice and become different ways of caring for the same biological inheritance. What fascinates me most is that this new understanding reaches far beyond physical health. Scientists are uncoveringintriguing linksbetween mitochondrial function and resilience,mood,personalitytraits, and even oursocial lives.For centuries we’ve tended to separate mind from body, as though thoughts somehow floated free of the flesh that produced them. The reality is that thoughts emerge from living tissue that must constantly capture, transform and use energy simply to exist.The mitochondrial psychobiologist Martin Picard has argued that we’ve become accustomed to thinking of ourselves as molecular machines, when it may be more useful to think of ourselves asenergetic processes. The brain is an organ whose every thought, memory and feeling depends on the continuous transformation of energy within billions of cells.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSeen this way, sleep is no longer simply rest, and exercise is no longer simply fitness. Food is no longer simply fuel. They’re different ways of sustaining the ancient biological partnership that allows our bodies – and our minds – to flourish.It’s remarkable to think that every idea you’ve ever had, every problem you’ve solved, every person you’ve loved and every hope you’ve held has depended upon an alliance forged more than 2bn years ago. The tiny descendants of that ancient bacterium have been quietly working inside us ever since, making possible not just movement or metabolism but thought itself.Perhaps that’s why the oldest health advice has survived every new scientific fashion. Long before we knew about ATP, oxidative phosphorylation or mitochondria, we recognised that people who slept well, moved regularly and ate nourishing food tended to flourish. We’re finally beginning to understand why.Hannah Critchlow is a neuroscientist and author ofThe 21st Century Brain(Torva).Further readingThe Song of the Cellby Siddhartha Mukherjee (Vintage, £14.99)Transformer: The Deep Chemistry of Life and Death by Nick Lane (Profile, £14.99How Life Works: A User’s Guide to the New Biology by Philip Ball (Picador, £14.99)Explore more on these topicsScience and nature booksThe big ideaNeuroscienceHealthSleepfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Voters are fed up’: Michigan primary forces Democratic party to accept leftwing shift | Democrats | The Guardian
description: With Abdul El-Sayed’s win, the party’s leftwing insurgency had breached the walls of a midwestern swing state, forcing a reckoning about Democrats’ direction and leadership
Author: David Smith
Headline: With Abdul El-Sayed’s win, the party’s leftwing insurgency had breached the walls of a midwestern swing state, forcing a reckoning about Democrats’ direction and leadership
Content: Abdul El-Sayed, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Zohran Mamdani.Illustration: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAbdul El-Sayed, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Zohran Mamdani.Illustration: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesThe Sunday readDemocrats‘Voters are fed up’: Michigan primary forces Democratic party to accept leftwing shiftWith Abdul El-Sayed’s win, the party’s leftwing insurgency had breached the walls of a midwestern swing state, forcing a reckoning about Democrats’ direction and leadershipDavid SmithSun 9 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareStanding beforeThe Spirit of Detroit, a landmark bronze statue in the city’s downtown, in the early hours of a Wednesday morning, Abdul El-Sayed channelled boxing great Muhammad Ali. “We shook up the world,” he declared.The 41-year-old former public health official had just delivered a knockout blow to the Democratic establishment,defeating the US congresswoman Haley Stevensto claim the party’s nomination for the Senate in swing state Michigan.El-Sayed hadcampaigned on a boldly progressive agendaof universal healthcare, halting military aid to Israel and sweeping campaign finance reform. The moderate Stevens had received $60m from outside groups, including $30m from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) and its affiliates.It was the latest and possibly biggest tremor in a political earthquake consuming the Democratic party. Its leftwing insurgency was no longer confined to deep blue coastal cities; it had breached the walls of a critical midwestern swing state. Now it is forcing a reckoning about the party’s leadership and its ideological direction ahead of the 2026 midterms and the 2028 presidential election.Matt Duss, executive vice-president of theCenter for International Policyand a former foreign policy adviser to the leftwing senator Bernie Sanders, said: “It’s dissatisfaction with the status quo. It’s dissatisfaction with the establishment. This is an anti-system moment.“We see this not just in our country but in democracies around the world. Voters are fed up with an elite establishment that is simply not delivering for them, that doesn’t feel their pain, that doesn’t seem to know or care about their struggles, and that’s part of why Abdul succeeded.”The past decade of US politics has been dominated by the rightwing populism ofDonald Trump. But leftwing populism has been running – and flourishing – on a parallel track since Sanders’ outsider campaign for president in 2016 was ultimately beaten back by Hillary Clinton and the Democratic establishment.Duss added: “The 2016 Sanders campaign was sort of the Big Bang for the rebirth of the progressive left in the United States. We’ve got a lot of others who joined Bernie. We’ve got a lot of great leaders on the progressive left now and are glad to have Abdul El-Sayed run.”Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a bartender who was an organiser for Sanders’s 2016 campaign,pulled off a stunning upsettwo years later against an incumbent in New York’s 14th district, becoming, at 29, the youngest woman ever to serve in the House of Representatives. She was joined by a small but vocal group of progressives known as “the Squad”.Sanders ran again in 2020 and, though he lost to establishment figure Joe Biden, his teamhad significant inputinto the surprisingly progressive agenda of the Biden presidency. But the events of 2024 – Biden’s abortive run for a second term, Kamala Harris’s coronation and Donald Trump’s return to power – exposed a chasm between the party leadership and the grassroots.Last November, Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist laser focused on affordability, beat establishment favourite Andrew Cuomo to become the first Muslim mayor of New York. He then helped three insurgent candidates win Democratic primary elections in New York. The “Mamdani effect” swept through Colorado, Illinois, Michigan, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Washington state, Wisconsin and Washington DC.The driving factors include frustration with Trump,the cost of living, corporate money in politics and the ongoing conflict in Gaza.Reuters/ Ipsos pollingshowed Israel’s favorability among Democrats plummeting from 59% in 2018 to just 22% in May 2026. The influx of Aipac money into political campaigns has become toxic for younger voters.In Michigan, which has the highest percentage of Arab Americans relative to population, El-Sayed accused Israel of committing genocide and built his campaign around a demand to end unconditional US military aid to the country. This positioned him directly against Stevens, who defended the US-Israel relationship and benefited from massive Aipac spending.El-Sayed’s ultimate victory – coupled with wins for progressivesWill LawrenceandDonavan McKinneyin House races in Michigan – marked a watershed moment, a high-stakes proof of concept challenging the myth that leftwing populists cannot win elections outside Democratic strongholds.Larry Jacobs, director of the Center for the Study of Politics and Governance at the University of Minnesota, perceives a general break within the party flowing from various sources including the “staleness” of its current leaders, Chuck Schumer in the Senate and Hakeem Jeffries in the House – both ardent supporters of Israel. “Gaza and Israel has become a lightning rod for all the other issues,” he added. “There’s a sense that the Democrats have been patsies in the face of Donald Trump. When Democrats say they want to fight back, they mean it.“Donald Trump has radicalised the Democratic party,” he said. “This revolt within the party would not have happened without Donald Trump. He is provoking a kind of earthquake, raising lots of unsettling questions within the Democratic party - its direction, its leadership, its policy priorities, its beholdenness to big donors.”Trump has rattled the old orthodoxies that prevailed in US politics for decades. If the right can conceive a radical programme in documents such asProject 2025, why can the left not be similarly ambitious? There is little appetite to return to the pre-Trump era, a broken system that led to his rise in the first place, but rather to reimagine wealth redistribution, stronger unions, democratic reform and a just foreign policy.Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of Our Revolution, a group born out of Sanders’ 2016 run, said: “You’re seeing a maturation of the progressive movement. You’re seeing the infrastructure that’s been built over a decade come into play. There’s a resonance of the message in reaction to the failed populism of the right but you’re also seeing increased sophistication in the organisation of the left.”The rise of groups such as theDemocratic Socialists of America(DSA) has occurred in tandem with a crisis of confidence and identity within the centrist wing of the Democratic party. At a moment when Trump paints the landscape in big and bold primary colours, the moderates are widely seen as timid incrementalists who lack ideas or superstars to compete with El-Sayed, Mamdani and Ocasio-Cortez.Geevarghese commented: “Because some of their funding depends on corporate donors, moderates have to pull punches. They are not able to articulate the causes of people’s problems. You’ve got progressives who are able to call out the corporate class and the corruption of our politics and how that affects people’s standard of living.”Even as they recognise the ground shifting beneath their feet, progressives warn that centrists are not likely to surrender the power they enjoy courtesy of Wall Street and Silicon Valley without a fight.Norman Solomon, director of RootsAction and executive director of the Institute for Public Accuracy, said: “One might say that hell has no fury like corporate Democrats scorned. I’m thrilled by the results in Michigan but at the same time I’m a bit apprehensive about the blowback from the powerful forces that have been accustomed to literally running the national Democratic party for many decades, arguably since the Democratic Leadership Council (DLC) was so successful at the beginning of the 1990s.”The DLC was founded by Al From,who in 1989 handpicked Bill Clintonto steer the Democratic party toward the centre ground, creating the “Third Way” movement that was pivotal to his 1992 victory and later emulated by Tony Blair in Britain.From reflected this week: “We’ve been focusing on beating Republicans and the democratic socialists have been focused on beating us.We’ve got to fight back. We’ve got to make it harder for them.”When Clinton first campaigned for president, 43% of Americans thought of themselves as moderate, compared to 36% conservative and 17% liberal. That picture has changed radically in the intervening years of polarisation.“Our formula is the right formula,” From insisted. “Obviously we’re in a different world and you have to communicate it different and you’ll need ideas that further the same underlying values, as we did, but they’ve got to be modern ideas, maybe different ideas because circumstances have changed. Our platform was for the 1990s, not for the 2030s, but the principles are the same.“The democratic socialists want a different system. They don’t want to further democratic values. You look at their platform: they want to get rid of the Senate, the presidency, the supreme court; they want ownership of business; they want to get rid of police; they don’t want to fund the military.”“That isn’t the historic Democratic party. It’s not the party of Roosevelt that saved capitalism and saved democracy in the world in World War II. It’s a different ideology, it’s a different party. “The true test of viability for El-Sayed – a Rhodes scholar, doctor and son of Egyptian immigrants – will come in November when he facesMike Rogers, a former Republican congressman, in a race that could determine the balance of power in the Senate. After an unusually rancorous campaign, El-Sayed was quick to urge “the things that unite us are so much bigger than the things that divide us,” and Stevens was equally quick to back him.Indeed, progressives and moderates across the country are likely to maintain an uneasy co-existence for the midterms as each plays to their demographical and geographical strengths in common cause against Republicans. Trump and the House speaker, Mike Johnson, have been seeking torevive a cold war-style panicby branding democratic socialists as “radical Marxists” and “godless communists”.Donna Brazile, a political strategist and former interim chair of the Democratic National Committee, said: “The question is, can two different wings of the same party function, unify and function as a governing majority if the Democrats win the majority? I contend that the answer is yes. We’ll agree on very important matters like the economy, improving the lives of the American people, making things more affordable again and not focusing on vanity projects, so the extent that we’re all running on the same message of affordability, the answer is yes.”But then comes 2028 and a time for choosing. The centrist group Third Way is planning a new $15m effort to discredit democratic socialism between now and the next presidential election,the New York Times reported. Some Democrats argue that progressives have won only a handful of races – albeit high-profile ones – among hundreds taking place across the country and the extent of the insurgency is exaggerated. Others believe the Michigan result means the leftwing lane just got wider.Geevarghese commented: “All of the electoral energy and enthusiasm is on the left and, at the end of the day, for a candidate to be viable in the 2028 presidential, they’re going to have to articulate a full-throated economic populism. That’s what’s needed to make it through the primary and ultimately that’s what’s going to be needed to be the antidote to Donald Trump.”Speculation is already swirling around who might carry the progressive banner into the next presidential primary. Mamdani, born outside the US, is not eligible to run, and said he does not want to. Congressman Ro Khanna of California, who campaigned for El-Sayed, is frequently mentioned but the most intense focus is onOcasio-Cortez, who is 36.Henry Olsen, a senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center thinktank in Washington, said: “If I were AOC’s advisers, I would look her in the eye and say, ‘Do you want to be president? If you want it to be president, the time is now. You will never have a better chance to own a lane that wants a leader.’“One of the things we’ve seen across the world in the last decade is young female leaders captivating the left. Why not a 39-year-old AOC?”

title: ‘They kidnapped a hard-working kid off our streets’: the gardener seized by ICE – and the New York town fighting back | US immigration | The Guardian
description: Gerson Turcios was 17 when he fled violence in Honduras to build a new life in the US. Six years later, he was mowing lawns in his home town of Rhinebeck when immigration officers took him. Within hours, friends, neighbours and local celebrities sprang into action. Could they stop his deportation?
Author: Alex Hannaford
Headline: Gerson Turcios was 17 when he fled violence in Honduras to build a new life in the US. Six years later, he was mowing lawns in his home town of Rhinebeck when immigration officers took him. Within hours, friends, neighbours and local celebrities sprang into action. Could they stop his deportation?
Content: Yorleny Weigel holds a photograph of Gerson Turcios.Photograph: Celeste Sloman/The GuardianView image in fullscreenYorleny Weigel holds a photograph of Gerson Turcios.Photograph: Celeste Sloman/The GuardianUS immigration‘They kidnapped a hard-working kid off our streets’: the gardener seized by ICE – and the New York town fighting backGerson Turcios was 17 when he fled violence in Honduras to build a new life in the US. Six years later, he was mowing lawns in his home town of Rhinebeck when immigration officers took him. Within hours, friends, neighbours and local celebrities sprang into action. Could they stop his deportation?Alex HannafordSun 9 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGerson Turcios didn’t recognise the men standing next to a couple of dark SUVs outside his house one July afternoon last year. He figured they were lost and approached to see if he could help. A slim 23-year-old with short dark hair and big brown eyes, Turcios had just finished work mowing lawns in the pretty town of Rhinebeck, in New York’s Hudson Valley. The men asked if he knew someone called Jimmy – he did, but Jimmy hadn’t lived in the small, white weatherboard house with Turcios, his brother and his brother’s girlfriend for a while.The men noted Turcios’s accent and asked where he was from. Turcios didn’t answer, so one took out his phone and snapped a photograph. The next thing Turcios knew, he was in handcuffs in the back of one of the SUVs and on his way to an ICE processing centre in Newburgh, New York, then on to a detention centre.Mass deportation has been the defining mission of Donald Trump’s second presidency. In the year since he took office, ICE – United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement – has deported nearly a quarter of a million people from inside the US (half a million including from its borders) as part of an immigration crackdown. Theseforceful apprehensions, which have in some casesresulted in fatal shootingsof potential deportees and bystanders, have resulted in protests – and sparked international outrage. Behind the statistics, though, are stories of hope and perseverance; of young immigrants who risked everything crossing rivers and deserts to build lives, start businesses and put down roots in communities that are now fighting to keep them.Back then, as he was shackled and led to his cell, sure he was about to be deported back to Honduras, Turcios – an immigrant who had made a terrifying journey as a teenager, fleeing violence there – had no idea that his community in Rhinebeck was already mobilising; that they would raise tens of thousands of dollars in days, galvanise support from Hollywood actors and film-makers who also called the town home, and even recruit the lawyer who essentially wrote the book on stopping ICE deportations around the nation to represent him.I’d moved to Rhinebeck with my own family from Texas during the pandemic, drawn to the bucolic countryside and good schools. Our own daughter now walks the same high school hallways Turcios once did. For me, and a lot of other people who call this small town home, Turcios’s arrest was personal.double quotation markIt was the first time I’ve ever used Instagram without being embarrassed about self-promotionView image in fullscreenActor Griffin Dunne, who has raised awareness of Turcios’s case.Photograph: Celeste Sloman/The Guardian“Well, it’s happened,”wroteactor Griffin Dunne on Instagram. “ICE has come to my beloved Dutchess County and kidnapped a hard working kid with his own local lawn care business, and without a criminal record, off our tranquil streets.” But he added, “This is only the beginning.” Dunne, who has a home in Rhinebeck, told his followers that the community had started a war chest to defend Turcios. “Our pressure has brought about a hearing for Gerson at 11:00 tomorrow morning at Thurgood Marshall Courthouse for those who wish to show support. To my Rhinebeck neighbors, a bus will leave from Tops [grocery store] at 7:00 am.”Six years earlier, around 9pm on a freezing December night, Turcios and three other migrants had stood by the southern banks of the Rio Grande river in Mexico, looking across into Texas as flames torched the desert brush behind them; Mexican soldiers had set it alight to flush them out.With nowhere left to go, Turcios turned to the others. “We are right here,” he told them. “The other side is the United States.” Another boy checked that everyone was able to swim – they were – but all Gerson could think about was alligators, which had occasionally been known to inhabit the Rio Grande.View image in fullscreenTurcios before he fled to the US …Photograph: courtesy of Henoch TurciosView image in fullscreen… and celebrating his birthday with his brother Henoch in the US in 2021.Photograph: courtesy of Yorleny WeigelThe four boys jumped into the black water together, fighting the current as it pushed them downstream. Along that stretch, near McAllen, Texas, the width of the Rio Grande ranges from 45 to 90 meters. Finally, soaking wet, they scrambled up a concrete wall on the US side. They ran through scrubland until headlights appeared behind them, then three German shepherds. A heavier boy was dragged down by the dogs as he scaled a fence; the others scattered. Turcios sprinted until three cars boxed him in andUS immigrationofficers emerged with guns drawn. “If you keep running,” they shouted, “we’re gonna shoot your legs.” Turcios stopped, put his hands up, then fell to his knees and felt a boot between his shoulder blades as they threw him to the ground and handcuffed him. He had spent six weeks on a journey that had nearly broken him. Against all odds, he had made it across the river. And now he’d been caught.In 2019, during the first Trump administration, an adult detained by Border Patrol crossing into the US was increasingly likely to be sent back to Mexico to wait for their immigration case to be heard. Turcios, though, was under 18, and the law dictated he be taken to refugee resettlement housing for minors. Turcios stayed at a facility in Long Island for almost a month until his brother, Henoch, and Henoch’s girlfriend, Yorleny Weigel, were allowed to pick him up and return to Weigel’s home in Rhinebeck.Henoch had come to the US in 2017 via a tortuous route, and Turcios hadn’t seen him for six years. Their first stop was a Wendy’s fast food joint for a burger – “So big,” Turcios now recalls, “I didn’t know how to eat it.”He would have to wait for the government to notify him of his first immigration hearing, but soon the Covid pandemic would throw the courts into chaos, with some hearings postponed indefinitely and others rescheduled then postponed again, leaving Turcios in limbo.Weigel showed Turcios his room, then drove him across the river to a big outlet store in the city of Kingston to buy clothes. He spoke no English, so Weigel registered him with a county language integration programme and with the local high school. In the summer of 2020, ahead of the start of the school year, he was introduced to Anna Lawson, who would be one of his classmates. Lawson was in advanced Spanish and, as Covid was still forcing people to meet virtually, they spoke regularly over Zoom. “He is a really lovely, positive person,” Lawson says. “He’d often be sitting outside, talking about how much he enjoyed Rhinebeck.”double quotation markHis English progressed very quickly. Each day we’d go outside and play basketballView image in fullscreenBrendan Dougherty, who shared a study hall with Turcios at school in Rhinebeck.Photograph: Celeste Sloman/The GuardianOn the first day of school, Turcios was afraid he’d be arrested by the police officer who sat outside in his car for an hour each morning as kids entered the building– just under half of US state schools have police patrol on campus – but after his first day, that fear passed. “After that I wasn’t afraid. I was excited,” he says. “But I didn’t speak any English at all.” Turcios immediately hit it off with his classmates. Brendan Dougherty shared a study hall with him. “Gerson is a very sociable guy, so it wasn’t difficult to strike up a conversation with him,” Dougherty says. “And his English progressed very quickly. Each day we’d go outside and play basketball.”Turcios finished high school in the early summer of 2022 and began working in the kitchen of a local French restaurant and, in his spare time, for a crew that did landscaping and house maintenance, and mowed lawns. One of his first clients was Jenny Friedberg, a creative director and producer who had moved up to Rhinebeck from the city during the pandemic. Turcios and the maintenance crew painted her basement in Brooklyn, and excavated 24in of bedrock under her barn in Rhinebeck. “Whatever they did, Gerson was always there,” Friedberg says. “He was the youngest of the crew, the smiliest, the most helpful, and my favourite.”In the summer of 2025, Turcios left the restaurant and went to work full-time with the crew. At 7.30pm on 18 July 2025, Friedberg’s phone rang. It was Carlos, Turcios’s boss. Turcios had been detained by ICE, he told her, and he didn’t know what to do.Friedberg made several calls that evening. The first was to Luciano Valdivia, a local restaurateur and president of Rhinebeck’s chamber of commerce. The next was to Amanda Miller, a local attorney. Then John Reinish, a political communications strategist she knew. Within 24 hours, they’d set up aSpotfund, an online fundraising platform, to raise money for Turcios’s legal battle. Miller called Gregory Copeland, a law school friend who had pioneered legal strategies to stop ICE deportations and had also moved to Rhinebeck.double quotation markWhatever the maintenance crew did, he was always there. He was the youngest, the smiliest, the most helpful, and my favouriteView image in fullscreenJenny Friedberg, a creative director and producer for whom Turcios had worked.Photograph: Celeste Sloman/The GuardianCopeland was a nationally recognised civil rights and immigration attorney, and co-founder of the Rapid Defense Network, a non-profit providing pro bono legal support to immigrants facing deportation. He was also the subject of the documentary Guerrilla Habeas, which looked at the legal strategy it employed to stop deportations at the last moment. That strategy hinged on filing habeas corpus petitions, which empower federal judges to compel the authorities to justify detentions, a power enshrined in the constitution. Doing this forces cases out of immigration courts and into federal court, where due process can be properly considered and immigrants have a fairer shot at justice.Miller says Copeland had experience fighting “the biggest machine there is – the federal government”. But since his move to Rhinebeck, he had stopped practising civil rights and immigration law, and had turned his attention to estate planning for clients. Still, Miller knew there was no one better to help Turcios.“It wasn’t clear to me immediately that I would help him, but I went into triage mode, gathering information and figuring out what our options were,” Copeland says. As soon as Copeland got Turcios’s “A-Number” – the alien registration number assigned by the US Department of Homeland Security to non-citizens– he could check his status in the system. He discovered that, years earlier, Turcios had been ordered deported “in absentia” for missing a hearing. During Covid, courts repeatedly moved locations; Turcios missed a notice despite living at the same address he’d always provided.Copeland knew it was now vital to get the Rhinebeck community to show up for him. “If you consider what the government evaluates when justifying someone’s detention, it’s whether they’re a danger to the community and a flight risk,” Copeland says. “The community is typically not going to show up for a dangerous person. And you’re less of a flight risk if there’s a strong community around you.”It was a matter of urgency to identify where Turcios was being taken and where he was going next. Copeland says it’s not an exact science, but after working these cases as long as he had, you get a feel for it. A red flag was if he had been sent to Louisiana, a staging location for deportations – at this point, he had not. However, Turcios had been detained with his passport – another red flag. “[The government] needs two things to remove you: a travel document and a final order of removal,” Copeland says. “They need something to show who you are because in immigration court one of the first things they need to establish is that you’re not a citizen.” If an immigrant picked up by ICE doesn’t have a travel document on them, that buys their attorneys more time.Meanwhile, Valdivia asked Leah Conklin, another resident who worked in international criminal justice reform, to get involved. Within days of Turcios’s arrest, a crack team was coming together, but time was of the essence. “One of the reasons they make arrests on Friday, I think, is because you can’t catch up,” Valdivia says, “and if you don’t know where they’re going, you don’t know how to stop it.”Copeland was looking at theonline detainee locator system, trying to get a feel for where Turcios was moving – through which processing centre; which detention centre. In New York state, if you are taken to Federal Plaza in Manhattan and then your location “goes dark”, that’s an indicator you could be bound for a deportation flight. “It’s very relevant for filing a habeas petition,” Copeland says, “because you have to file where they’re detained.” If you don’t know where your client is, you can’t file and they can be deported. “So it’s a game they’re playing – hiding the person.”Conklin had been calling around law firms but found it impossible to get a lawyer quickly enough. On Sunday, Copeland agreed to take on Turcios’s case himself. “I had created the Rapid Defense Network because there’s a small window in which you have to do this. It’s like a death penalty case: you have to strike while the iron’s hot or you’re dead.” By that evening, with Miller’s help, Copeland had filed an emergency petition on Turcios’s behalf, seeking a stay to allow him to consult with lawyers and challenge his removal order. Conklin says that the community came together in record time.double quotation markThey make arrests on Friday so you can’t catch up. If you don’t know where they’re going, you don’t know how to stop itView image in fullscreenLocal residents who joined the fight included Luciano Valdivia, restaurateur and former president of the Rhinebeck chamber of commerce …View image in fullscreen… and Leah Conklin, who worked in international criminal justice reform. Photographs: Celeste Sloman/The GuardianValdivia messaged some other Rhinebeck residents he knew could amplify Turcios’s story. He called Dunne, the actor and writer who had starred in An American Werewolf in London and After Hours, and whom Valdivia counted as a friend. He texted film-maker Andrew Jarecki, who donated, as did actor Paul Rudd, who co-owns a sweet shop in Rhinebeck and lives there with his family. Word spread. Other contributions came in from all over the US and beyond.Dunne began posting about Turcios’s case on social media. “It was the first time I’ve ever used Instagram without kind of being embarrassed about self-promotion because I had a movie coming out,” he says. “It made sense to me for the first time. I was just struck by the inhumanity and the contagion of cruelty.”Friedberg says that when Turcios was arrested, she had a reckoning with herself: “This sort of recognition of how we don’t often know the people that have been working for us or near us for years.” She had never asked about Turcios’s story.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTurcios spent his early childhood in the small town of Balfate on Honduras’s northern coast. His father, Juan, raised cattle. Irma, his mother, gave birth to 10 children. The disappearance of his eldest brother, Amilcar, is one of Turcios’s earliest memories. He was four when his brother went missing after travelling by boat to Roatán, a Honduran island, to seek a better life. Of the five people who made the trip, authorities recovered the bodies of three. Amilcar and the boat’s captain were never found. Turcios’s family never learned the truth; they suspect it had something to do with organised crime, but they’ve come to accept that Amilcar is dead.While there has been a drop in violent crime in the last couple of years, historically Honduras has been one of the most dangerous countries in the world, with gangs vying for control of drugs and extortion rackets. A decade ago, it frequently topped global lists of thehighest murder rates in non-war zone countries, fuelled by its position as a major transit hub for South American cocaine heading to the US.“My mother was afraid, so she decided we should move from that place where she lost her son,” Turcios says. The family relocated to just outside the large city of San Pedro Sula and stayed there for nine years. Turcios went to school, but eventually they sold up and moved to a house in the mountains. It was beautiful, he says, but dangerous; you could never be sure which was more deadly – the criminal gangs who stole livestock, or the venomous snakes and other wildlife.They had 10 cows to tend and a few horses, and they began constructing their own house. Laundry was done in a small stream and cooking over fire. Walking to the city took nine hours, over mountain passes; Turcios recalls jumping on his father’s shoulders to cross rivers.By the time Turcios moved to the mountains, his brother Henoch had already migrated to the US. Henoch says he travelled from Honduras, across Mexico by train, without any money and had to beg for food. He spent three months in Monterrey, where he almost had to have his left hand amputated due to an infection. A friend helped him pay for the medication – the same friend would eventually take in Henoch in Rhinebeck. After he’d recovered enough, he hitched a ride on a train to the border town of Sonoyta, then spent 22 days walking through the southern desert into Arizona. He says he nearly died after spending weeks without eating, surviving on nothing but water.‘Don’t go to the US – not with Trump in charge’: the UK tourist with a valid visa detained by ICE for six weeksRead moreEventually, Turcios’s parents decided to move back to town as they wanted his younger sisters, aged eight and 10, to go to school, and to be nearer to a hospital in case they got sick. Turcios stayed in the mountains, living alone for six months so his father wouldn’t have to sell his animals, but he was an hour away by foot from the nearest house. His father gave him a gun for safety and most nights he’d lie awake, clutching it, and listening to the cries of animals in the wilderness.After the 16-year-old son of his nearest neighbour was murdered over drugs, Turcios’s siblings decided it was time for him to leave Honduras. One day, when visiting his sister in town, he was told that the following morning a man would arrive who would help him cross into Mexico and travel to the US to join his brother. “I didn’t have a future in Honduras,” he says. “If you wanted to go to college, you had to pay a lot of money and my parents couldn’t afford it. And I knew if I went to the United States I would learn how to speak English and it would be better for me.”Two days later he was travelling across Guatemala by bus and car, under the “care” of a coyote – a people smuggler he had paid 12,000 Honduran pesos, the equivalent of about £350 – or, as he recalls, the amount he’d received for a cow he’d sold five days earlier. Turcios had been told the back route through the mountains would keep him safe. He, his coyote and a group of other migrants moved only at night, but safety proved elusive. At a bus stop in Guatemala, armed officers boarded and ordered passengers to strip. Turcios had hidden his money in his sock, out of sight. The coyote paid the officers off and they kept moving. Hours later, another police stop. This time the driver was pulled from the van, kicked and beaten while officers held a pistol to his head. Only when the driver produced 25,000 Mexican pesos (about £1,000) did they relent.After 16 nights in a safe house, one migrant demanded better treatment from the people smugglers and that they get moving. Three strangers dragged him outside and he never returned.double quotation markIt’s like a death penalty case: you have to strike while the iron’s hot or you’re deadView image in fullscreenCivil rights and immigration lawyer Gregory Copeland …View image in fullscreen… and fellow attorney Amanda Miller, who alerted him to Turcios’s plight. Photographs: Celeste Sloman/The GuardianThe journey took a month and a half. In early December, Turcios and his closest companion, Antonio, were roused at midnight and, together with four others, were packed into a van and dumped in desolate brush. Turcios and Antonio were from the same state in Honduras but hadn’t known each other before. The others were from different countries – El Salvador, Guatemala, Mexico. “I was 17. Antonio was 28 and like my older brother,” Turcios says. “His wife and kid had moved to the US a year before and lived in Georgia, so he was trying to reunite with them.”A guide led them through darkness for 30 minutes. By 3am they had joined 40 others alongside the Rio Grande, shivering in the winter cold. The border was not unguarded. Helicopters buzzed low, forcing them to hide in the grassland and scrub. Mexican army troops encircled them, weapons raised, setting fire to the surrounding brush to flush out the remaining migrants, most of whom fled into the night. Turcios surrendered his pesos and ran. Then, it was time to cross.After his capture, the US Border Patrol officers took Turcios to a room with a table and two chairs. An officer accused him of being an adult; of running drugs across the border. Turcios told them he was 17, that he had never muled drugs, and that he had gone three days without sleep or food. He produced his birth certificate, which they took and never returned. A doctor arrived, checked his teeth, and confirmed his age. Then the officers stopped yelling, moved him to a cell full of boys his age or younger, and gave him two cookies and a bottle of Kool-Aid – the best meal he had eaten in weeks.Two days later, he was given new clothes, a jacket for the cold, and told he was flying to New York. It was his first time on a plane, his first time seeing “ice fall from the sky”, as it was snowing that day in New York City. After 26 days in a Long Island shelter, showering each morning and night, and attending a little school inside the facility, he was met by Henoch and Weigel, who drove down from Rhinebeck to collect him.Six months after Turcios was detained outside his home in Rhinebeck, the campaign to help him had shifted from emergency response to sustained pressure. On a freezing Tuesday afternoon in January, more than 100 students walked out of Rhinebeck’s middle and high schools as part ofnationwide anti-ICE protests, defying district policies that required parental permission to leave campus.My daughter, Scout, then 14, helped organise the walkout, and I watched from the edge of the park as she stood on a podium and told the crowd how ICE had taken a Rhinebeck High School alumnus who had done nothing but contribute to the community and how his detention had affected everyone.Turcios has been shuffled between detention facilities across three states – New York, New Jersey and Louisiana – seemingly at random. Last August he was taken to the Alexandria Staging Facility in Louisiana, a factory for deportation flights. One morning he was led on to a plane bound for Honduras, but guards pulled him off just before departure after Copeland and other lawyers working on his case won a stay of removal. Over the next 48 hours, Turcios watched as 50 other migrants left the United States, before he was driven back to the detention facility.In June Turcios had his second court hearing; unlike the first, this one he was required to attend. Dunne says he couldn’t get out of his head the picture of this boy in ankle chains, flanked by guards, looking over at his friends and supporters in the public gallery. “And when he gave us a wave it was just heartbreaking.”It also brought up traumatic memories. Back in 1982, Dunne’s younger sister, Dominique, died after being strangled by her ex-boyfriend. “The last time I was in a courtroom was over 40 years ago, representing my sister who had been murdered,” he says. “I attended the trial every day … and every day felt like a situation where the system fails you. Seeing Gerson really, really shook me and I thought about things I hadn’t thought about in a long time – that feeling of helplessness.”On 18 July 2026 Turcios had been in detention for a full year. His fundraiser has reached more than $130,000 in donations from 1,121 different people, but his legal fight continues. After nine years living in Rhinebeck, Henoch self-deported back to Honduras. He says that, given what was happening to Latino people in the US under the Trump administration, he decided it was better to return. “Having to start over here in Honduras is tough, but it has to be done,” he tells me. Today he works on a cattle farm. Henoch’s former girlfriend, Yorleny Weigel, still lives in Rhinebeck.She misses Turcios. “I used to take him everywhere with me. People thought he was my son. I’d tell them he wasn’t, but in the end I just gave up and went with it. He loved to go dancing; he’d try to dance but he wasn’t very good.” She talks to Turcios most nights on the phone. “He’s changed,” she says. “He doesn’t want to admit it, but I think it’s breaking him a little bit.”double quotation markHe doesn’t want to admit it, but I think it’s breaking him a bitView image in fullscreenYorleny Weigel, former girlfriend of Turcios’s  brother Henoch, who gave him a home when he arrived in the US.Photograph: Celeste Sloman/The GuardianToday, now aged 24, Turcios is housed in the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn –the same buildingin which former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and Luigi Mangione, accused of murdering UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in New York City, are awaiting trial. Immigration detainees are kept separate, but are in the same facility.Turcios says he’s locked in his cell three times a day but allowed out for breakfast, lunch and dinner, and a few hours’ recreation – playing cards, watching TV. “There are four telephones in the unit and we need to line up to use them,” he says. “Sometimes there are eight people waiting and you don’t get to make a call.”He says the food is bad – breakfast is a packet of milk and a muffin; lunch is pasta with meat that is “old or cold and flavourless”; dinner is mashed potato, spinach and occasionally chicken. “We don’t see sunshine,” he says. “There is a small room where we play basketball and there’s a big opening like a cage, with no glass, and we can see a little piece of the sky.” He speaks to his parents, Irma and Juan, once a week, but calls are expensive – $10 to call Honduras.Turcios often thinks about how Trump campaigned on deporting all criminal undocumented immigrants. “But the criminals are on the outside,” he says. “And inside, most of these people here with me just came to the United States to work, to try to build our lives and make things better.”He wants to return to his home in Rhinebeck. “I knew the community was full of incredible, nice people,” Turcios says. “I never expected everyone would get together to help me out. I was so surprised and happy.”Turcios’s lawyers are challenging his prolonged detention – under a supreme court ruling, the government may detain someone it wants to deport who has a final order of removal for 90 days; between 90 and 180 days, it must show special justification to keep holding them; and after 180 days, it must prove they are “wildly dangerous”. Copeland says this is a level that even a history of gang-related homicide has in the past failed to meet. He argues that Turcios should have been released by October, roughly 90 days into his detention, and that ICE failed to properly notify him of a custody review hearing. In addition, Copeland is pursuing Turcios’s claim for asylum in the US.Meanwhile, Turcios’s high school friend Anna Lawson, who recently graduated from McGill University in Canada and is taking a gap year before starting law school, is in disbelief that Turcios has been identified by her government as someone who doesn’t belong here. “Gerson is someone who is a benefit to our community and has only enriched it and helped people. I think the American dream really does live in him. He is such an embodiment of what it’s supposed to mean.”Explore more on these topicsUS immigrationICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)featuresShareReuse this content
