title: Canadian government steps in as ‘out of control’ wildfires force thousands to flee | Canada | The Guardian
description: British Columbia battling 102 fires day and night across province, as breakneck speed hampers firefighters’ efforts
Author: Olivia Bowden
Headline: British Columbia battling 102 fires day and night across province, as breakneck speed hampers firefighters’ efforts
Content: Firefighters would traditionally get a break during nightfall, as cooler air would slow the burning, but this is no longer the case.Photograph: BC Wildfire Service/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFirefighters would traditionally get a break during nightfall, as cooler air would slow the burning, but this is no longer the case.Photograph: BC Wildfire Service/AFP/Getty ImagesCanadaCanadian government steps in as ‘out of control’ wildfires force thousands to fleeBritish Columbia battling 102 fires day and night across province, as breakneck speed hampers firefighters’ effortsOlivia Bowdenin TorontoSun 9 Aug 2026 14.20 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 22.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCanada’s federal government has announced it will provide urgent assistance to British Columbia after an onslaught of unprecedented fast-moving wildfires forced about 22,000 people to flee their homes in frantic evacuations.A total of 102 wildfires were raging across the province on Sunday, of which nearly half were categorised as “out of control”, according to the BC Wildfire Service. Of those fires, 78 ignited during the past week.The entire community of Summerland, about 30 miles south-west of the city of Kelowna and home to about 12,000 people, was evacuated overnight on Saturday, along with a further 8,000 people around nearby Peachland. About 10,000 others have been told to prepare to evacuate at a moment’s notice.Anette Boulet was among residents who fled Summerland along Okanagan Lake in British Columbia. As she and her family left around 4.30am Saturday, their home was shrouded in smoke.“You couldn’t see barely. It was just dark, and the ridge, the ridge of fire just coming towards you,” said Boulet, who evacuated to a centre in Penticton.“There’s no words to express it, the fear.”In a social media post on Sunday, Eleanor Olszewski, Canada’s minister of emergency management and community resilience, said she had “approved a request for federal assistance from British Columbia to provide shelter and accommodations for people who have been forced to leave their homes”.“I have tasked federal officials, led by the government operations centre at Public Safety ‌Canada, to work with the province to ensure support reaches those who need it most,” she ​said.MapEfforts to battle the Bald Range wildfire have been hampered by the breakneck speed of its spread.The blaze was first detected late on Friday evening, and grew within hours to more than 40 sq miles (100 sq km) – nearly twice the size of the island of Manhattan – as it raced nearly nine miles toward Okanagan Lake.The province’s premier, David Eby, declared a state of emergency late on Saturday, telling reporters that the blaze had been “like a bomb going off.”Cliff Chapman, BC Wildfire Service’s director of provincial operations, said the prolonged hot and dry weather the province has faced this summerhad resulted in “explosive” fire conditionsnever seen before. Lightning caused by thunderstorms forecast this week could make the situation still worse, he said.Residents were shaken awake in the middle of the night to flee their homes. Jennifer Pascoa, who lives in Summerland, told the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that she had begun to pack when she saw flames licking the nearby mountains.“It happened so quickly. We came home from the beach, we saw the plume of smoke, and then within an hour, the sky was covered in dark, black clouds,” she said.The British Columbia Wildfire Service said 10 standard helicopters and one night-vision helicopter were involved in the response, but had been hindered by thick smoke, turbulence ​and large fires.Thousands told to evacuate in British Columbia as wildfire growsThe Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the country’s federal police force, said an 80-year-old woman died while trying to escape the wildfire that forced evacuations in the Okanagan Lake region.Mike Flannigan, a professor of wildland fire at Thompson Rivers University in Kamloops, BC, said the rapidity of the fires’ spread was indicative of increasingly extreme blazes springing up in Canada and the US.Southern BC and the pacific north-west in the US had had little to no rain in the past six weeks, leaving the regions “bone dry”, he said. “You walk through the forest, it crunches; if you look sideways, you start a fire.”These conditions were being driven by human-caused climate change, he said. “We’re seeing higher intensity fires today than the past … the shorter the timeframe, the more challenging it is.”Before this decade, fire agencies’ policy was that if a blaze was 20km (12 miles) away from a community, there was no cause for immediate concern. The ferocity and speed of these fires meant that such calculations no longer held, said Flannigan, warning that all homes in at-risk regions should have an emergency kit ready to go.“If a fire can run 60km in a day, you should be worried about it,” he said.The Bald Range fire was also an example of how fires could metastasise through the night, he said.Traditional firefighting practices would usually give firefighters a break during nightfall, as the cooler air would slow the burning. “That’s not the case any more. The fire roars through the evening, through the night, and we’re seeing this more and more,” he said.Drought and the sheer power and size of the fires during the day allow them to keep momentum even in the dark. Fire management agencies in BC and Alberta now fight fires after dark using night-vision helicopters.Current conditions indicated that the fire season in BC and the US states of Washington and Oregon could extend into the autumn, Flannigan said.“It looks grim … there’s no rain,” he said, adding that, like California, Canada may begin to have “fire years” instead of a summer fire season.“I’m scared for the coming weeks.”In the US, crews in Washington that for over a week have been fighting three wildfires that began burning in the Spokane area continued clean-up near containment lines. None of the fires were growing, officials said. The fires have damaged or destroyed about 920 structures.Earlier in the week a man was arrested and charged with intentionally setting the biggest of the three Spokane-area blazes.Explore more on these topicsCanadaWildfiresAmericasClimate crisisDroughtnewsShareReuse this content

title: Costa Rican diplomat emerges as strong contender to be first female head of UN | United Nations | The Guardian
description: Rebeca Grynspan seen as continuity candidate with tacit support from current secretary general, António Guterres
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Rebeca Grynspan seen as continuity candidate with tacit support from current secretary general, António Guterres
Content: Rebeca Grynspan’s parents were refugees from the Holocaust. If elected she would be the UN’s first Jewish secretary general.Photograph: Santiago Mazzarovich/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRebeca Grynspan’s parents were refugees from the Holocaust. If elected she would be the UN’s first Jewish secretary general.Photograph: Santiago Mazzarovich/AFP/Getty ImagesUnited NationsCosta Rican diplomat emerges as strong contender to be first female head of UNRebeca Grynspan seen as continuity candidate with tacit support from current secretary general, António GuterresPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorSun 9 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 03.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Costa Rican diplomat and former vice-president whose parents were refugees from the Holocaust has become the surprise frontrunner to lead theUnited Nationsas its first female secretary general.Rebeca Grynspan, whose parents emigrated to Central America from Poland – and whose maternal grandparents were killed by the Nazis – is the current head of the UN conference on trade and development (UNCTAD), a body that has exhaustively tallied the economic damage inflicted by Israel’s occupation of the Palestinian territories.The current secretary general, António Guterres, will complete his second term on 31 December 2026 and under an informal system of regional rotation his successor is expected to come from Latin America.In a secret first straw poll of the UN security council, the five permanent and 10 temporary members were asked to say whether they supported, objected to or were neutral about each of seven candidates.Grynspan secured 10 “encourage” votes, four “no opinion” votes and one “discourage” vote. The identity of the discourage vote is not known, but the fact that she had only one objection places her in a strong opening position. The process is likely to conclude in October.Grynspan’s closest rival is Carolyn Rodrigues-Burkett, Guyana’s former UN envoy, with nine encourages, two discourages and four no opinions. At the close of a Bloomberg-sponsored debate at the general assembly last month she secured 49% of the vote among those attending, with Grynspan second on 14%.“Grynspan is seen by some as the continuity candidate, having the tacit support from Guterres,” said one western diplomat. “But the key is the source of the candidate’s discouragement votes: if [the votes] are coming from Russia, China or the US, there is a risk of deadlock.”The election comes at a critical moment for the legitimacy of multilateralism, as the UN suffers 20% job cuts and the secretary general’s role as mediator is supplanted by other actors, leaving the world body as a largely ignored moral conscience, or as a venue in which all sides vent their well-rehearsed differences.If elected, Grynspan would be the UN’s first Jewish secretary general. The UN has been criticised for overly focusing on Israel in its debates, but Grynspan has invoked her Jewish heritage to argue for the importance of ending conflict.She told the UN general assembly: “Peace is what made it possible for my parents, two refugees from the second world war, to find respect and dignity in a small country,Costa Rica. I am the daughter of this peace, a demonstration of what peace makes possible.”Her sister moved to Israel as a 17-year-old to study chemistry at the Hebrew University. As a result, her niece and nephew have completed compulsory service in the Israel Defense Forces.Under her leadership, however, UNCTAD has factually and starkly documented the economic damage wrought by Israel’s long-term occupation of the Palestinian territories.Its landmark February 2026 report found that “cumulatively, the Palestinian economy lost an estimated $212.2bn (in constant 2015 dollars) from 2000 to 2024. This partial, estimated lost potential, equivalent to nearly 20 times the entire Palestinian GDP of 2024, stems directly from Israeli occupation policies, restrictions, closures, and recurrent military operations.”In November 2025 Grynspan pointed out that Gaza’s GDP per capita had plummeted to $161 per person per year, one of the most severe economic contractions in modern history.Three other candidates, including Michelle Bachelet, have probably met with too much influential opposition to secure the job. Bachelet, the former president of Chile and a former UN human rights commissioner, faces opposition from the US government, which claims she was soft on China’s human rights record. But the Trump administration’s recent suggestion that the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, should get the job symbolises America’s drift away from the UN mainstream.The secretary general is elected to serve an initial four-year term after the 193-strong general assembly is requested to endorse a single recommendation by the security council. A candidate needs nine positive votes and no veto by a security council member.The new candidate must be elected by the end of the year, and there will be further meetings of the security council to test opinion.Explore more on these topicsUnited NationsCosta RicaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Typhoon Dolphin makes landfall in China as its strongest storm this year | China | The Guardian
description: Tropical cyclone brings torrential rain and high winds to east coast after hitting Japan’s southern Okinawa province
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Tropical cyclone brings torrential rain and high winds to east coast after hitting Japan’s southern Okinawa province
Content: People watch huge waves hit a waterfront in Sanmen county, Zhejiang province, as Typhoon Dolphin approachesPhotograph: cnsphoto/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople watch huge waves hit a waterfront in Sanmen county, Zhejiang province, as Typhoon Dolphin approachesPhotograph: cnsphoto/ReutersChinaTyphoon Dolphin makes landfall in China as its strongest storm this yearTropical cyclone brings torrential rain and high winds to east coast after hitting Japan’s southern Okinawa provinceReuters in BeijingSun 9 Aug 2026 14.13 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 14.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTyphoon Dolphin, the most powerful tropical cyclone to hitChinathis year, has made landfall on the country’s east coast, bringing torrential rain and strong ⁠winds and triggering warnings ​of flooding and landslides.The storm has already swept through Japan’s southern Okinawa prefecture, injuring six people and cutting power to more than 50,000 buildings.Dolphin made landfall near Yuhuan in Zhejiang province at about ⁠5:30pm (0930 GMT) on Sunday, China’s meteorological authorities said. It brought maximum sustained winds of 94mph (151 km/h) near its centre at landfall, equivalent to a category 1 hurricane on the Saffir-Simpson scale.In addition to evacuating at least 30,300 people, Shanghai has cancelled about 1,500 flights, according to the flight-tracking data provider VariFlight.View image in fullscreenA struggles against high winds and driving rain in Dongsha, Zhejiang province, as Typhoon Dolphin makes landfall.Photograph: Huang Zongzhi/Xinhua/APAuthorities moved offshore ⁠workers to safety, ordered vessels back to port and increased checks at reservoirs, mountain streams, landslide-prone areas, construction sites and tourist locations.Torrential ​rain is forecast for Monday across Zhejiang, Shanghai, northern Fujian, ‌north-eastern Jiangxi, central and southern Anhui, and ‌much of Jiangsu. Parts of central and eastern Zhejiang could receive 250-500 mm (10-20 inches) of rain, according to forecasters.Dolphin was forecast to track ‌westward before slowing over central and south-western China and gradually losing strength, the chief forecaster at the National Meteorological Centre, Wang Haiping, told the state broadcaster CCTV.That could prolong heavy rain and increase the risk of flooding and landslides, especially in mountainous areas and along smaller rivers.1:12Typhoon Dolphin batters parts of east and south-east Asia – videoTransport was widely disrupted across the east of the country and more than a million people were evacuated from their homes.A 42-year-old tourist from Guangdong, surnamed Chen, said he had been stranded in Shanghai ‌after his family’s flight, scheduled to depart on Sunday, was cancelled.He said the family had been rebooked on a flight at 10pm on Monday, although they were unsure whether it would be able ​to take off.“To us Guangdong people, this typhoon is as ordinary as having a meal and feeling the wind. It’s just part of everyday life,” he said, adding that the storm did not appear particularly strong by the standards of China’s southern coast.View image in fullscreenA woman wades through floodwater in Shanghai.Photograph: cnsphoto/ReutersIn neighbouring Zhejiang province, the city of Wenzhou relocated more than 900,000 people and opened more than 1,000 emergency shelters. In Fujian province, authorities evacuated 98,900 people from high-risk areas, according to Xinhua.Fujian maritime authorities ​said 55 coastal passenger ferry routes had been suspended, ​all 115 offshore construction projects halted and 290 construction ​vessels moved to sheltered waters.The water resources ministry said the Qiantang, Yong, Jiao and Shuiyang rivers could experience major ​flooding, while smaller rivers in the ‌hardest-hit areas could rise above ​warning levels.Authorities issued an alert for the risk of geological disasters in parts of Zhejiang. Residents in areas covered by a red mountain-torrent warning were told to follow local evacuation orders.Shanghai’s Yangshan port had cleared ships from its berths and moved more than 500 small and medium-sized vessels to shelter as Dolphin approached, the city’s maritime safety administration said.Scientists say global warming has made extreme weather more likely, including more powerful typhoons.Explore more on these topicsChinaAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Chinese EV sales surge to new high in Europe putting tariffs under scrutiny | Automotive industry | The Guardian
description: Imports this year now account for 14% of the market amid claims vehicles are being dumped in the EU and UK
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Imports this year now account for 14% of the market amid claims vehicles are being dumped in the EU and UK
Content: A Leapmotor production line in Jinhua, China. The company has increased sales in Italy by exploiting a purchase subsidy scheme.Photograph: VCG/GettyView image in fullscreenA Leapmotor production line in Jinhua, China. The company has increased sales in Italy by exploiting a purchase subsidy scheme.Photograph: VCG/GettyAutomotive industryChinese EV sales surge to new high in Europe putting tariffs under scrutinyImports this year now account for 14% of the market amid claims vehicles are being dumped in the EU and UKJasper JollySun 9 Aug 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 11.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChinese electric car sales have risen acrossEuropeto a record high driven by strong demand and low tariffs in the UK and a surge in buyers in Italy.Against a backdrop of claims that Chinese carmakers are “dumping” state-subsidised vehicles in the EU and UK to gain market share, the figures will give impetus to calls for quotas and higher tariffs to protect European manufacturers.The share of electric cars sold by Chinese brands rose to 14.2% across western European markets – or one in every seven battery electric vehicles (BEVs) – in the first five months of this year, according to Schmidt Automotive Research. The 171,800 sales represented an increase in market share of nearly five percentage points versus the same period in 2025.Brands including BYD, Chery, SAIC and Xpeng have targeted Europe for exports, as theChinese industry seeks to dominatethe global electric vehicle market. This has put traditionalEuropean manufacturers under intense pressurewhen tougher emissions rules are forcing them to increase their own BEV sales.Chart showing how China has increased its market share in electric vehicle sales in Europe from 9.4% to 14.2%The increase in European sales comes despiteEU tariffs of up to 35.3%for electric cars made by some Chinese manufacturers, on top of the standard 10% import duty.The UK is the largest European market for Chinese cars because the government hasdeclined to follow the EU’s leadin imposing extra levies. The UK accounted for a quarter of Chinese BEV sales across the 18 biggest Western European markets.AlthoughItalyaccounted for a fifth of the total, Schmidt said this was an “anomaly”. One manufacturer, Leapmotor, sent thousands of its cheap T03 electric cars into the country to take advantage of purchase subsidies from the government. The subsidies meant that the T03 was as cheap as €5,000 at one point – far below even the most keenly priced models sold by rivals.Chinese manufacturers have sold more than 120 different models in Europe this year – compared with about 100 from European brands.However, Matthias Schmidt, the founder of Schmidt research, said China’s share of the BEV market may have peaked, in part because they have shifted some of their focus to plug-in hybrid electric vehicles. PHEVs, which combine a polluting petrol engine with a smaller battery, are not yet subject to EU tariffs.“I think they are hitting a wall when it comes to pure electric models,” said Schmidt. “They will prioritise PHEVs over the next 12 months given hybrids are omitted from extra tariffs placed on BEVs only. With that loophole set to close in the next 12 months, they will aim to maximise that gap in the door for as long as possible.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Given shipping capacity remains limited, more PHEVs means fewer BEVs, which have likely peaked for now. BEVs will take priority again once local EU production comes online.”Oliver Blume, the chief executive of Volkswagen, last month called for that to change. Blume said European PHEVs were uncompetitive against Chinese equivalents. The German newspaper Handelsblatt has reported that the EU is considering extending the levies to PHEVs.The figures also showed a rebound in sales for Tesla across Europe. The US carmaker suffered a steep decline in sales last year amid abacklash against chief executive Elon Musk’s alliancewith Donald Trump and European far-right political parties.Tesla sales rose by 60% year-on-year, helped by an increase in demand for cheaper versions of its Model 3 and Model Y. The Model Y was the bestselling individual model across Europe during the period.Explore more on these topicsAutomotive industryElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsEuropeChinaItalyManufacturing sectorAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Thailand school shooting toll rises to nine after 12-year-old dies, police say | Thailand | The Guardian
description: Teenage girl treated in hospital after Friday’s school shooting has died, police say
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Teenage girl treated in hospital after Friday’s school shooting has died, police say
Content: Friends of an injured school teacher, who has been carried into the ambulance, embrace at the site of a school shooting, in Thailand's Nonthaburi province.Photograph: Wason Wanichakorn/APView image in fullscreenFriends of an injured school teacher, who has been carried into the ambulance, embrace at the site of a school shooting, in Thailand's Nonthaburi province.Photograph: Wason Wanichakorn/APThailandThailand school shooting toll rises to nine after 12-year-old dies, police sayTeenage girl treated in hospital after Friday’s school shooting has died, police sayStaff and agenciesSat 8 Aug 2026 22.11 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 02.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe death toll from a school shooting inThailandrose to nine on Saturday, after police said a 12-year-old girl caught up in Friday’s incident had died.Police at the Plai Bang Police Station in Nonthaburi Province said the girl, who had been treated at hospital with critical wounds, had died, a day after a 14-year-old boy allegedlyshot his grandparents and then killed more peopleat his school before turning the gun on ⁠himself.Thailand school shooting: eight killed including suspected attacker, police sayRead moreThe 14-year-old wounded more than 30 people in the ⁠shooting at the Debsirin Nonthaburi school northwest of Bangkok. Fourteen people remained in hospital on Saturday evening, seven of them in critical condition.Police are questioning more witnesses as part of their investigation, including the suspect’s parents. The boy had lived with his grandparents for 12 years after his parents had separated, Atthapol Anusit, deputy commissioner of the Provincial Police Region 1, ‌told reporters on Sunday.The suspected attacker fired at least 26 bullets with a gun belonging to his grandfather, and was found with 34 additional ammunition rounds.Police on Sunday told reporters the teenager had an air ⁠gun confiscated by a teacher last year and had watched violent content online and used social media to learn how to ⁠use a firearm.“According to witness interviews, the perpetrator had begun showing interest in ​studying the use of firearms ‌for some time, about one ‌to two years,” Atthapol said.Atthapol, who said police had so far interviewed 17 witnesses, said a knife had also been found in the boy’s bag and other evidence found at the crime scenes included a firearm, spent cartridge cases, and a personal computer.On the day of the incident, the suspected shooter remained inside the school after reports of the attack emerged, Arsit Sampantharat, the permanent secretary of the interior ministry, told PPTV.A lockdown at the school was declared over in about half an hour. Images from the scene showed students running with only socks on their feet as they were evacuated from the school.Thailand’s prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, has vowed to implement new gun laws, telling reporters only government officials on duty would be allowed to carry guns. However, he did not provide any ⁠specifics, including whether the legislation would tighten gun ownership requirements.Thailand has the highest rate of civilian gun ownership in south-east Asia, and in 2017 the Switzerland-based Small Arms Survey placed the country 13th worldwide for small-gun possession.A number of mass shootings have occurred in recent years in Thailand, including incidents at schools and a large Bangkok mall, and a 2022 attack in the country’s north-east that ‌killed 37 people including 22 children.Explore more on these topicsThailandGun crimeAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: China expresses ‘grave concern’ as internal documents reveal suicide warning before death in Melbourne immigration detention | Australian immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Serious questions raised about whether Chinese citizen was properly monitored at centre run by US prison giant
Author: Christopher Knaus
Headline: Exclusive: Serious questions raised about whether Chinese citizen was properly monitored at centre run by US prison giant
Content: A Chinese national took her own life in a centre run by Secure Journeys, an Australian subsidiary of US-based prison multinational MTC.Illustration: Victoria Hart/Guardian designView image in fullscreenA Chinese national took her own life in a centre run by Secure Journeys, an Australian subsidiary of US-based prison multinational MTC.Illustration: Victoria Hart/Guardian designAustralian immigration and asylumChina expresses ‘grave concern’ as internal documents reveal suicide warning before death in Melbourne immigration detentionExclusive:Serious questions raised about whether Chinese citizen was properly monitored at centre run by US prison giantFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastChristopher KnausandAriel BogleSun 9 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 17.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US private prison company running Australia’s immigration detention system was warned that a newly detained Chinese citizen expressed suicidal ideation and had a history of self-harm less than 24 hours before she died by suicide in a Melbourne detention centre, internal documents show.The death has raised serious questions about whether the detainee was properly monitored and whether she was placed in an appropriate room, given her state of mind.It has also triggered an intervention from Australia’s biggest trading partner, Guardian Australia can reveal.Escapes, fires, stabbing: catastrophic security failures revealed in Australia’s immigration detention networkRead moreThe Chinese embassy has confirmed it has “lodged solemn representations and expressed grave concern to the Australian side” about the circumstances of the death.“China will closely follow the case and safeguard the safety and legitimate rights and interests of Chinese citizens,” an embassy spokesperson said.China’s public intervention creates a fresh headache for the home affairs minister,Tony Burke, who is already furious about a string of security lapses involving the government’s new immigration contractor, Secure Journeys, a local subsidiary of the US-based prison multinational Management and Training Corporation.In Maythe Guardian revealedthat a series of failures had allowed the escape of high-risk detainees, caused ill-equipped staff to be stabbed and hospitalised and triggered multiple investigations, one of which warned that MTC’s “minimalist staffing model” was putting workers and detainees at risk.Burke took the extraordinary step of hauling in the global president of MTC for a face-to-face dressing down in September 2025, just six months after the company was awarded the $2.3bn onshore immigration detention contract.On 10 July Australian Border Force issued a short statement saying a detainee had been found dead in the Melbourne immigration detention centre that morning.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe detainee was a Chinese citizen in her mid-30s who had been picked up the day before for allegedly overstaying an English-language studies visa, internal documents seen by the Guardian show. She had no criminal history.The ABF transferred her into the custody of Secure Journeys on the afternoon of 9 July.The ABF made clear to Secure Journeys that she had previously attempted self-harm and had “recently thought about self-harm/suicide”, the documents show.She was found hanging in her room in the Broadmeadows residential precinct, part of the Melbourne immigration detention centre, early the next morning.Victoria police are investigating the death, which they described as non-suspicious. The coroner’s court of Victoria said it had directed police to prepare a brief of evidence.Quick GuideContact us about this storyShowThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know.If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods.Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don't already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDrop, instant messengers, email, telephone and postIf you can safely use the Tor network without being observed or monitored, you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Illustration: Guardian Design / Rich CousinsWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.There were 360 reported incidents of threatened and actual self-harm across Australia’s onshore immigration detention network between July 2025 and March 2026, according to parliamentary records. There have been at least two deaths this year.A Secure Journeys spokesperson said the company offered its “deep condolences to the family and friends of the female detainee” but could not comment further due to the investigation.“Secure Journeys’ commitment to maintaining safe and secure operations, as well as both staff and detainee welfare remains our top priority,” the spokesperson said.The Department of Home Affairs offered sincere condolences to the woman’s family and friends. “Due to our privacy obligations to the deceased and the ongoing investigation into this matter, it would not be appropriate to comment further,” a spokesperson said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChina experts described the embassy’s statement as “firm but not excessive”.The Australia-China Relations Institute’s director, Prof James Laurenceson, said the fact that representations had been made and the embassy had expressed “grave concerns” showed it was taking the death seriously.But Laurenceson said he didn’t read the embassy’s statement as “excessively aggressive”.Labor plans migration cuts as Tony Burke pulls out of major speechRead more“It is the case that Australia and China have been trading tersely worded diplomatic statements more frequently in recent months over everything from Taiwan, China’s maritime claims in the South China Sea, its cyber operations, the Jimmy Lai case, Darwin Port, and more,” he said. “But I am not convinced that China’s statement in this case should be interpreted as some sort of diplomatic slap back for Australian complaints about Chinese actions in other contexts.”MTC’s performance in running Australia’s onshore detention network has triggered multiple investigations, including by the federal work safety regulator Comcare.Internal documents show Comcare has set up a dedicated inspection program to scrutinise immigration detention, citing an “increase in notifiable incidents, the severity and the profile of the reported incidents involving the [contractor]”.The regulator privately warned the department this year that it had received numerous reports of “serious injury or illness to both workers and others (detainees)”, “self-harm ideations and death involving detainees” and “detainee on detainee violence”.One of Comcare’s key concerns is that the risk-assessment system used in the centres is not effective and is putting staff and detainees at serious risk of violence and other harms.Understaffing has been a key concern since MTC took over.A March report by the National Preventive Mechanism, an independent monitor of places of detention,reported that “critically” low staffing levelswere compromising the centres’ safety.The understaffing is also causing seriously ill detainees to miss medical appointments because MTC lacks workers to escort them to health centres.* Do you know more? Email christopher.knaus@theguardian.com or ariel.bogle@theguardian.comIn Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsAustralian immigration and asylumPrisonsTony BurkeChinanewsShareReuse this content

title: Sydney gardener fined almost $200,000 for removing 287 trees to improve harbourside mansion’s water views  | Sydney | The Guardian
description: Local council described incident as ‘worst act of environmental vandalism in Lane Cove history’
Author: Joe Hinchliffe
Headline: Local council described incident as ‘worst act of environmental vandalism in Lane Cove history’
Content: The native forest canopy that was cleared had stood since at least 1943 and included an ‘estuarine swamp oak endangered ecological community’.Photograph: supplied by Lane Cove councilView image in fullscreenThe native forest canopy that was cleared had stood since at least 1943 and included an ‘estuarine swamp oak endangered ecological community’.Photograph: supplied by Lane Cove councilSydneySydney gardener fined almost $200,000 for removing 287 trees to improve harbourside mansion’s water viewsLocal council described incident as ‘worst act of environmental vandalism in Lane Cove history’Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJoe HinchliffeSun 9 Aug 2026 01.35 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 06.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt began with a gardener being hired to trim grass at a harbourside mansion in Sydney – and escalated to payments being left in a shoe for the unlawfulfelling of hundreds of native treesin protected bushland.Now a court has fined Yi Wang $187,500 for his role in organising and carrying out the destruction of 287 trees from council-owned foreshore bushland at Woodford Bay in Longueville in late 2023.TheNew South Walesland and environment court justice Rachel Pepper convicted Wang last week for helping to orchestrate the clearing of 1,210 sq metres of land beside a waterfront property on Lucretia Avenue.Wang pleaded guilty to three offences in relation to the unlawful clearing, which Pepper heard destroyed potential habitat for a range of protected and threatened animals, including powerful owls and microbats. It could take three decades to recover.View image in fullscreenThe tree vandalism occurred on public land on the foreshore of Woodford Bay in Longueville.Photograph: supplied by Lane Cove councilThe unlawful tree clearing also greatly reduced the natural protection previously afforded to an Aboriginal midden, the court heard.When it sold in 2014 for $7.6m, real estate agents described the Lucretia Avenue property as an “exclusive waterfront” residence commanding “water views from every room”. It boasted a private beach and was “bordering lush reserves”.The director ofSydneyGarden Home, Wang was hired by the stepdaughter of the owner of the adjacent property to the bushland, Yao Wu, for grass trimming work in November 2023.‘Outrageous’ tree vandalism devastates harbourside suburb in SydneyRead moreThe next day, Wu asked Wang to clear trees as well, including on public land.“This is my back yard,” Wang would later claim Wu repeatedly told him.Wang then hired casual labourers, including a chainsaw operator, and chopped down and removed trees over a 12-day period. The gardener sent regular updates on the progress of the work to his employer via WeChat and was paid in cash, which was often left in a shoe at the front of the adjacent property for Wang to collect.Lane Cove council would later call those dozen days “the worst act of environmental vandalism” in the area’s history. The mayor, Scott Bennison, said the “outrageous” act needed to be “prosecuted to the full extent possible”.In September 2024, the council installed ahuge double-sided banner on the siteof what it labelled “tree vandalism”, demonstrating its “commitment to obscure” harbour views gained by the destruction of the habitat and pledging it would remain in place until the trees grew back “to a suitable height”.View image in fullscreenThe banner to block views after the removal of almost 290 trees.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianIn addition to the fine and the publication of notices about the case in newspapers, Pepper ordered Wang to pay Lane Cove council’s legal costs.In a statement, the council said it welcomed the judgment, describing it as “a win for native bushland”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs it was awaiting the outcome of another matter before the court relating to the same location, the council declined to comment further.The case first came to light through a tip-off from a member of the public. A council ranger then visited the site the day after the last day of clearing. Council officers discovered no approvals, permits, or consents had been issued for any tree removal and private investigators were engaged.Recorded interviews from those investigators, as well as CCTV footage and invoices from a nearby dump, which showed Wang and the chainsaw operator disposing of ute loads of branches and vegetation, provided evidence for a timeline of events and facts that Wang did not dispute.The council commissioned expert reports on the impact of the clearing, including by an arborist, a geologist and a senior archaeologist.View image in fullscreenThe foreshore of Woodford Bay.Photograph: Lane Cove councilView image in fullscreenAerial images show the extent of the destruction.Photograph: NSW land and environment courtWang argued his conduct was not reckless but rather negligent at its highest.Pepper accepted references from his wife, mother and friend that Wang was otherwise a person of good character and was unlikely to reoffend.The native forest canopy he helped clear had stood since at least 1943 and included an endangered ecological community.Regeneration of the trees to a comparable ecological condition would probably take 20 to 30 years, a period during which regrowth would be susceptible to pathogens and weed invasion, the court heard.Explore more on these topicsSydneyNew South WalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Labour seeking ‘deeper relationship’ with EU under Burnham, new minister says | Brexit | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Hamish Falconer wants ‘sense of renewed pace’ in post-Brexit talks while staying within Labour’s red lines
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Exclusive: Hamish Falconer wants ‘sense of renewed pace’ in post-Brexit talks while staying within Labour’s red lines
Content: Hamish Falconer: ‘We have made some real initial progress on resetting but now we’ve got to deliver.’Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHamish Falconer: ‘We have made some real initial progress on resetting but now we’ve got to deliver.’Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianBrexitLabour seeking ‘deeper relationship’ with EU under Burnham, new minister saysExclusive: Hamish Falconer wants ‘sense of renewed pace’ in post-Brexit talks while staying within Labour’s red lines‘I was on my honeymoon!’: Hamish Falconer’s surprise call-up to Burnham’s cabinetJessica ElgotandLisa O’CarrollSun 9 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK will move faster and be more ambitious on achieving closer ties with Europe under Andy Burnham’s government, his new chief post-Brexit negotiator has said.Hamish Falconer, the new cabinet minister in charge of the EU reset talks, said there was “room to be ambitious” within Labour’s red lines onEurope, which exclude reopening discussions on the single market and customs union, and he would look at the “art of the possible”.He said greater cooperation on services – which might include visa-free travel for British people working in the EU, or mutual recognition of qualifications–was the next big area where the UK hoped to make progress. “I would want a deeper relationship, a more ambitious relationship with the EU,” Falconer told the Guardian.What the EU wants from Andy BurnhamRead more“There’s also a whole range of areas in relation to services where I’d really like it to be progressed. Services is obviously an area where the EU itself is less closely integrated and there’s a lot of discussion within the EU about where to take the productivity challenge for them – that’s a challenge we can recognise here in the UK as well. So, particularly on services, I’m really interested in where we can go further.”Falconer, the son ofthe Labour grandee Charlie Falconer, is a former Middle East minister and diplomat who has experience as a Foreign Office negotiator. He said he wanted “a sense of renewed pace” in the talks – though there is still no new summit date in sight. The long-awaited reset summit, whichhad been proposed for July, was postponed after Keir Starmer resigned as prime minister in June.“We’re committed to our manifesto red lines, but all of my experiences as a negotiator and the art of the possible is in part shaped by the nature of the relationship between two people negotiating,” Falconer said.“I used to be a negotiator with the Taliban. With the EU, this is a negotiation with our friends, with whom we share our values and with whom we feel solidarity.”Earlier this summer, EU diplomats expressed concern that the talks under Starmer had lost momentum, with the second annual summit of EU and UK leaders repeatedly delayed astalks stalled over a youth mobility scheme.Falconer,who returned from his honeymoon when he was offered the post of Europe ministerby Burnham, has spoken already to the EU trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, and senior bloc figures hope he will bring a new energy to talks.View image in fullscreenHamish Falconer arriving at 10 Downing Street in July.Photograph: Thomas Krych/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOne said of his predecessor Nick Thomas-Symonds: “I really liked him but the problem was the UK didn’t open up a window, create the political space for a deal.”They complained that instead of seizing opportunities to get a deal over the line and bank a political win to move on to the next phase, the UK negotiators “kept trying to add things” such as an agreement on services.A source close to Thomas-Symonds disputed this and said good progress had been made on all areas under discussion in advance of the planned July summit.It is believed that the next summit may not be held until October to give Falconer time to get across the detail, and for Burnham to flesh out his foreign policy.Resolving the terms of a youth mobility deal is a key priority, to allow tens of thousands of European and British young people to live and work in each other’s territories.Talks remained deadlocked due to the UK’s reluctance to allow EU students to pay the lower fees charged to UK students, something opposed by cash-strapped universities.Falconer said the deal should “work for both sides” and was mindful of financial pressures on the university sector. “In my constituency in Lincoln, there’s two universities. I’ve got those issues very much at the forefront of my mind,” he said. “It is vital that as we go through this, we have real respect on both sides for what some of the constraints are for each of us.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFalconer said he wanted to apply Burnham’s“Makerfield test”to the EU negotiations, ensuring they would deliver tangible change to ordinary people struggling with the cost of living, including in his own very heavily leave-voting constituency.But he said he would continuously emphasise principles of “European solidarity”, which he said went beyond trade and were backed by shared values, including on defence and security and on how countries could tackle growing dangers such as wildfires caused by the climate crisis.Starmer and Thomas-Symonds had been due to host the second UK-EU summit on 22 July, withprogress already announcedon a deal easing barriers for food and drink exports expected to come into force before summer 2027.The EU that the UK left no longer exists | Mujtaba RahmanRead moreThough there was a warm relationship between Starmer and the EU’s Ursula von der Leyen, the UK had also faced difficulty in fulfilling some of the promised changes agreed atthe last UK-EU summit, including an inability to reach agreement on the UK’s entry into the €150bn Safe fund for defence investment.Talks over UK participation in Safe collapsed last Novemberwith France blamed for setting too high a price for British involvement. Seasoned observers in Brussels say it was also embarrassing for the EU and was “a failure of statecraft” on both sides.Falconer said: “I think that we have made some real initial progress on resetting but now we’ve got to deliver.”Having Downing Street support to give Falconer the political space that EU diplomats want created will be key. And he says he has the experience to deliver.“I used to be a negotiator in the Foreign Office, often doing really hard negotiations. Ultimately, the character of the wider relationship is really important,” he said. “Yes, there are some really important technical questions that we have got to get right.”“But we also need to put this in the big picture … there is also a massive wider European agenda, which is really important to us, and Britain is really important to that agenda too. Security, defence, tech. We are a big part of those discussions and those dilemmas.”Falconer said he would use his role – now at cabinet level – to boost the UK’s participation in solving Europe-wide challenges outside the EU. “We are part of Europe and we feel the threats to Europe, whether it’s in eastern Europe from Russia invading Ukraine, or even wildfires and that shared sense of challenge in dealing with that.”Explore more on these topicsBrexitForeign policyLabourAndy BurnhamEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Italy condemns Spain’s ‘unacceptable’ border controls as Ceuta fallout intensifies | Migration | The Guardian
description: Travellers caught up in migration row as Madrid introduces checks on visitors from Italy in retaliation for Rome’s move
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Travellers caught up in migration row as Madrid introduces checks on visitors from Italy in retaliation for Rome’s move
Content: Spanish police check the documents of travellers from Italy at Madrid-Barajas airport.Photograph: Spanish Police/ReutersView image in fullscreenSpanish police check the documents of travellers from Italy at Madrid-Barajas airport.Photograph: Spanish Police/ReutersMigrationItaly condemns Spain’s ‘unacceptable’ border controls as Ceuta fallout intensifiesTravellers caught up in migration row as Madrid introduces checks on visitors from Italy in retaliation for Rome’s moveAshifa Kassamin MadridSun 9 Aug 2026 10.59 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleItaly’s foreign minister has called Spain’s decision to impose retaliatory checks on travellers fromItaly“incomprehensible and completely unacceptable” as people making their way between the two EU countries were left grappling with the effects of the escalating feud.Spain startedcarrying out spot checkson visitors from Italy at midnight on Saturday. The tit-for-tat move came after Rome infuriated Madridby launching checkson 1 August for travellers from Spain in response to the recent influxof about 72,000 peopleinto Ceuta, a Spanish territory in north Africa.Spanish officials were swift to point out that the Italian checks made little sense, given that by 1 August, the border in Ceuta was back under control and the vast majority of those who had arrived had been returned toMorocco. Ceuta is not part of the Schengen free-movement zone, Madrid has repeatedly stressed, meaning there is little chance of onward travel to continental Europe without EU citizenship or residency.‘We have no tents or blankets’: Ceuta migrants struggle to survive brutal heat and freezing nightsRead moreThe checks by Italy had led to “intolerable” scenes at Italian airports, Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, told reporters. “This measure is, first and foremost, an attack on the dignity of the Spanish people, but, secondly, it is a torpedo fired at the hull of European unity,” he said.In an interviewpublished on Sundayin La Stampa, Italy’s foreign minister defended the move by Rome. “Some order needs to be brought in: we’re not against Spain, but we have a duty to protect our borders,” said Antonio Tajani, voicing concerns about some of the migrants potentially holding jihadist views. “What is incomprehensible and completely unacceptable is Spain’s reaction.”He pushed back against the suggestion that Rome’s actions were symbolic, given the remote possibility of anyone making it to Italy from Ceuta. “Where do they go after arriving inSpain? Italy, as a destination, is the country most at risk. We’re not Germany or Norway.”When asked if Italy’s response was proportionate, Tajani pointed to the reports of fresh calls online for a mid-August mass crossing. “We hope to be able to lift the suspension soon, as soon as the risk is no longer present,” he said.Italy’s interior minister publicly praised Spain last week for its handling of the crisis, but Tajani blasted Spain for not being “as vigilant” as it should have been.View image in fullscreenPassengers caught up in the border controls speak to the media in Madrid.Photograph: Chema Moya/EPAHe linked the influx to Spain’s recent regularisation programme, describingthe move to provide working migrants with papersas a “negative message that puts everyone’s safety at risk,” despite the EU’searlier dismissalof any connection between the Ceuta influx and regularisation.Italy’s government has long criticised Spain’s efforts to regularise undocumented migrants, even as it quietly works on similar plans to give nearly 1.1 million work permits to foreign workers by 2028. Speaking to the Financial Times, oneresearcher describedthe Italian government’s efforts as a “disguised amnesty.”Spain and Italy both have a long history of regularisation programmes. In 2002, Tajani’s party, Forza Italia,carried outone of Italy’s largest such programmes, issuing just over 634,000 permits.Even so, the perception of differences in their approach to migration has pitted Madrid and Rome against each other, with Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, seeking to position herself as a hardliner on migration while Spain’s Pedro Sánchez – who hasdefended the needfor foreign workers to grow Spain’s economy and stave off demographic collapse – said Italy had registered the highest number of irregular crossings in recent years in the EU, with figures that are double those of Spain.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMigrants who crossed into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in north Africa last month.Photograph: Pedro Nunes/ReutersIn recent days, the row has widened to include people making their way between the two countries, a route used by more than 8 million last year.“It’s ridiculous that we’re in this situation,” Elisa Fabbri, 41,told Spanish news siteEldiario.es as she left Madrid-Barajas airport on Saturday. Israel Pérez, a Cuban-born Spanish citizen, described it as an “absurd spiral” that risked pulling everyone down. “If we keep imposing checks on each other, in the end we’ll all end up losing,” he said. “This shouldn’t be happening between two European countries.”In Italy, opposition politicians accused Meloni of unleashing an “unfounded diplomatic crisis” that would ultimately harm Italians. “The cynical propaganda of the Meloni government has produced what was predictable: a boomerang that Italians will pay dearly for,” said Nicola Fratoianni, the leader of the Greens and Left Alliance. “This is a colossal mistake.”The EU commissioner for migration, Magnus Brunner, said on Saturday that he had been in contact with the interior ministers of the two countries. “Both confirmed that the internal border controls are temporary,” he said on social media. “Spanish authorities assured us the events in Ceuta will have no lasting effect on the Schengen area. That is why there are signals from Italy that controls could be lifted soon.”The row between Rome and Madrid after the events in Ceuta hints at sensitivities over migration across the EU, particularly as governments in Italy, France and Poland prepare to face off against far-right challengers in upcoming elections.But the latest Eurobarometer poll, which tracks public opinions every quarter, suggests the focus on migration may be out of step with Europeans’ top priorities. Whenasked about the topicsthat should be a priority for the European parliament, migration ranked sixth, behind issues such as the cost of living, the defence and security of the EU and the economy and job creation.Explore more on these topicsMigrationEuropeSpainItalyEuropean UnionGiorgia MeloniPedro SáncheznewsShareReuse this content

title: Russian family denied asylum in Finland fear reprisals for pro-Ukraine activism | Finland | The Guardian
description: Nikita and Olga Belov say they will be persecuted on return to Moscow but are yet to convince Finnish authorities
Author: Miranda Bryant
Headline: Nikita and Olga Belov say they will be persecuted on return to Moscow but are yet to convince Finnish authorities
Content: Nikita and Olga Belov have tried to claim asylum in Finland but have so far found their case rejected.Photograph: Nikita BelovView image in fullscreenNikita and Olga Belov have tried to claim asylum in Finland but have so far found their case rejected.Photograph: Nikita BelovFinlandRussian family denied asylum in Finland fear reprisals for pro-Ukraine activismNikita and Olga Belov say they will be persecuted on return to Moscow but are yet to convince Finnish authoritiesMiranda BryantNordic correspondentSun 9 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 12.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Russian family faces deportation fromFinlandafter repeatedly being denied asylum – despite the threat of arrest, imprisonment and potential torture for their pro-Ukrainian activism.Nikita and Olga Belov fled their homeland in 2022 after attracting the attention of Russian authorities – including military summons, threatening messages and attempts to locate them – after expressing opposition to thefull-scale invasion of Ukraine.Nikita, 25, left his engineering job at a research institute in Moscow specialising in metallurgical technologies after finding out the work he was doing was connected to the Russian war effort.Since arriving in Finland on visas, Nikita and his mother, Olga, 55, a nurse anaesthetist, have been vocal supporters ofUkraineand public in their active support and coordination of aid sent to the country and its armed forces. But the Finnish immigration service told the mother and son that despite this they face “no real risk” if they return to Russia.In April, they were detained by Finnish authorities pending deportation. They were later released after a court interventionbut are now awaiting a decision that could result in them being deported within weeks.View image in fullscreenNikita Belov and his mother, Olga, are strong supporters of Ukraine and critics of Putin’s war.Photograph: Nikita BelovThe Belov case is understood to be one of many of Russians being denied asylum in neighbouring Finland where legal experts deem their future risk and human rights have not been sufficiently assessed.Between February 2022 and June 2026, the Finnish immigration service deported 1,039 Russians according to official statistics: the most of any nationality. During the same period, 1,109 of 1,342 Russians were refused entry to Finland in connection with a negative asylum application.Since Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Finland’s relationship with its neighbour hasshifted drastically. Previously, Finland was a popular tourism destination for Russians and there were several well-used border crossings. It has since indefinitely closed its entire border, accusing Moscow of directing asylum seekers to Finland in a “hybrid operation”.Russia has also expanded its military bases on the border, while Nato –which Finland joined in 2023– has conducted training exercises in the country.View image in fullscreenNikita and Olga have been in Finland since 2022.Photograph: Nikita BelovNikita said his problems in Russia started when he realised that his boss had lied when he had told him that the project he was working on was not linked to the war effort. When he tried to come off the project, he said his boss threatened him with arrest or being sent to the frontline.“After that I realised I cannot leave this job without consequences and that we had to think about the situation,” Nikita said. His mother, he said, was then called by the military to ask about him and their house was visited by police. They soon came to the conclusion that they had no option but to leave Russia. “Now we realise if we come back we will be arrested immediately and go to jail and be tortured,” Nikita said.In Finland they have volunteered at their local Ukraine centre and contributed to humanitarian support, including help for first aid, food, clothes, Starlink equipment and a 3D printer, for which they received a video thank you message from Ukrainian soldiers.“We try to adapt, try to support Ukraine, try to state our opinion, because it is very important to help Ukraine. Help them strike back,” he said.View image in fullscreenNikita and Olga Belov continue to volunteer for pro-Ukraine causes.Photograph: Nikita BelovThe mother and son first applied for asylum in Finland in 2022 but it was refused, after which they unsuccessfully appealed. This year they applied again and were refused and were sent a deportation order. They were then placed in a detention centre awaiting deportation but after a court intervention were allowed to go home before a final decision. “There were all bad things in our minds. It was like the start of torture because it was a totally traumatic experience,” Nikita said. “At the time we really tried to prepare for our death.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSince then they have suffered with their mental health and undergone panic attacks as they wait for the decision of the court.Their lawyer, who requested not to be named for security reasons, said the Belovs are very likely to be at risk if they are deported to Russia. Nikita’s work history will also put them at risk, the lawyer said. In a previous role he said he had access to confidential government information.While it has long been difficult to get asylum in Finland, the lawyer said that recent changes on the border and to asylum procedure, including reduced access to legal aid, has made it even harder. “It’s even more difficult to get refugee status, even with clear political opinion showing. We really have to fight these cases to get the status that was earlier easier to get.”Blinded by War: documenting the aftermath of injury in Ukraine – photo essayRead moreThe political activist and Putin criticBill Browder, who is the head of the Global Magnitsky Justice Campaign, said the case is “a defining test of Europe’s commitment to protecting those who have risked everything to oppose Putin’s war”.Browder, whose friend and lawyer Sergei Magnitskydied at the hands of Putin’s regime, added: “If people who refused to support aggression, openly opposed the regime, and now face persecution are denied protection, it could create a dangerous precedent that discourages others from taking a stand against authoritarianism.”A Finnish immigration service spokesperson said it could not comment on individual cases.Antti Lehtinen, the director of the department for international protection, which is part of the Finnish immigration service, added: “The situation of each applicant is assessed individually, taking into account their personal circumstances.“For example, opposition to the war in Ukraine and related activities may constitute grounds for persecution based on political opinion. If we assess that a person’s political opinion or activities place them at risk of persecution or serious harm in Russia, they will be granted international protection.”Explore more on these topicsFinlandUkraineRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Netanyahu rejects US-led 15-point Gaza peace plan in rare public break with Trump | Israel-Gaza war | The Guardian
description: Israeli PM says IDF will not withdraw until Hamas is disarmed and rebukes US pressure to end wars without his country’s buy-in
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Israeli PM says IDF will not withdraw until Hamas is disarmed and rebukes US pressure to end wars without his country’s buy-in
Content: Trump will have to decide whether to increase pressure on Netanyahu if he wants his Gaza peace plan to succeed.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTrump will have to decide whether to increase pressure on Netanyahu if he wants his Gaza peace plan to succeed.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesIsrael-Gaza warNetanyahu rejects US-led 15-point Gaza peace plan in rare public break with TrumpIsraeli PM says IDF will not withdraw until Hamas is disarmed and rebukes US pressure to end wars without his country’s buy-inAndrew Rothin WashingtonSun 9 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTFirst published on Sun 9 Aug 2026 14.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael’s prime minister,Benjamin Netanyahu, has rejected a US-backed 15-point peace plan for Gaza in a rare public break with Donald Trump.In a statement on Sunday, Netanyahu said that he was confronting a “wave of rumours about Israeli weakness and Israeli withdrawals on all fronts” and rebuked US pressure to end wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran without Israel’s buy-in.On Gaza, he said: “Israel does not accept the 15-point document. The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal untilHamasis disarmed. And when I say the disarming of Hamas, it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry. And we are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament. Right now, we are talking with the Americans about this issue.”Trump’s Board of Peace in July proposed the 15-point plan, which mandated that Hamas disarmin exchange for providing a full Israeli military withdrawalfrom the Gaza Strip and an eventual transition of power to an independent Palestinian National Committee. Trump had said that the agreement would be implemented in stages, but Netanyahu on Sunday said that he wanted a full disarmament first in order to implement the deal.View image in fullscreenIsraeli attacks have continued on Gaza despite a ceasefire brokered last October.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesThe Israeli leader’s main target in his remarks was the US. Israel has emerged as a key stumbling block in the Trump White House’s plans to broker peace in the region, in Israel’s conflicts inGazaand Lebanon as well as in the war begun by joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran. And Netanyahu, who is facing tough elections in October and pressure from hardliners in his own government, appears ready to test his relationship with Trump in public in order to shore up his reputation as a defender of Israel at home.Israel had already signalled that it would reject the US-led plan. Soon after Trump announced it last month,Israel stepped up its bombing campaign in the Palestinian territory– strikes killed 18 people last Sunday. Netanyahu’s office had previously indicated it would not back the plan, saying: “The version that has been made public does not reflect Israel’s positions.”But Sunday’s rejection was far more forceful and direct, and appeared targeted at the Trump White House, as Trump and Netanyahu both face difficult elections. “Unlike all those who lecture us, we do what needs to be done for Israel’s security, and we can and know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary,” Netanyahu said.The head of Trump’s Board of Peace hit back on Sunday, saying the plan remained the “only way forward”. Nickolay Mladenov, the board’s high representative for Gaza, told Israeli television: “The option we are offering today is the only way forward that ensures this tragedy does not happen again.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIran plots to deal Trump a blow in midterms by keeping him entangled in warRead moreNetanyahu’s rejection is a blow to Trump’s desire to be seen as a broker of peace in foreign conflicts. With US midterm elections due in November, the White House is desperate to negotiate a peace in Iran in order to reopen the strait of Hormuz and help bring down oil and petrol prices.But the conflicts in the Middle East are interconnected and parallel US efforts have continued to bring peace to Lebanon, where Israel has occupied land in what it says is a buffer zone against Hezbollah, and Gaza, where Gulf allies of the US have decried what they say is an ethnic cleansing campaign being carried out by Israel.Like US presidents before him, Trump has found that Netanyahu can be a difficult ally. Bill Clinton, after meeting Netanyahu for the first time in 1996, is reported to have said: “Who’s the fucking superpower here?”More recently, the Biden administration found that its concerns about the human toll in Gaza were ignored, but continued to publicly back Netanyahu and did not significantly suspend military aid to the country for fear of the political blowback that Netanyahu and his allies in the US could cause.In Trump, however, Netanyahu has found a far more unorthodox and unpredictable counterpart in the White House. Netanyahu is a natural ally for Trump, and he has attacked Democrats before the midterm elections for being weak on supporting Israel.Yet more broadly,support for Israel and its war in Gaza is eroding in the Democratic party, and the Republicans have a presidential frontrunner for 2028 in the vice-president, JD Vance, who ispublicly sceptical of Israeland the war in Gaza.Trump will have to decide whether to increase pressure on Netanyahu, potentially alienating some pro-Israel allies, or to allow his efforts for a Gaza peace plan to stall, perhaps indefinitely.The answer will depend heavily on the US president’s own political instincts – are US voters hoping to see Trump emerge as a statesman capable of ending one of the world’s bloodiest recent wars in Gaza, or would a public clash with Netanyahu provoke a revolt among his base? With both countries entering tumultuous election cycles anda generational shift in support for Israel among US voters, the result could redraw the alliance between Israel and the US.Explore more on these topicsIsrael-Gaza warIsraelGazaBenjamin NetanyahuDonald TrumpMiddle East and north AfricaHamasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Netanyahu rejects Trump’s Gaza plan and vows no withdrawal until Hamas disarms – as it happened | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: This live blog is now closed.
Author: Victoria Bekiempis
Headline: This live blog is now closed.
Content: 15.47 EDTThe day so farWe’re wrapping our live coverage of the Middle East crisis for today. Here are Sunday’s top developments:Israel has rebuffed Donald Trump’s Gaza plan.The country said it would not leave Gaza unless Hamas was “genuinely” disarmed. Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that they were discussing their concerns with the US. “They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters,” Netanyahu said.Donald Trump said he’s “low keying it” with Iran as the Strait of Hormuz remains closed.Trump’s comments to Axios came after Iran said it would not agree to a deal until the US met its demands, which included never speaking insulting the country. “We are only semi-negotiating with them,” Trump also told Axios.Although Donald Trump has rebuffed claims that the US is running low on weapons crucial to its war on Iran, a leaked memo indicates that his military leadership is concerned by falling stockpiles.Per the Washington Post, deputy US defense secretary Steve Feinberg on Wednesday told defense industry leaders that they must “drive significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production for critical capabilities.”Meanwhile,Trump’s war on Iran continues to draw prominent criticism in the US. New York’sAlexandria Ocasio-Cortez said Trump’s complaints about rising costs clash with his policies that has made daily life more expensive. “Donald Trump may be saying that oil companies are making too much money, but what Donald Trump is doing is starting a reckless war in Iran, having closed door meetings with oil companies before his election, saying, you know, you give me money, you give me campaign contributions, and I will do whatever you want,” Ocasio-Cortez said on ABC.ShareUpdated at15.54 EDT

title: Iran-aligned Houthis claim they attacked oil refinery in Saudi Arabia | Houthis | The Guardian
description: Drone strike comes after Riyadh signs defence pact and Iran issues tough demands to reopen strait of Hormuz
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Drone strike comes after Riyadh signs defence pact and Iran issues tough demands to reopen strait of Hormuz
Content: A satellite image shows trail of smoke rising from Aramco’s Jazan refinery in south-west Saudi Arabia.Photograph: European Union/Copernicus Sentinel-2/ReutersView image in fullscreenA satellite image shows trail of smoke rising from Aramco’s Jazan refinery in south-west Saudi Arabia.Photograph: European Union/Copernicus Sentinel-2/ReutersHouthisIran-aligned Houthis claim they attacked oil refinery in Saudi ArabiaDrone strike comes after Riyadh signs defence pact and Tehran issues tough demands to reopen strait of HormuzGuardian staff and agenciesSun 9 Aug 2026 11.11 EDTFirst published on Sun 9 Aug 2026 08.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYemen’s Tehran-aligned Houthis have claimed responsibility for an attack on a refinery in Saudi Arabia, two days after the kingdom signed ⁠a defence pact with Turkey ⁠and Pakistan in response to ​growing regional instability caused by theUS-Israel war on Iran.The attack early on Sunday came afterIran said tough new demands would have to be met before it would reopen the strait of Hormuz, and after the United Arab Emirates said one of its ships had been targeted by an Iranian missile, as a deal to open the waterway remained out of reach.Iran’s supreme national security council said the strait would not open until the US corrected its “behaviour”.The US must never threaten Iran again and permanently end the war with Tehran and its armed allies in the region, said the statement from the council’s secretary, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, a former commander in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).‘Like being in prison’: the ship crews stuck in Gulf since FebruaryRead moreHe added that the US must also end the naval blockade of Iranian ports and withdraw its military from the area, “completely compensate” Iran for war damage, lift sanctions and “unconditionally” release frozen assets.There was no immediate comment from the US. According to the memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed by the US and Iran in June, a timetable to end sanctions and a plan for compensation would be part of a final peace deal, and negotiations would address frozen assets.The Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said on Saturday that Iran and Oman were close to reaching anagreement on navigationthrough the strait, “specifically the determination of a transit route”.But the waterway’s reopening was contingent on other conditions, Araghchi said, in remarks shared on social media. He blamed the situation on what he called the US violation of the June MoU.Oman, which is mediating and has made relatively few comments on the Hormuz talks, said on Saturday that the discussions were continuing “in a positive and constructive atmosphere”. It condemned attacks on ships in the strait.When it comes to decision-making in Tehran, the final say rests with the supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not been seen in public since an airstrike killed his father and predecessor on the first day of the war.View image in fullscreenThe Hamshahri newspaper carries front-page headline: ‘The Oman deal doesn’t mean the reopening of the strait of Hormuz.’Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAState media said on Sunday that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, met Khamenei in late July.Pezeshkian has given differing accounts in recent ⁠weeks about his access to the supreme leader, saying in July that interactions with ​Khamenei were “increasing day by ‌day”, only to note weeks later that communicating with him was “very difficult”.With Iran and the US still arguing over the parameters for peace, the Houthis last month declared a naval blockade againstSaudi Arabiain the Red Sea, citing what they said was a Saudi siege on them, an allegation Riyadh denies.The Saudi energy ministry said a fire had broken out at Aramco’s Jazan refinery early on Sunday but was later extinguished with no injuries and authorities were dealing with the ⁠incident, without giving a cause.TheHouthisused a drone to target the refinery in south-west Saudi Arabia, Yahya Saree, a military spokesperson for the rebel group, said in a post on X. They had struck Aramco sites before in ​Jazan, which processes 400,000 barrels of crude oil a day. They had also hit Yanbu, an oil export hub ‌on the Red Sea.In a separate statement, Saree said the Houthis had carried out missile and drone strikes on the Yemeni Red Sea port city of Mocha, which is controlled by the country’s internationally recognised, Saudi-backed governing body in Aden.View image in fullscreenTurkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, left, with Saudi Arabia’s Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistan’s Shehbaz Sharif on Friday.Photograph: Turkish Presidency Press Office/AFP/Getty ImagesThe UAE said on Saturday that a ship affiliated with its state oil company had been targeted by an Iranian missile. There was no immediate comment from Iran, whose IRGC has previously attacked ships, saying they had not coordinated their passage through the strait with Tehran.Tehran and its allied Shia armed groups have been striking Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states and blockading their ‌energy shipments since the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran on 28 February.The escalation of the conflict, which has disrupted global energy supplies and rattled the world’s economy, prompted Saudi Arabia on Friday to form an alliance with US allies Turkey and Pakistan.The accord is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression and stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three would be regarded as ⁠an attack on all.The Turkish foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, said the alliance was not directed against Iran or ​any other country, but rather served as a general ​pledge to support the security of Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.It was ​not clear whether or how either Pakistan or Turkey would join in any Saudi response to the latest attacks.Explore more on these topicsHouthisSaudi ArabiaUS-Israel war on IranStrait of HormuzYemenUS foreign policyMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham vows crackdown on ‘rip-off’ business practices to ease cost of living | UK cost of living crisis | The Guardian
description: First of PM’s ‘everyday fixes’ to be banning fake discounts and making it easier to cancel unwanted subscriptions
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: First of PM’s ‘everyday fixes’ to be banning fake discounts and making it easier to cancel unwanted subscriptions
Content: Andy Burnham is seeking to put the cost of living at the heart of his premiership.Photograph: Fred Duval/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham is seeking to put the cost of living at the heart of his premiership.Photograph: Fred Duval/SOPA Images/ShutterstockUK cost of living crisisBurnham vows crackdown on ‘rip-off’ business practices to ease cost of livingFirst of PM’s ‘everyday fixes’ to be banning fake discounts and making it easier to cancel unwanted subscriptionsAndy Burnham: I’ll end the rip-offs that people hateAletha AduPolitical correspondentSun 9
