Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 20.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has promised a series of measures to tackle the cost of living, including a ban on fake discounts and making it easier for people to escape unwanted subscriptions.The crackdown on “rip-off” business practices is expected to benefit consumers to the tune of £400m a year and will be the first in a range of “everyday fixes” to be implemented in the coming months.Writing for the Guardian, the prime minister said his government would step in wherever it could as he sought to put the cost of living at the heart of his premiership.“We won’t be able to solve every frustration overnight,” he wrote. “But where the government can save people money, remove an unnecessary obstacle or simply make something work better, we should and we will.”The government will ban misleading pricing practices that retailers use to make discounts appear better than they really are, including fake “was” prices, invented reductions and misleading recommended retail prices.View image in fullscreenThe government wants to ensure RRP prices cannot be used misleadingly.Photograph: Rosemary Roberts/AlamyMinisters will consult in the autumn on the precise practices covered and how the ban will work, before introducing the changes through secondary legislation.Downing Street hopes the measures can be implemented as soon as possible and does not expect a lengthy parliamentary process.The changes are intended to stop retailers inflating the price of an item before cutting it to give shoppers the false impression they are receiving a bigger discount.Burnham wrote: “If something is advertised as half price, it should actually be half price. We’ll make sure that when families snatch a deal, they can be confident they’re actually saving. That’s the least they deserve when budgets are so tight.”The government is also speeding up new protections against subscription traps, bringing forward their introduction from next spring to January. The rules will force businesses to provide clearer information when people sign up, regularly remind customers about their subscriptions and make it easier for them to cancel. Customers will also be given a 14-day cooling-off period after a trial ends or a long-term contract renews.The average person has about three subscriptions and spends about £500 a year on them, according to government figures. There are about 155m active subscriptions across the UK, and about £1.6bn a year is spent on unwanted ones.View image in fullscreenNew rules will make subscriptions clearer and easier to cancel.Photograph: Srdjan Randjelovic/AlamyMinisters estimate consumers will save an average of £14 a month for each unwanted subscription they are able to leave early.“Too many companies want you to sign up in seconds but then make it feel impossible to leave. It’s exhausting,” Burnham wrote.The challenge for the prime minister will be whether smaller consumer-oriented interventions can provide savings households notice when many are still under pressure.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe two measures will be followed by more over the coming months as he attempts to show voters his government can make a noticeable difference to household finances.Burnham also promised “bigger plans to make life easier and fairer for people over the longer term”, but Downing Street has yet to set out what those will include.Burnham wrote: “As far as I’m concerned, whatever the size, big or small, if it’s a problem for you, it’s a problem for us. That’s why I’ve made it clear from day one that creating room to breathe is my number one priority, and the whole of government is united on that.“Every single unexpected payment, rip-off or hidden catch chips away at hope. That might sound dramatic – but it’s true. Every single one is another message that thiscountry is built to catch people out rather than help them get on.”Citizens Advice welcomed the changes but said they “can’t be the end of the story”.The announcement comes as Burnham prepares to spend the rest of his summertravelling around Britainin an attempt to reconnect the government with voters, particularly in areas where Labour has lost support.“I’ll be asking people what action they want to see on the cost of living,” Burnham wrote. “Because if we want to find the problems that make everyday life harder, we need to listen to the people dealing with them.”Downing Street has not said whether what Burnham hears on the tour will shape the next round of “everyday fixes”.Explore more on these topicsUK cost of living crisisLabourAndy BurnhamRetail industryEconomic policyConsumer affairsnewsShareReuse this content

title: London mayor orders council to drop plan to ban new pubs and bars in Soho and West End | London | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Sadiq Khan urges Westminster council to adopt ‘positive vision of economic growth’ of nightlife
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Exclusive: Sadiq Khan urges Westminster council to adopt ‘positive vision of economic growth’ of nightlife
Content: People ‘vertically drinking’ outside the Dog and Duck pub in Soho.Photograph: fotoVoyager/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople ‘vertically drinking’ outside the Dog and Duck pub in Soho.Photograph: fotoVoyager/Getty ImagesLondonLondon mayor orders council to drop plan to ban new pubs and bars in Soho and West EndExclusive: Sadiq Khan urges Westminster council to adopt ‘positive vision of economic growth’ of nightlifeHelena HortonSun 9 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSadiq Khan has ordered Westminster council to scrap a policy that would ban new pubs and bars from opening in Soho and the West End of London.This comes after the Guardian revealedthe council’s new licensing policyasks pubs to stop customers from standing up while consuming beverages, which it calls “vertical drinking”. The policy is under consultation and also asks pubs to have table service rather than allowing orders at the bar.There was widespread anger at the plans to direct those applying to open new bars and restaurants in Westminster to implement the restrictions.The mayor ofLondonhas new powers, granted by the government this year, to intervene in licensing decisions. He is using these for the first time to ask the council to rewrite the draft policy.The Conservative Westminster councillors decree in the draft policy that newly licensed pubs should have to serve last orders at 10pm, and nightclubs should shut by 11.30pm on weekdays and at midnight on weekends.It also labels the entirety of Soho and theWest Endas a “cumulative impact zone”, which means no more pubs, bars or night clubs should be allowed to open unless under exceptional circumstances. This is despite the West End being one of the most popular nightlife areas in Europe.Khan pointed out that Home Office alcohol licensing data shows that only 41 licence applications were made in the West End cumulative impact area in 2023-24, with only 16 granted.Data also shows only 3.5% of applications that went to a licensing subcommittee in Westminster were approved exactly as applied for between 2023 and 2026, and pub and wine bar applications were down 80% in 2022-24.There are also plans to label Mayfair and the Victoria area as special zones where nightlife is restricted due to noise and other “nuisance behaviours”.Khan is asking the council to scrap all of these zones and allow new bars and pubs to open, in his formal response to the consultation. He is also directing it to get rid of the “core hours” policy and allow venues to be open late into the night.The prime minister, Andy Burnham, waded into the rowthis weekwhen he said standing up to drink in pubs was “British life” and should not be curtailed by local councillors.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Guardian view on pubs: football gave them a boost – now they need another | EditorialRead moreKhan said: “Licensing decisions that could make or break our city’s nightlife have, in my view, been skewed towards the interests of a handful of highly vocal residents and councillors, without giving enough weight to the effects on London’s wider economy and culture.”He added that the draft proposals “undermine City Hall’s efforts to make London’s nightlife the best in the world”.In his formal response he asks the council to “remove this cumulative impact policy altogether, instead setting out a positive vision of the economic growth that is being promoted, rather than the activity that is to be restricted”. This means the ban on opening new bars and pubs in Soho and the West End other than in exceptional circumstances would be lifted.The mayor said that Manchester city council is an example of a local authority that allows economic growth and supports bars, pubs and restaurants.Khan said: “Manchester city council’s policy has adopted a more enabling approach, with no core hours policy, no cumulative impact policy and a clear vision for what they are looking to promote across their different local neighbourhoods.“As envisioned by the Licensing Act 2003, there is a presumption to grant licences for pubs, bars, clubs and other premises where applicants can demonstrate effective management and compliance with the licensing objectives.”Westminster city council has been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsLondonHospitality industrySadiq KhanWest EndPubsRestaurantsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pakistani grooming gang suspect ‘refuses to give date for return to UK’ | UK news | The Guardian
description: Rukhsar Ahmed was recently elected an MP in Pakistan while on bail over alleged child rape in 1990s Manchester
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Rukhsar Ahmed was recently elected an MP in Pakistan while on bail over alleged child rape in 1990s Manchester
Content: Rukhsar Ahmed is the owner of a former restaurant, the Gujjar Palace, near Manchester’s curry mile.Photograph: SuppliedView image in fullscreenRukhsar Ahmed is the owner of a former restaurant, the Gujjar Palace, near Manchester’s curry mile.Photograph: SuppliedUK newsPakistani grooming gang suspect ‘refuses to give date for return to UK’Rukhsar Ahmed was recently elected an MP in Pakistan while on bail over alleged child rape in 1990s ManchesterShah Meer BalochandRajeev SyalSun 9 Aug 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA grooming gang suspect released on bail in the UK and then re-elected as an MP in Pakistan has reportedly declined to say when he would return to face rape charges.The Guardian disclosed that Rukhsar Ahmed, a former Pakistan state minister, was arrested at Manchester airport in July 2024 on suspicion of raping and trafficking at least two underage girls from care homes in the city’s Rusholme area during the 1990s.He was released on bail and flew to Pakistan nearly two months ago, missing an appointment at a police station after telling officers he was too unwell to fly back to the UK.He was elected an MP for prime minister Shehbaz Sharif’s centre-right Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz party days later.He did not respond to requests for a comment when approached by the Guardian last week.View image in fullscreenRukhsar Ahmed.Photograph: SuppliedIt emerged on Sunday that Ahmed, 61, had been located in his office in Khari Sharif, a village in Mirpur district.According to the Mail on Sunday, he told a reporter he would fly back to Britain to meet his bail conditions, but declined to give a date. “Everything is with my legal team in Manchester and London, they told me I can’t discuss this,” he told the newspaper.“What they done, this media in the United Kingdom and Europe, is out of order. I have not been convicted of anything nor charged for anything, so what is going on? I don’t want to discuss it, because if I discuss it, things may go wrong.”Asked directly whether he had raped two underage girls, he refused to answer, telling the reporter: “You are doing wrong now, I told you not to talk to me like this … please don’t talk to me like this, I told you I have nothing to do with it, OK.”Ahmed published a statement on his Facebook account on Friday. It read: “I categorically deny all the allegations against me and will address these matters through the appropriate forums. On legal advice, I will not comment further while these matters remain ongoing.”Ahmed was a minister in various state governments from 2006 until he lost his seat in 2021.The Guardian understands that Greater Manchester police (GMP) had wanted to restrict Ahmed’s ability to travel abroad as part of his bail conditions, but a judge rejected tougher measures in July 2024.Ahmed was arrested at Manchester airport on 18 July 2024 in relation to past child sexual abuse allegations linked to the Rusholme area, where he lived for many years.According to the report, he received a string of visitors in his office. He is the owner of a former restaurant, the Gujjar Palace, near Manchester’s curry mile.The ongoing investigation relates to allegations from several women about sexual abuse of children at care homes in the early 1990s, when Ahmed was in his late 20s.He is understood to be expected to answer police bail in the next six weeks. If he does not attend, GMP may issue a warrant for his arrest or take steps to extradite him.The Guardian has approached Ahmed for comment again.Richard Scorer, the head of abuse law at Slater and Gordon who has acted in many Manchester grooming gang cases said: “Rusholme has regularly featured in grooming gang investigations over the past 30 years, with many cases involving allegations of children being abused in and around the area.“Not all of those allegations have been adequately investigated. I hope that a comprehensive investigation is taking place here”.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Three Banksy artworks in London have cost taxpayers nearly £150,000 | Banksy | The Guardian
description: Costs of security and removal efforts have reignited debate over whether work is vandalism or valuable public art
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Costs of security and removal efforts have reignited debate over whether work is vandalism or valuable public art
Content: Banksy’s artwork outside the Royal Courts of Justice in London.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBanksy’s artwork outside the Royal Courts of Justice in London.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesBanksyThree Banksy artworks in London have cost taxpayers nearly £150,000Costs of security and removal efforts have reignited debate over whether work is vandalism or valuable public artNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentSun 9 Aug 2026 10.09 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThreeBanksyartworks have cost taxpayers almost £150,000 in removal efforts, security and other costs, with the bill expected to rise.The largest bill relates to a mural painted on the Royal Courts of Justice in London in September 2025, where efforts to remove it and provide security have so far cost more than £85,000,according to the BBC.The mural depicted a judge in a wig beating a protester with his gavel.Banksyconfirmed the work was his by posting an image on his website and Instagram account.The Ministry of Justice told the BBC, after a freedom of information request, that £50,000 had been spent trying to remove the paint from the wall of the Grade II-listed building on Carey Street. A further £35,000 had been spent on overtime and security.Banksy confirms statue of man blinded by flag in London is his workRead more“The Royal Courts of Justice is a listed building and HMCTS are obliged to maintain its original character,” the HM Courts and Tribunals Service said.The costs have reignited a debate over whether Banksy’s work constitutes vandalism or valuable public art, particularly when it appears on historic buildings. The artist,who emerged from Bristol’s graffiti scene in the 1990s,is one of the world’s most famous street artists. His work has sold at auction for upwards of £18m.The shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, said it was “outrageous” that taxpayers’ money was being spent cleaning up after the artist. “Our courts are a national symbol of justice and the rule of law,” he said. “Banksy’s vandalism should be stopped and he should foot the bill for the costs he imposes on others.”But the art critic Estelle Lovatt defended Banksy’s work and highlighted the benefits for tourism. “Some people visit Buckingham Palace and others visit Banksy’s art,” she told the BBC. “His work brings people together in a way that politics can divide us. He’s like the Pied Piper or a town crier.“It can be intimidating if a mural appears on your building, in terms of the crowds, but he makes art accessible because there’s no gallery fee.”Initial attempts to remove the mural were unsuccessful and contractors have since been using laser technology. If Westminster city council considers the result inadequate, another cleaning method will be required. As a final option, the affected stonework could be removed and replaced.A listed building consent application has also been submitted for railings to be installed across the wall where the mural appeared. The cost of the installation is not yet known.Another Banksy work has generated almost £60,000 in costs for Westminster city council.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenBanksy artwork in Waterloo Place.Photograph: Richard A Brooks/AFP/Getty ImagesA statue of a man carrying a flag appeared in Waterloo Place in the capital, near Trafalgar Square, in April. Banksy claimed responsibility by posting a video of the overnight installation on Instagram.The council said it had spent almost £60,000 on safety barriers, administration and a security guard to monitor the statue.“Ownership of the statue now sits with the council as landowner,” it said. “The council has notified the artist’s agent that it is reviewing options for the short, medium and long term.”In August 2024, another Banksy work appeared on a City ofLondonpolice sentry box. The artist painted a shoal of piranha fish over the box, which had been installed in the 1990s as part of security measures against the IRA.The box was subsequently removed at a cost of £2,200 and was never replaced. It is due to go on display at the London Museum when it reopens in November.Explore more on these topicsBanksyArtLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Most X accounts posting about Belfast and Southampton unrest were based outside UK | The far right | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Analysis shows 55% of accounts were overseas – and seven of 12 most-read posts came from US
Author: Carmen Aguilar García
Headline: Exclusive: Analysis shows 55% of accounts were overseas – and seven of 12 most-read posts came from US
Content: The analysis underlines that US rightwing actors are seeking to influence the UK and boost their position on X in moments of disorder.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe analysis underlines that US rightwing actors are seeking to influence the UK and boost their position on X in moments of disorder.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe far rightMost X accounts posting about Belfast and Southampton unrest were based outside UKExclusive: Analysis shows 55% of accounts were located overseas – and seven of 12 most-read posts came from USCarmen Aguilar García,Michael Goodier,Pamela DuncanandDan SabbaghSun 9 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than half the accounts that posted on Elon Musk’s X about the rioting in Belfast and the civil disorder inSouthamptonin June were based outside the UK, an analysis by the Guardian can reveal.Of the 8,672 accounts whose combined posts about the events exceeded 1,000 views, just 45.3% were shown as from the UK, according to the social media platform’s own location function.One in six (16.8%) came from the US, 4.5% from Ireland, and about a quarter from all European countries other than the UK.Seven of the 12 most-read tweets aboutBelfastand Southampton came from the US – including one from Musk himself and two other US “alt-right” commentators – while an eighth was linked to North America.The analysis underlines that US rightwing actors are seeking to influence the UK and boost their position onXin moments of disorder – an exploitation of flashpoint events that has only intermittently attracted political attention in Britain.Q&AMethodologyShowThe Guardian collected 43,000 tweets mentioning Belfast, Southampton, Henry Nowak or Vickrum Digwa posted on X during the period of the unrest in both cities.This covered the period from 2 June to the end of 3 June for Southampton and from the evening of 8 June to the end of 9 June for Belfast.For X accounts whose combined tweets reached more than 1,000 views, we extracted their location and the number of times they have changed their username as shown in the “about this account” tab.Using a large language model (LLM), the team first classified which posts were directly related to the protests in Belfast and Southampton, and then categorised them as containing explicit or implicit racist language or anti-immigration comments. For those about Belfast, we also classified tweets as containing calls inciting to violence.A team of three people manually verified more than 5,500 posts, statistically testing the accuracy of the model to be robust and in line with academic standards.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Nearly a third of all 43,000 posts on X relating to the two incidents contained racist or anti-immigration comments. Almost one in 10 relating to Belfast contained calls for violence or paramilitary or vigilante action.Imran Ahmed, the chief executive of the Centre for Countering Digital Hate, said the data demonstrated that X had become “a weapon of choice” for hostile foreign actors seeking to manipulate shocking and divisive content.Their goal, he added, was “to amplify local tragedies and crises, intensify racist narratives, and incite violence in communities they have never set foot in and to whom they have no real connection.”A post from Musk after the life sentencing of the killer of 18-year-old Henry Nowak, who had been falsely accused of racism by police after being stabbed in Southampton, has been viewed more than 28m times.“Legacy mainstream media, same ones who wrote about George Floyd millions of times, are dead silent about Nowak,” Musk posted shortly before 3pm on 2 June, in effect promoting his own platform at a time of heightened tension and disorder in the Hampshire port.View image in fullscreenElon Musk posted about race and immigration in the UK twice as often as he did about SpaceX in the run-up to the aerospace company’s IPO in June.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersEleven police officers were injuredon the night of 2 June in Southampton as people claiming to protest over Nowak’s murder marched to the site of his death. This followed a rally, addressed by the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, outside the city’s main police station.Musk is based in the US and has not visited the UK since November 2023. A Guardian analysislast monthfound he posted about race and immigration in the UK twice as often as he did about SpaceX in the run-up to the aerospace company’s initial public offering in June.Security experts including Fiona Hill, a former adviser to the US and UK governments, have warned that the UK is asoft target for online manipulationby overseas actors because it does not take the idea of civil, or “psychological”, defence seriously.Dr Julia Ebner, a researcher at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue and the University of Oxford, said flashpoint episodes such as in Southampton and Belfast had become “strategic events” for far-right actors seeking to amplify and exploit them.“They are using the UK as a negative example, smearing the UK to promote their own narratives of western civilisational decay or social collapse,” Ebner said. “But the other purpose is to influence UK politics, and European politics more widely,” using crisis moments to “promote a strong, strengthened far-right wave across the world”.Four of the top 12 most-seen tweets came from UK accounts: two were by the leader of the Restore Britain party, Rupert Lowe, whom Musk has endorsed; another was from GB News, while the most popular, with 37.6m views, was written by the “anti-woke” rightwing political commentatorKonstantin Kisin.Other accounts located in the US were anonymous, though familiar. @EndWokeness posted a blurry still image of a black man attacking a white man in Belfast on 8 June, saying the full video was “too graphic” to post. It attracted 16.3m views.The assault, a stabbing in which the victim, Stephen Ogilvie, lost an eye, promptedthree nights of racially motivated riotingtargeting non-white people in Belfast. An asylum seeker from Sudan was charged with attempted murder and at least 23 people were arrested.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA vehicle set alight during riots in Belfast in June.Photograph: Peter Morrison/APThe @EndWokeness account, which has 3.9m followers, was cited by aparliamentary committeeafter it amplified a false claim that the 2024 attack in Southport, in which three girls were killed, was carried out by a Muslim man.The account has been linked byan open source analystto Jack Posobiec, a rightwing influencer who promoted the Pizzagate conspiracy, a false accusation that leading US Democrats were engaged in satanic child abuse at a child-friendly pizza restaurant in Washington DC.Another leading poster was the US rightwing influencer Benny Johnson, who accused the New York Times of writing nothing about Nowak and thousands of pieces about the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis in 2020 – though Nowak was murdered in the UK.The analysis of the most-viewed accounts did not reveal any posts from Russia or China – bothcountries that have been behind online disinformation campaigns – though it is possible that posters successfully disguised their locations using virtual private networks (VPNs).X shows location data for most profiles, inferred by the platform from user IP addresses, though government accounts are excluded. Last November, after the feature was introduced, X’s then head of product,Nikita Bier, said it was more than 99% accurate. When it was launched, it revealed that some pro-Scottish-independence accounts were based in Iran.But there weresigns of inauthenticityin popular posts. Two of the top most-seen tweets came from the US-based C3 (@C_3C_3) account, accusing “legacy media” of not reporting about the Nowak case. Its profile picture is a baby wearing a Make America Great Again cap; the username has changed 14 times previously.One UK account, which tweeted at least six times about the murder of Nowak, with almost 3,800 combined views, had changed its name more than 400 times. NewsSceneUK – subsequently changed to BritifyFooty – wrote in one tweet about the “huge crowd of patriots outside #Southampton Police Station”.Accounts posting from overseas that changed their usernames more than 20 times included one in Kenya that wrote after the Belfast stabbing: “When the state fails to protect people, the streets find their own language.” Another, from Europe, described the Nowak case as “a globalized, calculated and malicious evil” affecting “every White person and every White nation”.Close to a third – about 13,000 – of the Belfast and Southampton tweets, whether from the UK or abroad, were racist or anti-immigrant, according to the Guardian analysis. When analysed separately, a quarter of the posts that were only about Southampton were racist or anti-immigrant, compared with a third of those that were only about Belfast.One UK-based poster, writing a day after the Belfast stabbing, claimed they hoped the attacker was British-born because “race is the issue, not immigration status”. The post registered 2m views.Valerie Wirtschafter, an expert on online foreign influence operations from the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank, said she believed violent events such as those in Belfast and Southampton were “a point of exploitation” in which “outside agitators” had an opportunity to make a disproportionate impact.Their position was helped by X and other social media companies cutting content moderation, she said, but in particular by “algorithms and how they collide with the basic cognitive processes of humans. We are more attracted to things that are shocking.”Explore more on these topicsThe far rightXElon MuskFar rightFar right (US)InternetBelfastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump appoints staff secretary Will Scharf as new White House counsel | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Scharf, who helped president win approval for $400m ballroom, to replace David Warrington on 1 September
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Scharf, who helped president win approval for $400m ballroom, to replace David Warrington on 1 September
Content: Will Scharf in the Oval Office with the president last week.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APView image in fullscreenWill Scharf in the Oval Office with the president last week.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APDonald TrumpTrump appoints staff secretary Will Scharf as new White House counselScharf, who helped president win approval for $400m ballroom, to replace David Warrington on 1 SeptemberStaff and agenciesSun 9 Aug 2026 18.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump announced on Sunday that ⁠Will ​Scharf, the staff secretary who helped secure approval for the $400m White House ballroom project, will become ⁠White House counsel and assistant to the president.Effective 1 September, Scharf will replace David Warrington, who will be leaving the administration to join the private sector. Warrington ​formerly served ​as a ​personal counsel and a ​lawyer ‌for Trump’s ​2024 campaign.Trump noted that Scharf previously served as a federal prosecutor and represented him in a number of cases, including at the supreme court. Scharf also led the National ‌Capital Planning Commission, which approved the president’s construction ​of the White House ballroom.“Will is Tough, Strong, and Smart! He also loves our Country, and respects the Law,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Will Scharf will do a great job as White House Counsel!”Appeals court halts construction of Trump’s $400m White House ballroomRead moreThe shakeup in the White House counsel’s office comes at a critical juncture – just months ahead of the midterm elections, where Trump’s Republican party will be fighting to hold on to control of Congress.Democrats have vowed to pursue investigations into Trump and his administration if they are successful in November.The White House counsel’s job is to advise on legal and policy questions related to the presidency. The office is the primary White House contact for the justice department, and it handles presidential pardons, works on judicial appointments and reviews legislation. The office also helps investigate and manage congressional investigations into the administration and lawsuits against the president when he is sued in his official capacity.Trump in July 2025 had named Scharf as chair of the National Capital Planning Commission, the executive branch agency with jurisdiction over construction and major renovations to government buildings in the region.Trump’s ballroom won final approval from the NCPC in April, though a divided federal appeals court ruled Friday that construction onthe project must stopbecause Congress had not approved it. Trump has vowed to appeal to the supreme court.The project is already well on its way and has begun to rise above ground on the east side of the White House.The Associated Press and Reuters contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez announces decision to freeze her eggs | Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez | The Guardian
description: US congresswoman to share journey online as she criticizes Trump administration’s attacks on reproductive care
Author: Victoria Bekiempis
Headline: US congresswoman to share journey online as she criticizes Trump administration’s attacks on reproductive care
Content: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez on the steps of the Capitol in July.Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAlexandria Ocasio-Cortez on the steps of the Capitol in July.Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty ImagesAlexandria Ocasio-CortezAlexandria Ocasio-Cortez announces decision to freeze her eggsUS congresswoman to share journey online as she criticizes Trump administration’s attacks on reproductive careVictoria BekiempisSun 9 Aug 2026 18.06 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 18.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlexandria Ocasio-Cortezhas announced she is going to freeze her eggs and will be sharing the process online.The progressive New York congresswoman, 36, revealed her decision to undergo fertility treatment in a series of Instagram stories this weekend. “This is a choice that I am making to feel more in control of my life,” Ocasio-Cortez said.Ocasio-Cortez said she had been saving for the procedure for a very long time, and said there was not a lot of information for women interested in doing so.“As women in general, we are not taught about our bodies, we are not prepared for our own lives, whether that is in puberty, whether that is in pregnancy, whether that is in perimenopause, menopause, whether that is in so many different aspects of our lives,” shesaidin one of the stories.Ocasio-Cortez recognized the balancing act that comes with undergoing fertility treatment with her work as a congresswoman. Ocasio-Cortez told viewers that she would be taking her shots in the dressing room before a scheduled ABC interview on Sunday.“I want you all to see that,” Ocasio-Cortezsaid. “Because women can do anything. And I think it’s badass that I’m gonna be giving myself shots in the green room, get my glam on, roll out, talk international events, domestic policy, elections, pop out, live my life, do my thing.”Ocasio-Cortez also showed the medicines and tools, such as syringes and alcohol wipes, used in the process, which involves injecting multiple forms of medication over a period of time that typically lasts around 10 days or more. She joked she would not be injecting herself on a live feed, quipping: “Maybe I should start an ASMR egg-freezing channel.”“Don’t be weird about this, even I know though all of you will be,” she said with a slight smile moments before finding an injection site on her abdomen.She exhaled, injected the medication, and then remarked: “That wasn’t so bad!”During her Sunday interview on ABC, Ocasio-Cortezdiscussedher decision further.“In this political environment where this administration is denying reproductive care to women across the country, from abortion rights to the ability to carry out a healthy pregnancy, I think it’s important for us as leaders to have these conversations and share these processes, especially for working women across the country and normalize them,” she said.Ocasio-Cortez’s announcement drew praise.Amanda Litman, co-founder and president of Run for Something, a political action committee that supports young progressive candidates,saidon X: “I’m just so grateful for her honesty & vulnerability.”Xochitl Hinojosa, a Democratic strategist,respondedto Litman’s post by saying: “THIS. We don’t talk about women freezing their eggs or what women have to go through to start a family. Thank you @AOC for your bravery.”Explore more on these topicsAlexandria Ocasio-CortezDemocratsUS politicsHouse of RepresentativesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Zuckerberg faces questions over why superyacht reportedly declined to help stranded boat | Alaska | The Guardian
description: Small cruise ship rescued skiff in south-east Alaska even though Meta billionaire’s $300m megayacht was closer
Author: Eric Berger
Headline: Small cruise ship rescued skiff in south-east Alaska even though Meta billionaire’s $300m megayacht was closer
Content: A spokesperson for Zuckerberg said the ‘assist was already under way’ by the time the yacht crew reviewed the radio request.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersView image in fullscreenA spokesperson for Zuckerberg said the ‘assist was already under way’ by the time the yacht crew reviewed the radio request.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersAlaskaZuckerberg faces questions over why superyacht reportedly declined to help stranded boatSmall cruise ship rescued skiff in south-east Alaska even though Meta billionaire’s $300m megayacht was closerEric BergerSun 9 Aug 2026 15.06 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 20.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMark Zuckerberg has faced questions over why a small cruise ship in south-east Alaska rescued a stranded skiff and its crew when his 387ft superyacht had been closer.The Silicon Valley billionaire’s yacht, worth a reported $300m, is said to have “repeatedly” declined to assist when a nearby boat called for help last week.Zuckerberg, CEO of Facebook and Instagram owner Meta Platforms, was not on board at the time, a spokespersontold Forbes.When a nearby 21ft skiff ran out of fuel between Petersburg and Juneau, theAlaska Beaconreported operators of a cruise ship that was further away than Zuckerberg’s yacht came to the rescue.“I’m on a small-ship Alaska cruise with my son,” a passenger on the UnCruise Adventures ship Wilderness Legacy postedon Bluesky.“Our boat rescued a stranded vessel last night and apparently we did that after the Coast Guard radioed Mark Zuckerberg’s yacht – which was closer – and they repeatedly refused to respond. (There was near unanimous booing when the captain announced this).”But Brian Baker, a spokesperson for Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, told Forbes that the couple were not on board his yacht, named Launchpad. The yacht crew had been operating on a different radio channel, Baker told Forbes. “The assist was already under way” by the time they reviewed the broadcast, he said.Even if he was not on his ship, the report is unlikely to boost public opinion of Zuckerberg, who has faced criticism over the societal impact of his social media platforms; his newwarm relationshipwith Donald Trump; andhis lavish,insular lifestyle.“I live in Juneau and I’ve been having to look at that excessive eyesore parked up in [Auke Bay] for too long now,” aReddit userwrote of the yacht in response to the rescue story. “Fuck Zuckerberg.”Explore more on these topicsAlaskaMark ZuckerbergMetanewsShareReuse this content

title: Perseid meteor shower set to dazzle northern hemisphere this week | Meteors | The Guardian
description: Astronomers say viewing conditions promising for this year’s shower, and 50 to 100 meteors an hour may be visible
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Astronomers say viewing conditions promising for this year’s shower, and 50 to 100 meteors an hour may be visible
Content: Ancient statues are seen during the Perseid meteor shower atop Mount Nemrut in southeastern Turkey in August 2024.Photograph: Emrah Gürel/APView image in fullscreenAncient statues are seen during the Perseid meteor shower atop Mount Nemrut in southeastern Turkey in August 2024.Photograph: Emrah Gürel/APMeteorsPerseid meteor shower set to dazzle northern hemisphere this weekAstronomers say viewing conditions promising for this year’s shower, and 50 to 100 meteors an hour may be visibleAssociated PressSun 9 Aug 2026 14.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Perseid summer light show is back, and viewing conditions are especially promising across the northern hemisphere.The meteor shower’s is expected to peak on Wednesday night into Thursday morning, and coincides with a total solar eclipse across Spain, Iceland and Greenland and a six-planet parade – though the best time to view the fireballs will come after totality.As many as 50 to 100 meteors per hour may be visible under ideal conditions, according to NASA. The American Meteor Society estimates 30 to 50 meteors per hour could be seen from rural regions in the US.Random meteors are visible in dark skies on any given night. Meteor showers tend to put on dazzling celestial shows and happen at predictable times every year when the Earth plows through trails of debris left behind by comets and, sometimes, asteroids. Those remnants collide with Earth’s atmosphere at extremely high speeds, producing streaks of light known as shooting stars.The Perseids are debris from comet 109P/Swift-Tuttle, an icy ball that orbits the sun every 133 years and is not scheduled for a return visit until 2125. Observations of this meteor shower date back over 2,000 years.The Perseids are a perennial favorite because they tend to produce brilliant fireballs. Summer temperatures also make this shower popular.“We don’t have to suffer through a cold winter night to get a good view of meteors,” said astronomer Zach Vanderbosch with McDonald Observatory in Texas.The moon will be in its new moon phase during the Perseids’ peak, making viewing conditions even better.“The moon is beautiful, but it’s such a diva,” said astronomer Aparna Venkatesan with the University of San Francisco. “New moon means we don’t have moonlight flooding the sky, and you tend to see way more meteors as a result.”To spot the meteors, go outside after dark, away from clouds and city lights. Venkatesan plans to drive to the Sierra Nevada.The best views will be between midnight and dawn when the constellation Perseus is high in the northern sky. The meteors will appear to radiate from that constellation.Look up and give your eyes a half hour to adjust to the darkness. Vanderbosch recommends picking a patch of sky to focus on until a quick, bright streak passes by – even in your peripheral vision – and to avoid looking at your phone.“There’s just something magical about it,” Vanderbosch said.Explore more on these topicsMeteorsAstronomySpacenewsShareReuse this content

title: Lake Mead plummets to historic low water level as Colorado River struggles | Colorado river crisis | The Guardian
description: Levels at reservoir along Arizona-Nevada border dipped below previous record set in 2022, amid water crisis in west
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Levels at reservoir along Arizona-Nevada border dipped below previous record set in 2022, amid water crisis in west
Content: A paddle boat in Lake Mead near the Hoover Dam, far below the bathtub ring of light minerals indicating the lack of water, near Boulder City, Nevada, on 7 August.Photograph: Ty ONeil/APView image in fullscreenA paddle boat in Lake Mead near the Hoover Dam, far below the bathtub ring of light minerals indicating the lack of water, near Boulder City, Nevada, on 7 August.Photograph: Ty ONeil/APColorado river crisisLake Mead plummets to historic low water level as Colorado River strugglesLevels at reservoir along Arizona-Nevada border dipped below previous record set in 2022, amid water crisis in westGuardian staff and agenciesSun 9 Aug 2026 14.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLake Mead, the largest reservoir in the United States, has plummeted to its lowest water level since it was filled some 90 years ago, the latest sign of adeepeningwater crisisin the American west.Water levels at the reservoir, which straddles the Arizona-Nevada border outside Las Vegas, hit 1,040.4ft (317.1 meters) above sea level on Friday, according to federal data. That’s just below the record set on 28 July 2022, according to the US Bureau of Reclamation.The reservoir is a critical storage system on Colorado River, a massive waterway that supplies roughly 40 million people across seven US states, tribal nations and Mexico, and irrigates millions of acres of farmland.Water cuts loom as US unveils long-awaited response to Colorado River crisisRead moreBut theColorado River basinis facing enormous pressure due to a combination of overuse, prolonged drought and extreme heat, and a lack of snowmelt to replenish the river. Lake Powell, the second major reservoir on the Colorado River, isalso at historiclow levels.“It’s extremely significant and extremely concerning. You have three-quarters of the population of the Colorado River basin, some 30 million people, who are directly impacted by risks to Lake Mead,” said JB Hamby, the chair of the Colorado River board of California and a board member of the Imperial Irrigation District, the largest user of the river’s water. Hamby said it is vital for states that use Colorado River water to reduce water use.Drought and dry conditions have stretched along the length of the Colorado and are particularly intense at its source in the Rocky Mountains.View image in fullscreenWater lines are visible on the rocky banks of Lake Powell on 1 August 2026 in Page, Arizona.Photograph: Justin Sullivan/Getty ImagesMelting snow provides important water for the river. This past winter, however, saw the worst snowpack on record for the Colorado River basin, adding more stress on farmers, industry, wildlife and hydropower producers, as well as the cities and towns that rely on the waterway.Years of overuse combined with drought and rising temperatures have been depletingLake MeadandLake Powell, the country’s second-largest reservoir. Both are the lowest they have been in nearly seven decades.To protect the strained system’s ability to produce hydropower, federal officials said Thursday that they will not release cool Lake Powell water from Glen Canyon Dam in northern Arizona to protect a threatened native fish, thehumpback chub, whose habitat is between the reservoirs.Federal officialsrecently announceda short-term proposal to stave off a crisis in the beleaguered waterway, after states that rely on it – California, Colorado, Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico, Wyoming and Utah –failedto reach an agreement on how to share the dwindling resource in the long term.The federal proposal called for the Lower Basin states of Arizona, California andNevadato take less water. The Bureau of Reclamation, which released the plan, said it was flexible: deeper cuts could happen in drier times, while states would have more time to collectively agree on how to manage the scarce resources.Lake Powell, a vital reservoir, plunges toward unprecedented low levels as water crisis deepens in US westRead moreThe government is expected to release a so-called “record of decision” in the coming weeks offering more details on the plan, butexperts have warnedit might not be enough to solve the problems facing the imperiled river.Severe drought in 2022 on Lake Mead, which is held back by Hoover Dam,exposed human remainsand forced water officials in Las Vegas to pump water from deeper within the reservoir to continue to supply water to millions of people.Levels at Lake Powell have dropped so much that it has become difficult to descend far enough to reach the water. Boat ramps have had to move, shut down or be built anew.Lake Mead and Lake Powell are not alone. Of the 54 western reservoirs tracked by the federal Bureau of Reclamation, nine recently recorded their lowest levels in the last three decades.Federal officials do not believe the record will stay where it is. According to modeling done in July, Lake Mead is forecast to continue dropping through much of the rest of the year.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsColorado river crisisArizonaNevadaWaternewsShareReuse this content

title: Don Nelson, legendary coach and five-time NBA champion as player, dies at 86 | NBA | The Guardian
description: Don Nelson, the second-winningest coach in NBA history who won five championships as a player with the Boston Celtics, died on Sunday
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Don Nelson, the second-winningest coach in NBA history who won five championships as a player with the Boston Celtics, died on Sunday
Content: Don Nelson had success as a player and coach.Photograph: Manuela Soldi/EPAView image in fullscreenDon Nelson had success as a player and coach.Photograph: Manuela Soldi/EPANBADon Nelson, legendary coach and five-time NBA champion as player, dies at 86Nelson had second-most coaching wins in NBA historyWon five titles with Boston Celtics in 1960s and 70sHelped develop stars Steph Curry and Dirk NowitzkiAssociated PressSun 9 Aug 2026 15.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 17.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDon Nelson, the second-winningest coach in NBA history who won five championships as a player with theBoston Celtics, died on Sunday. He was 86.“On Sunday morning our beloved husband, dad, grandfather and great-grandfather Don Nelson ⁠peacefully went to be ⁠with the ​Lord, surrounded by his loving family,” a statement from his family read. “Throughout his last week, friends and family encircled him with love, sharing the ⁠blessing of his friendship and revisiting treasured memories.”The Nelson family did not divulge a cause of death.Nelson is one of two coaches inNBAhistory to have at least 250 wins with three different franchises – Milwaukee , Dallas and Golden State – also serving as general manager for all three franchises. He was a three-time coach of the year and made the playoffs 18 times in 31 seasons. He went to the conference finals three times with the Bucks and once with the Mavericks, although he never won an NBA title as a coach.He also acted as a mentor for players he coached early in their careers, including Dirk Nowitzki and Stephen Curry.“One of the big reasons I was drafted by the Warriors was because of Don Nelson. The story is he never liked rookies, but from Day 1 he challenged me and gave me an opportunity to be my best self on the court,” Curry said on Sunday. “He had an immeasurable impact on the sport and will go down as one of the greatest minds in the history of the game. He’s a true icon and will be missed by the countless number of people he touched, including myself, during a legendary career. Sending my love to Joy, his family and all those who were fortunate enough to know him.”How the ABA changed basketball forever: Dr J, George Gervin and the league that dared to be differentRead moreNelson introduced what is now known as the point forward, and his up-tempo style of offense created a buzz. He said the idea of shifting from the dominant big men of the 1970s to an offense focused on speed and the fast break came from his playing days under Celtics Hall of Fame coach Red Auerbach.Nelson played 11 of his 14 seasons in Boston and was on five Celtics championship teams under four different coaches. He became an assistant coach in Milwaukee after retiring as a player, then took over after coach Larry Costello resigned 18 games into the 1976-77 season. Nelson coached the Bucks for 11 seasons starting in 1976 and won seven straight division titles.His fast-paced offenses were probably best on display with Golden State in the “Run TMC” era featuring future Hall of Famers Tim Hardaway, Mitch Richmond and Chris Mullin. Nelson said he wanted them on the court at the same time.Nelson spent 11 seasons over two stints with Golden State. The first one was punctuated by a rift with rookie star Chris Webber, who was traded away a month into his second season. Nelson, demoralized by the trade, missed nine games that season due to illness and resigned under pressure three months later in February 1995.In between, Nelson was fired after less than one season in New York in 1995-96, then coached in Dallas for eight seasons, taking time off after being diagnosed with cancer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNelson’s son, Donnie, joined his father as an assistant coach with the Mavericks in 1998, later became general manager and remained with the organization until 2021. Together they persuaded 20-year-old German star Nowitzki to pass up European basketball and join the Mavericks. Don Nelson also developed Steve Nash into one of the NBA’s top point guards before Nash went on to win back-to-back MVPs with the Phoenix Suns in 2005 and 2006.At Golden State, Nelson’s “We Believe” Warriors led by Baron Davis upset Nowitzki and the top-seeded Mavericks in the first round of the 2007 playoffs in one of the biggest shocks in NBA history. In his final season as a coach, Nelson mentored rookie Curry in 2009-10.Nowitzki and Davis were among those who paid tribute to Nelson. Davis said: “That time in my life and career was truly special, and Nellie was a huge part of making it possible. I’ll always be grateful for the memories, the laughs and everything we accomplished together,” while Nowitzki said: “I’ve said it a million times and I will always say it: I don’t think my career could have turned out how it did without you being my first coach and giving me the freedom to play my game. I can only say THANK YOU. For everything.”Steve Kerr, the current Warriors head coach who built on Nelson’s work to win four NBA championships with the franchise, said: “So much of what is now commonplace in the modern NBA can be traced back to the way Nellie approached the game. His impact on the Warriors is just as significant. He helped shape some of the most memorable teams and moments in franchise history and built a lasting connection with generations of Warriors fans. His legacy will always remain an important part of this organization.”Curry, the key player in those championship wins, added his tribute: “One of the big reasons I was drafted by the Warriors was because of Don Nelson. The story is he never liked rookies, but from Day 1 he challenged me and gave me an opportunity to be my best self on the court. He’s a true icon and will be missed by the countless number of people he touched, including myself, during a legendary career.”Nelson retired as the NBA’s career coaching wins leader with 1,335, just ahead of Lenny Wilkens’s 1,332. Nelson kept that top spot for nearly 12 years before close friend and now-retired San Antonio coach Gregg Popovich passed him in March 2022.Explore more on these topicsNBABoston CelticsGolden State WarriorsDallas MavericksBasketballUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tour de France Femmes: Vollering wins second title but tactics row rumbles on | Tour de France Femmes | The Guardian
description: Demi Vollering won the final stage to seal her second Tour de France Femmes title but runner-up Kasia Niewiadoma reiterated her unhappiness with her rival team’s tactics on the penultimate stage
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Demi Vollering won the final stage to seal her second Tour de France Femmes title but runner-up Kasia Niewiadoma reiterated her unhappiness with her rival team’s tactics on the penultimate stage
Content: Demi Vollering lifts up her bike in delight after winning the Tour de France Femmes.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDemi Vollering lifts up her bike in delight after winning the Tour de France Femmes.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesTour de France FemmesTour de France Femmes: Vollering wins second title but tactics row rumbles onDutch cyclist finishes 1:18 clear of Kasia Niewiadoma‘I know what’s right and what’s not,’ runner-up saysJeremy Whittlein NiceSun 9 Aug 2026 14.32 EDTFirst published on Sun 9 Aug 2026 13.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the end, there was no debate. Demi Vollering went clear on the Col d’Èze, overlooking Nice, to win her secondTour de France Femmesfrom rival Kasia Niewiadoma, champion in 2024, by one minute and 18 seconds.The decisive attacks came on the narrow snaking climb of the Chemin du Vinaigrier, past swimming pools and art deco villas, where breakaway rider Isabella Holmgren was finally overhauled and ­Vollering and Niewiadoma again went head-to-head.Tour de France Femmes 2026: Vollering wins stage eight after dramatic late break – as it happenedRead moreThe Polish rider’s last-ditch attack saw her replicate the effortsshe had made on Mont Ventouxon Friday, but it was not enough to dislodge Vollering, who remained glued to her back wheel on the 15% gradients, before finally breaking clear just 600 metres from the top of the final ascent of the Èze.However, Vollering’s stage victory and overall success was set against the backdrop of the row between her and Niewiadoma over what were described as “dirty” tactics employedat the foot of the crucial climbof Saturday’s stage, from Sisteron to Nice.The pair have history and their spat goes back to the 2024 race, when Vollering crashed while wearing the yellow jersey on stage five, and Niewiadoma rode on to the finish, eventually winning the race overall by just four seconds.“I have a lot of respect for Kasia,” Vollering said before the stage, but added that she had been “disappointed when I saw her interview yesterday [Saturday], directly after the finish line, because she really attacked my teammates, and I think it’s not so fair to do that.“I didn’t forget what she did when I was on the ground two years ago. So, if she’s speaking about fair play, then I think she’s not the one that can really say something about that. I find it sad that we attack each other like this after the finish line.”Niewiadoma had angrily confronted Vollering’s French FDJ United-Suez teammate, Célia Gery, at Saturday’s finish on the Promenade des Anglais, accusing her of blocking her path as she tried to follow the Dutch rider on the final climb of the stage.The row continued into Sunday afternoon and was inflamed further when Vollering’s manager, Stephen Delcourt, demanded an apology from Niewiadoma.View image in fullscreenWinner Demi Vollering (centre) alongside runner-up Kasia Niewiadoma (left) and third-placed Elisa Longo Borghini.Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images“For the credibility of her sport, I prefer she apologises,” Delcourt said before the start of the final stage. “Célia is 20 years old, she made the corner fast. I’m sure it was never in Célia’s mind to do something wrong.”Lars Boom, Vollering’s sports director, said that Gery was being “torn apart on social media and is receiving death threats”.“I’ve seen the footage and, from what I can see, there isn’t much in it. Gery still leaves space,” Boom said.Even in the race itself the debate continued. On the first ascent of four, of the Col d’Èze, Vollering and ­Niewiadoma rode alongside each other, deep in discussion before the Dutch rider wagged her finger at Niewiadoma, who then rode off.“I’ve been racing for years,” Niewiadoma said on Sunday morning. “I know what’s right and what’s not. It’s not like I’m making things up. I expressed how I felt, and nothing has changed since then.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenKasia Niewiadoma (right) tries to dig in as Demi Vollering increases the pressure on the final stage.Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images“Demi was extremely strong. It’s an honour to fight against her. I don’t want to take anything away from her performance. I just want to race fairly against her.”Niewiadoma’s husband, former world champion Taylor Phinney, went even further. “Is it illegal? I don’t think so,” he posted on social media, of Gery’s move. “Is it dirty riding? To me, yes.”Dogs, descents and dehydration: Tour de France Femmes 2026 – in picturesRead moreHe compared Gery’s move to “something you would see in a junior race, not a move you’d expect from one of the world’s best teams in the biggest race of the year.”“People can ride how they want, race with respect for others or not,” Phinney wrote. “I met many riders who rode without respect in my day. The peloton remembers who races with class and who does not.”It was also a bitter final day for Marlen Reusser,winner of the stage four time trialin Dijon, who fell on a right-hand bend, while descending the Col d’Èze, and tearfully got to her feet, to finish the stage. The Swiss rider, who had started the day third overall, tumbled down the standings to finish 14th in the general classification.Afterher Ventoux exploits, Niewiadoma yet again had to be content with a podium finish, her fifth in five years. “A day like today only motivates me to come back even stronger,” she said.But this race was Vollering’s vindication, two years after her bitter tears at Alpe d’Huez. “I wanted to make it clear that we didn’t win because of an incident on Saturday,” she said. “I wanted to make it clear that we, as a team, deserved to win a beautiful Tour de France Femmes with humility and pride.”Explore more on these topicsTour de France FemmesCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: La Liga president Javier Tebas says ‘Infantino era is over’ at Fifa | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Javier Tebas, the La Liga president, has accused Gianni Infantino of ‘destroying the essence of football’ and said his time is up at Fifa
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: Javier Tebas, the La Liga president, has accused Gianni Infantino of ‘destroying the essence of football’ and said his time is up at Fifa
Content: Javier Tebas has added to the mounting pressure on Gianni Infantino during an interview with Le Monde.Photograph: Ted Shaffrey/APView image in fullscreenJavier Tebas has added to the mounting pressure on Gianni Infantino during an interview with Le Monde.Photograph: Ted Shaffrey/APFifaLa Liga president Javier Tebas says ‘Infantino era is over’ at FifaTebas says Swiss is ‘destroying essence of football’Any reform at highest levels must be ‘genuine’Paul MacInnesSun 9 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJavier Tebas says Gianni Infantino’s position as Fifa president is untenable, claiming he is “destroying the very essence of football” while calling for reform at the highest levels of the game.TheLa Ligapresident, who is a longstanding and vociferous critic of the current Fifa regime, said “the Infantino era is over” and called for control of the game to be expanded beyond the current “elite”.Fifa defends Gianni Infantino and launches attack after ‘effort to undermine’ presidentRead moreWhile Tebas’s remarks will surprise no one within the game, they maintain the drumbeat of criticism directed against Infantino following his determination to continue in post despite his secret and subsequently quashed plans to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors.In an interview with French newspaper Le Monde, Tebas repeated his call for Infantino to resign, an appeal first made after the World Cup but before the sell-off scandal. “For me, Gianni Infantino’s time has long since passed,” he said.“I’m not saying this because of recent events; I have noticed this style of management for a long time, though everyone else seems to be discovering it only now.“Gianni Infantino is not someone who contributes to the growth of football. On the contrary, his projects are destroying the very essence of the sport: the national leagues.“Football is not limited to the elite. For me, the Infantino era is over. What remains to be seen is when that will take effect and how the succession will unfold. I hope it is not just a matter of swapping out some people for others, but of a genuine overhaul.”View image in fullscreenGianni Infantino has received the backing of Fifa in spite of Uefa’s threat to boycott all its tournaments.Photograph: Sam Corum/PAInfantino is battling to stay in post despite an increasingly coordinated attempt by European football officials and others to unseat the 56-year-old Swiss.Uefahas made it clear they regard Infantino’s continued leadership of world football as untenable, the Norwegian FA has called for the president to stand down and a number of European associations have withdrawn letters endorsing Infantino for another term at the head of Fifa.Uefa confirmed on Saturday that a“departure payment”had been made to a female employee who is alleged to have been in a relationship with Infantino while he was the organisation’s general secretary more than a decade ago.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Daily Telegraphreportedon Friday night that the woman received a six-figure sum after the alleged relationship, allegations Fifa dismissed as “categorically untrue”.On Saturday night,Fifapublished a statement accusing Infantino’s critics of attempting to remove him from office before the presidential election next March. “Those who do not have the support of Fifa’s member associations should not seek to achieve through allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through Fifa’s established democratic processes,” the statement read.Infantino has also garnered support from prominent nations outside Europe, including the World Cup co-host Mexico and the finalists Argentina. Uefa say a proposed boycott of all Fifa tournaments remains in prospect, with the women’s Under-20 World Cup due to start in Poland on 5 September.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoLa LigaUefaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Where are the Ugandan boxers? Four are latest athletes to vanish after UK sports events | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Team manager has ‘no idea’ why they disappeared, after reports one of Commonwealth Games athletes said they intended to claim asylum
Author: Robyn Vinter
Headline: Team manager has ‘no idea’ why they disappeared, after reports one of Commonwealth Games athletes said they intended to claim asylum
Content: Nuhu Batte, the captain of Uganda’s Commonwealth Games boxing team, is one of four Ugandan boxers who have gone missing.Photograph: James Fearn/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNuhu Batte, the captain of Uganda’s Commonwealth Games boxing team, is one of four Ugandan boxers who have gone missing.Photograph: James Fearn/Getty ImagesBoxingWhere are the Ugandan boxers? Four are latest athletes to vanish after UK sports eventsTeam manager has ‘no idea’ why they disappeared, after reports one of Commonwealth Games athletes said they intended to claim asylumRobyn VinterSun 9 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 05.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYears of arduous preparation and training had come to fruition and the pressure was finally lifted. After competing for their country in theCommonwealth Gamesin Glasgow, athletes from Uganda were afforded a couple of days’ sightseeing time before catching their plane home on Tuesday.But when the flight took off, there were four empty seats.Only two of the team of six boxers returned to Uganda. Ibrahim Kemis, Emily Nakalema, Angel Katushabe and the captain, Nuhu Batte, were missing.One of the athletes reportedly told the Ugandan news website NBS Sport they were intending to claim asylum in the UK where there are better training facilities. But the team manager for the Ugandan Commonwealth Games teamtold the BBChe had “absolutely no idea” what basis they would have for an asylum claim in the UK.“It’s nothing political, it’s nothing to do with gender or something [like that] – I have absolutely no idea why they would be doing that,” said the team’s chef de mission, Godwin Kayangwe.The first indication something was amiss was that their phones were turned off – against the rules of the Ugandan team camp, as athletes need permission to come and go. And then they vanished.The Guardian understands the foursome were initially taken in by a boxing gym in Glasgow but are no longer inScotland. The owner of the gym did not respond to queries about the missing boxers.Kayangwe hoped they would make the “right decision” and return to Uganda.View image in fullscreenEmily Nakalema (foreground) of Team Uganda competing during the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.Photograph: James Fearn/Getty ImagesThe Pakistani boxer Qudratullah was also missing, having not joined his teammates on the flight home. He was not in his room when officials went to search for him.The events have been the subject of gossip in the boxing world, with rumours abound that the Ugandans had paid money to a Scottish coach to help them disappear. One man involved in boxing, who did not want to be named, said he believed there was “something very, very suspicious going on” and that their location was a closely guarded secret..Police Scotland said it had received reports of athletes not returning home and that it was working with the Home Office to assess the situation.AGlasgow2026 spokesperson said the organisers were working closely with authorities – including Police Scotland, Border Force and UK Visas & Immigration – to ensure that 3,000 athletes from 74 nations and territories could safely and securely participate.This is not the first time athletes have disappeared after tournaments in the UK. The Home Office carries out enhanced checks on participants before big sporting events, due to how prevalent it is.It is estimated 27 people did not leave after the Manchester Commonwealth Games in 2002, 66 after Glasgow 2014, and 17 after Birmingham in 2022. After the 2012 Olympics in London, several athletes chose to stay. Tribunal decisions from asylum applications show a number of people, including athletes from Cameroon and Sudan, and the Ethiopian Olympic flag bearer, all attempted to claim asylum in the UK.The stories go back decades. More than 600 former East German athletes defected before the fall of the Berlin Wall, some of them exposing compulsory doping going on in their home country.Pete Carvill, a boxing commentator and author, said there were many examples of boxers not going back to their home countries because it was possible to have a more lucrative career elsewhere.“Most of the guys who do defect don’t make the best of the opportunity,” he said. “They leave behind the discipline of their amateur programmes and usually end up with lifestyle issues.”He said they often “put weight on that is hard to take off, they begin drinking and partying, they stop training. A lot of them also get taken advantage of, signing contracts that they don’t understand and blowing the purses that they receive.”There are examples of athletes who have stayed in the UK after big tournaments facing legal trouble. Last year, Philip Pariyo, a Ugandan rugby player who claimed asylum after the 2014 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, was imprisoned for raping a woman in Cardiff. A team Pakistan boxer, Nazeer Ullah Khan, was convicted of harassing a woman he met while working in a kebab shop after failing to return to his home country when the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham ended.There are far more success stories, however. Many athletes have made a life in the UK and had families, and some still compete. Eritrean-born Weynay Ghebresilasie was the fastest Scottish man at the London Marathon this year, having claimed asylum and settled in Glasgow after the 2012 Olympics.Cyrille Tchatchet, a Cameroonian-born weightlifter, won a silver medal for Team GB at the Commonwealth Games last week, 12 years after he refused to go back to his home country.View image in fullscreenCyrille Tchatchet after winning a weighlifting silver medal at the Games in Glasgow.Photograph: Dean Mouhtaropoulos/Getty ImagesHe disappeared after the 2014 Games, sleeping rough and eventually being granted refugee status in 2016. He told the BBC: “I remember talking to [my mum] when I left the Commonwealth village. I told her I didn’t have a place to go and she was very concerned.”Tchatchet, who now works as a nurse in the West Midlands, said: “Going back to Glasgow, competing and actually winning a silver medal … I’m very, very proud and honoured to have been given this opportunity to represent England.”Explore more on these topicsBoxingCommonwealth GamesCommonwealth Games 2026GlasgowImmigration and asylumScotlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Iraola says Liverpool have work to do as familiar frailties in defence prove costly | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: Andoni Iraola was disappointed by Liverpool’s inability to sustain their good first half as they surrendered a two-goal lead to lose 3-2 against Monaco
Author: Dominic Booth
Headline: Andoni Iraola was disappointed by Liverpool’s inability to sustain their good first half as they surrendered a two-goal lead to lose 3-2 against Monaco
Content: Lewis Koumas (right) congratulates Alexander Isak after he opened the scoring at Anfield.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenLewis Koumas (right) congratulates Alexander Isak after he opened the scoring at Anfield.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersLiverpoolIraola says Liverpool have work to do as familiar frailties in defence prove costlyHead coach frustrated by ‘tired’ performanceMonaco come from two down to win 3-2 at AnfieldDominic Boothat AnfieldSun 9 Aug 2026 13.55 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndoni Iraola told his Liverpool team they have work to do after ­squandering a 2-0 lead against Monaco to lose a second successive pre-season friendly.The former Bournemouth coach last managed a game at Anfield almost exactly a year ago in the memorable opener to the 2025-26 Premier League season, a game the Cherries wereunfortunate to lose 4-2. Now on his debut in the home dugout, Iraola saw his team produce a similarly open display and lose again. It became clear Liverpool’s longstanding defensive frailties are still to be eliminated.Leeds stage thrilling comeback to sink Liverpool in Chicago friendlyRead moreAlexander Isak and Florian Wirtz scored in the first half as the hosts exhibited some free-flowing ­football, butMonacodominated a ­second half that became fragmented as Iraola and Monaco’s Filipe Luís made wholesale changes.“As soon as we have made some changes they start to get tired, we cannot sustain that level, so we have work to do,” Iraola told LFCTV on Liverpool’s “frustrating” regression after a bright start. “They were much better in the second half, in the same way we were better in the first half.”After Liverpool beat Wrexham and Sunderland during a pre-season tour to the US, a4-2 defeat against Leedsbrought back memories of the struggles of last season. This result will cause some concerns with transfer activity dragging.Ronald Araújo is at least due to arrive on loan from Barcelona. Although that deal is not yet complete and Alexis Mac Allister is still to return from World Cup duty, Iraola’s team to face Monaco was strong, with Ifeanyi Ndukwe, 18, and Lewis Koumas, 20, the only fringe players to start if you exclude Kostas Tsimikas, back from a loan at Roma. Jérémy Jacquet and Curtis Jones were not considered because of fitness doubts, with Iraola at pains not to “rush” Jaquet, whosigned from Rennes for £50m, into action after a chequered time with injury.Iraola said: “Jérémy, we were in doubt whether to pick him today, he should be fine for the next one. Curtis [there is] something wrong with his hip, [it] didn’t make sense to risk [him].”Wirtz was sharp, testing Lukas Hradecky with an early shot. Isak’s opener on 16 minutes was met with a hearty cheer from the home faithful, perhaps not surprising given it was just the fourth time the Anfield crowd have been able to celebrate an Isak goal, competitive or otherwise.View image in fullscreenAndoni Iraola was disappointed after watching Liverpool slip to a second successive friendly defeat.Photograph: Lewis Storey/Danehouse/Getty ImagesThe strike came after Ryan ­Gravenberch and Dominik ­Szoboszlai’s slick midfield exchange, the former then finding the Swede, who rifled low into the corner. Koumas and Wirtz both squandered presentable chances, but it was soon 2-0 when the German forced home after a ­goalmouth scramble.Iraola cut a relaxed figure on the touchline throughout and was content with his side’s attacking fluidity. The Spaniard’s preference for a high defensive line was evident throughout, though Alisson was tested far less often than Hradecky until he had to face a 44th-minute penalty after Virgil van Dijk’s trip on Aleksandr Golovin. The Russian stroked home the spot-kick himself to make it 2-1 at the break, giving ­Alisson no chance.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWataru Endo for Ndukwe and Giorgi Mamardashvili for Alisson were the only half-time substitutions from Iraola, who made more sweeping changes just before the hour, with Rio Ngumoha, Milos Kerkez and the summer signing Víctor Muñoz among those introduced.By that stage it was 2-2, after Mamardashvili had saved from Mika Biereth only to see the striker tap in the rebound. Monaco’s goals were greeted with eerie silence given there were almost no away fans. There were some groans from home supporters frustrated at seeing their side fritter away a two-goal lead but Ngumoha’s name was sung when he came on.That Ngumoha was selected on the right wing – Mohamed Salah’s old stomping ground – was lost on nobody, nor was the fact that both the youngster and Muñoz were brought on rather than Federico Chiesa. The Italian did appear after 74 minutes along with Harvey Elliott, who was welcomed warmly back to Anfield after his nightmare on loan at Aston Villa.Monaco carved out the better chances in the search for the next goal, with Flávio Nazinho firing wide, and Oumar Konaté failing to seize on a good through ball, before their 88th-minute winner stemmed from a corner swung in from the left, which Paris Brunner met with a sweet header.There was no Anfield roar to push the hosts on to equalise as there would have been in a competitive match, and Liverpool’s side resembled a reserves squad by the end, but it was still a tame finish nonetheless. Only a double-header against Como – the first of which will be played behind closed doors – now remains before Iraola’s competitive debut away at Newcastle on 23 August, with his home league debut coming against Nottingham Forest a week later. The manager will demand an improvement in the next fortnight.Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolAndoni IraolaMonacoFriendliesnewsShareReuse this content
