The priorities of working-class voters, meanwhile, are an afterthought.A new report from Jared Abbott, the director of the Center for Working Class Politics, and Joan Williams, author of Outclassed: How the Left Lost the Working Class and How to Win Them Back, looks at ways to bridge the yawning class divide that threatens the possibility of forming a winning coalition.They developed an original survey to explore the various attitude “gaps” between the broad working class (defined as non-college educated, middle income workers) and the liberal upper middle class (Democratic-leaning college graduates with a household income in the top 25%).Democrats need to rethink their image of a ‘man of the people’ | Judith LevineRead moreThe resulting report, titledThe Left’s Coalition Crisis: Understanding the Massive Divide Between Working Class and College Educated Voters, and How to Bridge it, is, according to the authors, “the most comprehensive review available to date” of class-based political attitudes across a number of issue areas.The first thing to note about the gaps between the educated upper middle class and the working class is that the latter overwhelmingly prioritize economic issues, while the former lean toward cultural ones.Of the top 12 political priorities listed by working-class respondents, 11 are economic concerns. The only non-economic issue prized by the working class was a desire to lower the crime rate. Meanwhile, educated upper-income respondents rated cultural and symbolic issues over economic concerns. Of their top 12 priorities, only six were economic. They also rate abstract ideals over concrete, material ones. Educated voters prioritized “resisting authoritarianism” above “protecting social security” and “ending racism” above “protecting Medicaid”.On an issue by issue basis, the largest gaps that Abbott and Williams found were along culture, climate, crime and immigration issues. That is, the very issues many college-educated liberals have built their political identities around. Maybe that wouldn’t be such a problem if these issues were largely downplayed by Democratic party leaders, in favor of shared economic grievances. But that’s hardly the case.Not only do the cultural priorities of the privileged fail to speak to working-class voters’ economic frustrations, but, because Democratic party primaries are dominated by educated upper-income voters, these appeals have come to define liberalism itself.No doubt, the surest way to get a huge cheer at a liberal political rally is to simply mention racism or authoritarianism. Bonus points if you bravely proclaim your unwillingness to “throw X group under the bus”. Such rhetorical gestures have the added benefit of committing candidates to nothing in particular, and thus never threaten potential rich donors.You might say, so what? Who cares if candidates say some throwaway lines about the “marginalized” at a campaign rally; what’s the harm?As Abbott and Williams demonstrate, signaling allegiance to such political priorities is far from costless. Embracing the values and slogans of the privileged tells working-class voters that you are either aloof to, or ignorant of, their priorities.And worse, that you don’t respect working people as political actors. As the authors note, college graduates in Europe and the United States “are more biased against the less-educated than any other stigmatized group”, including racial, religious, and sexual minorities. Blue-collar workers can sense liberal condescension in smarmy injunctions to “be kind”, and they resent what they perceive as upper-class attempts to morally re-educate them.It gets worse. Even if upper-income progressives steer clear of cultural condescension, their economic priorities are also class-bound. While working-class voters prioritize jobs, wages and economic growth, the educated knowledge workers are mainly concerned with high costs. This, too, is a function of the latter’s relatively privileged class position.Democrats are counting on Trump’s unpopularity to save them. It won’t | Osita NwanevuRead moreDespite recent wage erosion, the college-educated set still make much more than their non-college educated counterparts – between 60% and 80%moreon average. This wage premium, combined with our K-shaped economy, means that the well-educated and well-heeled, those in the top 20% of the income hierarchy, nowdrivenearly 60% of all consumer spending.For many educated, upper-income voters – especially those in corporate careers – the defining feature of their economic lives is consuming, not producing. As such, they are extremely sensitive to price increases.Working-class voters are too, but for very different reasons. It’s the devaluing of work that drives their frustrations. As the authors point out, for the working class, and especially for blue-collar workers, it’s work, not consumption, that defines their lives.But long-term wage stagnation, and the disappearance of good stable jobs, has meant that essential goods have become even more difficult to afford. Here, globalization plays a major role. And, on that issue, the data show yet another chasm between the popular classes.While some liberal appeals to “affordability” emphasize the need to scrap tariffs and embrace more liberal immigration rules in order to broaden consumer demand (and lower the agricultural wage-bill), working-class voters are rightly skeptical of these solutions.Restrictions on trade and immigration represent efforts to address the long neglected problems of wage stagnation. Free-trade has devastated the working class, shuttering thousands of factories and sinking many into drug-addiction and despair. At the same time, mass migration has eroded the wage packet for manual workers. For them, addressing affordability must mean policies that speak to the essentially place-bound character of blue-collar life.While professional-class status is portable – effectively equivalent in London, New York, Paris or Washington DC – working-class status is not so liquid. Seniority in a job or trade is not typically a transferrable credential. For these reasons place-loyalty matters a great deal to working-class people.On the other hand, globalization and the growth of “knowledge work” has supercharged select high-income metro areas, where many professionals live and where progressives thrive. Democrats nowrepresentnine of the top 10 highest-income congressional districts in the country.The truth is, educated upper-income voters, be they progressive or moderate, largely benefit from low-wage immigrant labor and cheap foreign goods. Contrary to the place-based loyalty of blue collar workers, they prize their status as global-citizens and cosmopolitan consumers.Navigating these tensions isn’t easy, but Abbott and Williams did find a number of issues that could serve as a foundation for a progressive program of popular-class unity.Getting it right means addressing both the wage and the price side of the affordability equation, downgrading the cultural priorities of the privileged (including on abortion and transgender issues), and grappling with the tension between globalist affinities and local loyalty.By focusing only on those issues that win more than two-thirds of support from both working-class and educated upper-middle-class respondents, they propose a political program with the following planks: allow Medicare to negotiate lower prescription drug prices, protect and improve social security, spend $150bn on infrastructure, expand Medicaid, ratchet up education spending, and raise the minimum wage.The Democrats have one last chance to halt the erosion of US democracy – and it’s less than 100 days away | Timothy Garton AshRead moreThat’s a great start. But it could be improved by an even greater emphasis on working-class priorities. We need new trade rules, revitalized national industry and real pro-labor immigration reform that can help right the wrongs of globalism.We ought to advocate expansive and generous policies that emphasize the importance of family life. Why not make giving birthentirely free, implement national paid-parental leave, and provide affordable childcare?And finally, we need to make expanding and improving badly underfunded local police and fire departments a national priority in order to make every neighborhood and community safe. Such priorities speak directly to felt needs and they signal a genuine political attempt at reorganizing politics around working-class demands, rather than the preferences of the professionals.Putting working-class priorities first will no doubt result in political tensions. Flashpoints around gender, immigration and even class itself, will break out. Getting through those fights will be necessary if progressives ever hope to expand their coalition by reaching into the working class.Plus, who knows, maybe professional-class progressives could learn a thing or two from their working-class counterparts.Dustin Guastella is a research associate at the Center for Working Class Politics and the director of operations for Teamsters Local 623. He is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsDemocratsOpinionUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Subscriptions you can’t easily cancel, sales that aren’t sales – I’ll end the rip-offs that British people hate | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: These everyday hassles are small, but they add up – especially in a cost of living crisis. That’s why my government will tackle them head-on, says UK prime minister Andy Burnham
Author: Andy Burnham
Headline: These everyday hassles are small, but they add up – especially in a cost of living crisis. That’s why my government will tackle them head-on, says UK prime minister Andy Burnham
Content: ‘Each everyday fix will be designed to put a bit more money back into people’s pockets.’Photograph: mihailomilovanovic/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Each everyday fix will be designed to put a bit more money back into people’s pockets.’Photograph: mihailomilovanovic/Getty ImagesOpinionLabourSubscriptions you can’t easily cancel, sales that aren’t sales – I’ll end the rip-offs that British people hateAndy BurnhamThese everyday hassles are small, but they add up – especially in a cost of living crisis. That’s why my government will tackle them head-onAndy Burnham is the UK prime ministerBurnham vows crackdown on ‘rip-off’ business practicesSun 9 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareIt’s remarkable how much of modern life can seem designed to wear us down. Every “sale” seems to come with an asterisk. Consumer contracts often find a way of costing more than you expected. And too many companies want you to sign up in seconds, but then make it feel impossible to leave. It’s exhausting.They might not be the issues that keep you up at night. But they’re often the reason you go to bed ticked off. Westminster has got used to telling people that these everyday hassles are just part of life. The response has too often been a shrug of the shoulders or just calling it bad luck.I don’t think that’s right. Because these everyday hassles affect millions of people. And they add up. Every single one is an unnecessary cost. And when the cost of living continues to weigh heavily on so many people’s lives, we need to be pulling every single lever we can to help ease that.But they add up in another way too. Every single unexpected payment, rip off or hidden catch chips away at hope. That might sound dramatic – but it’s true. Every single one is another message that this country is built to catch people out rather than help them get on.I want people to start believing in Britain again. But we’ll only get there by building a country that feels fair. And that means getting a grip on those issues that get people’s backs up day in, day out. So we are going to do things differently. We are going to get on with the everyday fixes that make life easier and more affordable. As far as I’m concerned, whatever the size, big or small, if it’s a problem for you, it’s a problem for us.That’s why I’ve made it clear from day one that creating room to breathe is my number one priority, and the whole of this government is united on that. We won’t be able to solve every frustration overnight. But where the government can save people money, remove an unnecessary obstacle or simply make something work better, we should – and we will.We are kicking off with a couple of first steps on those everyday hassles that people tell me about time and time again.First, we are putting an end to phoney bargains. We are taking on poor practices that make people’s lives harder. If something is advertised as half price, it should actually be half price. We will make sure that when families snatch a deal, they can be confident they’re actually saving. That’s the least they deserve when budgets are so tight.Second, we are making it as easy to leave a subscription as it is to join, and businesses won’t be able to renew a subscription without notifying you. New rules will come into force in January 2027, in time for when people often start new subscriptions, or cancel the ones they have, for the year ahead.There are about 155m active subscriptions in the UK, with consumers spending an estimated £1.6bn a year on ones they don’t actually want – a direct hit to family budgets. The changes we are introducing will save an average of £14 a month for every unwanted subscription.These are just a couple of our everyday fixes. There will be more to come over the next few months and bigger plans to make life easier and fairer for people over the longer term.Each everyday fix will be designed to put a bit more money back into people’s pockets, to make daily life a little fairer and to give people a bit more hope that politics really can work for them again.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI will also be asking people what action they want to see on the cost of living. Because if we want to find the problems that make everyday life harder, we need to listen to the people dealing with them.So over the summer, I will begetting out to regions across countryto hear directly from people about the challenges they face and the changes they want to see.Westminster has spent too long asking people to wait for life to get better. This government is determined to make it better and to bring back hope. My message to people is simple: this will be a cost-of-living government and we will be on your side to prevent you being overcharged, trapped or misled.Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United KingdomExplore more on these topicsLabourOpinionConsumer rightsUK cost of living crisisFamily financescommentShareReuse this content

title: The idea of ‘sin’ can cause shame and trauma. But what if it’s used as a cue to act? | Jackie Bailey | The Guardian
description: Instead of ‘being’ or ‘doing’ the wrong thing, a more useful understanding of sin may be of ‘missing the mark’ – a sense of not quite right-ness
Author: Jackie Bailey
Headline: Instead of ‘being’ or ‘doing’ the wrong thing, a more useful understanding of sin may be of ‘missing the mark’ – a sense of not quite right-ness
Content: ‘Shame arising from a sense of deep unworthiness pushes me into the fetal position, rather than into action.’Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Shame arising from a sense of deep unworthiness pushes me into the fetal position, rather than into action.’Composite: Getty ImagesMaking sense of itSpiritualizedThe idea of ‘sin’ can cause shame and trauma. But what if it’s used as a cue to act?Jackie BaileyInstead of ‘being’ or ‘doing’ the wrong thing, a more useful understanding of sin may be of ‘missing the mark’ – a sense of not quite right-nessMaking sense of itis a column about spirituality and how it can be used to navigate everyday lifeSun 9 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 19.18 EDTShareAs a child, I was taught we are inherently unworthy of God’s love. “Forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us,” I would intone at Sunday mass, along with the other parishioners. I was imploring God, not just to overlook my theft of the last cookie in the pantry, but for something more fundamental. I asked him to remove the heavy weight of shame from my eight-year-old shoulders.I had absorbed the doctrine of “original sin” into the marrow of my bones, even though it was hard to square with another key teaching of my church: God is love. Surely, I reasoned, a loving God would not send me to hell if I failed to believe in Him?Eventually I left the religious institution of my childhood, but core ideas have stuck to me like burrs on the back of a (sacrificial) lamb. Looking for a way to live an ethical life outside religion, I ask myself: is there utility in a doctrine of sin?In the Christian faith, sin can be broadly understood as twofold: original sin and actual sin. Actual sins can be named and listed, as in the Ten Commandments. In many Christian traditions, original sin is the foundational state of being human. It refers to a broken state of being. The remedy is understood to be singular: God, the source of salvation, is humanity’s only hope of returning to a state of grace.Many religions have ethical codes that outline acceptable behaviours without the doctrine of originalsin. For example, Muslims believe that humans are born untainted (fitrah), with the potential to move towards God and goodness, while the Jewish tradition and some Christian sects teach that humans enter the world innocent.An act of kindness, or mitzvah, teaches us to be part of something bigger than ourselves | Nomi KaltmannRead moreIn these contexts, the idea of sin can still become problematic. For example, if the religion condemns a person’s gender or sexual orientation as sinful, this can cause significant personal shame and trauma. It can also lead to the punishment and exile of a person from their families and communities.Chet (חֵטְא) orchata, (חָטָא),a Hebrew word for sin, andhamartia (ἁμαρτία),the biblical Greek term for sin, are translated as “to miss the mark”. This might be a more useful understanding of sin than being inherently wrong, or doing the wrong thing. It reminds me of the Buddhist termdukkha,commonly translated as suffering, but which can also be understood as being off-kilter, like a wheel off its axis. Perhaps sin is asense that the world is spinning slightly out of alignment with a benevolent universe.Sin understood as disharmony could be personal, communal or cosmic. I might feel the need for more balance in my life, perhaps between work and play, or generosity and self-interest. Relationally, I might feel a disconnect between myself and others, or between me and nature, or me and my sense of something bigger than myself. At a societal level, I could conceptualise sin as the issues that I and my community must take responsibility to change, like systemic racism in the law, or the ever-increasing gap between the rich and poor. At the universal level, I can seekto cocreate goodness and positively to influence the way my species affects the direction of the cosmos.Perhaps the idea of sin has utility when it encourages what the Buddhists term “right action”. If I feel a sense of not-quite-rightness, rather than assuming it means there is something wrong with me or humanity, I can understand it as a cue to act.Shame arising from a sense of deep unworthiness pushes me into the fetal position, rather than into action. But a sense of things being out of whack could be inspiring. With a little help and the right tools, I could fix a wobbly wheel. I could set it true and start driving.Jackie Bailey is an award-winning author whose latest book is The Outrageous Good Fortune of Living (HarperCollins). Jackie works as a funeral celebrant and pastoral care practitioner, supporting people to navigate death and dyingExplore more on these topicsSpiritualizedMaking sense of itcommentShareReuse this content

title: As AI guzzles water and energy, we are already facing a choice: datacentres or homes? | John Harris | The Guardian
description: Whitehall wants to triple their number in the UK. Yet in Slough, I saw the impact they’re having on communities, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: Whitehall wants to triple their number in the UK. Yet in Slough, I saw the impact they’re having on communities, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: Illustration: R Fresson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: R Fresson/The GuardianOpinionDatacentresAs AI guzzles water and energy, we are already facing a choice: datacentres or homes?John HarrisWhitehall wants to triple their number in the UK. Yet in Slough, I saw the impact they’re having on communitiesSun 9 Aug 2026 07.03 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareAmid headlines aboutthe UK’s drought, Europe’s wildfires and impossible global temperatures, it was 28C when I arrived in Slough last Monday. I was there to look around Slough Trading Estate, a place that might once have conjured up images of the TV comedyThe Office, many of whose laughs came at the expense of this overgrown patch of suburbia, 20-odd miles west of London.But these days, this area of town – an incongruous mixture of old-school businesses such as Mr Clutch and Angling Direct, and vast, metal-clad leviathans that look like something pulled from JG Ballard – hasbecome a bywordfor the constant expansion of datacentres, those hulking symbols of the vast computing power that big tech now requires, not least because of the ever-more complex workings of artificial intelligence.In many people’s minds, datacentres are also a byword for the two totemic issues of yet another searing summer:heat and water. Across the world, the huge amounts of electricity they demand, mostly generated using fossil fuels, indelibly connects them to the climate emergency. The constant machinations of their crammed-in servers require cooling processes that also use vast amounts of water. So it is that the 21st century’s dominant means of communication intensifies our era’s most terrifying threats.The first building I loitered around was a datacentre owned by the California-based company Equinix. There were 100 or so cars in its “visitor” and “staff” spaces, no corporate branding to be seen – and, up close, the constant sound of a low industrial whirr. On the other side of the street, poetically enough, was a set of offices occupied by ThamesWater, a few of whose employees were taking a break outside. I pointed across the road: did they know what the building contained?“There’s loads of AI bits in there,” said a twentysomething woman called Louise. “I saw something about it on Instagram: all the water they use.” She rolled her eyes. “It’s ridiculous. Loads and loads of water because of all the AI.” On her phone, she foundone of the postsshe had seen. “Slough is quietly running Britain’s AI boom but there’s a problem,” it said. “When a heatwave hits, the machines get thirsty too. Cooling systems work overtime in hot weather, spiking demand for power and water.”Someone suggested I make the five-minute journey to nearby Britwell, a housing estate built for bombed-out Londoners after the second world war. The first person I encountered was a mum from the area called Sheryl. “You notice the noise at night: like a whirring, buzzing sound,” she said. “And since we’ve had all these [new] ones up here, there seems to be more heat round here.”Early research, including arecent preprintof a paper authored by researchers at Cambridge University earlier this year, does suggest that datacentres can have a “heat island” effect, pushing up temperatures in their immediate vicinity by an average of 2C, and as much as 9C. Last month, the trading estate’scorporate owners saidthey had “not seen conclusive evidence demonstrating that datacentre operations on Slough Trading Estate are causing increases in local temperatures”.View image in fullscreenSlough Trading Estate, which houses some of the 40 datacentres in the area.Photograph: Education Images/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesSlough has thedensest cluster of datacentresin western Europe: as many as 40, with more to come. What has happened here is bound up with the trading estate’s recent history as a partly deregulated “simplified planning zone”, the town’s proximity to London (the faster that digital financial transactions can happen, the better), and the apparently flukish fact that Slough sits atop the cables that connect Britain to the US and Ireland. The datacentres the town hosts are owned and maintained by companies that are far from being household names – Equinix, Digital Realty, Iron Mountain – but serve famous customers including Amazon, Google, Oracle and Microsoft.Fierce arguments about datacentres are a big part of the discourse surrounding the upcoming US midterm elections, with Donald Trump taking apredictable position: “You have to convince your community how great these things [are] … You can’t fight it.” But actually, you can. Resistance is now pouring into the US political mainstream: midway through last month, New York became the first state to impose aone-year pauseon new “hyperscale” datacentres, and, as litigation is fought out across the country, there is mounting pressure for other parts of the US to follow suit. The leftist insurgent Abdul El-Sayed, who last week won a Democratic Senate primary in Michigan, has crisply captured the mood: “People really effing hate datacentres,” he says. Even the Republican governor of Texas hascalled for a banon their development in rural areas, and last week ordered that new centres won’t join the state’s power grid until regulators have reviewed their use of water and energy.Increasing numbers of US facilities have their own dedicatedgas turbines; in the UK, high-ups at the energy regulator Ofgem say that100 planned centreshere aim to do the same. US sites are putting added pressure on existing power grids that also use coal and oil, and backup generators powered by diesel are a standard industry feature. Green datacentres areattracting growing interest, but many insiders insist that renewables simply don’t cut it: “Our datacentres have to run 100% of the time so we can’t even consider using [renewables] as a primary source,” one industry kingpintold the Financial Timeslast year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDemocracy is at stake when foolish humans bet on machines being intelligent | Rafael BehrRead moreWith good reason, not many people are minded to listen to private water companies. But only a fortnight ago, Water UK, the organisation that represents firms in the four nations, said that the government’s existing water forecasts were “fatally flawed” and “explicitly exclude” datacentres, which can use up to5m gallons a day, equivalent to the consumption of up to 50,000 people. What that omission says about our readiness for more datacentres – and what will happen during inevitable future droughts – is an interesting question. Would the public be expected to stoically limit their use of water while datacentres carried on guzzling it?All sorts of tensions could soon explode. For all Andy Burnham’s talk of local decision-making, Whitehall’s official aim is still to triple the UK’s number of datacentres by 2030, which could be aided by the fact that they are nowclassed ascritical national infrastructure. In December, a report by the London assemblyrevealedthat datacentres’ electricity requirements had led to stalled housebuilding in the capital; last week brought news of the returned housing secretary, Angela Rayner,approving a redevelopmentof the old Truman Brewery site in east London that had been called in by her predecessor, Steve Reed. It will include a datacentre handling transactions in the City, offices and 44 homes, in contrast to plans supported by the local council centred on 350 new dwellings. Whatever that represents, it doesn’t sound like what the new PM calls “good growth in every postcode”. There may, in fact, be a stark choice lurking in such stories that politicians will soon have to face: homes or servers?On my way out of Britwell, I had a chat with a woman called Jodie, on her way home from Lidl. “My brother said he saw something on TikTok that said if there was a war, Slough would be a target because of the datacentres,” she said. I grimly laughed: “Come friendly bombs and fall on Slough”, and all that? “Let’s hope not,” she said. In the middle distance, the increasingly gigantic datacentres whirred on, and I thought of a few lines from another of John Betjeman’s poems: “And over all the land, instead of trees / Clean poles and wire will whisper in the breeze / We’ll keep one ancient village just to show / What England once was when the times were slow.”John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDatacentresOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingWatercommentShareReuse this content

title: Is your ill fate bad luck or a curse? You could ask Ted Lasso, but why not consider the psychology  | Helen Pilcher | The Guardian
description: From Mayo to Birmingham City, sports lore is rife with powerful hexes. There’s nothing mystical about the dread and self-doubt they can induce, says science writer Helen Pilcher
Author: Helen Pilcher
Headline: From Mayo to Birmingham City, sports lore is rife with powerful hexes. There’s nothing mystical about the dread and self-doubt they can induce, says science writer Helen Pilcher
Content: Mayo celebrate winning the 2026 All-Ireland Gaelic football title after 75 years – and 11 finals losses.Photograph: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMayo celebrate winning the 2026 All-Ireland Gaelic football title after 75 years – and 11 finals losses.Photograph: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesOpinionPsychologyIs your ill fate bad luck or a curse? You could ask Ted Lasso, but why not consider the psychologyHelen PilcherThe hit TV show confirms that sports lore is rife with powerful hexes. But there’s really nothing mystical about the dread and self-doubt they can induceSun 9 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 05.06 EDTShareAs the new season of Ted Lasso started, I was reminded of one of the show’s stranger storylines. When Dani “Football is life!” Rojas gets injured, his teammates blame the incident on a curse said to haunt the treatment room.Absurd? Perhaps. But sports curses aren’t just fictional plot devices. Football is fertile ground for stories of mysterious forces, blamed for everything frommissed penalties to decades of failure.Take Mayo’s Gaelic football team. After they won the All-Ireland title in 1951, the story goes that a local priest cursed them, declaring they would not win another final until every member of that team had died. Over the next 75 years, Mayo reached 11 more finals – and lost them all. Paddy Prendergast, the last surviving member of the 1951 squad, died in 2021. Then Mayo made it to the final again last month and won. This prompted the Canadian prime minister Mark Carney, who has family ties to Mayo, to announce on X: “The curse is broken.”Birmingham City – a team close to my heart – has its own curse story. The club is said to have endured decades of disappointment after a100-year hexwas placed on its home ground in 1906. And this year, Harry Kane missed a close-range chance in England’s Fifa World Cup match against Ghana, shortly after a “witch-doctor” claimed to havecast a spell on him. Coincidence?There are, of course, many possible explanations. Maybe supernatural forces really were at work. Maybe the teams had bad luck, made tactical errors or were simply beaten by better opponents. Or maybe, once the curse became part of the team’s folklore, it acquired a life of its own. In this scenario, it doesn’t matter whether the “spells” were ever cast, or whether players personally believed in them. What matters is that the idea gained a cultural foothold. Retold by fans, journalists and commentators, the stories shaped expectations about what might happen next. And expectations can have very real effects.Psychology has a name for the power of negative expectations: the nocebo effect. The phenomenon is best known in medicine. A person takes aplacebopill but is warned it may cause side-effects. Often, they experience them anyway.The symptoms are real, even though the tablet isn’t causing them. The same principle can play out in sport. Philip Hurst and colleagues at Canterbury Christ Church University have shown that when runners are given an inert supplement but told it will negatively affect their sprint performance,they run slower. Give them the same supplement but tell them it will improve their performance, it has little effect. This hints that in sport, negative expectations may have more of an impact than positive ones.View image in fullscreenTed Lasso tries to lift his team’s curse with a late-night cleansing ritual.Photograph: YouTubeNow, imagine a football player walking on to the pitch. The trigger hardly matters. A “curse”, a run of defeats or a teammate’s throwaway comment can all plant a seed of doubt. After that, every misplaced pass, heavy touch or missed chance can seem like proof that something is off. Confidence falters. A game that once felt instinctive becomes something to overthink, until doubt itself starts to undermine performance.What begins in one player’s mind can also become a team-wide narrative. Players absorb cues from team members, supporters, critics and the media, quietly internalising the atmosphere that surrounds a team. Psychologists call this social contagion: the spread of emotions, behaviours and beliefs through groups. Over time, these shared beliefs can become part of a team’s identity, shaping how it responds under pressure. The result is a feedback loop: the story shapes expectations, expectations shape behaviour, and behaviour can appear to confirm the original story. The question is: how do you break the cycle?Perhaps we can learn a thing or two from Ted Lasso and the real-life managers who faced similar scenarios. Lasso’s solution was a late-night cleansing ritual, with players throwing treasured possessions into a container which he set alight. Meanwhile Birmingham City’s Barry Fry tried a more “fluid” approach, by urinating on the pitch’s four corners.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhether these rituals had any mystical power is beside the point. Their value was psychological. They created a reset – a chance for the team to draw a line under the past and start expecting a brighter future. For Mayo, that reset has finally arrived. The next generation of players and supporters will inherit a different memory – not of the final they could never win, but of the one they finally did. As former Mayo player Colm Boyle put it after their victory: “The shackles are off.” The curse may only have been a story, but now Mayo can tell a different one.Helen Pilcher is a science writer and author of Life Changing: How Humans Are Altering Life on Earth and This Book May Cause Side EffectsExplore more on these topicsPsychologyOpinionTV comedyIrelandcommentShareReuse this content

title: The hill I will die on: Remove those earphones – you’re blocking out the music of humanity | Stefan Stern | The Guardian
description: Beyond the white noise lies a vibrant world of possibility, so take your headphones off and listen to your surroundings. It may even save your life, says author Stefan Stern
Author: Stefan Stern
Headline: Beyond the white noise lies a vibrant world of possibility, so take your headphones off and listen to your surroundings. It may even save your life, says author Stefan Stern
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onTechnologyThe hill I will die on: Remove those earphones – you’re blocking out the music of humanityStefan SternBeyond the white noise lies a vibrant world of possibility, so take your headphones off and listen to your surroundings. It may even save your lifeSun 9 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 13.31 EDTShareEr, excuse me. Hello? I’m sorry, but would you mind taking your … I SAID, WOULD YOU MIND TAKING THOSE EARPHONES OUT FOR A SECOND, PLEASE?I try, in the main, to be a live-and-let-live kind of person. Patient. Considerate. But this patience is being tested to breaking point by the proliferation, the epidemic, of almost-ubiquitous earphones.The world must be shut out, apparently. The wearer has nothing to learn or gain by listening to anybody else in their vicinity. They would rather be elsewhere, plunged into music or a novel or maybe a noisy pavement phone call, which will remain, sadly for the accidental eavesdropper, a slightly odd one-way exchange only.The hill I will die on is that there is a fascinating and beautiful world out there, filled with conversation and laughter and the possibility of making new friends and acquaintances. But instead of taking part in all that, people prefer to plug in their earphones, tune in and drop out.*This phenomenon seems to be 21st-century proof of Pascal’s belief that the “inability to sit quietly in a room alone” is the source of all our problems. There must be constant, piped-in noise. Silence is the enemy.The hill I will die on: I really don’t like ‘like’ – or other imprecise and redundant speech | Louis de BernièresRead morePerhaps this is another consequence of Covid lockdowns. We got used to being on our own, working at home, earphones in, to save flatmates or family members from the distraction of other conversations. Back in the workplace, the earphones have stayed in. Maybe this can help with concentration, a protest against the enforced intimacy of the open-plan office. But it makes life harder for colleagues who may want to ask a quick question, or for a benign boss – other types of boss are available – to show some interest in you, when they are “managing by walking around”.Imagine if, two centuries earlier, Wordsworth had wandered lonely with his AirPods in. Would he have ever heard the “still, sad music of humanity, / Not harsh nor grating, though of ample power / To chasten and subdue”?OK, maybe it is polite on the bus or the train to stick the earphones in and avoid creating noise pollution. People who are neurodivergent may want to block some things out. But personally, I usually enjoy listening to the conversations you can hear, in a range of languages, on public transport. I knowthat Nigel Farage objects to that sort of thing, but the rest of us don’t have to.I say: take the earphones out, lend me (and everyone else) your ears and enjoy the world around you. Choose real life. At the very least, staying alert could save you from getting run over, or mugged.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd, you know, if there weren’t so many of these earphones permanently on display, then maybe people would stop launching so manypodcasts.* I make an exception forthe new audio version of my latest book, you’re allowed to listen to that.Stefan Stern is co-author of Myths of Management and the former director of the High Pay Centre. His latest book is Fair or Foul: The Lady Macbeth Guide to AmbitionExplore more on these topicsTechnologyThe hill I will die onWork & careerscommentShareReuse this content

title: Game of Thrones: The Mad King review – an action-packed saga of dry ice and fire | Theatre | The Guardian
description: This prequel to the TV series has one joust after another, spectacular stagecraft and plenty of modern resonance
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: This prequel to the TV series has one joust after another, spectacular stagecraft and plenty of modern resonance
Content: Reminiscent of Olivier? … Michael Shaeffer as King Aerys II Targaryen in Game of Thrones: The Mad King.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenReminiscent of Olivier? … Michael Shaeffer as King Aerys II Targaryen in Game of Thrones: The Mad King.Photograph: Johan PerssonTheatreReviewGame of Thrones: The Mad King review – an action-packed saga of dry ice and fireRoyal Shakespeare theatre, Stratford-upon-AvonThis prequel to the TV series has one joust after another, spectacular stagecraft and plenty of modern resonanceMark LawsonSun 9 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDuring the RSC’s 65 years, numerous Lears have lost their minds and frequent Caesars been slaughtered by their courts. Now, though, a tyrant new to its stages faces both fates. He is King Aerys II Targaryen, ancestor of one warring bloodline inGame of Thrones, the dramatisation of George RR Martin’s A Song of Ice and Fire series of fantasy novels that helped TV streamers’ rise to global domination during eight HBO seasons from 2011 to 2019.Some may balk at an institution named for England’s greatest dramatist staging an American drama franchise. There is, though, a compelling economic imperative:rising costs due to current wars(a frequent problem for Martin’s ancient oligarchs too) and Covid-era debts now exacerbated by paying back government loans means that the RSC could use another big commercial transfer – asits musical Matildamay not be immortal.View image in fullscreenChloe Lamford’s striking sacred tree … Noah Ritter as Prince Rhaegar Targaryen in Game of Thrones: The Mad King.Photograph: Johan PerssonThere is also an artistic rationale. Martin has always credited Shakespeare’s English history plays as a model. DramatistDuncan Macmillan– starting from an unexplored reference in the books to a consequential tournament in this universe in 281AC (after conquest) – and director Dominic Cooke bow even deeper to the presiding genius: Michael Shaeffer’s King Aerys, with long white beard and flower-braided hair, strongly resembles Laurence Olivier’s television Lear.You don’t need to read the entrails of a raven to guess the target of the title The Mad King: the various Brutuses plotting his fall conclude that the “paranoid and delusional” monarch will destroy their civilisation. The focus, though, is not just Trumpian. Macmillan references two wider international crises – the instability of heads of state and the weather – and a UK national concern: the endurance of a royal bloodline. The RSC’s patron, King Charles III, might skip this one.There are already two HBO prequels –House of the DragonandA Knight of the Seven Kingdoms– but while those are set up to 200 years before the TV series, Macmillan’s is a much closer prologue. That is a harder task, as he must match up with the season one box set. Fans will be attracted by back stories of telly-legendary characters: one young man is addressed as Eddard Stark, but pleads to be known as Ned. Two leads in the main TV show are babies at the end of the RSC’s three hours and 45 minutes.Macmillan’s dialogue is quasi-Shakespearean with a rough iambic beat. A heavily pregnant princess is “overloaded with the hopes of the realm”. One of many violently bereaved characters tells another: “If a beloved has been wrenched from you, then we are fellow countrymen.” The problem comes when this plausible pastiche of Elizabethan politicking collides with Martin’s supernaturalism.View image in fullscreenVisceral … Elizabeth Ayodele as Princess Elia Martell and Tanisha Spring as Ashara Dayne in Game of Thrones: The Mad King.Photograph: Johan PerssonThe steeds of puppetry and movement directors Nick Barnes and Finn Caldwell – vast skeletal frames manipulated by squads of actors – carry characters in rather too many jousts and battles. Dogs and dragons are similarly simulated. But whatever the efforts and budgets expended, theatre can’t match the stunning dollars-to-burn televisual atmospherics. Chloe Lamford’s set, though, includes a striking sacred tree, intermittently formed by a huge trunk rising to dock with flowered foliage descending. Real flames and mock fog frequently swirl on a cruciform walkway that quarters the stalls of the Royal Shakespeare theatre: a scene of dry ice and fire.‘Can’t stop smiling!’ The wait is over for epic Game of Thrones prequel The Mad KingRead moreActors in adaptations of screen material – such as the currentThe Silence of the Lambs– can choose whether to be avatars of the TV or film stars. Here, the performers must be plausible previews of their future television inheritors. Maxim Ays as Jaime Lannister, Michael Abubakar’s Ned Stark, the Cersei Lannister of Daisy Franks and Hughie O’Donnell’s Lord Varys might all be earlier portraits of the famous, but youth and new lines leave leeway for their own intonations. Even so, the greatest impact is made by characters featured in the main TV show only in dialogue or flashback: Princess Elia Martell and Prince Rhaegar Targaryen, viscerally played by Elizabeth Ayodele and Noah Ritter.The play’s end intriguingly leaves a 14-year gap until the TV series, perhaps allowing for more instalments. Purists will object that, rather than staging Shakespeare-adjacent populist spin-offs, the RSC should be offering its house dramatist’s royal dramas plain. The counter argument is that hitching on to a cultural juggernaut may bring in new sources of income and audiences.The review star system can struggle with shows that some might sell their house to see but others would be reluctant to leave home for. This feels like a five-star production for most devoted throners but a three-star for those who haven’t seen the TV series. Thereby, to channel this show’s infectious tones, the Judging One has trod a path between those stellar prophecies.AtRoyal Shakespeare theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, until 5 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreRoyal Shakespeare CompanyGame of ThronesGeorge RR MartinDuncan MacmillanDominic CookereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘If you’d done that in the 90s, you’d have been torn to pieces!’: comedy icons share their Edinburgh fringe survival tips with first-timers | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: How do you deal with nerves or bad reviews? What if you don’t sell any tickets? For debutants, the list of potential worries is huge. So we paired a few up with veterans to talk past mistakes, coping strategies – and the odd celebrity encounter
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: How do you deal with nerves or bad reviews? What if you don’t sell any tickets? For debutants, the list of potential worries is huge. So we paired a few up with veterans to talk past mistakes, coping strategies – and the odd celebrity encounter
Content: Portraits: Antonio Olmos; Styling: Sam DeamanEdinburgh festival 2026‘If you’d done that in the 90s, you’d have been torn to pieces!’: comedy icons share their Edinburgh fringe survival tips with first-timersHow do you deal with nerves or bad reviews? What if you don’t sell any tickets? For debutants, the list of potential worries is huge. So we paired a few up with veterans to talk past mistakes, coping strategies – and the odd celebrity encounterBinge on the fringe: the must-see shows at Edinburgh 2026Explore the rest of our coverage of the Edinburgh festival 2026Rich PelleySun 9 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 10.30 EDTShareEveryone has to start somewhere – even at the Edinburgh festival fringe. But what made Smack the Pony actor Fiona Allen take up standup in her 50s? Why is veteran TV entertainer Joe Pasquale making his fringe debut in his 60s in an ensemble comic play? How many taboos will newcomer Sepideh Kaav, a Berlin-based Iranian comic in her early 30s, break by talking about sex? And what will the 78-year-old, seven-time Edinburgh veteranGyles Brandrethmake of debutant Brandy Bex, a 50-year-old NHS nurse performing in drag? We paired six fringe stalwarts with relative newcomers to compare their hopes, fears and survival tactics for this year.Frank Skinner (five previousfringes) and Cecily Hitchcock (fringe debut)View image in fullscreenFrank Skinner and Cecily Hitchcock. Styling: Sam Deaman. Makeup: Neusa Neves using Code8 cosmetics, Benefit eyebrows and Lashify. Frank Skinner wears Gresham Blake suit and Gieves & Hawkes shirt and tie. Cecily Hitchcock wears Vivienne Westwood dress from Mytheresa and Coeur De Lion necklace.Composite: Antonio Zazueta Olmos/Getty ImagesThe veteranBlack Country comic, back with a new work-in-progress show, chats with the newcomer, whose 2000s-themed show is set to be silly for silly’s sakeFrank SkinnerMy worry is that my first Edinburgh was so long ago – 1987 – that any advice I give will be archaic. I did it completely the wrong way. I went up with a play, was blown away by alternative comedy, then booked a venue for the following festival having never done standup. I wasn’t even planning to practise until someone pointed out that I probably should.Cecily HitchcockDid it work?FSMy biggest audience was nine people. One day, nobody came at all. That’s how people get their hearts broken at Edinburgh.CHI wouldn’t mind a couple of people, as long as they liked me. Is there anything I should avoid?FSI’d say: “Don’t read your reviews,” but everyone likes talking about the bad ones. I got two reviews that year. They both essentially said: “This guy clearly doesn’t know what he’s doing,” but insinuated: “He’s got something.” That was just enough crumbs to keep me going. Apparently, younger comedians are now obliged to have a theme or theatrical element. Someone like me, who just does jokes, is old-fashioned.CHSince Fleabag everybody feels they need some tragedy. But it’s not frowned upon to be silly. My show is silly for silliness’s sake, although it does have a theme of nostalgia and childhood innocence.FSEdinburgh used to feel like a folk festival. Anyone could turn up and do weird stuff. It’s much more professional now. The first time a comedian handed me a business card, I thought: “If you’d done that in the 90s, you’d have been torn to pieces.” The one word you couldn’t use on the circuit in those days was “ambition”. Now, people are very upfront about what can be gained from Edinburgh. I mean, this year, I’m doing work-in-progress, using Edinburgh in a way that it’s previously used me. I’d be happy just doing work-in-progress for the rest of my life – 80 people in a room, just tinkering, trying new stuff. Even one line working is like receiving nectar from the gods.CHHow do you avoid going mad, surrounded by other comics for a month?FSI used to have lots of “dressing-room friends”, and stay out until 4am, even if I was drinking Vimto. But years of solo shows turn you into a lonelier, more desolate outsider. Having friends on the circuit helps. Thinking “We’re all in this together” is a good stabiliser.CHThe last time I went, everyone wanted to see the man who eats a kilogram of cheese. Do you still feel you’re getting better?FSI think I’m funnier than I’ve ever been. But I’m biased. Obviously.Cecily Hitchcock: Family Recipeis at Pleasance Courtyard, to 30 August.Frank Skinner: Work in Progressrunsto 16 August;Crowd Work With Frank Skinner, 17 to 26 August; both at Assembly George Square Studios.Stephen K Amos (23 previousfringes) and Joe Pasquale (fringe debut)View image in fullscreenStephen K Amos and Joe Pasquale.Composite: Pål Hansen/Mark McGee/Getty ImagesTheEdinburgh stalwart and the television, panto and variety veteran are appearing together in11½ Angry Men, an ensemble spoof of the courtroom drama 12 Angry MenStephen K AmosHas Edinburgh never been on your radar before?Joe PasqualeIt’s always been on my radar. I’ve just never been asked. There’s always been this barrier between middle-of-the-road and alternative comedy.SKAMy first Edinburgh was in a package lineup in 1997. Back then, it was all about being discovered. Now the joy is the creativity: you’re surrounded by comedians of all ages.JPBefore Covid, I’d almost had enough of being on the road, stuck in traffic, eating crap. When the world disappeared for two years, I was just a bloke in his pants with nothing to do. Now I love younger comics’ energy and ambition. How do youngsters cope nowadays? How can they afford it?SKAThey can’t. Everything’s gone through the roof. Edinburgh felt corporate-y even when I started. It feels even more corporate-y now.JPI’m worried that I’m supposed to tap-dance. I phoned the director and said: “You do know I can’t tap-dance?” He said: “What do you mean you can’t tap-dance? You’ve been doing variety for 40 years!” I said: “I’ve never tap-danced in my life.” He said: “Well, you’ve got four months to learn.”SKADon’t read reviews. If you believe the good ones, you’ve got to believe the bad ones. Did I have a good time? Did the audience? That’s enough for me.JPNone of us are trying to get rediscovered, not at our age. I’m there for the experience of being on stage with you and the lads.11½ Angry Menis at Pleasance EICC Pentland theatreto 22 August.Ania Magliano (seven previousfringes) and Ele McKenzie (fringe debut)View image in fullscreenAnia Magliano and Ele McKenzie.Composite: Alexandra Cameron/ Rebecca Need-Menear/Getty ImagesThe Edinburgh comedy award nominee and SNL UK host discusses pre-gig routines with the actor-comedian presenting her debut standup hourEle McKenzieMy primary concern is that I won’t sell any tickets, and no one will come. The idea of being reviewed terrifies me.Ania MaglianoYou’ve got to have someone to throw under the bus as a scapegoat. That’s what directors and producers are for. Being misunderstood by the public shivers my timbers. Having said that, I still have a Google Alert set for my own name, which completely goes against my Zen Buddhist state.EMIt must be incredibly reassuring knowing your dates are sold out.AMTicket sales are a useful anchor. The fringe is so abstract, scary and unknown. Deep down, we’re all terrified of being exposed through our art. And it is art. It’s tough on your body because you burn through so much energy, but you’re fuelled by adrenaline.EMWhatdoyou eat?AMLast year, I stayed in a flat with an air fryer. I got into having a nice big egg frittata every morning and a banana before going on stage. The fringe is like managing depression: you need to remember basic self-care. A long shower can buy you an extra week of energy if you time it right.EMWhat time are you on?AM1.25pm.EMI’m envious that you can get up and get on with it. I’m on at 8.10pm, thinking: “How will I spend my days?” I usually have a pint or two before a gig, as an unhealthy pre-show ritual.AMI used to be precious about my pre-show routine because I wanted control. I’d meditate for five minutes in the toilet, to get in the zone. The bottom line is trusting yourself to do a good show, whatever gets thrown at you.EMI’m fully expecting to make plans – “I’m going to do this, I’m going to do that.” Then it’ll go to shit almost immediately.AMIt’s surreal performing comedy 28 days in a row. Whatever you need to do to get through it is fine, even if that means having a chocolate brownie before every show. Hashtag: be kind to yourself.Ele McKenzie: Bringing It All Back Homeis at Pleasance Courtyard, to30 August;Ania Magliano: Peach Fuzzis at Monkey Barrel, to 22 August.Fiona Allen (one previousfringe) and Sepideh Kaav (fringe debut)View image in fullscreenFiona Allen and Sepideh Kaav.Composite: Natasha Pszenicki/Oliver Look/Getty ImagesThe Smack the Pony actor, who began standup in her 50s, talks about late starts and homesickness with the Berlin-based Iranian comicFiona AllenI’ve only done one solo show – three years ago. I was acting, having babies, but hadn’t done standup. It was very much “mum on the run”. This time, it has more of a theme, set over a single day, where I wake up dreading having to go to a party that evening.Sepideh Kaav:That’s my struggle – do I need a theme? I already have one, as an Iranian woman in her early 30s. But there will be expectations.FAPeople’s expectations can be whatever they like. There are thousands of shows at Edinburgh. It sounds trite, but you should just do you.SKI am so scared of living away from home for a month. Do you get homesick?FAI’m a total homebird. I miss my dog. Bring your home comforts, your favourite PJs. A month sounds like for ever, but you’ll suddenly be halfway through.SKI mostly gig in Berlin, where I live. English is my second language, and words carry less emotional weight when they aren’t in your mother tongue. We don’t have a comfortable, everyday way of talking about sex, so discussing it in Farsi is very difficult. Speaking English makes everything easier. Few Iranian women do standup, and my comedy is quite dark. Even if I go to Edinburgh and fail, it might inspire somebody to think: “I can do better.”FAI was 54 and thought: “I hope somebody else is sitting there at my age, going: ‘Well, she’s done it. Now I’m going to do it.’” Edinburgh is like a club full of open-armed, like-minded people, so you’re going to have a lovely time.Sepideh Kaav: 1979 – Persianality Disorderis at Coco BoHo, 18 to 30 August;Fiona Allen: White Liesis at Gilded Balloon Teviot: Dining Room, to 29 August.Susie McCabe (seven previousfringes) and Gregor Fisher (one previousfringe, 45 years ago)View image in fullscreenGregor Fisher and Susie McCabe.Composite: Graeme Hunter/Andy Hollingworth/Getty imagesThe Rab C Nesbitt actor was last at the fringe when it was barely recognisable to today. The Scots standup with seven runs behind her shares her wisdomGregor FisherI haven’t done Edinburgh for 45 years. Back then, it was still church halls, not fancy venues that no fucker can afford. I did The Servant of Two Masters – a Scottish version of an Italian play – out of the back of a van. It was theatre for the people, funded by the government back when it cared about the arts.Susie McCabeI’m just fortunate to play these lovely theatres every night.GFIt’s not because you’re fortunate. It’s because you’re good. If you’re crap, you don’t survive. Don’t hide your light under a bushel, Susie. I was iffy about coming back. My daughter said: “Well, you might have fun, Dad.” I thought I should do it one last time because, you know – tick-tock. I’d forgotten that I have to get there every day, which is a big ask for an old boy like me.SMThe fringe is a bit like gay equality in the 70s. We all wanted it to be slicker and better but, once you’ve got it, you’ve lost a bit of what it was. The gay scene used to have this underground. Then we got equality and everybody’s like: “You don’t need to march any more.” I think the fringe is a bit like that.Having worked for a living, I hear comedians moaning: “This is my third gig of the day.” I think: “You’ve only worked half an hour!”GFWhat was your job?SMI was an electrician.GFYou’re the very person I need. I cannot get an electrician for love nor money.Susie McCabe: Coming of Rageis at Assembly George Square: Gordon Aikmantheatre, to 30 August;An (Early) Evening With Gregor Fisheris at Gilded Balloon Teviot: Debating Hall, 15 to 30 August.Gyles Brandreth (seven previous fringes) and Brandy Bex (fringe debut)View image in fullscreenGyles Brandreth and Brandy Bex.Composite: Andy Robinson/ Bill Black/Getty ImagesThe veteran broadcaster, former Tory MP and raconteur imparts his wisdom on the NHS major-trauma nurse making herfringe debut as a drag comedy characterGyles BrandrethI’ve been going to Edinburgh – alarmingly – since the 1950s. In the 90s, I was a Conservative member of parliament, but I lost my seat in 1997. My wife said: “You’ve got a clean slate. What do you most want to do in the world?” I said: “I want to be in a musical.” I had this brilliant idea – 100 musicals in 100 minutes. Then somebody said: “Go to Edinburgh,” and I was lucky enough to hit the jackpot. How long have you been a nurse?Brandy BexI qualified in 2009. I had a bit of an existential crisis when I turned 40, so I thought: “I’m going to create a comedy character and take the piss out of the NHS.”GBHa! So you’ve been taking the piss, just not in a specimen bottle. Two of my sisters were NHS nurses. One is 86 now. Where do you nurse?BBMajor trauma.GBThat can be your opening line. “By day, I work on major trauma. By night, I cause major trauma.” How are you on nerves? Do you take beta blockers?BBNo. I used to be quite nervous, but now I truly enjoy it.GBWell done, you! You and I may be the only people in Edinburgh not on drugs, prescription or otherwise.BBI imagine in a year or two, I probably won’t be in the NHS.GBThe other thing I wondered is: where will you change into your costume? Wherever you change, it will not be private – a telephone booth, a lavatory, a stairwell. I was doing a Rocky Horror Show skit as part of my musical montage, and decided to change in the flat before I set off. Looking out of the window, I saw a guy with binoculars taking pictures of me. It was quite exciting. Ian McKellen came; afterwards we had a coffee. I was back in my jeans and T-shirt. He said: “I bet you’re still wearing your suspenders.” I said: “As it happens, Ian, I am. How did you guess?” He said: “Because I’m still wearing mine!”Brandy Bex: Progressin Workis at Just the Tonic at Westside Rodeo, 23 to 27 August;Gyles Brandreth: Up Memory Lane!is at Assembly George Square: Gordon Aikman theatre,to 30 August.

title: Hostile review – surreal spaghetti western is a wild and wordless ride | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: At the Edinburgh international festival, Olivier Rannou’s lone cowboy encounters desert dangers in a mix of clowning, mime and visual trickery
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: At the Edinburgh international festival, Olivier Rannou’s lone cowboy encounters desert dangers in a mix of clowning, mime and visual trickery
Content: In extremis … Olivier Rannou in Hostile at Church Hill theatre, Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIn extremis … Olivier Rannou in Hostile at Church Hill theatre, Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewHostile review – surreal spaghetti western is a wild and wordless rideChurch Hill theatre, EdinburghAt the Edinburgh international festival, Olivier Rannou’s lone cowboy encounters desert dangers in a mix of clowning, mime and visual trickeryArifa AkbarSun 9 Aug 2026 06.39 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 06.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe lone ranger at the centre of Olivier Rannou’s family-friendly western initially appears as stranded and desolate as one of Samuel Beckett’s anti-heroes. Parched and prone across a table, with a knotted handkerchief on his head, he is marooned in a desert landscape with a water bottle full of sand, a desperate thirst and a scattering of human skeletal remains.He retains an edge of existential angst, struggling to survive in extremis, but also becomes more clown-like by turns. Rannou shows us, through movement, expression and sound, that this cowboy is a wanted man, on the run, wrestling with the dangers of his barren, unpeopled surroundings.There is the hallucinatory sound of dripping water, a fight with a rattlesnake and a saloon bar shootout, enacted solely by Rannou through mime and clowning, along with a delightful invention of props (the snake is conjured from string, the cacti from planks of wood).Émilie Rougier’s electronic compositions accompany his antics, charging the atmosphere with danger and flipping the mood from light to dark. Sometimes, this sound resembles an electric didgeridoo; at other times, tinkly fairground tunes. There is also some lovely lighting design by Alan Floc’h and Alexandre Musset that evokes a relentlessly glaring desert sun or eerie night.View image in fullscreenPlayful … Hostile at the Churchill theatre, Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianIt is comic, cartoonish and brooding. The skeletons are clear memento mori but with comic edges, and there is exuberant silliness alongside this as well as a Beckettian sense of “failing better” that shows him stoically fending off the repeated, Road Runner-like mishaps that befall him.[seagull] review – silence proves golden in innovative if puzzling shot at ChekhovRead moreProduced by French theatre company Bakélite, it is an eccentric and entertaining show. Rannou brings great, easy physicality, although some of it feels rather abstract and you wonder where this one-man spaghetti western is going or what it is ultimately saying.A highlight comes with the visual playfulness of the set, also designed by Rannou. The original table morphs into other objects, ever bigger and more elaborate, including, at one point, a wooden horse which comes to life and slowly clops off the stage. It is all constructed, carpenter-like, by Rannou before our eyes, and it seems as if he is engaged in a delightful act of wood origami.It absolutely amuses, but as a wordless show that does not try to explain itself, it is rather bemusing too.AtChurch Hill theatre, Edinburgh, until 11 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsTheatreComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)ClownsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Chris Martin seems nice – but Coldplay make me feel carsick!’: Lucy Beaumont’s honest playlist | Music | The Guardian
description: As a tween, Hull’s finest learned the rap from Waterfalls – now she blubs to prog. But which song from a British singer-songwriter is her guilty pleasure?
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: As a tween, Hull’s finest learned the rap from Waterfalls – now she blubs to prog. But which song from a British singer-songwriter is her guilty pleasure?
Content: ‘I’ve never done karaoke in my life and I never will’ … Lucy Beaumont.Photograph: Debbie EllisView image in fullscreen‘I’ve never done karaoke in my life and I never will’ … Lucy Beaumont.Photograph: Debbie EllisHonest playlistMusic‘Chris Martin seems nice – but Coldplay make me feel carsick!’: Lucy Beaumont’s honest playlistAs a tween, Hull’s finest learned the rap from Waterfalls – now she blubs to prog. But which song from a British singer-songwriter is her guilty pleasure?As told toRich PelleySun 9 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first song I fell in love withCaravan of Love by the Housemartins, when I was four or five. They’re also from Hull, but I think I mainly liked it because my granny and grandad had a caravan in their garden that I used as a wendy house.The first single I boughtI remember buying Thriller by Michael Jackson from HMV in Hull, even though it was before my time. Everyone loved Michael Jackson so I was probably copying somebody at school.The song I inexplicably know every lyric toI know the lyrics to loads of songs, but I actually sat down and learned the rap from Waterfalls by TLC when I was about 12.The best song to play at a partySuperstition by Stevie Wonder.The song I can no longer listen toAnything by Coldplay – particularly Yellow. I have a visceral reaction. It’s not them – Chris Martin seems like a nice guy – but there’s something about the tone that makes me feel carsick.The song I secretly like, but tell everybody I hateSupermarket Flowers by Ed Sheeran. He wrote it about his grandmother dying, but from his mother’s point of view. I think it’s a really lovely song, but I’d never tell anybody.The song that changed my lifeAs a teenager, I was really into hard house. Then, when I heard the first Stone Roses album, it was like nothing I’d heard before. The opening bars of Waterfall are especially rock’n’roll, but also feel so spiritual. It had a massive effect on me.The song that gets me up in the morningMovin’ on Up by Primal Scream – perfect if I’m hungover and have a busy day.The song that makes me cryWish You Were Here by Pink Floyd has been played at a couple of funerals, and it always gets me. I always think how amazing it must be to write something that people play at their most vulnerable moments, and that somehow explains life.The song I do at karaokeI’ve never done karaoke in my life and I never will. But if someone put a gun to my head I’d do These Boots Are Made for Walkin’ by Nancy Sinatra.The song I want played at my funeralAt a funeral, you really listen to music as a group. So I’d have Try a Little Tenderness by Otis Redding.Lucy Beaumonttours the UK23 September to 20 June; tour starts Scunthorpe.Explore more on these topicsMusicHonest playlistComedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Chosen in the Wild with Bear Grylls review – in a world of toxic masculinity, this feels radical at points | Television | The Guardian
description: As the survivalist takes the cast of the Christian drama out in the wild to discuss faith, it’s surprisingly moving to find two very confident men so comfortable in their gentleness
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: As the survivalist takes the cast of the Christian drama out in the wild to discuss faith, it’s surprisingly moving to find two very confident men so comfortable in their gentleness
Content: ‘I thought I was going to die!’ Luke Simyan goes skydiving.Photograph: Amazon MGM StudiosView image in fullscreen‘I thought I was going to die!’ Luke Simyan goes skydiving.Photograph: Amazon MGM StudiosTV reviewTelevisionReviewThe Chosen in the Wild with Bear Grylls review – in a world of toxic masculinity, this feels radical at pointsAs the survivalist takes the cast of the Christian drama out in the wild to discuss faith, it’s surprisingly moving to find two very confident men so comfortable in their gentlenessLucy ManganSun 9 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJudas Iscariot is sonice! That’s a surprise. Just goes to show – you betray ONE messiah, the scroll-media gets to work and people forget everything else.I’m joshing, of course. I’m having a little religious joke because The Chosen in the Wild withBear Gryllshas put me in such a good mood. The Judas Iscariot in question is actually Luke Dimyan, the actor who plays him in The Chosen: the multi-season series about the life, death and resurrection of Jesus of Nazareth. The Chosen is a venture by evangelical Christian film-maker Dallas Jenkins that began as a crowdfunded project in 2017 and is now watched by an estimated 280 million people worldwide. Bear Grylls is a fan and a Christian – what could be more natural than him taking members of the cast for survivalist adventures in the Utah desert, to talk to them about faith in between ziplining across chasms, filtering water through socks and rappelling down cliffs?It is precisely because the result does feel so natural that I find myself in such a good mood. The actors are not asked to do too much. Some do a helicopter jump, some don’t. They each do a couple of small challenges, where neither the intrinsic difficulties nor the participants’ hesitations are lingered over, and then they stop for another chat about acting or God while Bear feeds them an MRE (military ready meal) or nugget of survivalist wisdom. No one becomes an emotional or physical wreck.Dimyan is Grylls’ first guest – a wise choice as he is a completely charming, self-confessed nerd (“I worry a lot! I’m constantly worried!”) who names rocks as he makes his way to meet Bear (“I think I’ve passed Jerry a few times,” he notes worriedly) but is willing to skydive on to the canyon trail from 10,000ft. “That’s amazing!” he says cheerfully when he lands. “I thought I was going to die!”At their first pit stop, they talk about Dimyan’s upbringing in a Coptic Egyptian family who didn’t want him to be an actor. “Get paid!” said his dad. “Be safe!” Now, he says, his parents say: “We’re glad we were wrong!” It’s really lovely.So too is the rapport between the men, who discuss their faith in unembarrassed fashion and talk about what Jesus means to them. “Acceptance,” says Dimyan. “He saw people and allowed them to be the best versions of themselves … if you love people unabashedly, they will take that chance.” None of the episodes goes deeply into matters of faith but they have a simple and touching authenticity to them.It is also unexpectedly moving to watch two men – here especially, but in other episodes, too – be so confident and yet so peaceful together. In a world full of toxic masculinity, it feels as radical as any religious profession to hear Bear compliment his companion on his gentleness and to have him poke fun at his own reputation (he tends to let scorpions go these days, he says, unless he’s really desperate to eat).They are also funny together. Dimyan, understandably, can’t quite believe he has to pee on his MRE to activate the heat pack that will make it palatable. Nor, when he has been convinced of the necessity, can he instantly muster the wherewithal. “Normally I can take direction,” he says with his back to us, concentrating. “It just needs a little bit,” Bear shouts over to him. “Look, you get what you get,” says Dimyan.The other episodes stick to this soothing formula, drawing in more of the cast: the Indian American actor Paras Patel, who plays disciple Matthew; Elizabeth Tabish (Lilith/Mary Magdalene); and, in the penultimate outing, Jonathan Roumie (Jesus himself – who gets to roam the Adirondacks instead of the desert, which I think suggests a VIP treatment quite out of keeping with His teachings). I did enjoy the fact that Dallas Jenkins got the final episode. If a director can, he will always place himself just above God.I don’t quite know how to square Grylls’ evident sincerity and good sense on show here with the fact that his most noteworthy recent appearance prior to this was at thebaptism of Russell Brand– after accusations by multiple women of rape and other abuses by the comedian were made public. Brand has since been charged with three counts of rape and other assaults. Grylls was asked during the publicity run for Chosen in the Wild whether his feelings about the baptism had changed. “I think all our faith changes and evolves, and I’d also say I have many doubts as well. I really struggle with so much of it,” he said. But “I think at heart, my faith says … not to judge people and to love people.” I look forward to Brand being judged in a court of law, and I don’t think that’s through a lack of Christian compassion. But on we go.The Chosen in the Wild with Bear Grylls is on Prime VideoExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewBear GryllsReality TVreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Even the good guys were doing bad things’: the wild, twisted story behind the new Tiger King | Documentary | The Guardian
description: Monsters of God is a jaw-dropping new series from the makers of the hit Netflix pandemic smash, exploring the murky world of exotic reptile smuggling
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: Monsters of God is a jaw-dropping new series from the makers of the hit Netflix pandemic smash, exploring the murky world of exotic reptile smuggling
Content: A still from Monsters of God.Photograph: HBO MaxView image in fullscreenA still from Monsters of God.Photograph: HBO MaxDocumentary‘Even the good guys were doing bad things’: the wild, twisted story behind the new Tiger KingMonsters of God is a jaw-dropping new series from the makers of the hit Netflix pandemic smash, exploring the murky world of exotic reptile smugglingAndrew LawrenceSun 9 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1993, a sci-fi blockbuster about an animal theme park that resurrected the dinosaurs sparked more than a flurry of interest in those long-extinct beasts. It left audiences jonesing for the next best thing: a close encounter with a bearded dragon or a ball python. Jeremy McBride, the Emmy-winning film-maker was one of them. “I wanted a pet iguana,” he said. In the wake of the Spielberg classic, reptiles have become fixtures of the modern imagination, adorning zoo exhibits, living room terrariums and every corner of pop culture while underpinning a multibillion-dollar pet trade.Monsters of God review – a messy feud between rival reptile smugglers gets the Tiger King treatmentRead moreBut just as in Jurassic Park, the urgent danger isn’t the prehistoric creatures with the teeth and venom. It’s the people willing to steal, smuggle and kill for them. People like the Pablo Escobar of animal trafficking. “Our next documentary is going to be called Who Backstabbed Who,” jokes Eric Goode, an Emmy-nominated director. “You never know when that knife is going to go in your back because everyone’s trying to make a deal with the feds, with another reptile dealer. Even the good guys were supposedly doing bad things. It’s messy.”Goode’s latest collaboration with McBride,Monsters of God, premiered on HBO this week, and it has all the ingredients to become another monoculture moment in the mold of Tiger King. Where Goode’s pandemic smash was a rabbit hole into the kooky subculture of private zoo owners, this five-part series, executive produced by McBride, explores the sprawling shadow enterprise of traffickers who ransack the globe for the rarest reptiles and sell them for staggering profits. What began as a criminal ecosystem connecting smugglers, individual collectors and major institutions such as the National Zoo soon expanded to include bad actors in other illicit industries who seized on the opportunity to use reptiles as camouflage for their own operations.Based on the 2008 true-crime book The Lizard King, Monsters of God traces the trade’s humble origins to the 1960s, when a cheese salesman named Hank Molt began publishing a reptile price list and mailing it to zoos as they began to recognize the enormous commercial potential in dedicated collections. Molt became an inspiration for reptile enthusiasts who envied his rare finds and the globe-trotting adventures that produced them, while the US Fish and Wildlife Service – dismissed as the “duck cops” – rightly feared his booming business wreaking havoc on native ecosystems and moved swiftly to rein him in.In 1977, Molt was federally indicted on more than 200 smuggling counts and served just 90 days in jail. But that leniency wasn’t enough to contain the reputational damage his case inflicted, particularly among institutions such as the Smithsonian’s National Zoo and its many patrons in Congress. After Molt’s prosecution, the reptile trade’s power structure was revealed: at the center of this tight-knit monopoly, there could be onlyone“lizard guy” inonetown (usually in Florida) – making reptile smugglers comparatively easier to investigate than, say, the mob. After Molt it was his apprentice Tommy Crutchfield, an ostentatious Floridian who poured nearly every dollar he made in trading reptiles back into the hunt for new ones and, fittingly, inspired the title for this series.After Molt dimed out Crutchfield in retaliation for stealinghisbusiness, igniting a decades-long feud between the two reptile obsessives, the crown passed on to Ray Van Nostrand, a Miami hustler who chased bulk profits from common species over rare specimens.
