Then he crossed paths with Mario Tabraue, a prolific cocaine and wildlife smuggler viewers might remember from Tiger King as the likely inspiration for the cult gangster flick Scarface. Together, they popularized a new method of concealment: packaging rare and venomous reptiles with drugs to disguise shipments and deter inspectors. But the “Pablo Escobar of animal trafficking” title was ultimately reserved for Malaysia’s Anson Wong, the reptile nerd kingpin whosesuspected tiesto Asia’s ruling families and underworld gangs made him law enforcement’s white whale.Monsters of God catches up with these men in their winter years, resulting in wistful reflections on their notorious pasts. Van Nostrand, who died during filming just short of his 80th birthday, was battling dementia and visibly struggles to access his memories in interviews.View image in fullscreenTom Holt in Monsters of God.Photograph: HBO MaxBut Goode and McBride found that they could bring back some of his old spark by pairing him with his son Michael, the Tony Soprano-like successor who expanded the family business while his father was imprisoned, only to wind up imprisoned for turtle trafficking himself. They also shot Van Nostrand at the family’s warehouse facility, ostensibly legitimate again, where he was surrounded by the reptiles that built, lost and rebuilt the family fortune. “We had a whole version of that story with him not in it in a contemporary way,” McBride says. “But we had one editor whose dad was going through dementia at the time who pushed us to show more of that. It’s not every day that you get to interview someone who doesn’t necessarily know what they’re talking about and show that in a way that’s compassionate.”Each hour-long episode raises the stakes, with reptile-loving axeman Slash literally underscoring the twists, turns and spitting-viper cutaways. “He’s such a sweet, normal guy, cares about the issue and wanted to contribute his time,” McBride says. “We’d send him music, and he’d play over it during a lot of particular scenes. We’re gonna put out the vinyl soon.”All the while, you can’t help wondering whether McBride and Goode, doing his Michael Moore thing while calling the shots behind the camera, are sticking their own necks out a bit too far. “What we’re really good at is getting people locked up behind bars,” Goode says, not entirely joking. “There was one guy who was under investigation and went to prison while we were filming him. I’ve decided I’m really good at putting people in prison inadvertently.”Bombs, heists and big cats: TV’s 25 best true-crime shows everRead moreCrucially, no animals were harmed in the production of Monsters of God – something, alas, that can’t be said for a black market that treated dead reptiles as little more than the cost of doing business. The film’s tales of “spoiled inventory” are every bit as shocking and heartbreaking as you’d expect. A longtime conservationist, Goode is relentless about getting viewers to see these creatures as he does, pressing his lens so close to vertical pupils, beaky maws and scaly brows that you can’t help harboring concern for his camera crew.Tabraue, the cocaine cowboy who ultimately served 12 years of a 100-year sentence for his 1989 conviction on narcotics and racketeering charges, had a near-death experience during one shoot after he was bitten by a Gila monster – the only venomous lizard native to the US, McBride hastens to note. “Fun fact: a compound in their venom led to the development of GLP-1 drugs,” he says. “So the very thing that can kill you is now saving people’s lives around the world.”View image in fullscreenEric Goode and Jeremy McBride at the premiere of Monsters of God.Photograph: Rob Latour/ShutterstockIn Monsters of God, the people are the ones framed as beasts – fueled by lust for power, wealth and the narcotic thrill of the chase. The longer you watch, the harder it becomes to distinguish the good guys from the bad. The federal agents who pursued these reptile smugglers are pitched into moral ambiguity the moment they step onto the beat. Some are willing to look the other way for the sake of a conviction; others come to believe their proximity to the trade entitles them to a piece of it.“It’s like the Harvey Keitel movie Bad Lieutenant,” says Goode.“Well,” McBride adds, “it’s even more pathological.”As the crime thriller unravels, the docuseries also shows how smuggling has ravaged reptile populations, pushing some species to the brink of extinction. But one of the documentary’s bigger ideas – how reptile imports have thrown native US ecosystems out of whack – was ultimately left on the cutting-room floor. “We filmed Burmese pythons in the South Florida Everglades,” Goode says. “We filmed iguanas dropping out of trees. The invasive species angle is a big deal, and it really does have an impact all around the world.”But Monsters of God doesn’t do much to help viewers who might have gone into it already feeling ambivalent about zoos. On the one hand, their money-making reptile exhibitions helped create the conditions for the wildlife smuggling business. On the other, where else would people encounter these creatures closely enough to understand why they are worth protecting? “The paradoxical effect of smuggling is that zoos are functionally seed banks for preventing animals from going extinct,” McBride says. “It’s no longer animals coming in. It’s animals going out.”Goode sees that contradiction as part of a larger reckoning. “It’s a bit like saying: how should I feel about America?” he says. “Zoos, like our culture, have a lot of skeletons. They were part of the civic planning of a city and built to be entertaining. But zoos also have a long history of evolving, just like we do in our country.”In the end, Monsters of God is not a spectacle for the sake of it. It’s the Jurassic Park cautionary tale come to life: fascination curdling into obsession.“We’re really interested in making entertaining content,” McBride says. “But we also want to try and tuck in a purposeful message. More than ever nonfiction stories matter a lot. People want to learn something, and we want to help educate them and not just have them watch a freak show all the time.”Monsters of God is available onHBOMaxExplore more on these topicsDocumentaryHBOFactual TVPolitics TVUS televisionTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Prophets review – a mysterious tale of faith at the end of the world | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: A researcher encounters an isolated community in thrall to a mysterious religious leader in Jack MacGregor’s atmospheric but elusive drama
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: A researcher encounters an isolated community in thrall to a mysterious religious leader in Jack MacGregor’s atmospheric but elusive drama
Content: Faith no more … Xander Cowan in Prophets at Assembly Roxy, Edinburgh.Photograph: Giulia FerrandoView image in fullscreenFaith no more … Xander Cowan in Prophets at Assembly Roxy, Edinburgh.Photograph: Giulia FerrandoEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewProphets review – a mysterious tale of faith at the end of the worldAssembly Roxy, EdinburghA researcher encounters an isolated community in thrall to a mysterious religious leader in Jack MacGregor’s atmospheric but elusive dramaMark FisherSun 9 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat impresses about Jack MacGregor as a playwright is their willingness to take us into the wider world.Nightlandswas set in a deserted Russian research base in Svalbard; Everything Under the Sun concerned militias in Mali; andOur Brotherplayed out in the Cambodia of Pol Pot. So it is with Prophets, which begins with the arrival of Kerris, a Scottish researcher, on the sparsely populated island of Saint John, a fictional British Overseas Territory in the South Pacific.Played by Rebecca Wilkie, she is as curious about the religious activities of the islanders as she is the archaeological record of plant life she is supposedly there to study. Welcomed by Joe, a former merchant seaman played by a multitasking Xander Cowan, she senses something is amiss in the nightly church services led by an elusive man they call the prophet. Her job is about the dawn of time, but the locals are readying themselves for the end of days.View image in fullscreenProphet motive … Xander Cowan and Rebecca Wilkie in Prophets.Photograph: Giulia FerrandoAll this starts promisingly in the well-acted production directed by Fraser Scott. MacGregor’s political sense suggests there could be some kind of cover-up going on behind the slow-moving administrative machinery of this faraway remnant of the British empire, compounding the impression of an out-of-control cult taking its lead from a rewritten Bible.Hostile review – surreal spaghetti western is a wild and wordless rideRead moreBut as Prophets plays out, it increasingly feels as if the real drama is somewhere else. Kerris, it transpires, has a personal interest in charismatic religious leaders, but her backstory is hazy and slow to reveal itself. We get too fleeting an insight into whatever trauma she went through in Scotland.And for as long as she is outside the cult looking in, we feel at one remove from the action on the island. It means we are left with the uncontroversial message that cults are a bad thing, and get only a shallow perspective on the social forces that make such religious conviction attractive in the first place.AtAssembly Roxy, Edinburgh, until 31 August.All our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Foriegner review – will drinking your own urine get you a US visa? | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Sohrab Haghverdi takes pleasure at winding up the audience in a subversively funny ‘anti-comedy’ of autobiographical insight and political provocation
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Sohrab Haghverdi takes pleasure at winding up the audience in a subversively funny ‘anti-comedy’ of autobiographical insight and political provocation
Content: A virtuoso artistic talent? … Sohrab Haghverdi in ForiegnerView image in fullscreenA virtuoso artistic talent? … Sohrab Haghverdi in ForiegnerEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewForiegner review – will drinking your own urine get you a US visa?Summerhall, EdinburghSohrab Haghverdi takes pleasure at winding up the audience in a subversively funny ‘anti-comedy’ of autobiographical insight and political provocationMark FisherSun 9 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSohrab Haghverdi says he wants to be liked. I’m not so sure. Would a needy actor be willing to try the audience’s patience by coughing and coughing, then coughing some more? Would they push their way through a hole in a Persian rug, while shouting about snakes and balancing empty suitcases on their head? Or wander off stage at random?No – this is a man who takes pleasure in winding us up. Whether it is collecting his own bodily fluids or launching into a splenetic rant in favour of Trump’s bombing of Iran, he has no interest in giving us an easy ride. This is punk theatre: irritating and brash.Yet Haghverdi can also be endearing. Foriegner – the misspelling is intentional – is billed as an “anti-comedy clown show” and, anti-comedy or not, it is frequently very funny.View image in fullscreenClowning around … ForiegnerThe US-based Iranian performer claims to have been misunderstood as a linear storyteller and equally misunderstood as creating “crazy” theatre, so is opting instead to do both at the same time. The result is a destabilising amalgam of meta-theatrical games, flashes of autobiographical insight and political provocation.In the Black review – rewarding drama about the Faustian pact of big businessRead moreSperm and urine are the recurring symbols. He claims that drinking his own piss will put him in line for an O-1B US visa for virtuoso artistic talent, an ironic conceit that would be hilariously subversive if true. But perhaps the connecting thread is the philosophy of Rumi, the 13th-century mystic who called for people to kill their false self in order to live truly.A show that is both wayward and intentional seems hellbent on destroying itself from within. Haghverdi does not want to be labelled as an Iranian, still less a minority; he resists being boxed in by his directors (Benjamin and Mason Rosenthal), and resents entertaining us even as he does so. His quest for perpetual reinvention leads to a Marmite show that is equal parts perplexing and delightful.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalComedy (Culture)Comedy (Stage)TheatreClownsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Paddy Young: Will Sir Be Laughing Alone? review – morose misadventures of a luckless bachelor | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The SNL UK star’s romantic failures and house-share humiliations make for a fun hour of downbeat yet twinkling comedy
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: The SNL UK star’s romantic failures and house-share humiliations make for a fun hour of downbeat yet twinkling comedy
Content: Sad-sack charm … Paddy Young at Monkey Barrel, Edinburgh.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanView image in fullscreenSad-sack charm … Paddy Young at Monkey Barrel, Edinburgh.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewPaddy Young: Will Sir Be Laughing Alone? review – morose misadventures of a luckless bachelorMonkey Barrel, EdinburghThe SNL UK star’s romantic failures and house-share humiliations make for a fun hour of downbeat yet twinkling comedyBrian LoganSun 9 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 12.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArecent star ofSaturday Night Live UK,Paddy Youngis enjoying a moment of life-changing fulfilment and success. But “I’ve brought the worst plus-one to the party,” he says – by which he means himself. If ever the truism that money can’t buy you happiness needed demonstration, look no further than Young’s new show, Will Sir Be Laughing Alone? It finds the 35-year-old lamenting (as ever) the circularity of his domestic life, a luckless perma-bachelor doomed for ever to watch on as his housemates graduate to more grown-up, loved-up lives elsewhere.Young has cultivated the perfect persona to sell this sorry tale: a plangent northerner, half-turned away from the audience and side-eyeing us coyly with this or that tale of hapless manboyishness. Is it an act? Well, no, it’s an exaggeration, and part of the fun is to work out how sincere sad-sack Paddy really is, halfway through his three score years and 10, stuck in a house share with “three PS2s and not a lamp in sight”. He’s bothered not that his flatmate is having sex too noisily, but that it’s not audible enough (“Let me in!”). Ghosted by a recent date, he has resorted to stalking his first teenage kiss on Facebook, then all the way to Copenhagen, fantasising about inserting himself into her wholesome family life.Sophie Duker: Hot Beef Injection review – bad encounters with men spun into great comedyRead moreYou might think this would get bleak. Certainly, Young’s downbeat sense of self pre-empts much comic momentum. Consolation is to be found in the Scarborough man’s evident relish for his own enfeeblement, and a strain of triumphalism at the small victories (his flatmate’s baldness versus Paddy’s flourishing head of hair, say) afforded even to those who lose at the lottery of life.That loserdom is offset too by Young’s standup skills, as evidenced tonight by some very adroit crowd-work, and by the kind of small-screen success that leads to audience members showing up in DIY Paddy Young T-shirts. How sustainable is Young’s shmuck shtick in the face of such adulation? On this evidence, you’d expect – and hope for – plenty more morose-but-twinkling comedy from a man whose Saturday nights may be live, but whose every other night is lived vicariously through long-lost girlfriends and his more sexually successful housemates.AtMonkey Barrel, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026ComedyEdinburgh festivalFestivalsSaturday Night LivereviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Andrew Lincoln narrates an impressive nature series  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Force of Nature has a powerful polemic edge as it explores oceans. Plus, the finale of chaotic climate crisis drama The Rapture. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: Force of Nature has a powerful polemic edge as it explores oceans. Plus, the finale of chaotic climate crisis drama The Rapture. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Clowning around … Force of Nature on ITV1.Photograph: Plimsoll Productions/ITVView image in fullscreenClowning around … Force of Nature on ITV1.Photograph: Plimsoll Productions/ITVTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: Andrew Lincoln narrates an impressive nature seriesForce of Nature has a powerful polemic edge as it explores oceans. Plus, the finale of chaotic climate crisis drama The Rapture. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Graeme Virtue,Priya Elan,Jack SealeandSimon WardellSun 9 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleForce of Nature6pm, ITV1This natural history series has an appropriately polemical edge – its exploration of various natural habitats is filtered through the increasing difficulties faced by animals hoping to thrive in them. It focuses on coastal regions in this episode, as unexpected extreme weather destroys flamingo colonies and ruins the anemone home of clownfish. It’s impressive but sobering, too, as an insight into the chaos wrought by humans.Phil HarrisonVan Der Valk8pm, ITV1So far, series four of the Amsterdam cop reboot has featured two gangland murders and a car bombing (even if the biggest crime remains the wishy-washy version of the classic theme tune). Marc Warren’s prickly Piet is determined to collar the culprit, though it will mean teaming up with a formidable criminal matriarch.Graeme VirtueRichard E Grant’s Very Modern Odyssey8pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenSoaking up the culture … Richard E Grant’s Very Modern Odyssey on Channel 4.Photograph: James Gavin Walker/Emporium ProductionsThe budget doesn’t compare to that enjoyed by Christopher Nolan but if you haven’t heard enough hot takes on Homer’s epic this summer, Richard E Grant’s road trip is one of the better ones. This time, he’s in Sicily where he explores the myth of Cyclops and performs, with endearingly luvvy-ish gusto, in an amphitheatre.PHNYO at the Proms8pm, BBC FourConducted by Thomas Adès, the 150-strong National Youth Orchestra will play a trilogy of pieces centring on the underworld: Liszt’s Mephisto Waltz No 1, based on Nikolaus Lenau’s Faust poem; Berlioz’s Symphonie Fantastique; and Part II of Adès’s own ballet score Dante: Purgatorio. Petroc Trelawny is your host.Priya ElanThe Rapture9pm, BBC OneThis chaotic but enjoyably eccentric drama concludes. Bethany is on the run and her drawings of her visions are becoming more apocalyptic still. With her professionalism being called into question, is Gabs going to risk everything to help her? The walls are closing in around both of them, so she might not have much choice.PHThe Piano9pm, Channel 4Claudia Winkleman and Mika arrive at Manchester Piccadilly, where their guest expert is German pianist Alice Sara Ott. Excelling on the concourse are a young composer whose piece is based on just two notes, a seven-year-old who has charm to match startling ability, and a musician who has spent time away from their most beloved instrument, but now makes a triumphant, tear-inducing comeback.Jack SealeFilm choiceSpeed, 9pm, Film4View image in fullscreenPrimed to explode … Speed on Film 4.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyIf Jan de Bont’s 1994 action thriller didn’t propel Keanu Reeves to stardom (Point Break arguably did that in 1991), it was his biggest box-office hit to date – and it was most definitely a breakthrough moment for Sandra Bullock. She is her co-star’s equal as a passenger who has to take the steering wheel of an LA bus primed to explode if it goes under 50mph. Reeves has the more superficially heroic role as a police bomb disposal officer, but both have their moments in a terrifically tense series of freeway set-pieces, while Dennis Hopper is reliably unhinged as their foe.Simon WardellLive sportMen’s Hundred Cricket: London Spirit v Birmingham Phoenix, 5.30pm, Sky Sports CricketAt Lord’s.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Grief became my brand’: Freya Bromley on writing about personal tragedy | Books | The Guardian
description: Touring her memoir and talking to others helped the author come to terms with her brother’s death, but the book’s success left her feeling guilty. Had she commodified her family’s pain?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Touring her memoir and talking to others helped the author come to terms with her brother’s death, but the book’s success left her feeling guilty. Had she commodified her family’s pain?
Content: ‘Why is it so difficult to be unhappy around the people you’ve known the longest?’ … Freya Bromley.Photograph: Patch StudiosView image in fullscreen‘Why is it so difficult to be unhappy around the people you’ve known the longest?’ … Freya Bromley.Photograph: Patch StudiosBooks‘Grief became my brand’: Freya Bromley on writing about personal tragedyTouring her memoir and talking to others helped the author come to terms with her brother’s death, but the book’s success left her feeling guilty. Had she commodified her family’s pain?Freya BromleySun 9 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen my memoir about my life after my brother’s death was published, I was very fortunate that people connected with it. It’s not easy to feel good fortune from the worst thing that’s ever happened to you. But I suppose I felt pleased when the experience that had once made me so lonely suddenly became a point of connection.I had not always been an open book. I was 22 when my brother died from a rare bone cancer. The people around me didn’t know what to say about this awful thing, so they pretended it hadn’t happened and I pretended, too. For a few years I was a ghost in my own life. Nothing felt real. I got very good at imitating normality, imagining I was in a video game called Office.There were other simulations such as Dating and Fun Friend Hangout where it was game over when I brought up death. A numbness settled in. Grief, and the subsequent silence around it, had obliterated my sense of who I was. My reality had been shattered, and I was unsure how I fitted within the life I once had. I found that, at this time of my life, even to be looked in the eyes was incredibly uncomfortable. The thought of someone seeing my pain was excruciating. Or perhaps it was the fear of them not searching for it at all.Maybe these years of feeling so unseen made me want to share myself with people through writing. My 2024 book The Tidal Year follows the year I swam in every tidal pool in Britain with a friend. I like to say it’s a memoir about swimming that isn’t really about swimming at all. It’s about loss, and how to find joy in your life as a young person after a tragedy. Readers knew my most intimate moments, and many shared their own. Late at night, I’d receive messages on Instagram with confessions of people’s PTSD. Sometimes people emailed me shocking, explicit details of a death close to them. I was moved that something I’d written had prompted them to contact me. Writing had transformed my life, and I believed that whether it was a book, email or a DM there was power in acknowledging your pain through words.double quotation markI opened up my grief like a suitcase and waited for people to unpack all their sadness into it, then I took it homeAt first, I felt an enormous pressure to reply with something articulate and wise. This was hardest in person. If someone started crying at the signing table, as they often did, there was an awkward distance between us. Should I stand up to hug them? What could I say to make it better? I learned that it wasn’t at all about what I replied. It was about listening. Most people, when they lose someone, don’t get to say the name of their loved one any more. The best thing I could say is: who’s the person you’re missing? What were they like?Having these conversations has been a real privilege. And I must admit I became rather addicted to them. I pitched myself for events, volunteered with bereavement charities, used all my holiday to travel the country visiting bookshops. However, the best thing about the book was also the worst: I’d alchemised my grief into something powerful, positive, productive and I soon became consumed by guilt that I’d commodified our family tragedy. Looking back, I think I felt that if the book did well enough, if it helped enough people, then perhaps I could be redeemed from writing it at all.At events, I opened up my grief like a suitcase and waited for people to unpack all their sadness into it, then I took it home again. On the train, I’d wonder where to put all the stories people had handed me. A brother collapses on a rugby pitch. A mother drowns in the sea. A sister is murdered by her husband … I was thinking about death all the time. Tragic events now seemed quite normal. Perhaps I could have protected myself more, put up a shield between myself and others so I wasn’t so affected by their stories, but what would be the point of having these interactions and not feeling them so deeply? What would be the point of listening and not truly hearing?That summer a men’s book club messaged me to say they’d chosen my book, and I was welcome to join them for a drink. The pub was one I’d mentioned and their attentive reading made me feel special. When I arrived, we had some drinks and spoke about their book club which had seen them through many seasons of their friendship. We drank some more. Someone quoted a passage they found amusing. I felt like the best, shiniest version of myself. Then someone shared that a member of the group had lost his sister recently. A new atmosphere fell over the table, and I realised why I was there. I was drunk now, and my cheeks were red. The man in question gripped his pint and told me he worried he’d never experience happiness again. “You look happy,” he said, “I can’t imagine you ever feel like that.” My stomach twitched with dread that I had performed the wrong version of myself.I often worried whether I looked sad enough, and if people felt I was heartless or fake if I didn’t. Sometimes at readings, people asked me why I wasn’t crying. In publicity meetings for my book, I’d been asked to come up with social media ideas. Are there any significant anniversaries you could post on, they asked. I didn’t want to turn any more sad moments into content, but maybe that’s what I’d signed up for. I suppose I made my brand grief, and I’ve often wondered what happens to the soul of a person with a brand like that.I recently saw the writer and climate justice organiser Mikaela Loach post about being hospitalised for a long-term undiagnosed illness. She said that during a recent meeting with Meta they showed a selection of her posts and revealed that when she cried, they performed best, so maybe she should create more like that. The next day I was served an advert by Instagram aimed at “Creators” that suggested a new Reel template going from “Sad Girl Winter” to “Hot Girl Summer” with space for selfies of crying to camera.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markFiction has given me new ways to untangle the life-changing force that is grief beyond reflecting only on my ownBefore we experience great tragedies, I think we all have this idea that death is something that brings families together. That we will hold each other and cry and bond. In some ways this is true. I have never been hugged tighter than when I saw my big brother, Lawrence, after we got the news that today would be the day. Lawrence had driven across London to pick me up so we could go to the hospital together. I have never been held like that, our bodies colliding on the street as our world fell apart.But what follows can be so devastating. You’re all trying not to knock the bruise. You’re all trying to get by, as best you can. There’s a lot of silence. There’s a lot of crying alone. There are a lot of misunderstandings because you’re all coping in different ways. No one is right, no one is wrong. But sometimes it’s easier to be angry about this, than it is to be angry about the person who’s been taken from you, because at least in one of those situations you have some semblance of control.Although I’d spent two years touring the country talking about grief, I still couldn’t talk about it with those closest to me. Why is it so difficult to be unhappy around the people you’ve known the longest? Even today, I don’t know that I can confidently share my feelings with the people I love. I am just too sad. And I love them too much to show them. I don’t want them to worry, after all we’ve been through. I’m sure that they feel the same.Most of the people who reach out to me aren’t only grieving a person. They’re grieving the version of themselves that existed before. My second book, A Real Piece of Work, is a novel about a family meeting for the fifth anniversary of a death. I wanted this fictional world to be an offering to everyone I’d met – a reckoning with what becomes of a family once the funeral is over. How do our relationships shift when life-changing loss ruptures our existing dynamics? I’m trying to start a family of my own now and I think it’s been important to me to create something real and thorny yet hopeful that captures how most of us are trying our best, even when we misunderstand each other. I do truly believe that.I don’t believe there is such a thing as moving on. We only ever move through and carry it with us. I carry the weight of a lot of stories now, but somehow it feels all the lighter because of the expansive conversations created between people through books.Fictionhas given me new ways to untangle the life-changing force that is grief beyond reflecting only on my own. I’ve just started a new book tour. I still sit at the signing table. And when someone tells me they’re struggling, I ask them about the person they’re missing, so they can say their name again.A Real Piece of Work by Freya Bromley is published by Hutchinson Heinemann.To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: We know sleep, exercise and diet are vital for health. But why? | Science and nature books | The Guardian
description: The benefits of all three come down to a crucial piece of cellular kit
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The benefits of all three come down to a crucial piece of cellular kit
Content: Illustration: Elia BarbieriView image in fullscreenIllustration: Elia BarbieriThe big ideaScience and nature booksWe know sleep, exercise and diet are vital for health. But why?The benefits of all three come down to a crucial piece of cellular kitHannah CritchlowSun 9 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 09.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSleep. Exercise. Eat well. It’s the oldest recommendation in medicine, repeated so often it’s become a cliche. We know the advice, even if we don’t always follow it. But have you ever stopped to wonder why these three seemingly different habits have such remarkably similar effects on our brains and bodies?For generations we’ve treated them as separate prescriptions – sleep restores us, exercise strengthens us and food fuels us. Yet neuroscience is beginning to suggest something rather more elegant: they’re all essentially doing the same job.What has changed is not the recommendations themselves, but our understanding of the biology beneath them. The more scientists study the brain, the clearer it becomes that cognition is astonishingly energy intensive. Although the brain makes up about 2% of body weight, it uses roughly a fifth of the body’s energy at rest. Every memory we retrieve, every decision we make and every creative insight carries a metabolic cost. Thought itself is an energy-hungry act.That raises an obvious question: where does all that energy come from? The answer lies deep in evolutionary history. More than 2bn years ago, a primitive cell engulfed a bacterium. Instead of being digested, the bacterium remained, forming a long-term partnership with its host.Over time, this arrangement became one of biology’s most important alliances. The bacterium became remarkably efficient at capturing the chemical energy stored in food and transforming it into ATP, the molecule that powers almost every biological process. The host offered protection, and together they made complex life possible.double quotation markIntelligence depends not simply on the brain’s wiring, but on the uninterrupted flow of energy through that wiringThat partnership is still running inside us today. Mitochondria – the descendants of that ancient bacterium – exist in almost every cell in the body. The exception is the mature red blood cell, which removes them to make space for haemoglobin and improve oxygen transport. Even here, biology reveals its logic: everything is shaped by trade-offs in energy efficiency.For decades, mitochondria were introduced in biology textbooks as the cell’s “powerhouses” – important, dependable but rather dull. The stars of the show were undeniably neurons. Today, that picture is changing.We’re discovering that neurons produce thought, ideas and emotions only because mitochondria continuously transform fuel into the energy they need. Intelligence depends not simply on the brain’s wiring, but on the uninterrupted flow of energy through that wiring. This is a subtle shift in perspective, but an important one.Emerging evidence suggests that healthy mitochondrial functionhelps give rise to intelligence, including drivingarithmetic and processing speed,working memory,healthier brain ageingand greaterresilience to stress. Mitochondria are no longer viewed as passive batteries but as active participants in the delicate balancing act that allows the brain to adapt, learn and flourish throughout life.Suddenly, the oldest health advice begins to make much more sense. Exercise doesn’t simply boost muscle mass, itbulks upthe hippocampus – a key region of the brain involved in learning and memory. It also encourages mitochondria to becomemore numerous and more efficient. We often imagine we’re training our bodies; we’re alsostrengtheningthe ancient energy system that allows our brains to work.Sleep performs a different kind of maintenance. While we’re unconscious, the brain is astonishingly busy. Memories are consolidated and worn-out cellular components – including mitochondria – arerepaired or replaced. So rather than thinking of sleep as simply rest, we can conceive of it, at least partly, as a mitochondrial maintenance shift, aimed at preparing the brain for another day of active learning, adapting and imagining.Then there’s food. Mitochondria rely entirely on what we eat to perform their remarkable chemistry. The quality of that fuel matters. Dietsrich in minimally processed foodsprovide the ingredients for efficient energy transformation, while diets that continually overwhelm the system appear to make that processless efficientover time.Seen through this lens, sleep, exercise and diet stop looking like three separate pieces of lifestyle advice and become different ways of caring for the same biological inheritance. What fascinates me most is that this new understanding reaches far beyond physical health. Scientists are uncoveringintriguing linksbetween mitochondrial function and resilience,mood,personalitytraits, and even oursocial lives.For centuries we’ve tended to separate mind from body, as though thoughts somehow floated free of the flesh that produced them. The reality is that thoughts emerge from living tissue that must constantly capture, transform and use energy simply to exist.The mitochondrial psychobiologist Martin Picard has argued that we’ve become accustomed to thinking of ourselves as molecular machines, when it may be more useful to think of ourselves asenergetic processes. The brain is an organ whose every thought, memory and feeling depends on the continuous transformation of energy within billions of cells.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSeen this way, sleep is no longer simply rest, and exercise is no longer simply fitness. Food is no longer simply fuel. They’re different ways of sustaining the ancient biological partnership that allows our bodies – and our minds – to flourish.It’s remarkable to think that every idea you’ve ever had, every problem you’ve solved, every person you’ve loved and every hope you’ve held has depended upon an alliance forged more than 2bn years ago. The tiny descendants of that ancient bacterium have been quietly working inside us ever since, making possible not just movement or metabolism but thought itself.Perhaps that’s why the oldest health advice has survived every new scientific fashion. Long before we knew about ATP, oxidative phosphorylation or mitochondria, we recognised that people who slept well, moved regularly and ate nourishing food tended to flourish. We’re finally beginning to understand why.Hannah Critchlow is a neuroscientist and author ofThe 21st Century Brain(Torva).Further readingThe Song of the Cellby Siddhartha Mukherjee (Vintage, £14.99)Transformer: The Deep Chemistry of Life and Death by Nick Lane (Profile, £14.99How Life Works: A User’s Guide to the New Biology by Philip Ball (Picador, £14.99)Explore more on these topicsScience and nature booksThe big ideaNeuroscienceHealthSleepfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sophie Duker: Hot Beef Injection review – bad encounters with men spun into great comedy | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The standup is on sparkling form as she mines a lifetime of baffling and alarming experiences for a smart, purposeful and very funny hour
Author: Anya Ryan
Headline: The standup is on sparkling form as she mines a lifetime of baffling and alarming experiences for a smart, purposeful and very funny hour
Content: Beef encounter … Sophie Duker is at Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 August.View image in fullscreenBeef encounter … Sophie Duker is at Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 August.Edinburgh festival 2026ReviewSophie Duker: Hot Beef Injection review – bad encounters with men spun into great comedyPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghThe standup is on sparkling form as she mines a lifetime of baffling and alarming experiences for a smart, purposeful and very funny hourAnya RyanSun 9 Aug 2026 10.48 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSophie Duker is done with men. She swears it. And, in her fourth hour, Hot Beef Injection – named after a crude euphemism from80s teen film The Breakfast Club– she is going to tell us exactly why.Duker has had her fair share of relationships, tracking all the way back to her adolescence. “I did hand stuff with a 16-year-old boy,” she announces at the show’s opening. On reflection, though, most of those experiences have left her feeling, well, weird.Hot Beef Injection presents a gallery of men who have intimidated, disappointed or baffled her, from the swaggering alpha male types of Soho to the repairman who deliberately leaves his tools behind in the hope of seeing her again. Later come more sinister stories: getting into a car with a strange man in a time of need and finding herself locked in a room with a man in a position of power at a comedy club. Taken together, they paint a bleak picture – one that will be familiar to many women and that, as Duker quips, Louis Theroux has only recently begun to notice. Throughout it all, Duker has learned to keep smiling.This leads us to the viral question at the show’s centre: would you rather be alone in a forest with a random man or a bear? You don’t need me to tell you which side Duker falls on – I mean, have you seen Paddington? She offsets all the darkness with her trademark breezy wit. And the audience is entirely under her spell. She joyfully targets the “milky whites”, interrogates the single straight white man who has come to her show of his own accord, and does roaring impressions of men in their cars drinking energy drinks.Hostile review – surreal spaghetti western is a wild and wordless rideRead moreThe final payoff feels a little too neat for a show that has, until that moment, been pretty dismissive of all things male. No matter – Duker’s presence is all good-time joy and delight, and this is a show so neatly crafted and intelligent that every routine serves a purpose.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalFestivalsSophie DukerComedy (Stage)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: OnlyFans for Therapy review – a brave and unsettling emotional exposure | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Veering from confident to crumbling, Verona Verbakel delivers a vivid show mixing humour with trauma
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Veering from confident to crumbling, Verona Verbakel delivers a vivid show mixing humour with trauma
Content: Big in Belgium … Verona Verbakel in OnlyFans for Therapy at Zoo Playground, Edinburgh.Photograph: Kaat Pype/Soraya AzbiriView image in fullscreenBig in Belgium … Verona Verbakel in OnlyFans for Therapy at Zoo Playground, Edinburgh.Photograph: Kaat Pype/Soraya AzbiriEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewOnlyFans for Therapy review – a brave and unsettling emotional exposureZoo Playground, EdinburghVeering from confident to crumbling, Verona Verbakel delivers a vivid show mixing humour with traumaMark FisherSun 9 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe are all familiar with the cliche of the influencer narrating their daily routines – or should I say, their journey? – and trying to convince us, and perhaps themselves, they are living their best life. We know, too, about the websites offering intimate access in exchange for cash.But what if the online medium were put to more honest purposes? What if, instead of endless positivity, it presented a painful recovery from trauma?View image in fullscreenHaunted … Verona Verbakel in OnlyFans for Therapy.Photograph: Soraya AzbiriIt would, suggests writer and performerVerona Verbakel, be cheaper than paying for therapy. After a back-of-the-envelope calculation, she estimates she would need 2,599 sessions with a psychiatrist at £70 a time to get her through a lifetime of recovery. The cost, either in cash or in continued trauma, has to be paid by someone.The exposure in her solo show, OnlyFans for Therapy, is of the emotional not the naked body kind. It concerns a woman haunted by the abuse she suffered as a five-year-old and the additional anguish of an investigation when she was 18. Confident and assured one minute, she crumbles the next – the damage for ever just beneath the surface, raw and inescapable.Part of the Big in Belgium programme, Karolien De Bleser’s production has a characteristically Belgian disregard for theatrical convention. Verbakel’s role is to sit, stony-faced at a laptop, occasionally catching our eye, and seemingly indifferent to the content of the first-person videos she shows in sequence.At turns upbeat and tearful, Verbakel appears in videos that vary from lying in bed wearing a sleep mask and reciting a drily comic list of emotional triggers to the actor making painful expeditions to the scene of the original abuse and breaking down as she does so. The direct-to-camera honesty of the online world makes the pain all the more vivid in a brave, unsettling show.AtZoo Playground, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsIn the UK, theNSPCCoffers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In the US, call or text theChildhelpabuse hotline on 800-422-4453. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact theKids Helplineon 1800 55 1800; adult survivors can seek help atBlue Knot Foundationon 1300 657 380.
