title: ‘I lose all sense of time in the hypnotic flow’: five writers on their favourite British rivers | United Kingdom holidays | The Guardian
description: From the source to the sea, our writers share their favourite ways to immerse themselves in nature by paddleboarding, canoeing, camping, walking and fishing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From the source to the sea, our writers share their favourite ways to immerse themselves in nature by paddleboarding, canoeing, camping, walking and fishing
Content: Jo Moseley paddleboarding on the Esk in North Yorkshire.Photograph: Mary DaviesView image in fullscreenJo Moseley paddleboarding on the Esk in North Yorkshire.Photograph: Mary DaviesUnited Kingdom holidays‘I lose all sense of time in the hypnotic flow’: five writers on their favourite British riversFrom the source to the sea, our writers share their favourite ways to immerse themselves in nature by paddleboarding, canoeing, camping, walking and fishingSun 9 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Paddleboarding the Esk in North YorkshireIt’s early afternoon on an unusually hot and sunny Yorkshire day. I’m standing on my paddleboard on the tidal section of the River Esk, near Whitby’s New Bridge, as cars stream across. The 28-mile-long Esk is special, as it is the only major river in Yorkshire that flows directly into the North Sea.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Ahead of me is a bustling marina, the famousabbeyand the West and East piers. The town is full to the brim with visitors in search of the best fish and chips, amusement arcades and tales ofDraculaandCaptain Cook. Later, in the autumn,gothsin their finery will parade the cobbled streets.Here on the river, however, it is tranquil. A salmon leaps from the water to my right, bubbles rise from the seaweed beneath my board, and to my left, the riverbank absorbs abandoned boats into its grassy knolls. On an evening paddle, you might spot the crews from one of the town’s three main rowing clubs (Whitby Coastal,FriendshiporFisherlads).View image in fullscreenA few miles inland from Whitby, the Esk passes under the Larpool Viaduct.Photograph: Maciej Olszewski/AlamyYou can launch from the slipway at the far end of the marina back car park near Coates Marine. Arriving by train or bus, it’s a few minutes’ walk from the station. Launch about one and a half hours before high tide and head right towards the New Bridge and Ruswarp. Be mindful, this section of the river is tidal and water levels do drop.After taking in the magnificent view, I turn and paddle towards Ruswarp, a couple of miles inland, passing under the Larpool Viaduct, which carries the 22-mileCinder Track. Branches of willow trees droop elegantly into the water offering welcome shade. Swans glide past and Highland cattle graze nonchalantly in the fields. A couple hike the path that runs alongside the river.double quotation markI first paddled on the Esk with my young sons in 2006. Twenty years later, it still remains a peaceful, hidden gemI first paddled on the Esk with my young sons in 2006. Twenty years later, it still remains a peaceful, hidden gem. We hired kayaks fromRuswarp Pleasure Boats(established 1874) just above the weir, which also rents rowing boats and now paddleboards. For a £5 fee, it offers a private jetty to launch your own craft, which is ideal as access to the river is very limited along this stretch. There is free parking on the roadside here, and with thenumber 95 busstop (Arriva) nearby, public transport is an option. Paddle up toPerry’s Plantsgarden centre at Briggswath just before Sleights and then turn back.You’ll pass theWaterside restaurantandWhitby Wellbeing’s wild saunaalong the way, so family and friends can eat, sweat or dip while you float along, letting the river carry your worries away. Afterwards, nip toBotham’sin Sleights for some Resolution tea and lovely iced lemon buns. I promise, it’ll be a grand paddleboarding day out in Yorkshire.Jo Moseley is the author ofStand-Up Paddleboarding in Great BritainWild camping on the Dart in DevonView image in fullscreenSian Lewis wild camping next to the River Dart.Photograph: Sian LewisOn the uplands of Dartmoor, two tributaries – the East Dart and West Dart – join beneath ancient woodland at the well-named hamlet of Dartmeet. They entwine as the River Dart, which flows for 47 miles from open moor into steep wooded valleys and passes peat bogs and tors, oak forest, market towns and rolling pasture before it runs into the sheltered waters of the south Devon coast.Its upper reaches retain a pristine wildness that feels increasingly rare in southern England. The Dartmoor national park is criss-crossed by some of the cleanest bodies of water in the country, home to salmon, sea trout and otters, while the wooded valleys below are rich remnants of ancient temperate rainforest.The Dart’s name is thought to derive from an old Celtic word meaning “river where oak trees grow”, and the lower banks are indeed lined with native oak trees, thick with mosses and ferns. It may be one of Britain’s smaller protected landscapes, but Dartmoor feels remarkably untamed. You can cross it on foot in a few days, yet it’s surprisingly easy to lose yourself in the rolling mists, twisting woodlands and miles of open moorland of this ethereal landscape.View image in fullscreenThe River Dart runs past tors in the Dartmoor national park.Photograph: Maciej Olszewski/AlamyIt’s that sense of freedom that keeps drawing me back. I love nothing more than stuffing a tent into my rucksack and heading out on foot for a riverside camp, following the Dart and its web of streams and creeks until I find a quiet bend or grassy bank for the night. I fall asleep to the steady rush and rumble of the water and wake up early for a swim in one of its deep, crystal-clear pools before packing up and walking on.I can roam about like this because Dartmoor is theonly place in Englandwhere wild camping is legally permitted. In the national park, “backpack”, or wild camping, is allowed for one or two nights in some areas, provided you stay away from roads and settlements and leave no trace of your visit.Sometimes, I have company on the riverbanks. I’ve huddled in bivouac bags with friends and woken totally covered in sparkling droplets of dew. I’ve camped on the water’s edge and woken in the middle of the night to what sounded like an invading army around my tent. It turned out to be a troop of scouts, arriving spectacularly late at their campsite and gamely pitching flimsy-looking tents by the light of their headlamps. And once, at dusk, I think I glimpsed the sleek head of an otter slipping into the current. But more often than not, once evening falls and I sit by the door of my tent watching the water darken, I have the Dart all to myself.Sian LewisFishing on the Dove in the Peak DistrictView image in fullscreenAndy Pietrasik considers his tactics beside the Dove.Photograph: Andy PietrasikThere’s a trout rising upstream from where I am standing on the bank of the River Dove in Beresford Dale, on the border of Staffordshire and Derbyshire. I mark the spot – just beyond that overhanging tree branch – and rue the fact that it will make casting a fly without getting snagged tricky. I need to get into the river and wade over to the other bank for a clear shot. But it’s a steep drop to the water and the pools look deep in this stretch; deep enough to go over my chest waders. I walk back downstream to a spot where I can safely enter the fast-flowing river, but realise it’s going to be a long wade upstream. Too long and splashy, which will disturb any fish and scatter them. So, I get out again and walk back to where I first spotted the feeding trout. I am caught in indecision, and repeat this pattern several times before giving up on this particular quarry.The meander at this section of the river has formed a little peninsula, and standing in the middle of it is a fishing hut, where I go to drink a coffee and consider my tactics. This isn’t any old fishing hut, however. This one is a substantial structure, built from stone, with pillars framing the door and with an inscription in Latin, “Piscatoribus Sacrum” (Sacred to all Fishermen).View image in fullscreenThe ‘little fishing house’ constructed on a peninsula in the Dove by the poet Charles Cotton.Photograph: Andy PietrasikIn the lintel stone is a cypher of intertwined letters: CC and IW, for Charles Cotton, the poet who built this “little fishing house” on his estate in 1674, and Izaak Walton, who wrote The Compleat Angler in 1653. Cotton added “Instructions how to angle for a trout or grayling in a clear stream” to accompany the fifth edition of Walton’s book, considered to be the first technical manual of fly-fishing and one of the most reprinted books in the English language.The River Dove is the spiritual home of fly-fishing because of Walton and Cotton, and it still holds a mythical place in fishers’ minds. As someone who grew up on the Staffordshire-Derbyshire border, and fished the Dove where it joins the River Trent at Newton Solney in my youth, I was well aware of the river’s special status. But, at that age, I wasn’t about to give myself the extra homework of reading a 17th-century treatise on fishing and nature. Instead, an English teacher who fished furnished me with the only line I needed to know: “you will find it one of the purest crystalline streams you have seen.”double quotation markThe River Dove is the spiritual home of fly-fishing because of Walton and Cotton, and it still holds a mythical place in fishers’ mindsThe stretch of the Dove I’m fishing – called the Temple beat after Cotton’s fishing house – races and tumbles through a narrow tree-lined dale hemmed in by limestone crags. Near the bridge above a section known as the Pike Pool, a family is splashing and paddling in the early summer sunshine. There’s a popular 4-mile loop that starts at Hartington village, and the path is too busy with walkers to fish, so I enter the river at the bridge and wade and fish “the vale it winds through like a snake” until I spot the rising trout and stop for my coffee break.Later that day, I lose all sense of time in the hypnotic flow of catching and releasing a series of small wild brown trout. Just beyond the fishing house, someone has carved a large hole into the base of a dead oak tree, the perfect place to sit and watch dippers skit along the banks and damselflies dance upon the surface. A little further on, a large Hereford cow is drinking from the river, framed by overhanging trees and with a verdant conical hill in the background. The scene strikes me as being a pastoral masterpiece, much like The Compleat Angler.Andy PietrasikA day ticket on the Temple beat can be booked throughFishing Breaks from £65skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSourcingthe Severn and Wye in mid-WalesView image in fullscreenKevin Rushby and Stevie: the Severn gets a finer ‘start in life’ than the Wye.Photograph: Kevin RushbyIt will prove to be the best of hikes, and in some ways the worst. I start out early from Eisteddfa Gurig on the A44, hoping to get going while the day is cool. My plan is to visit the sources of two of Britain’s greatest rivers – the Severn and the Wye which, by a fluke of geography, lie a couple of miles apart on a mountain ridge in mid-Wales.The path leads me up Pumlumon Fawr, a 752-metre (2,467ft) massif with magnificent views to the Irish Sea. The day is scorching hot and the bald sheep-nipped hills look only an inch of topsoil away from becoming a desert. Of the two rivers, the Severn gets the finer start in life. There is a marker post next to a deep, dark pool of water that is being squeezed from the bog. In ancient times, humans worshipped springs, but there are no garlands here, only a few sea shells carried upstream by hikers from the Bristol Channel on the 224-mile (360km)Severn Way.double quotation markA short walk downstream brings me into a deep valley where the Severn, already gathering force, bounces through ferny gladesA short walk downstream brings me into a deep valley where the Severn, already gathering force, bounces through ferny glades. It feels as if someone is caring for this river, determined to give it a good start in life. There is a usefulcar parkfurther down the valley, but I cut away through the forest to find the origin of its twin, the Wye.I have hopes of a dip in a mountain pool, but there are misgivings. Arguably the loveliest river in Britain, the Wye has been hitting headlines for a severedecline in water quality. Dead salmon have been found,algal blooms reported. Campaigners, however, have scored a major victory in creatinga charter of rights, including the right to flow and be free of pollution. Significant authorities, including Powys and Herefordshire, have adopted it. There is hope.View image in fullscreenA footbridge over the River Severn in Hafren forest, close to the river’s source.Photograph: Maddie Red/AlamyThe first omen is the defunctNant Iago lead mine, a reminder that human impact on the environment is nothing new. Government statistics show that about 900 miles (1,500km) of our rivers and estuaries arestill contaminated by 19th-century mines. I skirt around the old workings and walk up the valley. In the wrinkles of this hillside, the Wye has a moorland birth, a harsh ordeal. No sooner has the clean, bright water started out than it’s being crapped in by sheep and messed about by humans. Any thought of a dip in a pool, or even a sip from the source, is brutally quashed.The moorland/forested contrast with the Severn is not unplanned: scientists have been controlling andassessingthese non-identical twins since a time when flood risks and algal blooms were not issues. Whatever their conclusions, however, our expectations of rivers remain pitifully low. In 17th-century Britain, by contrast, salmon were so plentifully available for people to fish for themselves that there waslittle market for them.I carry on down theWye Valley Walk, a 136-mile route whose leaping salmon logo is looking sadly inappropriate. After a few miles, I turn west up a side stream that has a toxic reddish tint. Only a Martian would take a dip. This has become a grim trudge, but finally, up a side valley, I stumble on deep pools alive with tiny frogs. Spruce and pine have been planted. There are orchids and bog asphodels. Then, a magnificentgolden-ringed dragonflysettles next to me. My spirits are restored. Maybe the Wye can bounce back. I set off for nearbyLlangurigwhere there’s apub, the Bluebell Inn,and atearoom.Kevin RushbyCanoeingthe Tay in PerthshireView image in fullscreenAilsa Sheldon and her teenage son canoe the Tay.The Tay is Scotland’s longest river (117 miles) and Britain’s mightiest, discharging more water than the longer Thames and Severn combined. Rising on the slopes of Ben Lui in Argyll, gathering strength from Highland burns before widening through Perthshire and eventually reaching the North Sea at Dundee.It’s the middle stretch, from Killin to Dunkeld through Highland Perthshire, that I love best. At Killin, we’ve happily lost whole afternoons to picking wild raspberries, skimming stones and climbing trees. My boys climbed their first Munro here, Ben Lawers, when their legs were much shorter. We should have had beautiful loch views from the top, but reached the summit in cloud instead. They loved it.Further along the banks at Lawers and Kenmore is where my sisters and I head for restorative escapes: alternating freezing loch swims with a hot tub has become our preferred form of therapy.double quotation markWe pull the canoes ashore on a little island for a picnic, and as we eat our sandwiches, there’s a flash of iridescent turquoiseI’ve often walked by the river, but was curious to see it from a different angle: by canoe. Aberfeldy is a two-hour drive north from Edinburgh, so it’s an early start for me and my son Louis, 15. We’re welcomed atBeyond Adventurewith coffee and a briefing, then transferred upriver with two long orange canoes and our instructor, Kevin Meldrum.Our route begins on theRiver Lyonjust before its confluence with the Tay. In this calm eddy, we get a quick lesson in paddling and turning the boat. Louis is 6ft-plus and I am not, which seemed a recipe for paddling in circles. Kevin keeps us right, and Louis soon learns to calmly counteract any erratic paddling on my side. We meet the Tay over a gentle rapid and begin paddling downstream. We settle into the river’s rhythm, learning to read the current and steer around camouflaged anglers patiently waiting for salmon, and spotting herons standing guard in the shadows.View image in fullscreenKingfishers can sometimes be spotted on the banks of the Tay.Photograph: Alex Cooper/AlamyThe banks of the Tay are changing, thanks to the returning beaver population. We don’t spot any (they emerge at dusk), but we do see evidence of stripped bark and felled trees by the river. Paddling into a tree-lined eddy, we admire a carefully constructed beaver lodge.We pull the canoes ashore on a little island for a picnic lunch, and as we eat our sandwiches, there’s a flash of iridescent turquoise. My first ever sighting of a kingfisher.It’s great to be on the water with a guide who knows the river so well. At each stretch of rapids, we’re set a route, and navigate each one facing downstream, still smiling. As we return to Aberfeldy, we paddle underGeneral Wade’s Bridge, unchanged since it was built in 1733. We’ve been on the water for three hours, but it feels all too soon when we approach the Beyond Adventure base. Reluctant to leave, we find a deep, peaty pool for a swim.Heading home, we stop for a pizza (a teenage second lunch) and cold drinks atThe Taybankin Dunkeld. Watching the Tay flow past the beer garden, I realise the river looks different to me now. Once you’ve travelled with it, it’s hard not to wonder what’s waiting around the next bend.Ailsa SheldonBeyond Adventureoffers half-day discovery canoeing tours from£63 adults, £47.25 children, £199.50 for a family (two adults, two children)Explore more on these topicsUnited Kingdom holidaysWalking holidaysBoating holidaysWater sports holidaysWalkingWales holidaysFitnessfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to cook the perfect apricot galette – recipe | Dessert | The Guardian
description: A free-form fruit tart that’s easy to throw together with whatever seasonal fruit you have to hand
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: A free-form fruit tart that’s easy to throw together with whatever seasonal fruit you have to hand
Content: Felicity Cloake’s perfect apricot galette.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Johnny Bentham.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s perfect apricot galette.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Johnny Bentham.How to cook the perfect ...DessertHow to cook the perfect apricot galette – recipeA free-form fruit tart that’s easy to throw together with whatever seasonal fruit you have to handFelicity CloakeSun 9 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe galette takes its name from the pebble it’s said to resemble – as Elizabeth David observes, it takes many forms, all of them round and flat. For me the word conjures thebuckwheat pancakes of Brittanywhile French friends, in a quick straw poll, tend to think first of the frangipane-stuffed puff pastrygalette de roisserved at Epiphany, with one vote for a buttery Breton biscuit.Ask the English-language internet, however, and you’ll be served what is more commonly known as a tart(e), more specifically a charmingly rustic, free-form version which doesn’t require a tin. Though Anne Willan references prune and apple three-tier galette pies from the Pyrenees in her 1981 classic French Regional Cooking, and David includes a yeasted version that sounds more like a cobbler in French Provincial Cooking, most fruit galette recipes I find seem to be American. My hunch is thatAlice Waters’ traditionof a daily seasonal galette at Chez Panisse may have popularised the name across the pond, but the general idea never needed upselling. As a quick and easy way to turn a punnet of fruit into a dessert, it’s hard to beat, whatever you call it.The pastryThere are two popular options here: a rich shortcrust, or a rich rough puff. AsLouis Thompson observesin his incredibly comprehensive exploration of the galette on Nicola Lamb’s Kitchen Project Substack, “because you are eating such a small amount of pastry per portion in a galette, it can afford to be richer”. He, likeNicole Rucker, goes for a rough puff, as doesRose Levy Beranbaum, who writes in The Baking Bible that “in recent years, when I bake a pie, the pie crust I always turn to is this one”, which she describes as a “perfect flaky and tender cream-cheese pie crust”.View image in fullscreenIt’s a rough puff pastry for Nicole Rucker’s apricot galette. (All thumbnail images by Felicity Cloake)While Thompson keeps it simple with equal parts of butter and flour, Beranbaum swaps some of the butter for cream cheese and heavy cream. This makes for a softer and slightly more savoury crust next to Thompson’s buttery, shatteringly crisp base, which puts me in mind of the end of a croissant. Rucker opts for a plainer formula of 60% of the flour weight in butter, allowing the filling to shine. Also in the cream cheese, butter and cream camp areBrian Levy, and Helen Goh and Yotam Ottolenghi, whose rich shortcrust recipe in 2017’s Sweetactually contains more fat than flour, and, probably not coincidentally, proves a tester favourite.Brian Levy’s softer, crumblier, more pie-dough like version, which contains less butter, is instead enriched with an egg yolk.All stand up admirably to the task of containing the fruit’s juices without springing a leak, or even a suspicion of sogginess, but as a galette, in my mind at least, should be something one can knock up relatively easily, I’ve decided to opt for a rich, flaky shortcrust rather than anything that requires folding and layering, however minimally. I’ve based mine on theSweetformula, but because we all enjoyed the flavour of the wholemeal flour in Levy’s pastry so much, I’ve swapped in some of that (Thompson advises going for no more than half of the total weight if using something like spelt or rye in particular, on the basis that “beyond this, I find the flavour overwhelming and begin to experience unwanted textural changes due to the reduced gluten-forming capabilities”. After two delicious but less than perfect-looking attempts with a 50:50 mixture, I realise that wholemeal flour does make the dough softer and harder to work with, so I reduced the quantities to a third. (Note: if you decide to go for an alternative grain, you may find it needs more liquid to bring it together, so always trust your eyes… though it should only just clump into a dough. If it’s very dusty, scoop out the dough, and add a little more liquid just to the dry bits. I’ve also left out the vinegar, because as far as I can tell it’s only really helpful to stop the pastry discolouring if you’re storing it for long periods, and this is less important if you’re using wholemeal flour in any case.View image in fullscreenRose Levy Beranbaum swaps some of the butter for cream cheese and heavy cream.Probably the most important piece of advice: keep everything as cold as possible, particularly if you’re making this, as I was, in the height of summer. As there’s no tin to support the sides, it’s well worth chilling the shell both before filling and before cooking, in warm weather. If your kitchen is nice and cool, you may wish to skip one of these steps.The fruitI try recipes using apples, peaches, rhubarb and blueberry – from pineapple to pear, there aren’t many fruit that don’t work in a galette, so I’ll try to make this as general as possible while, perhaps controversially, opining that the drier the fruit, the prettier the galette, but the less satisfying the result.Thompson and Rucker’s apple galettes are beautiful, and undeniably delicious, but the low-profile nature of the galette – the real showstoppers tend to feature just one layer of thinly cut fruit – means that they lack the juicy generosity of the stone fruit versions. They’re works of art, but I prefer my apples in a deeper pie –GohandOttolenghi’s rhubarb and blueberry combination works well, though given the season you might prefer their alternative suggestion of fig and raspberry as a combination, but Beranbaum and Levy’s peaches prove the crowd favourites. For my perfect recipe, I’ve chosen to use apricots, first because we grow such beautiful ones in south-east England at this time of year, and second because wherever they’re from, apricots are a fruit that’s almost always enhanced by cooking.Whatever you use, however, you need to assert your authority over its juices. Goh and Ottolenghi toss the fruit with a little tapioca starch or cornflour to help thicken them, and cook it immediately, before the sugar starts to draw them out, and Levy does the same but with ground almonds. Beranbaum takes the opposite approach, macerating the fruit with sugar and lemon juice for up to 90 minutes before draining off the resulting juice, reducing it with butter to a rich syrup, and then returning it to the fruit along with some cornflour to further thicken it in the oven. Rucker employs a simpler version, spreading some of the sugared juices on top of the fruit before baking, and turning the remainder into a glaze for the top.View image in fullscreenGoh and Ottolenghi toss the fruit with a little tapioca starch or cornflour to thicken.Thompson, after taking advice from Chez Panisse-trained pastry chef Sarah Johnson, author ofFruitful, does nothing at all: “A common mistake,” Johnson tells him, “is adding sugar to the fruit before baking. I like to put the galette in the oven without sugar, then gradually add it as it cooks. This helps preserve the fruit’s shape and prevents excess liquid from escaping, which can lead to leaks”. As well as sprinkling a little on top (though Thompson cautions against adding too much, especially to tarter fruits like rhubarb or (red) plums “as these are particularly juicy fruits which will leach buckets of juice”), the main job of “managing the sweetness of the fruit instead comes from a flavourful glaze applied after baking”.Given a shiny glaze is the easiest way in the world to give even the most rustic of tarts a professional looking finish, this approach, in which you prioritise keeping the fruit intact during baking, and then adjust the sweetness in a more controlled fashion once it’s out of the oven, seems sensible.Personally, I like the colour, and texture of roasted fruit skin, so I haven’t peeled them, but if you’d like to, dunk them in boiling water for a minute, then run them under a cold tap; the skins should just peel off. How you cut the fruit also matters: “if you know the fruit you’re using is particularly juicy,” Thompson explains, “it is helpful to place it less densely and in larger slices – for apricot and plum galettes, I only cut the fruit into quarters”. For something like an apple or a firm, unripe pear, however, you can get away with slices about 5mm thick.The spongeView image in fullscreenLouis Thompson’s apricot galette contains ‘the most delicious frangipane I’ve ever tasted’.Rucker and Beranbaum, who have, of course, already macerated their fruit, throw caution to the wind and add it straight to the pastry without a mediator (which works fine with apples, but does mean Beranbaum’s is better eaten soon after cooling, before the juices have had time to mingle too much with the base. That said, this is the best time to eat it in any case). Famously, however, the Chez Panisse galette, which may well be the patient-zero of this modern galette phenomenon, utilises something called “moon dust” to act as an absorbent layer between fruit and pastry, much as one might thickly butter a tomato sandwich to stop the bread going soggy.Another alumnus,David Lebovitz, recalls that it was a mixture of “flour, almond meal, sugar and crushed amaretti cookies” and also that “because I can never leave anything alone, I nicknamed [it] ‘Lunar Lint’”. Goh and Ottolenghi also utilise amaretti, mixed with flour, sugar and cinnamon while Levy, whose book focuses on using fruit, rather than refined sugars, as a sweetener, cleverly whizzes up dried apricots and orange juice to make a chunky jam layer that works really well.The most popular approach comes from Thompson, who makes the most delicious frangipane I’ve ever tasted simply by dint of roasting whole almonds in their skins and grinding them himself, before mixing with butter, sugar and egg. I also add a little flour, in deference to the juiciness of the fruit I’m using, and sprinkle some extra on top, as he recommends.The glazeView image in fullscreenBrian Levy cleverly whizzes up dried apricots and orange juice to make a chunky jam layer that works really well.Goh and Ottolenghi forgo a glaze, perhaps on the basis that such things would be gilding the lily for such a rustic bake. Beranbaum uses excess juices drained from her fruit and Levy and Rucker both suggest the standard smooth apricot jam. Though I’ve gone for the last approach, because it’s easy and it works with the fruit I’ve chosen, I must give an honourable mention to Thompson’s apple stock, made from the pectin-rich skins and cores of the fruit simmered with water, and then mixed with sugar and cornflour; it’s very clever indeed, and certainly worth considering if you’re working with apples or pears.Levy finishes his tart with chopped pistachios rather than the usual crunchy sugar. Swapping these for almonds feels like the obvious move given how well they go with apricots, and the fact you’ll be roasting some anyway for the frangipane.Make aheadThis is best eaten on the day it’s cooked, but you could make the individual elements (pastry shell, frangipane, cut fruit) ahead of time and assemble just before baking.Perfect apricot galetteWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep50 minChill1 hr 15 minFreeze1 hrCook45 minServes8For the pastry125g cold butter, cut into 2cm cubes120g plain flour, plus extra to dust60g wholemeal plain flour¼ tsp fine salt⅛ tsp baking powder80g full-fat cream cheeseFor the filling (or use 50g crumbled amaretti mixed with the same amount of flour and sugar)100g skin-on almonds50g caster sugar20g plain flour30g butter, softenedA pinch of salt1 egg, beatenFor the topping650g apricotsor other stone fruit1 tbsp cornflour2 tbsp caster sugar2 tbsp smooth apricotor other jamTo make the pastry, freeze the butter for at least an hour, until solid. Measure the flours, salt and baking powder into a bowl and freeze them, too.Put the flours in a food processor and add the cream cheese. Pulse to combine, then add the butter. Pulse until the mixture looks like coarse breadcrumbs with some larger chunks of butter remaining visible. Alternatively, do this in a bowl and use your fingertips to flatten the chunks. Cautiously add just enough iced water (probably two tablespoons) that when you squidge a piece between two fingers it becomes a dough. At this point tip out on to a clean work surface and use your hands to press it together – if any pieces still look a bit dusty, then add a little more water to them separately before adding to the rest, so as not to over hydrate it. Form into a ball, then flatten into a circle. Wrap and chill for at least 45 minutes.View image in fullscreenMeanwhile, heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Put the whole almonds on a baking tray and roast for 12 minutes. Once cool (turn off the oven for now), roughly chop them. Set aside 10g and blitz the rest to a fine powder, then mix in the sugar, flour, butter, salt and just enough egg to make a paste, keeping the remainder for the egg wash.Roll out the dough on a large, floured piece of baking paper to a rough circle about 32cm across. Carefully move to a baking sheet and chill while you prepare the fruit.Cut the apricots in half and remove the stones (no need to peel unless you want to). If very large, cut into quarters.View image in fullscreenTrim the pastry to neaten the edge, then use a plate or lid about 25cm wide to draw a circle in the middle, being careful not to cut all the way through. Spread the circle with the frangipane, then scatter with the cornflour and one tablespoon of the sugar. Finally, arrange the apricot halves across the tart, skin-side up, cutting the last pieces to fill any gaps.Fold the rim of the pastry towards the centre all the way around, crimping slightly to make it look a bit prettier – there should be a wide circle of fruit still visible in the middle. Put back in the fridge for 30 minutes unless your kitchen is very cool. Heat the oven, and a baking sheet, back up to 200C/180C fan/gas 6.View image in fullscreenBrush the pastry with beaten egg. Slide the paper and tart on to the hot baking sheet and bake for 15 minutes, then scatter the fruit with the remaining tablespoon of sugar. Put back in the oven for 30 more minutes or until the pastry is nicely browned, turning halfway if it’s colouring unevenly. Take out of the oven and slide off the paper on to a wire rack to cool.Heat the jam in a microwave or small saucepan until runny. Once the tart has cooled for about 15 minutes, paint the fruit and pastry with jam and scatter with the reserved chopped nuts.Whether you call it a galette or a tart, what are your top tips for success in the free-form, open-top pastry department? Puff, rough puff or shortcrust? Frangipane or moon dust? And is Alice Waters responsible for the galette label?Explore more on these topicsDessertHow to cook the perfect ...FoodFrench food and drinkBakingPastryFruitCakerecipesShareReuse this content

title: Bullgogi, Manchester M1: ‘Highly decent, amenable, human-free dining’ – restaurant review | Food | The Guardian
description: Bullgogi’s largely automated hospitality will either delight or horrify you, but the food is serious
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: Bullgogi’s largely automated hospitality will either delight or horrify you, but the food is serious
Content: Bullgogi, Manchester M4: the UK’s largest Korean barbecue restaurant.Photograph: Shaw & Shaw/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBullgogi, Manchester M4: the UK’s largest Korean barbecue restaurant.Photograph: Shaw & Shaw/The GuardianGrace Dent on restaurantsFoodReviewBullgogi, Manchester M1: ‘Highly decent, amenable, human-free dining’ – restaurant reviewBullgogi’s largely automated hospitality will either delight or horrify you, but the food is seriousGrace DentSun 9 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 14.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBullgogi, a whopping new interactive multiscreen Korean restaurant in Manchester’s Piccadilly Plaza, has arrived, heralding the end of traditional hospitality – again. It’s the UK’s largest Korean barbecue restaurant – 165 covers, traditional tabletop grills at every booth – but has no servers with notepads, just screens. Yourgyeran jjim, yourdolsot bibimbap, yourbulgogi: jab the at-table screen and it will arrive, ferried by human hand. Think McDonald’s, but as a gargantuan restaurant. Jae Cho and hisMaguro Grouphave built an empire of 21 locations across London and Manchester, but this is their biggest venture to date. We arrive without reservation, which is no problem, because Bullgogi is the size of a small planet. We order pots of barley tea and pints of Asahi at £6.90, and sit back to enjoy the Blade Runner vibes.Bullgogi’s largely human-free hospitality will either delight or horrify you. Personally, I greet our new robot hospitality overlords with calm scepticism. Over the past few decades, I have staggered through theCovid QR menuwilderness, prised my dinner from the temperamental jaws of robot fridges in rural farm shops, and watched with mirth as the robot chef at arecent Soho yakitorijoint still required a human to load every skewer into it before performing. For these reasons, I greet Bullgogi with a raised eyebrow. In fact, the moment we flag, via the screen, a food intolerance at our table, a bright, chipper human appears immediately to check through the menu for said offending item.View image in fullscreenBullgogi’s ‘crisp and crimped’ chicken dumplings.Bullgogi is a restaurant that’s hoping to serve all palates. Experienced Korean food lovers can head straight for thedoenjang jjigae, an earthy, soya bean paste broth with beef, or thesundubu jjigae(silken tofu with seafood). If you’re preparing for war, there isbudae jjigae, the Korean army stew in which spam, ham, kimchi and noodles are simmered into something rib-sticking enough to fuel a march to the 38th parallel. There is wobblygyeran jjim(steamed egg custard), Korean beef tartare seasoned with sesame oil, andgimmari, or crispy seaweed rolls stuffed with glass noodles. For pan-Asian regulars who might knowbibimbapand the likes of double-fired Korean fried chicken orkimchipajeon(fermented kimchi pancake), Bullgogi has them covered, too. You’ll see Korean students from Manchester university using it as a canteen alongside tables of pensioners from Rochdale encountering Korean food for the first time. This is a harder trick to pull off than it sounds, and the screen ordering seems to appeal to both.View image in fullscreenThe ‘highly decent’ chicken bibimbap, at Bullgogi in Manchester.Bullgogi is not necessarily a place to linger. It is cheap, strip-lit, sparsely decorated; this is a bold new opening that feels more like a 1990s service station than a restaurant; I’ve had glitzier dinners atForton Services. Even so, there is a sense that food is taken seriously here. The Korean dumplings arrive too hot to devour immediately, but they are crisp and crimped, with a peppery, minced vegetable filling. Ordering the cheese potato pancake, orgamja jeon, was probably an error: no health authority in the world would smile upon me for eating four pieces of deep-fried shredded potato and barrowfuls of melted mozzarella. My lifespan decreased with each mouthful. A stone bowl of silken tofusundubu jjigaeturned up in a fabulous seafood broth – one of the best things we ate – followed by a chickendolsot bibimbap, which was also highly decent.View image in fullscreenBullgogi’s cheese potato pancake: ‘My lifespan decreased with each mouthful.’We didn’t use the tabletop grill, and neither did anyone else. The future of the Korean tabletop grill looks patchy. Restaurateurs quietly admit they are hell to service and expensive to run. Modern customers, meanwhile, love the idea of them and then don’t use them, though thebulgogi,LA-stylegalbi,iberico collarand spicy pork are waiting should you choose to.Bullgogi is a pleasant, amenable, albeit slightly hollow dining experience. We ate, we paid, we left. There were no desserts. No one noted our departure, as seemingly no robot had alerted them that we were a dine and dash. The drive-thru Costa Coffee-ification of British restaurants continues. Treasure your servers while you have them. You’ll miss them when they’re gone.Bullgogi, 6A Piccadilly Plaza, Manchester M1 4AH, 0161-553 1141. Open all week, noon-10pm (10.30pm Sat, 9.30pm Sun). From about £30 a head à la carte; lunch menu Mon-Fri, about £13 a head, all plus drinks and serviceExplore more on these topicsFoodGrace Dent on restaurantsRestaurantsKorean food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content
